topics.name: Unit 1: Exploring One-Variable Data and Collecting Data
topics.description: Explore the foundations of statistical thinking. Learn to collect, organize, and describe data using tables, graphs, and summary statistics. Master sampling methods, identify bias, and design experiments.

concepts.title: Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?
concepts.content_html:
Introducing Statistics: What Can We Learn from Data?

Statistics is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data to answer questions about the world. Unlike pure mathematics, statistics always deals with real-world information and requires context to be meaningful.

Why Context Matters

A number by itself — say, 72 — is meaningless. Is it a test score? A temperature? A heart rate? In statistics, we always describe results in context, meaning we reference the specific variables, individuals, and setting of the study.

Population vs. Sample

A population is the entire group of individuals or objects we want to study. The number of individuals in a population is denoted \( N \).

A sample is a subset of the population that is actually examined. The number of individuals in a sample is denoted \( n \).

We study samples because it is usually impractical or impossible to study an entire population. For example, to estimate the average screen time of all U.S. teenagers (population), a researcher might survey 500 teenagers (sample).

Data vs. Datum

Data are the values of a variable (or variables) recorded for individuals in a study. A single observed value is called a datum.

Data can be numbers (heights, scores) or categories (eye color, brand preference). The type of data determines which statistical tools we use.

Putting It All Together

Every statistical study involves:

  • Individuals — the objects described by the data (people, animals, things)
  • A variable — a characteristic measured on each individual
  • A population — the full set of individuals of interest
  • A sample — the subset actually observed
Key Idea: Always answer statistical questions in context. Instead of saying "the mean is 3.2," say "the mean number of hours of sleep lost per week among surveyed college students is 3.2 hours."
AP Exam Tip: The AP graders award points for answers written in context. Vague answers that omit who, what, and where will lose credit.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Introducing Statistics

problems.question_html: A researcher wants to determine the average amount of time high school students in California spend on social media per day. She surveys 200 students from 10 randomly selected high schools. What is the population in this study?

choices.text: The 200 students surveyed
The 10 randomly selected high schools
All high school students in California
All students who use social media

hints.text: The population is the entire group the researcher wants to learn about, not just the group actually studied.
The researcher wants information about all high school students in California. The 200 surveyed students are the sample.

solution_steps.text: The population is the entire group of interest. The researcher wants to know about high school students in California.
Therefore, the population is all high school students in California. The 200 surveyed students are the sample drawn from that population.

problems.question_html: A school principal collects data on the GPA of every senior (\( N = 312 \)) in the school. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: \( N = 312 \) refers to the sample size because the principal only looked at seniors.
\( N = 312 \) refers to the population size because every senior was included.
\( N = 312 \) is a statistic because it describes the seniors.
\( N = 312 \) cannot be determined without more information.

hints.text: Consider whether the principal studied every individual in the group of interest or just a subset.
Since the principal collected data on every senior (the entire group of interest), this is a census. \( N \) denotes population size.

solution_steps.text: The principal's group of interest is all seniors in the school, and data was collected on every one of them.
Since every individual in the population was included, \( N = 312 \) is the population size. This is a census, not a sample.

problems.question_html: A sports analyst wants to study the free-throw percentage of all NBA players during the 2024–2025 season. She randomly selects 60 players and records their free-throw percentages. Which of the following correctly identifies the population and sample?

choices.text: Population: the 60 selected players; Sample: all NBA players
Population: all NBA players during the 2024–2025 season; Sample: the 60 selected players
Population: all basketball players worldwide; Sample: all NBA players
Population: the 60 selected players; Sample: their free-throw percentages

hints.text: The population is the full group the analyst wants to learn about. The sample is the smaller group she actually collected data from.
The analyst is interested in all NBA players in the 2024–2025 season (population) and selected 60 of them (sample).

solution_steps.text: The analyst's research question is about all NBA players during the 2024–2025 season, so that is the population.
She actually collects data from only 60 players, so those 60 players are the sample. Free-throw percentages are the variable, not the sample.

problems.question_html: A nutritionist surveys 150 college students about their daily water intake. She reports: "The average daily water intake is 5.4 cups." Why might a statistics instructor mark this conclusion as incomplete?

choices.text: She should have used the median instead of the mean.
She did not specify units.
She did not describe the result in context — she should specify who was studied and what was measured.
She should have surveyed the entire population.

hints.text: Think about what is missing from the sentence. Does it tell you who the individuals are and what specific variable is being described?
In statistics, conclusions must be stated in context: reference the individuals (college students), the variable (daily water intake), and the setting.

solution_steps.text: The statement "the average daily water intake is 5.4 cups" lacks context. It does not specify the group studied.
A proper in-context statement would be: "The average daily water intake among the 150 surveyed college students is 5.4 cups." Answering in context is essential on the AP exam.

problems.question_html: A biologist tags 45 deer in a national forest to estimate the total deer population. In this study, the number 45 represents which value?
problems.correct_answer: n||sample size

hints.text: The 45 deer are a subset of all deer in the forest. What letter do we use for the size of a subset?
A sample is a subset of the population. The sample size is denoted \( n \) (lowercase), while the population size is \( N \) (uppercase).

solution_steps.text: The population is all deer in the national forest. The 45 tagged deer are only a subset — the sample.
The size of a sample is denoted \( n \) (lowercase). So 45 represents \( n \), the sample size.

problems.question_html: A meteorologist records the high temperature in Phoenix every day for one year. Each individual daily high temperature value is called a __________ (singular).
problems.correct_answer: datum||data point

hints.text: We use a specific term for a single piece of data. It is the singular form of "data."
A single observed value is called a datum. "Data" is the plural — the collection of all observed values.

solution_steps.text: "Data" refers to the entire collection of observed values. The singular form — one individual observation — is called a datum.
Each individual daily high temperature is a single observation, so it is called a datum.

problems.question_html:
An environmental agency measures the mercury level in water samples from 30 lakes across a state. The entire group of lakes the agency wants to draw conclusions about consists of 1,200 lakes. Identify \( N \) and \( n \) for this study.

\( N = \) __________

hints.text: \( N \) represents the size of the entire group the agency wants to draw conclusions about.
The population is all 1,200 lakes. \( N \) (uppercase) = population size = 1,200. The sample consists of 30 lakes, so \( n = 30 \).

solution_steps.text: The population is all 1,200 lakes in the state, so \( N = 1{,}200 \).
The sample is the 30 lakes actually tested, so \( n = 30 \).

problems.question_html: A company surveys 500 of its 12,000 employees about job satisfaction. A single employee's response of "satisfied" is an example of a __________.
problems.correct_answer: datum||data point||observation

hints.text: This is a single recorded value from one individual. What is the singular of "data"?
A single observation is called a datum. The full set of 500 responses constitutes the data.

solution_steps.text: One employee's response is a single observation — a datum.
All 500 responses together make up the data. Each individual value is a datum.

problems.question_html:
A city council wants to know whether residents support building a new community park. They mail a survey to 800 randomly selected households out of the city's 25,000 households.

(a) Identify the population and the sample in this study.

(b) A council member summarizes the results by saying, "68% of people support the park." Rewrite this conclusion so that it is properly stated in context.

(c) Explain why studying a sample rather than the entire population is practical in this situation.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) The population is all 25,000 households in the city. The sample is the 800 randomly selected households that received the survey.
(b) "Based on the sample of 800 randomly selected households, approximately 68% of responding city residents support building a new community park."
(c) Surveying all 25,000 households would be costly and time-consuming. A well-chosen random sample of 800 households can provide a reliable estimate of the city's opinion at a fraction of the cost and effort.

hints.text: For part (a), ask yourself: who does the council want to learn about (population), and who did they actually contact (sample)?

For part (b), make sure your rewritten statement mentions who (city residents/households), what (support for the park), and the basis (the sample). For part (c), think about cost, time, and feasibility.

solution_steps.text: (a) The population is all 25,000 households in the city. The sample is the 800 randomly selected households.
(b) A proper in-context statement: "Based on the sample of 800 randomly selected city households, approximately 68% of respondents support building a new community park."
(c) Surveying all 25,000 households would require significantly more time, money, and effort. A random sample of 800 provides a practical and reliable way to estimate the population's opinion.

problems.question_html:
A school district wants to evaluate the effectiveness of a new math curriculum. They test 250 students from 5 middle schools at the end of the school year.

(a) Identify the individuals, the variable, the population, and the sample.

(b) The report states: "The mean score was 78." Explain what is wrong with this statement and rewrite it in context.

(c) Would \( n = 250 \) or \( N = 250 \) be the correct notation for the number of students tested? Justify your answer.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Individuals: middle school students. Variable: math test score at the end of the year. Population: all middle school students in the district. Sample: the 250 students tested from 5 schools.
(b) The statement lacks context — it does not say who was tested or what was measured. A better version: "The mean end-of-year math test score among the 250 sampled middle school students was 78 points."
(c) \( n = 250 \) is correct because the 250 students are a sample, not the entire population of middle school students in the district. Lowercase \( n \) denotes sample size.

hints.text: Individuals are the objects being studied. The variable is what is measured on each individual.
For part (b), add who, what, and where. For part (c), recall that \( N \) = population size and \( n \) = sample size. Are the 250 students the entire population or a subset?

solution_steps.text: (a) Individuals: middle school students. Variable: math test score. Population: all middle school students in the district. Sample: the 250 students from 5 schools.
(b) "The mean score was 78" is not in context. Better: "The mean end-of-year math test score among the 250 sampled middle school students was 78 points."
(c) \( n = 250 \) is correct. The 250 students are a sample (subset) of all middle school students in the district, so we use lowercase \( n \) for the sample size.

concepts.title: Variables
concepts.content_html:
Variables

In any statistical study, we measure characteristics of individuals. These characteristics are called variables because their values vary from one individual to another.

Observational Units

An observational unit (or individual) is a single entity on which data are collected. Observational units can be people, animals, objects, or even time periods — anything being measured or observed.

Types of Variables

Variables come in two fundamental types:

Categorical (Qualitative) Variables place individuals into groups or categories. Examples include:

  • Favorite social media platform (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube)
  • Class year (freshman, sophomore, junior, senior)
  • Whether a coin lands heads or tails

Quantitative (Numerical) Variables take on numerical values for which arithmetic operations make sense. Examples include:

  • Height in centimeters
  • Number of text messages sent per day
  • Annual household income
Key Idea: If you can meaningfully average the values, the variable is quantitative. If averaging makes no sense (e.g., the "average" zip code), the variable is categorical — even if the labels happen to be numbers.

Parameter vs. Statistic

A parameter is a number that describes the population. A statistic is a number that describes the sample.

We usually do not know the true parameter, so we use the statistic to estimate it.

DescribesExample Notation
ParameterPopulation\( \mu \) (population mean), \( p \) (population proportion)
StatisticSample\( \bar{x} \) (sample mean), \( \hat{p} \) (sample proportion)
AP Exam Tip: A common trick question uses numerical labels (like jersey numbers or zip codes) to see if you recognize them as categorical. Numbers used only as labels are categorical variables.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Variables

problems.question_html: A survey asks students: "How many hours per week do you exercise?" and "What is your favorite sport?" Which variable is quantitative?

choices.text: Favorite sport
Hours of exercise per week
Both variables are quantitative
Neither variable is quantitative

hints.text: A quantitative variable takes numerical values where arithmetic (like finding a mean) is meaningful.
Hours of exercise is numerical and can be averaged — it is quantitative. Favorite sport places people into categories — it is categorical.

solution_steps.text: "Favorite sport" assigns individuals to categories (basketball, soccer, etc.) — categorical.
"Hours of exercise per week" is numerical and it makes sense to compute a mean — quantitative.

problems.question_html: A researcher records the jersey numbers of players on a basketball team. Which type of variable is "jersey number"?

choices.text: Quantitative, because jersey numbers are numerical
Categorical, because jersey numbers serve as labels rather than measurements
Neither quantitative nor categorical
Both quantitative and categorical

hints.text: Ask yourself: does it make sense to find the average jersey number of a team?
Even though jersey numbers are digits, they are used as identifiers, not measurements. Averaging them is meaningless, so they are categorical.

solution_steps.text: Jersey numbers look numerical but serve only as labels to identify players.
Computing the "average jersey number" has no real-world meaning. Therefore, jersey number is a categorical variable.

problems.question_html: A health study records each participant's blood type (A, B, AB, O) and cholesterol level (mg/dL). Which of the following correctly classifies both variables?

choices.text: Blood type is quantitative; cholesterol level is categorical
Both variables are categorical
Blood type is categorical; cholesterol level is quantitative
Both variables are quantitative

hints.text: Can you compute a meaningful average for each variable? Categories like A, B, AB, O cannot be averaged.
Blood type places people into groups (A, B, AB, O) — categorical. Cholesterol is measured in mg/dL and can be averaged — quantitative.

solution_steps.text: Blood type assigns individuals to categories (A, B, AB, O) with no numerical ordering — categorical.
Cholesterol level is a numerical measurement in mg/dL — quantitative. The correct pairing is categorical and quantitative.

problems.question_html: The true proportion of all registered voters in a state who support a ballot measure is \( p = 0.62 \). A polling firm surveys 1,000 voters and finds \( \hat{p} = 0.59 \). Which value is the parameter and which is the statistic?

choices.text: \( p = 0.62 \) is the statistic; \( \hat{p} = 0.59 \) is the parameter
Both are parameters
\( p = 0.62 \) is the parameter; \( \hat{p} = 0.59 \) is the statistic
Both are statistics

hints.text: Recall: a parameter describes the population; a statistic describes a sample.
\( p \) is the true population proportion (parameter). \( \hat{p} \) is computed from the sample of 1,000 voters (statistic).

solution_steps.text: \( p = 0.62 \) describes all registered voters in the state — it is the population parameter.
\( \hat{p} = 0.59 \) was computed from the sample of 1,000 voters — it is the sample statistic.

problems.question_html: A sample of 80 college students has a mean GPA of \( \bar{x} = 3.21 \). The value 3.21 is an example of a __________.
problems.correct_answer: statistic||sample statistic

hints.text: This value was computed from a sample, not the entire population.
A number that describes a sample is called a statistic. A number that describes the population is a parameter.

solution_steps.text: The value \( \bar{x} = 3.21 \) was calculated from a sample of 80 students.
Because it describes a sample (not the entire population), it is a statistic.

problems.question_html: Classify the variable: "the number of apps installed on a student's phone." This is a __________ variable.
problems.correct_answer: quantitative||numerical

hints.text: Is the value a number where arithmetic operations are meaningful, or is it a category?
The number of apps is a count — you can compute a mean number of apps. It is a quantitative (numerical) variable.

solution_steps.text: The number of apps is a numerical value (e.g., 23, 47, 85). Computing a mean is meaningful.
Therefore, it is a quantitative (numerical) variable.

problems.question_html: A survey records each student's grade level (9, 10, 11, 12). Even though the values are numbers, this variable is best classified as __________.
problems.correct_answer: categorical||qualitative

hints.text: Would computing the "average grade level" be a meaningful summary?
Grade level (9, 10, 11, 12) is used to group students into classes, not to measure a quantity. It is categorical even though the labels are numbers.

solution_steps.text: Although 9, 10, 11, and 12 are numbers, they represent categories (freshman, sophomore, junior, senior).
Computing an average grade level is not meaningful. The variable is categorical (qualitative).

problems.question_html: In a study, the observational units are individual trees in a forest. The researcher records each tree's species and height in meters. The observational units in this study are the __________.
problems.correct_answer: trees||individual trees

hints.text: Observational units are the individual entities on which measurements are taken.
Each tree is measured for species and height, so the observational units are the individual trees.

solution_steps.text: An observational unit is the entity being measured. Here, each tree has its species and height recorded.
The observational units are the individual trees in the forest.

problems.question_html:
A fitness company collects data from 500 users of its smartwatch app. For each user, the company records: age (years), resting heart rate (bpm), subscription plan (Free, Basic, Premium), and daily step count.

(a) Identify the observational units.

(b) Classify each variable as categorical or quantitative.

(c) The company reports that the mean daily step count for the 500 users is 7,450 steps. Is this value a parameter or a statistic? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) The observational units are the 500 smartwatch app users.
(b) Age: quantitative. Resting heart rate: quantitative. Subscription plan: categorical. Daily step count: quantitative.
(c) This is a statistic because it describes a sample of 500 users, not the entire population of all smartwatch app users.

hints.text: Observational units are the individuals being measured. For each variable, ask: does averaging make sense?
Subscription plan has categories (Free, Basic, Premium) — categorical. Age, heart rate, and step count are numerical — quantitative. The 500 users are a sample, so any summary value is a statistic.

solution_steps.text: (a) The observational units are the 500 individual smartwatch app users.
(b) Age (years): quantitative. Resting heart rate (bpm): quantitative. Subscription plan: categorical (Free, Basic, Premium are categories). Daily step count: quantitative.
(c) The mean of 7,450 steps is computed from a sample of 500 users. Since it describes the sample, it is a statistic. The population parameter would be the mean step count of all users of the app.

problems.question_html:
A school counselor wants to understand the relationship between class year and post-graduation plans. She surveys 200 seniors and asks each: "What is your class year?" and "What do you plan to do after graduation? (college, workforce, military, gap year, other)."

(a) Identify the observational units and both variables. Classify each variable.

(b) The counselor finds that 64% of the 200 surveyed seniors plan to attend college. Is 64% a parameter or a statistic? Justify your answer.

(c) If the school has 530 seniors total, explain what the corresponding parameter would represent.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Observational units: the 200 surveyed seniors. Variables: class year (categorical) and post-graduation plan (categorical — college, workforce, military, gap year, other).
(b) 64% is a statistic because it was calculated from the sample of 200 seniors, not from all 530 seniors in the school.
(c) The corresponding parameter would be the true proportion of all 530 seniors in the school who plan to attend college.

hints.text: Both variables place students into groups. Think about whether 200 students are the whole population or a subset.
Class year and post-graduation plan are both categorical. The 200 students are a sample of the 530 seniors, so 64% is a statistic estimating the population parameter.

solution_steps.text: (a) Observational units: the 200 seniors surveyed. Class year: categorical. Post-graduation plan: categorical (college, workforce, military, gap year, other).
(b) 64% is computed from 200 of the 530 seniors — a sample. Therefore, 64% is a sample statistic (\( \hat{p} = 0.64 \)).
(c) The parameter would be the true proportion \( p \) of all 530 seniors who plan to attend college. This is the value we are estimating with the sample statistic.

concepts.title: Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics for One Categorical Variable
concepts.content_html:
Tabular Representation and Summary Statistics for One Categorical Variable

Once we collect categorical data, we need ways to organize and summarize it. The most common tools are frequency tables and relative frequency tables.

Frequency Tables

A frequency table lists each category and the count (frequency) of observations in that category.

Favorite Streaming ServiceFrequency
Netflix45
YouTube30
Disney+15
Other10
Total100

Relative Frequency Tables

A relative frequency table shows the proportion (or percentage) of observations in each category.

\[ \text{Relative frequency} = \frac{\text{Frequency}}{\text{Total}} \]

Favorite Streaming ServiceRelative Frequency
Netflix0.45 (45%)
YouTube0.30 (30%)
Disney+0.15 (15%)
Other0.10 (10%)
Total1.00 (100%)

The relative frequencies must sum to 1 (or 100%). Small rounding discrepancies are acceptable.

Summary Statistics for Categorical Data

For categorical data, the main summary statistics are:

  • Mode: the category with the highest frequency
  • Proportions: the fraction of observations in each category

Note: Mean, median, and standard deviation are not appropriate for categorical data because the categories have no inherent numerical order.

Key Idea: Relative frequencies allow comparisons between groups of different sizes. If School A surveys 200 students and School B surveys 500, raw frequencies are misleading — use relative frequencies instead.
AP Exam Tip: On the AP exam, always check that your relative frequencies sum to 1 (or 100%). If they don't, you may have made an arithmetic error.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Tabular Representation for Categorical Data

problems.question_html:
A survey of 200 students asked about their preferred mode of transportation to school. The results are shown below.

TransportationFrequency
Car80
Bus60
Bike35
Walk25

What is the relative frequency for "Bus"?

hints.text: Relative frequency = frequency of the category divided by the total number of observations.
\( \text{Relative frequency for Bus} = \frac{60}{200} = 0.30 \)

solution_steps.text: The frequency for Bus is 60 and the total number of students is 200.
\( \text{Relative frequency} = \frac{60}{200} = 0.30 \), or 30%.

problems.question_html: A frequency table shows the following counts for favorite ice cream flavor among 150 people: Chocolate (52), Vanilla (38), Strawberry (27), Mint (18), Other (15). What is the mode?

choices.text: Vanilla
Chocolate
Strawberry

hints.text: The mode is the category that appears most frequently.
Chocolate has the highest frequency (52), so Chocolate is the mode. Note: the mode is the category name, not the frequency count.

solution_steps.text: The mode is the category with the highest frequency. Comparing: Chocolate (52), Vanilla (38), Strawberry (27), Mint (18), Other (15).
Chocolate has the highest count at 52, so the mode is Chocolate. The mode is the category name, not the number 52.

problems.question_html: A school surveys 400 students about their favorite school lunch. The results are: Pizza (140), Tacos (100), Salad (80), Chicken Nuggets (60), Other (20). What percentage of students prefer either Tacos or Salad?

hints.text: Add the frequencies for Tacos and Salad, then divide by the total.

solution_steps.text: Tacos: 100 students. Salad: 80 students. Combined: \( 100 + 80 = 180 \) students.
\( \frac{180}{400} = 0.45 = 45\% \). So 45% of students prefer either Tacos or Salad.

problems.question_html: Two classes take the same survey about preferred study location. Class A (30 students): Library 12, Home 10, Café 8. Class B (50 students): Library 20, Home 18, Café 12. A student claims "More students in Class B prefer the library, so Class B likes the library more than Class A does." Is this reasoning valid?

choices.text: Yes, because 20 is greater than 12.
No, because we should compare relative frequencies: Class A has 40% and Class B has 40% — they are the same.
No, because the sample sizes are too small.
Yes, because Class B surveyed more students.

hints.text: When comparing groups of different sizes, raw counts can be misleading. What should you use instead?
Class A: \( 12/30 = 0.40 \). Class B: \( 20/50 = 0.40 \). The relative frequencies are equal, so the claim is not valid.

solution_steps.text: To compare groups of different sizes, use relative frequencies. Class A: \( 12/30 = 0.40 \) (40%). Class B: \( 20/50 = 0.40 \) (40%).
Both classes have the same proportion preferring the library (40%), so the student's reasoning based on raw counts is not valid.

problems.question_html: In a survey of 250 households, 75 have dogs, 90 have cats, 45 have fish, and 40 have no pets. What proportion of households have cats?

hints.text: Proportion = count in category divided by total count.
\( \text{Proportion with cats} = \frac{90}{250} = 0.36 \) or 36%.

solution_steps.text: The number of households with cats is 90. The total number of households is 250.
\( \text{Proportion} = \frac{90}{250} = 0.36 \), which is 36%.

problems.question_html: A relative frequency table for eye color shows: Brown = 0.42, Blue = 0.30, Green = 0.12, Hazel = 0.10. The relative frequency for "Other" must be __________.

hints.text: All relative frequencies must sum to 1.00 (100%).

solution_steps.text: Sum the given relative frequencies: \( 0.42 + 0.30 + 0.12 + 0.10 = 0.94 \).
Since all relative frequencies must sum to 1.00: Other = \( 1.00 - 0.94 = 0.06 \) (6%).

problems.question_html: A survey of 500 adults asked about their primary news source. Results: TV (175), Online (200), Newspaper (55), Radio (40), Social Media (30). What is the relative frequency for Online news?

hints.text: Divide the frequency for Online by the total number of adults surveyed.

solution_steps.text: Online frequency: 200. Total surveyed: 500.
\( \text{Relative frequency} = \frac{200}{500} = 0.40 \), or 40%.

problems.question_html: A frequency table for 300 students' favorite season shows: Summer (105), Fall (72), Winter (48), Spring (75). The proportion of students who chose Winter is __________.

hints.text: Divide the Winter frequency by the total.

solution_steps.text: Winter frequency: 48. Total: 300.

problems.question_html:
A community center surveyed 360 members about their preferred fitness class. The results are shown below.

ClassFrequency
Yoga108
Spin90
Zumba72
Weights54
Pilates36

(a) Construct a relative frequency table.

(b) What is the mode? Interpret it in context.

(c) What proportion of members prefer either Yoga or Zumba? Interpret this value in context.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Yoga: 108/360 = 0.30, Spin: 90/360 = 0.25, Zumba: 72/360 = 0.20, Weights: 54/360 = 0.15, Pilates: 36/360 = 0.10. Total = 1.00.
(b) The mode is Yoga. Among the 360 surveyed community center members, Yoga was the most frequently preferred fitness class.
(c) Proportion = (108 + 72)/360 = 180/360 = 0.50. Half (50%) of the surveyed community center members prefer either Yoga or Zumba.

hints.text: To find each relative frequency, divide each frequency by 360. The mode is the category with the highest count.
Yoga: 108/360 = 0.30, Spin: 0.25, Zumba: 0.20, Weights: 0.15, Pilates: 0.10. The mode is Yoga. For part (c), add the frequencies for Yoga and Zumba before dividing by 360.

solution_steps.text: (a) Divide each frequency by 360: Yoga = 0.30, Spin = 0.25, Zumba = 0.20, Weights = 0.15, Pilates = 0.10. Sum = 1.00.
(b) Yoga has the highest frequency (108), so Yoga is the mode. In context: among surveyed members, Yoga was the most preferred fitness class.
(c) \( \frac{108 + 72}{360} = \frac{180}{360} = 0.50 \). In context: 50% of surveyed community center members prefer either Yoga or Zumba.

problems.question_html:
An environmental group surveys 800 residents about their recycling habits. The frequency table is:

Recycling HabitFrequency
Always240
Usually200
Sometimes176
Rarely120
Never64

(a) Calculate the relative frequency for each category.

(b) What proportion of residents recycle at least "Usually" (i.e., "Usually" or "Always")? Interpret in context.

(c) A second town surveys 500 residents and finds that 175 "Always" recycle. Can we conclude that Town 1 has more dedicated recyclers than Town 2? Justify using relative frequencies.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Always: 240/800 = 0.30, Usually: 200/800 = 0.25, Sometimes: 176/800 = 0.22, Rarely: 120/800 = 0.15, Never: 64/800 = 0.08. Total = 1.00.
(b) (240 + 200)/800 = 440/800 = 0.55. In context: 55% of the surveyed residents recycle at least "Usually."
(c) Town 1 "Always" relative frequency: 240/800 = 0.30. Town 2 "Always" relative frequency: 175/500 = 0.35. Town 2 actually has a higher proportion of residents who always recycle (35% vs. 30%), so we cannot conclude Town 1 has more dedicated recyclers. We must compare relative frequencies, not raw counts, when sample sizes differ.

hints.text: Divide each frequency by 800. For part (c), compare relative frequencies, not raw counts, because the towns surveyed different numbers of residents.
Town 1: 240/800 = 0.30. Town 2: 175/500 = 0.35. Even though 240 > 175, Town 2 has a higher proportion — so raw count comparisons are misleading.

solution_steps.text: (a) Always: 0.30, Usually: 0.25, Sometimes: 0.22, Rarely: 0.15, Never: 0.08. Total = 1.00.
(b) \( \frac{240 + 200}{800} = 0.55 \). In context: 55% of surveyed residents recycle at least "Usually."

(c) Town 1: \( 240/800 = 0.30 \) (30%). Town 2: \( 175/500 = 0.35 \) (35%). Despite having a lower raw count, Town 2 has a higher proportion of "Always" recyclers. Comparing raw frequencies across different-sized groups is misleading.

concepts.title: Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable
concepts.content_html:
Graphical Representations for One Categorical Variable

Tables organize data numerically, but graphs give us a visual summary that makes patterns easier to spot. For categorical data, the two most common graphs are bar charts and pie charts.

Bar Charts

A bar chart displays each category as a separate bar. The height (or length) of each bar represents the frequency or relative frequency of that category.

Key features of bar charts:

  • Gaps between bars: bars do not touch because the categories are distinct (not continuous)
  • Bars can be arranged in any order (alphabetical, by frequency, etc.)
  • The vertical axis can show frequency (count) or relative frequency (proportion/percentage)

A Pareto chart is a special bar chart where the bars are arranged in order from tallest to shortest, making it easy to see which categories are most common.

Pie Charts

A pie chart (circle graph) shows each category as a slice of a circle. The angle of each slice is proportional to that category's relative frequency.

\[ \text{Slice angle} = \text{Relative frequency} \times 360° \]

Pie charts work best when:

  • There are a small number of categories (ideally 5 or fewer)
  • You want to emphasize part-to-whole relationships
  • The parts represent all possible categories (sum to 100%)

When to Use Each

FeatureBar ChartPie Chart
Best forComparing categoriesShowing part-to-whole
Many categoriesWorks wellBecomes cluttered
Comparing two groupsSide-by-side bars workNeed two separate charts
Exact valuesEasier to read preciselyHarder to read precisely
Key Idea: Bar charts are generally preferred over pie charts because it is easier for the human eye to compare bar heights than slice areas. The AP exam tends to use bar charts more frequently.
AP Exam Tip: When interpreting a graph, always refer to the specific categories and values rather than making vague statements. State which category is largest, give its approximate value, and use context.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Graphical Representations for Categorical Data

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a key reason why bars in a bar chart for categorical data should have gaps between them?

choices.text: To make the chart look more attractive
To indicate that the categories are distinct and not continuous
To leave room for error bars
Gaps are optional and have no statistical meaning

hints.text: Think about what the gaps communicate about the nature of the data. Are the categories connected on a number line?

Categorical data have distinct, separate categories with no natural ordering or continuity. Gaps between bars emphasize this. Histograms (for quantitative data) have no gaps because the data are continuous.

solution_steps.text: In a bar chart, each bar represents a distinct category (e.g., types of pets, favorite colors).
Gaps between bars visually indicate that the categories are separate and not part of a continuous scale. This distinguishes a bar chart from a histogram.

problems.question_html: A bar chart shows the favorite social media platforms of 500 surveyed teens: Instagram (175), TikTok (150), Snapchat (90), YouTube (55), Other (30). Which platform is the mode?

choices.text: TikTok
Instagram
Snapchat

hints.text: The mode is the category with the tallest bar (highest frequency).
Instagram has the highest frequency (175), so Instagram is the mode. Remember: the mode is the category name, not the count.

solution_steps.text: The mode corresponds to the tallest bar — the category with the highest frequency.
Instagram has the highest frequency at 175. Therefore, the mode is Instagram (the category, not the number 175).

problems.question_html: A Pareto chart of customer complaints at a restaurant shows bars in this order (tallest to shortest): Wait Time, Food Quality, Cleanliness, Price, Service. What distinguishes a Pareto chart from a regular bar chart?

choices.text: A Pareto chart uses horizontal bars instead of vertical bars.
A Pareto chart arranges bars in order from most frequent to least frequent.
A Pareto chart does not have gaps between bars.
A Pareto chart can only display relative frequencies.

hints.text: Look at the order of the bars: Wait Time has the most complaints and Service has the fewest.
A Pareto chart is a bar chart with bars arranged in descending order of frequency. This makes it easy to identify the most common categories at a glance.

solution_steps.text: A Pareto chart is a special type of bar chart where bars are ordered from tallest (most frequent) to shortest (least frequent).
This ordering highlights the most common categories. Regular bar charts may use alphabetical or arbitrary ordering.

problems.question_html: A student creates a pie chart to compare the favorite sports of students at two different schools. A statistics teacher says this is not the best choice. Why?

choices.text: Pie charts cannot display sports data.
Comparing two groups requires two separate pie charts, making direct comparison difficult. A side-by-side bar chart would be more effective.
Pie charts can only show data for one variable.
The teacher is wrong — a pie chart is the best choice for comparing two groups.

hints.text: Think about what happens when you try to put two groups on one pie chart — or how hard it is to compare two separate pie charts.

Comparing proportions between two groups on separate pie charts is difficult because the human eye struggles to compare angles/areas across charts. Side-by-side or segmented bar charts allow direct comparison.

solution_steps.text: To compare two schools, you would need two separate pie charts, making visual comparison difficult.
A side-by-side bar chart (or segmented bar chart) places the two groups next to each other, allowing direct comparison of category proportions.

problems.question_html: In a pie chart, a category that represents 25% of the data would have a central angle of __________ degrees.

hints.text: The total angle in a circle is 360°. Multiply the relative frequency by 360°.

solution_steps.text: The slice angle equals the relative frequency multiplied by 360°.
\( 0.25 \times 360° = 90° \). A category representing 25% of the data gets a 90° slice.

problems.question_html: A researcher has data on the primary language spoken at home for 2,000 households, with 12 different languages represented. Which graph would be more appropriate — a bar chart or a pie chart? Answer: __________
problems.correct_answer: bar chart||bar graph

hints.text: Consider how each graph handles a large number of categories.
With 12 categories, a pie chart becomes cluttered and hard to read. Bar charts handle many categories well, so a bar chart is more appropriate.

solution_steps.text: Pie charts work best with about 5 or fewer categories. With 12 languages, many slices would be thin and hard to distinguish.
A bar chart is more appropriate because it can clearly display many categories side by side, making comparisons easier.

problems.question_html: A pie chart for transportation methods shows: Car = 144°, Bus = 108°, Bike = 72°, Walk = 36°. What percentage of people use the bus?

hints.text: To convert a slice angle to a percentage, divide the angle by 360° and multiply by 100.

solution_steps.text: The bus slice has a central angle of 108°. The full circle is 360°.
\( \frac{108}{360} = 0.30 = 30\% \). So 30% of people use the bus.

problems.question_html: A bar chart uses relative frequency on the vertical axis. The bar for "Strongly Agree" reaches 0.35, and 200 people were surveyed. How many people selected "Strongly Agree"? Answer: __________

hints.text: Relative frequency times total gives the frequency (count).
\( 0.35 \times 200 = 70 \) people.

solution_steps.text: Relative frequency = 0.35 and the total is 200.
\( \text{Frequency} = 0.35 \times 200 = 70 \). So 70 people selected "Strongly Agree."

problems.question_html:
A school newspaper published the following data on 600 students' favorite music genres:

GenreFrequency
Pop180
Hip-Hop150
Rock108
Country90
Other72

(a) Calculate the central angle for each genre if these data were displayed in a pie chart.

(b) Which type of graph — bar chart or pie chart — would better allow a reader to determine the exact number of students preferring each genre? Explain.

(c) A student says, "Pop is almost twice as popular as Rock." Justify whether this claim is supported by the data.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Pop: (180/600) × 360° = 108°, Hip-Hop: (150/600) × 360° = 90°, Rock: (108/600) × 360° = 64.8°, Country: (90/600) × 360° = 54°, Other: (72/600) × 360° = 43.2°. Total = 360°.
(b) A bar chart is better for reading exact values because readers can compare bar heights against a numerical axis. In a pie chart, it is difficult to estimate exact counts from slice areas.
(c) Pop: 180 students (30%). Rock: 108 students (18%). The ratio is 180/108 ≈ 1.67, which is less than 2. So Pop is not quite twice as popular as Rock. The claim is not precisely supported, though Pop is substantially more popular.

hints.text: For part (a), use the formula: angle = (frequency/total) × 360°. For part (b), think about which graph makes it easier to read precise values.
For part (c), compute the ratio 180/108 and compare to 2. Also compare the relative frequencies: Pop = 30%, Rock = 18%.

solution_steps.text: (b) A bar chart is better for reading exact values. Bar heights are compared against a numerical axis, which is more precise than estimating slice areas in a pie chart.
(c) Pop = 180, Rock = 108. Ratio: \( 180/108 \approx 1.67 \). Since 1.67 < 2, Pop is not quite twice as popular as Rock. The claim is not precisely supported by the data.

problems.question_html:
A city council surveys 1,000 residents about their preferred method of public communication from the city. The results are:

MethodFrequency
Email newsletter320
Social media280
City website200
Mail120
Phone alerts80

(a) A council member creates a pie chart of this data. Calculate the central angle for "Social media" and "City website."

(b) Another council member creates a bar chart of the same data. Explain one advantage of the bar chart over the pie chart for this data set.

(c) If the council wanted to prioritize the top two methods, which two would they choose? What combined percentage of residents do these two methods cover?
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Social media: (280/1000) × 360° = 100.8°. City website: (200/1000) × 360° = 72°.
(b) A bar chart makes it easier to compare frequencies precisely because readers can use the numerical axis to determine exact values. In the pie chart, the slices for Social media (100.8°) and Email (115.2°) are close in size and hard to distinguish visually.
(c) The top two methods are Email newsletter (320, 32%) and Social media (280, 28%). Combined: 320 + 280 = 600, which is 60% of residents.

hints.text: For part (a), multiply the relative frequency by 360°. For part (c), identify the two categories with the highest frequencies.
Social media angle: (280/1000) × 360° = 100.8°. The top two methods are Email (320) and Social media (280), combining for 600/1000 = 60%.

solution_steps.text: (a) Social media: \( \frac{280}{1000} \times 360° = 100.8° \). City website: \( \frac{200}{1000} \times 360° = 72° \).

(b) The bar chart allows more precise comparison because bar heights can be read against a numerical axis. The pie chart slices for Email (115.2°) and Social media (100.8°) are similar in size and difficult to compare visually.
(c) Top two: Email newsletter (320, 32%) and Social media (280, 28%). Combined: \( 320 + 280 = 600 \), which is \( \frac{600}{1000} = 60\% \) of residents.

concepts.title: Representing a Quantitative Variable with Graphs
concepts.content_html:
Graphical Representations for One Quantitative Variable

Quantitative (numerical) data can be displayed using several types of graphs. Each graph type reveals different features of the data distribution.

Dotplots

A dotplot places a dot above a number line for each data value. Repeated values stack vertically. Dotplots are ideal for small data sets because every individual value is visible.

Example: Quiz scores of 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 9, 10 would show one dot above 7, two dots above 8, three dots above 9, and one dot above 10.

Stem-and-Leaf Plots

A stem-and-leaf plot (stemplot) splits each data value into a stem (leading digit(s)) and a leaf (trailing digit). Leaves are listed in order on each row.

For the data 23, 25, 31, 34, 37, 38, 42:

2 | 3 5
3 | 1 4 7 8
4 | 2

Key: 3 | 4 means 34

Split stems break each stem into two rows (leaves 0–4 and 5–9) when a single stem has too many leaves, providing a more detailed picture of the distribution.

Histograms

A histogram groups data into equal-width bins (intervals) and uses bars to show the frequency (count) or relative frequency (proportion) in each bin. There are no gaps between bars because the variable is continuous.

Key Idea: Relative frequency \(= \frac{\text{frequency in bin}}{\text{total number of observations}}\). The sum of all relative frequencies equals 1 (or 100%).

Bin width affects the appearance of a histogram. Too few bins can hide patterns; too many bins can make the graph noisy. A common guideline is 5–15 bins for most data sets.

Choosing a Graph

  • Dotplot: best for small data sets (\(n < 30\)); shows every value
  • Stemplot: good for small to moderate data sets; preserves actual values
  • Histogram: best for large data sets; groups data into bins

Relative frequency of the 70–79 bin \(= \frac{12}{40} = 0.30\).

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a key difference between a histogram and a bar chart?

choices.text: Histograms use colors; bar charts do not.
Histograms display quantitative data with no gaps between bars; bar charts display categorical data with gaps.
Bar charts can only show frequencies; histograms can show relative frequencies.
Histograms always have vertical bars; bar charts always have horizontal bars.

hints.text: Think about what type of data each graph is designed for and how the bars are arranged.
A histogram represents a continuous quantitative variable, so the bars touch. A bar chart represents categories, so gaps separate the bars.

solution_steps.text: A histogram displays quantitative (numerical) data. The bars touch because the variable is continuous — each bar covers an interval of values.
A bar chart displays categorical data. Gaps between bars emphasize that the categories are distinct.

A histogram of daily high temperatures (°F) in a city during June has the following bins and frequencies:

What proportion of days had a high temperature of at least 80°F?

solution_steps.text: Days with temperature at least 80°F: \(10 + 6 + 2 = 18\).

problems.question_html: A student constructs a histogram with bins of width 5. If the smallest data value is 12 and the largest is 47, what is the minimum number of bins needed to include all data values?

hints.text: Start the first bin at or below 12 and make sure the last bin includes 47. Each bin covers 5 units.
Starting at 10: bins are 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39, 40–44, 45–49. That's 8 bins to cover 12 through 47.

solution_steps.text: A natural starting point at or below 12 is 10. With bin width 5, the bins are: 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–29, 30–34, 35–39, 40–44, 45–49.
The value 47 falls in the 45–49 bin, so we need 8 bins.

The following stem-and-leaf plot shows the ages of participants in a community fun run:

1 | 5 7 8
2 | 0 2 3 5 6 8
3 | 1 4 5 9
4 | 0 3
5 | 2

Key: 2 | 5 means 25

How many participants are in their 30s?

hints.text: Look at the row with stem 3. Each leaf represents one participant in their 30s.
Stem 3 has leaves 1, 4, 5, 9 — that is 4 participants.

solution_steps.text: The stem 3 row contains leaves: 1, 4, 5, 9.
Count the leaves: there are 4 participants in their 30s.

problems.question_html: A dotplot of the number of pets owned by 20 students shows the following: 0 pets (4 dots), 1 pet (7 dots), 2 pets (5 dots), 3 pets (3 dots), 4 pets (1 dot). What is the total number of pets owned by all 20 students?

hints.text: Multiply each pet count by its frequency, then add the products.

solution_steps.text: Total = \(0 \times 4 + 1 \times 7 + 2 \times 5 + 3 \times 3 + 4 \times 1\)

problems.question_html: A stem-and-leaf plot uses split stems. The stems shown are 2L, 2H, 3L, 3H. A data value of 37 would be placed on which stem?
problems.correct_answer: 3H

hints.text: In a split-stem plot, L holds leaves 0–4 and H holds leaves 5–9.
The value 37 has stem 3 and leaf 7. Since 7 is in the range 5–9, it goes on the 3H stem.

solution_steps.text: In a split-stem plot, the "L" row contains leaves 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and the "H" row contains leaves 5, 6, 7, 8, 9.
For 37: stem = 3, leaf = 7. Since 7 is in the 5–9 range, it belongs on the 3H stem.

A histogram of commute times (in minutes) for 50 employees has these relative frequencies:

0–90.10

Relative frequency for less than 20 min: \(0.10 + 0.24 = 0.34\). Number of employees: \(0.34 \times 50 = 17\).

Combined relative frequency: \(0.10 + 0.24 = 0.34\).

problems.question_html:
A teacher records the following quiz scores for 15 students:

72, 75, 78, 80, 82, 84, 85, 85, 88, 90, 91, 93, 95, 97, 100

(a) Construct a stem-and-leaf plot for these data. Use stems 7, 8, 9, 10.

(b) Describe one advantage of using a stem-and-leaf plot instead of a histogram for this data set.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Stem-and-leaf plot:
7 | 2 5 8
8 | 0 2 4 5 5 8
9 | 0 1 3 5 7
10 | 0
Key: 8 | 5 means 85

(b) A stem-and-leaf plot preserves the individual data values, so you can recover the exact scores. A histogram only shows the count within each bin, not the actual values.

hints.text: For the stem-and-leaf plot, the tens digit is the stem and the units digit is the leaf. List leaves in order for each stem.
For part (b), think about what information is lost when you group data into histogram bins versus keeping each value visible.

solution_steps.text: Organize by stems (tens digits): 7 → leaves 2, 5, 8; 8 → leaves 0, 2, 4, 5, 5, 8; 9 → leaves 0, 1, 3, 5, 7; 10 → leaf 0.

The stem-and-leaf plot is:
7 | 2 5 8
8 | 0 2 4 5 5 8
9 | 0 1 3 5 7
10 | 0
Key: 8 | 5 means 85

Advantage: The stem-and-leaf plot retains the exact data values, whereas a histogram only shows frequencies per bin. This makes it possible to find the median, identify repeated values, and see the shape of the distribution at the same time.

problems.question_html:
An environmental scientist measures the concentration of a pollutant (in parts per million) at 25 sites along a river. She creates a histogram with the following bins and frequencies:

Bin (ppm)Frequency
0–42
5–96
10–149
15–195
20–242
25–291

(a) What proportion of sites have a pollutant concentration of less than 15 ppm?

(b) Describe the shape of the distribution. Is a dotplot or histogram more appropriate for displaying this data set? Explain your reasoning.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Sites with concentration < 15 ppm: 2 + 6 + 9 = 17. Proportion = 17/25 = 0.68.

(b) The distribution is roughly unimodal and slightly skewed to the right (the tail extends toward higher concentrations). A histogram is more appropriate than a dotplot because with 25 observations and a continuous variable, grouping into bins gives a clearer picture of the distribution's shape than plotting individual dots.

hints.text: For part (a), add the frequencies of all bins below 15 ppm and divide by 25.
For part (b), consider where the peak of the histogram is and which direction the tail stretches. Also think about sample size when choosing between a dotplot and histogram.

solution_steps.text: (a) Bins with concentration < 15 ppm: 0–4 (2), 5–9 (6), 10–14 (9). Total = \(2 + 6 + 9 = 17\).
Proportion \(= \frac{17}{25} = 0.68\). About 68% of sites have concentrations below 15 ppm.

(b) The histogram peaks in the 10–14 bin (unimodal) and has a longer tail on the right side (skewed right). A histogram is more appropriate because with 25 data points and a continuous measurement, bins provide a clearer visual summary than individual dots would.

concepts.title: Describing the Distribution of a Quantitative Variable
concepts.content_html:
Describing Distributions Using SOCS

When describing the distribution of a quantitative variable, use the SOCS framework — always in context of the data.

S — Shape

Common shapes include:

  • Symmetric: The left and right sides are approximately mirror images.
  • Skewed right (positively skewed): The right tail is longer. Most values cluster on the left.
  • Skewed left (negatively skewed): The left tail is longer. Most values cluster on the right.
  • Unimodal: One clear peak.
  • Bimodal: Two clear peaks (may suggest two subgroups).
  • Uniform: All values occur with roughly equal frequency; no clear peak.

O — Outliers / Unusual Features

Mention any outliers (data points that fall far from the rest), gaps (regions with no data), or clusters (groups of data separated by gaps). At this stage, outliers are identified informally — values that appear to be unusually far from the main body of data.

C — Center

Describe the typical value. You might reference the approximate center of the distribution (e.g., "The typical household income is around $55,000"). Formal measures (mean, median) come in Topic 1.7.

S — Spread

How much do values vary? Describe the range informally (e.g., "Scores range from about 40 to 100"). Formal measures (range, IQR, standard deviation) come in Topic 1.7.

Key Idea: Always describe shape, outliers, center, and spread in the context of the data. Don't just say "skewed right" — say "The distribution of household incomes is skewed to the right, with most households earning between $30,000 and $70,000 but a few households earning over $200,000."

Common Mistakes

  • Confusing skew direction: the skew is named for the direction of the tail, not the peak.
  • Forgetting context: always reference the variable and units.
  • Using "normal" loosely: save "normal" for the specific normal distribution; use "symmetric" or "approximately symmetric" when describing shape.

choices.text: Unimodal and symmetric
Bimodal with a gap
Skewed right
Uniform

hints.text: How many peaks (modes) does the distribution have? Are there regions with no data?
Two clusters with peaks at 2 and 7 hours mean two modes (bimodal). The region between them with few dots is a gap.

Two peaks = bimodal. The region between the clusters with very few values represents a gap.

diagram.caption: Bimodal dotplot of study hours with clusters at 2 hours and 7 hours

problems.question_html: A histogram of the ages of runners in a 5K race is roughly bell-shaped with a peak around 35 years, and the youngest runner is 18 while the oldest is 52. There are no apparent gaps or unusual values. Which of the following is the best description of this distribution?

choices.text: The distribution of ages is skewed right with a center around 35 years.
The distribution of ages is approximately symmetric and unimodal, centered around 35 years, with ages ranging from 18 to 52 and no apparent outliers.
The distribution of ages is uniform, ranging from 18 to 52.
The ages are bimodal with centers at 18 and 52.

hints.text: A complete description should address all four components of SOCS: shape, outliers, center, and spread.
Bell-shaped = approximately symmetric and unimodal. Center is about 35, spread is 18 to 52, and no outliers are mentioned. The best answer addresses all four parts in context.

solution_steps.text: Shape: roughly bell-shaped → approximately symmetric and unimodal.
Outliers: no apparent outliers or unusual features.
Center: peak around 35 years.
Spread: ages range from 18 to 52.
The answer that addresses all four SOCS components in context is the correct choice.

problems.question_html: A student describes a histogram of daily rainfall amounts as follows: "The graph goes up and then comes down." What critical elements of the SOCS framework is this student missing?

choices.text: The student only described shape; they are missing outliers, center, spread, and context.
The student gave a complete description.
The student only needs to add the word 'symmetric.'
The student described spread but is missing shape.

hints.text: Compare the student's description against the full SOCS framework. Does the student mention outliers? Center? Spread? Context?

"Goes up and then comes down" vaguely describes shape but lacks specificity (is it symmetric? unimodal?). The student omits outliers/unusual features, center, spread, and any reference to the variable (rainfall) or its units.

solution_steps.text: The student vaguely addressed shape ("goes up then comes down") but did not use proper vocabulary (symmetric? unimodal?).
Missing: outliers/unusual features, center (typical rainfall), spread (range of values), and context (no mention of rainfall or units).
A complete SOCS description requires all four components and must be stated in the context of the variable being measured.

problems.question_html: When describing a distribution, the "S" at the end of SOCS stands for what concept?
problems.correct_answer: spread||variability||Spread||Variability

hints.text: SOCS stands for Shape, Outliers, Center, and ____.
The final S refers to how much the data values vary — their spread.

solution_steps.text: SOCS stands for Shape, Outliers (and unusual features), Center, and Spread.
Spread describes how much variability or dispersion there is in the data.

problems.question_html: A distribution of test scores is described as "skewed left." In which direction does the longer tail extend?
problems.correct_answer: left||Left||toward lower values

hints.text: The name of the skewness tells you the direction of the tail.
"Skewed left" means the tail extends to the left, toward lower values.

solution_steps.text: In a skewed-left distribution, the longer tail extends to the left (toward lower values).
The bulk of the data is concentrated on the right (higher values), with a few unusually low values pulling the tail to the left.

problems.question_html: In a distribution that is skewed right, most of the data is concentrated on which side?
problems.correct_answer: left||Left||lower||the left

hints.text: If the tail goes right, where is the bulk of the data?
In a right-skewed distribution, the tail is on the right, so most data is on the left (lower values).

solution_steps.text: In a right-skewed distribution, the long tail extends to the right (toward higher values).
Therefore, the majority of data values are concentrated on the left side (lower values).

problems.question_html: A distribution of reaction times in an experiment has one main cluster between 200 ms and 400 ms, but there is an isolated group of three values near 800 ms. The feature at 800 ms is best described as a(n) ________ in the distribution.
problems.correct_answer: cluster||outlier||gap||cluster of outliers

hints.text: Think about what we call data points that are far away from the main body of data.
The isolated group at 800 ms, far from the main cluster (200–400 ms), represents outliers. The separation between the groups is a gap.

solution_steps.text: The three values near 800 ms are far removed from the main cluster of data (200–400 ms).
These isolated values are best described as outliers (or a cluster of outliers). The empty region between the main body and these values is a gap.

problems.question_html:
The histogram below shows the distribution of scores on a standardized math test for 200 students. The scores range from 300 to 800, with a peak near 500 and the distribution is approximately symmetric.

(a) Using the SOCS framework, write a complete description of this distribution. Be sure to use context.

(b) A counselor says, "Most students scored in the 500s, so the test is too easy." Explain why this conclusion may not be valid based on the distribution.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Shape: The distribution of standardized math test scores is approximately symmetric and unimodal. Outliers: There are no apparent outliers or unusual features. Center: The distribution is centered around 500, suggesting a typical score of about 500. Spread: Scores range from about 300 to 800, a spread of approximately 500 points.

(b) The counselor's conclusion is not valid. In a symmetric distribution centered at 500, roughly half the students scored below 500. The range of 300 to 800 shows substantial variability. A center of 500 on an 800-point scale does not indicate the test is 'too easy' — it suggests the test differentiates across a wide range of abilities.

hints.text: For part (a), address each letter of SOCS separately and always mention 'standardized math test scores' to provide context.
For part (b), consider what 'centered at 500' means for a scale of 300–800. Does a center in the middle really mean the test is easy?

solution_steps.text: (a) Shape: The distribution of standardized math test scores is approximately symmetric and unimodal, with a single peak near 500.
Outliers: No apparent outliers or unusual features are visible.
Center: The typical score is approximately 500.
Spread: Scores range from about 300 to 800 (a range of about 500 points), indicating considerable variability.

(b) The counselor's reasoning is flawed. An approximately symmetric distribution centered at 500 means roughly half of students scored below 500 and half scored above. The wide range (300 to 800) shows the test produces a variety of scores. A center near the middle of the scale suggests the test is appropriately calibrated, not too easy.

diagram.caption: Approximately symmetric histogram of standardized math test scores for 200 students, peak near 500

problems.question_html:
Two dotplots show the distribution of daily tips (in dollars) for two servers at a restaurant over 30 days.

Server A: Tips range from $15 to $95, with most values between $40 and $60 and one value at $95.

Server B: Tips range from $30 to $70, evenly spread with no clear peak.

(a) Describe the shape of each server's tip distribution.

(b) Compare the two distributions in terms of center, spread, and any unusual features.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Server A: The distribution of daily tips is unimodal and skewed right, with most tips clustered between $40 and $60 and a tail extending toward $95. Server B: The distribution of daily tips is approximately uniform, with tips spread fairly evenly from $30 to $70.

(b) Center: Server A's typical tip appears to be around $45–$55. Server B's typical tip is around $50 (the middle of the uniform spread). The centers are similar. Spread: Server A has a wider range ($15 to $95 = $80 range) compared to Server B ($30 to $70 = $40 range). Unusual features: Server A has a potential outlier at $95, which is far above the main cluster. Server B has no apparent outliers.

hints.text: For part (a), decide whether each distribution is symmetric, skewed, unimodal, bimodal, or uniform. For part (b), compare center, spread, and outliers.
Server A's cluster at $40–$60 with one high value at $95 suggests right skew with a possible outlier. Server B's even spread with no peak is approximately uniform.

solution_steps.text: (a) Server A: Unimodal (peak in $40–$60 range) and skewed right due to the tail extending to $95.
Server B: Approximately uniform — tips are evenly distributed from $30 to $70 with no dominant peak.
(b) Center: Both servers have a typical tip around $50. Server A's center is slightly harder to pin down because of the skew.
Spread: Server A's range is $95 − $15 = $80. Server B's range is $70 − $30 = $40. Server A has more variability.
Unusual features: Server A has a potential outlier at $95 (far above the main cluster). Server B has no apparent outliers.

diagram.alt_text: Two rows of dots: Server A has most dots between $40-$60 with one at $95, Server B has dots evenly spread from $30 to $70
diagram.caption: Two dotplots comparing daily tips for Server A (right-skewed with outlier at $95) and Server B (uniform, $30-$70)

diagrams.caption: Histogram of a right-skewed distribution with the tail extending to the right, showing mean pulled above the median

concepts.title: Summary Statistics for a Quantitative Variable
concepts.content_html:
Summary Statistics for One Quantitative Variable

Summary statistics are numbers that describe the center and spread of a distribution. Understanding which statistics to use — and when — is essential for AP Statistics.

Measures of Center

Mean (\(\bar{x}\)): The arithmetic average of all data values.

\[\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n} = \frac{x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}{n}\]

Median: The middle value when data are arranged in order.

  • If \(n\) is odd, the median is the middle value (position \(\frac{n+1}{2}\)).
  • If \(n\) is even, the median is the average of the two middle values.

Measures of Spread

Range = maximum − minimum. Simple but sensitive to outliers.

Quartiles: \(Q_1\) (25th percentile) and \(Q_3\) (75th percentile) divide the ordered data into quarters.

  • \(Q_1\) is the median of the lower half of the data.
  • \(Q_3\) is the median of the upper half of the data.

Interquartile Range (IQR): \[\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1\] The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

Standard Deviation (\(s\)): Measures the typical distance of data values from the mean.

\[s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum(x_i - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}\]

A larger standard deviation means data values are more spread out from the mean.

Resistant vs. Non-Resistant Measures

Key Idea: A statistic is resistant (robust) if it is not heavily affected by outliers or extreme values.
ResistantNon-Resistant
MedianMean
IQRRange
\(Q_1\), \(Q_3\)Standard deviation

Effect of Outliers

Outliers pull the mean toward the tail. In a right-skewed distribution, the mean is typically greater than the median. In a left-skewed distribution, the mean is typically less than the median. In a symmetric distribution, the mean and median are approximately equal.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Summary Statistics for a Quantitative Variable

problems.question_html: Find the mean of the following data set: 12, 15, 18, 20, 25.

hints.text: The mean is the sum of all values divided by the number of values.

problems.question_html: A data set contains: 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 100. Which measure of center is more resistant to the outlier at 100?

choices.text: The mean, because it uses all data values.
The median, because it depends only on the middle value(s).
The range, because it measures spread.
The standard deviation, because it accounts for variability.

hints.text: A resistant measure is not greatly affected by extreme values. Which center measure changes less when an outlier is present?
The median is the middle value (8). The mean = \(\frac{145}{7} \approx 20.7\), pulled up by 100. The median (8) better represents the typical value.

solution_steps.text: Median of {3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 100} is 8 (the 4th value).
The outlier (100) pulls the mean far above the typical values, but the median stays at 8. The median is more resistant.

problems.question_html: The salaries (in thousands of dollars) of 6 employees at a small company are: 35, 38, 42, 45, 50, 200. What is the mean salary? What is the median salary?

hints.text: The mean is the sum divided by 6. The median of 6 values is the average of the 3rd and 4th values.

solution_steps.text: Mean = \(\frac{410}{6} \approx 68.33\) thousand, or $68,333.
Median: with 6 values, average the 3rd and 4th: \(\frac{42 + 45}{2} = 43.5\) thousand, or $43,500.
The outlier salary of $200,000 pulls the mean far above the median.

problems.question_html: Which of the following pairs of statistics are both resistant to outliers?

choices.text: Mean and standard deviation
Mean and IQR
Median and IQR
Median and range

hints.text: A resistant statistic is not greatly affected by outliers. Check each option — are both statistics in the pair resistant?
Median is resistant (based on middle values). IQR is resistant (based on Q1 and Q3). Range and standard deviation are not resistant because they depend on extreme values or all values.

solution_steps.text: Resistant measures: median, Q1, Q3, IQR.
Non-resistant measures: mean, range, standard deviation.
The only pair where both are resistant is median and IQR.

problems.question_html: The ordered data set is: 4, 7, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24. Find the interquartile range (IQR).

hints.text: First find Q1 (median of the lower half) and Q3 (median of the upper half), then compute IQR = Q3 − Q1.

solution_steps.text: With 8 values, split into lower half {4, 7, 9, 12} and upper half {15, 18, 21, 24}.

problems.question_html: A data set has 9 values, arranged in order: 2, 5, 5, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17, 20. What is the median?

hints.text: For an odd number of values, the median is the middle value. What position is the middle value?
With 9 values, the median is at position \(\frac{9+1}{2} = 5\). The 5th value is 10.

solution_steps.text: There are 9 values. The median is at position \(\frac{9+1}{2} = 5\).
The 5th value in the ordered list is 10. The median is 10.

problems.question_html: A data set has a mean of 50 and contains the values: 40, 45, 48, 55, \(x\). Find the value of \(x\).

hints.text: Use the mean formula: \(\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}\). You know the mean is 50 and there are 5 values.

problems.question_html: The data values are: 3, 4, 4, 5, 7. Calculate the standard deviation \(s\). Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: First find the mean, then compute each deviation \((x_i - \bar{x})\), square them, sum them, divide by \(n - 1\), and take the square root.

problems.question_html:
The following data represent the number of home runs hit by 10 players in a season:

5, 8, 12, 14, 15, 18, 22, 25, 30, 45

(a) Calculate the mean, median, Q1, Q3, and IQR.

(b) A sports analyst reports the "average" number of home runs as 19.4. A different analyst reports the "typical" number as 16.5. Explain which measure each analyst is using and which better represents the typical player. Justify your answer.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Mean = (5+8+12+14+15+18+22+25+30+45)/10 = 194/10 = 19.4. Median = (15+18)/2 = 16.5. Q1 = 12 (median of lower half: 5,8,12,14,15). Q3 = 25 (median of upper half: 18,22,25,30,45). IQR = 25 − 12 = 13.

(b) The first analyst (19.4) is using the mean. The second analyst (16.5) is using the median. The median better represents the typical player because the distribution is skewed right by the outlier at 45 home runs, which pulls the mean above most of the data. The median is resistant to this outlier.

hints.text: For part (a), remember: with 10 values, the median is the average of the 5th and 6th. Q1 is the median of the lower 5 values, Q3 is the median of the upper 5.
For part (b), compare mean (19.4) and median (16.5). Which is pulled by the high value of 45? The resistant measure better represents 'typical.'

solution_steps.text: Median: average of 5th (15) and 6th (18) values = \(\frac{15+18}{2} = 16.5\).
Lower half: {5, 8, 12, 14, 15}. \(Q_1 = 12\) (the 3rd value).

(b) 19.4 is the mean; 16.5 is the median. The high value of 45 pulls the mean up. The median (16.5) is resistant to this outlier and better represents the typical number of home runs for these players.

problems.question_html:
A teacher gives a quiz to two classes. The results are summarized below:

Class AClass B
Mean7878
Median8076
Standard Deviation512
IQR618

(a) Both classes have the same mean. Explain why the median tells us something different about the two distributions.

(b) Compare the spread of the two classes using both standard deviation and IQR. What do these statistics tell you about the consistency of scores in each class?

(c) Based on the relationship between mean and median for each class, what can you infer about the shape of each distribution?
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Class A has median (80) > mean (78), suggesting a slightly left-skewed distribution — a few low scores pull the mean down. Class B has median (76) < mean (78), suggesting a slightly right-skewed distribution — a few high scores pull the mean up. The medians show the distributions are centered differently despite having the same mean.

(b) Class A: SD = 5, IQR = 6 — scores are tightly clustered around the mean, indicating consistent performance. Class B: SD = 12, IQR = 18 — scores are much more spread out, with greater variability. Class A students performed more consistently than Class B.

(c) Class A: mean < median → slightly skewed left. Class B: mean > median → slightly skewed right.

hints.text: Compare mean and median for each class. When mean < median, what does that suggest about skew? Also compare the spread statistics.
Class A: median > mean → slight left skew. Class B: median < mean → slight right skew. Class B has much larger SD and IQR, indicating more variability.

solution_steps.text: (a) Although both classes have mean 78, Class A's median (80) is above the mean while Class B's median (76) is below. This tells us the distributions are shaped differently — the 'typical' student in Class A scored higher than the 'typical' student in Class B.
(b) Class A has SD = 5 and IQR = 6, meaning scores are tightly grouped. Class B has SD = 12 and IQR = 18, meaning scores are much more variable. Class A performed more consistently.

(c) Class A: mean (78) < median (80) → the distribution is slightly skewed left (a few low scores pull the mean below the median). Class B: mean (78) > median (76) → the distribution is slightly skewed right (a few high scores pull the mean above the median).

concepts.title: Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics
concepts.content_html:
Boxplots and the Five-Number Summary

A boxplot (box-and-whisker plot) provides a visual summary of a distribution using five key values.

The Five-Number Summary

The five-number summary consists of:

  1. Minimum (smallest value)
  2. \(Q_1\) (first quartile — 25th percentile)
  3. Median (50th percentile)
  4. \(Q_3\) (third quartile — 75th percentile)
  5. Maximum (largest value)

Constructing a Boxplot

  1. Draw a number line spanning the range of the data.
  2. Draw a box from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\). This box represents the middle 50% of the data (the IQR).
  3. Draw a vertical line inside the box at the median.
  4. Extend whiskers from each end of the box to the minimum and maximum values.

Modified Boxplots

A modified boxplot identifies outliers explicitly using the 1.5 × IQR rule:

Outlier Rule: A data value is an outlier if it falls more than \(1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) below \(Q_1\) or above \(Q_3\).
Lower fence: \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\)
Upper fence: \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\)
Any value below the lower fence or above the upper fence is classified as an outlier.

In a modified boxplot:

  • Whiskers extend to the most extreme data values that are not outliers (within the fences).
  • Outliers are plotted as individual dots or symbols beyond the whiskers.

Mean vs. Median and Shape

The relationship between the mean and median tells us about skewness:

  • Skewed right: mean > median (the mean is pulled toward the right tail)
  • Skewed left: mean < median (the mean is pulled toward the left tail)
  • Symmetric: mean ≈ median

On a boxplot, right skew appears as a longer right whisker and more space between the median line and \(Q_3\). Left skew shows the opposite pattern.
