problem_sets.title: Practice: Graphical Representations of Summary Statistics

problems.question_html: A data set has the following five-number summary: Min = 10, \(Q_1\) = 25, Median = 35, \(Q_3\) = 50, Max = 90. What is the IQR?

hints.text: IQR = Q3 − Q1.

problems.question_html: A boxplot of exam scores shows the median line closer to \(Q_1\) than to \(Q_3\), and the right whisker is much longer than the left whisker. What does this indicate about the distribution?

choices.text: The distribution is approximately symmetric.
The distribution is skewed left.
The distribution is skewed right.
The distribution is bimodal.

hints.text: Look at where the median sits within the box and which whisker is longer. The longer tail indicates the direction of skew.
The median closer to Q1 and a longer right whisker both indicate the distribution stretches more to the right — it is skewed right.

solution_steps.text: When the median line is closer to \(Q_1\), more of the box's area is between the median and \(Q_3\) — the upper half of the middle 50% is more spread out.
A longer right whisker confirms the distribution extends further to the right.
Both features indicate a right-skewed distribution.

problems.question_html: The five-number summary for daily step counts of 30 adults is: Min = 2,100, \(Q_1\) = 5,400, Median = 7,800, \(Q_3\) = 10,200, Max = 18,500. Is the maximum value (18,500) an outlier according to the 1.5 × IQR rule?

choices.text: Yes, because 18,500 is much larger than the median.
Yes, because 18,500 exceeds \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 17,400\).
No, because 18,500 is within \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR} = 19,200\).
No, because the maximum can never be an outlier.

hints.text: Calculate the IQR and then the upper fence. Compare 18,500 to the upper fence.

solution_steps.text: Since \(18{,}500 > 17{,}400\), the maximum is an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule.

problems.question_html: A distribution of housing prices in a city is skewed right. Which of the following statements is true?

choices.text: The mean is less than the median.
The mean is approximately equal to the median.
The mean is greater than the median.
The mean is always double the median.

hints.text: In a skewed distribution, the mean is pulled toward the tail. Which direction is the tail in a right-skewed distribution?
Skewed right → the tail extends to the right (high values) → the mean is pulled to the right → mean > median.

solution_steps.text: In a right-skewed distribution, the tail extends toward higher values.
The mean is pulled toward the tail (higher values), so mean > median.
For housing prices: a few very expensive homes pull the mean above the median.

problems.question_html: A data set has \(Q_1 = 20\), \(Q_3 = 40\), and IQR = 20. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, what is the upper fence for identifying outliers?

hints.text: The upper fence = \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\).
Upper fence = \(40 + 1.5(20) = 40 + 30 = 70\). Any value above 70 is an outlier.

solution_steps.text: Any data value greater than 70 would be classified as an outlier.

problems.question_html: In a modified boxplot, a data point appears as an individual dot beyond the right whisker. This point is classified as a(n) ________.
problems.correct_answer: outlier||Outlier

hints.text: In a modified boxplot, what are individual points plotted beyond the whiskers called?
Points beyond the whiskers in a modified boxplot are outliers — values that fall outside the fences.

solution_steps.text: In a modified boxplot, whiskers extend to the most extreme values within the fences.
Points plotted individually beyond the whiskers are classified as outliers (values beyond \(Q_1 - 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\) or \(Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}\)).

problems.question_html: A data set has the five-number summary: Min = 15, \(Q_1 = 28\), Median = 36, \(Q_3 = 44\), Max = 52. What is the lower fence for identifying outliers using the 1.5 × IQR rule?

hints.text: First find IQR = Q3 − Q1, then compute lower fence = Q1 − 1.5 × IQR.

solution_steps.text: Any value below 4 would be an outlier. The minimum (15) is well above 4, so there are no low outliers.

problems.question_html: Two boxplots are displayed side by side comparing the marathon finish times (in minutes) for runners aged 20–29 and runners aged 50–59. The 20–29 boxplot has a smaller box (IQR) and shorter whiskers than the 50–59 boxplot, but both have similar medians. What does this comparison tell us?
problems.correct_answer: The typical finish times are similar, but the 50-59 age group has more variability.||Both groups have similar centers but the older group has greater spread.

hints.text: Compare the medians (center) and the box widths/whisker lengths (spread) of the two groups.
Similar medians mean the typical finish times are comparable. A smaller box and shorter whiskers for 20–29 mean less variability — the 50–59 group has more spread in their finish times.

solution_steps.text: Similar medians indicate that the typical marathon finish time is about the same for both age groups.
The 20–29 group has a smaller IQR (narrower box) and shorter whiskers, indicating less variability in finish times.
The 50–59 group has a wider box and longer whiskers, indicating greater variability — finish times are more spread out among older runners.

problems.question_html:
The following data represent the number of points scored by a basketball player in 12 games:

8, 12, 14, 16, 18, 19, 20, 22, 24, 26, 28, 45

(a) Calculate the five-number summary.

(b) Use the 1.5 × IQR rule to determine whether there are any outliers.

(c) Describe how the boxplot for this data would look. Would you recommend using a regular or modified boxplot? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Min = 8, Q1 = 15, Median = 19.5, Q3 = 25, Max = 45.

(b) IQR = 25 − 15 = 10. Lower fence = 15 − 1.5(10) = 0. Upper fence = 25 + 1.5(10) = 40. Since 45 > 40, the value 45 is an outlier. No values are below 0, so no low outliers.

(c) The box extends from Q1 = 15 to Q3 = 25 with a median line at 19.5. The left whisker extends from 15 down to 8. For a modified boxplot, the right whisker extends to 28 (the largest non-outlier value), and 45 is plotted as an individual point. A modified boxplot is recommended because it clearly identifies the outlier at 45, which a regular boxplot would hide by simply extending the whisker to 45.

hints.text: With 12 values, the median is the average of the 6th and 7th. Q1 is the median of values 1–6, Q3 is the median of values 7–12.
After finding the five-number summary, compute fences: lower = Q1 − 1.5(IQR), upper = Q3 + 1.5(IQR). Check if any data values fall outside these fences.

solution_steps.text: Min = 8. Max = 45. Median = average of 6th and 7th = \(\frac{19 + 20}{2} = 19.5\).
Five-number summary: 8, 15, 19.5, 25, 45.
(b) IQR = 25 − 15 = 10. Lower fence = 15 − 15 = 0. Upper fence = 25 + 15 = 40.
45 > 40 → outlier. No values below 0 → no low outliers.

(c) A modified boxplot is recommended. The box spans 15 to 25, median at 19.5, left whisker to 8, right whisker to 28 (largest non-outlier). The value 45 appears as a dot beyond the right whisker, clearly flagging it as an outlier.

diagram.alt_text: Horizontal box plot showing min 8, Q1 15, median 19, Q3 25, max 28 with an outlier dot at 45
diagram.caption: Box plot of basketball player points per game with outlier at 45

problems.question_html:
Side-by-side boxplots compare the annual rainfall (in inches) for two cities over 20 years:

City A: Min = 20, \(Q_1\) = 30, Median = 38, \(Q_3\) = 42, Max = 50. No outliers.

City B: Min = 10, \(Q_1\) = 25, Median = 40, \(Q_3\) = 55, Max = 70. One outlier at 70.

(a) Compare the centers of the two distributions.

(b) Compare the spreads of the two distributions using IQR.

(c) The mayor of City B claims, "Our city gets about the same rainfall as City A." Evaluate this claim using the boxplot information.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) City A's median rainfall is 38 inches and City B's median is 40 inches. The centers are close, so in a typical year both cities receive similar rainfall.

(b) City A: IQR = 42 − 30 = 12 inches. City B: IQR = 55 − 25 = 30 inches. City B has much more variability in annual rainfall (IQR is 2.5 times larger).

(c) The mayor's claim is partially correct — the median rainfall is similar (38 vs. 40 inches). However, City B's rainfall is much more variable (IQR = 30 vs. 12), with years as dry as 10 inches and as wet as 70 inches. So while the 'typical' year is similar, City B's rainfall is far less predictable.

hints.text: Compare medians for center, and IQRs for spread. Consider what the mayor means by 'about the same.'
The medians are similar (38 vs. 40), supporting the mayor's claim about center. But City B's IQR (30) is much larger than City A's (12), meaning City B's rainfall varies much more year to year.

solution_steps.text: (a) City A median = 38 in., City B median = 40 in. The centers are similar — both cities typically receive around 38–40 inches of rainfall per year.
(b) City A IQR = 42 − 30 = 12 in. City B IQR = 55 − 25 = 30 in. City B has 2.5 times the variability of City A.

(c) The mayor is correct that the typical (median) rainfall is similar. However, the claim is misleading because it ignores variability. City B ranges from 10 to 70 inches with an IQR of 30, while City A ranges from 20 to 50 with an IQR of 12. City B's rainfall is much less consistent from year to year.

diagram.caption: Side-by-side box plots comparing annual rainfall for City A and City B
