concepts.title: Comparisons of Distributions for One Quantitative Variable
concepts.content_html:
Comparing Distributions

When we have a quantitative variable measured across two or more groups, we need tools to compare those distributions side by side. The AP Statistics CED emphasizes three graphical displays for comparison and an important numerical tool—the z-score.

Back-to-Back Stemplots

A back-to-back stemplot shares a common stem column, with leaves for one group extending to the left and leaves for the other extending to the right. This works best for small to moderate data sets with two groups.

Example: comparing quiz scores for two class sections. The shared stems make it easy to see whether one section tends to score higher, whether the spreads differ, and whether either distribution has outliers.

Parallel (Side-by-Side) Boxplots

When comparing two or more groups, parallel boxplots drawn on the same number line let you quickly compare centers (medians), spreads (IQRs), and potential outliers. They are especially useful when you have more than two groups or larger data sets where stemplots become unwieldy.

When describing comparisons, always address shape, center, spread, and unusual features in context.

Comparative Dotplots

Comparative dotplots stack dotplots for each group on a common axis. They preserve individual data values and reveal shape, clusters, gaps, and outliers more clearly than boxplots for small data sets.

Z-Scores: Comparing Across Distributions

A z-score (standardized score) tells you how many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean:

\[z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\]

  • A positive z-score means the value is above the mean.
  • A negative z-score means the value is below the mean.
  • A z-score of 0 means the value equals the mean.

Z-scores allow you to compare values from distributions with different means and standard deviations. The observation with the higher z-score performed better relative to its group.

Key Takeaway: When comparing individual values from different distributions, always use z-scores rather than raw values. A score of 85 on one test may be more impressive than a 90 on another if the first test had a lower mean and smaller standard deviation.
Common Mistake: Students often compare raw scores from different distributions without standardizing. Always compute z-scores first when distributions have different centers or spreads.
concepts.content_raw: Comparisons of Distributions for One Quantitative Variable

problem_sets.title: Practice: Comparing Distributions

problems.question_html: Two classes took the same exam. Class A had a mean of 78 and a standard deviation of 6. Class B had a mean of 82 and a standard deviation of 10. A student in Class A scored 90 and a student in Class B scored 92. Which student performed better relative to their class?

choices.text: The student in Class B, because 92 > 90
The student in Class A, because their z-score is 2.0 compared to 1.0
They performed equally well relative to their classes
It is impossible to compare without knowing the shapes of the distributions

hints.text: To compare values from different distributions, calculate the z-score for each: \(z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\).
Class A: \(z = \frac{90 - 78}{6} = 2.0\). Class B: \(z = \frac{92 - 82}{10} = 1.0\). The higher z-score indicates a better relative performance.

solution_steps.text: Calculate the z-score for the Class A student: \(z_A = \frac{90 - 78}{6} = \frac{12}{6} = 2.0\).
Calculate the z-score for the Class B student: \(z_B = \frac{92 - 82}{10} = \frac{10}{10} = 1.0\).
Since \(z_A = 2.0 > z_B = 1.0\), the student in Class A performed better relative to their class, even though the Class B student had a higher raw score.

problems.question_html: Parallel boxplots are drawn for the daily high temperatures in three cities during July. City X has a median of 88°F with an IQR of 4, City Y has a median of 85°F with an IQR of 12, and City Z has a median of 90°F with an IQR of 7. Which city has the most consistent temperatures?

choices.text: City X, because it has the smallest IQR
City Y, because it has the lowest median
City Z, because it has the highest median
City Y, because a larger IQR means more data was collected

hints.text: Consistency means less variability. Which measure of spread is shown in a boxplot?
The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of data. A smaller IQR means more consistent (less variable) data.

solution_steps.text: Consistency refers to low variability. In boxplots, the IQR (length of the box) shows the spread of the middle 50%.
City X has the smallest IQR of 4, meaning its daily high temperatures are the most tightly clustered around the median.
Therefore City X has the most consistent temperatures.

diagram.alt_text: Three horizontal box plots showing City X median 88 IQR 4, City Y median 85 IQR 12, City Z median 90 IQR 7
diagram.caption: Parallel box plots of daily high temperatures for three cities in July

problems.question_html: Back-to-back stemplots are constructed comparing the number of hours of sleep for students at two schools. School A's leaves range from 5|2 to 9|5, while School B's leaves range from 4|8 to 8|3. School A's distribution is roughly symmetric, while School B is left-skewed. Which of the following is a valid comparison?

choices.text: School A students tend to sleep more and have a more symmetric distribution than School B students
School B students sleep more because left-skewed means most values are high
The schools have the same typical amount of sleep because they share the same stems
We cannot compare the distributions because they have different shapes

hints.text: Compare shape, center, and spread. For a left-skewed distribution, the tail extends to the left (lower values), and the mean is pulled below the median.
School A ranges from about 5.2 to 9.5 hours (symmetric), while School B ranges from 4.8 to 8.3 hours (left-skewed with a tail toward fewer hours). School A's center appears higher.

solution_steps.text: School A ranges from about 5.2 to 9.5 hours and is roughly symmetric, so the center is around 7–7.5 hours.
School B ranges from 4.8 to 8.3 hours and is left-skewed, meaning the tail extends toward fewer hours of sleep. The center is pulled below the middle of the range.
School A students tend to sleep more (higher center) and the distribution is more symmetric. It is valid to compare distributions even if they have different shapes.

problems.question_html: In a back-to-back stemplot comparing test scores for two classes, the stem represents tens digits and the leaves represent units digits. If a score of 73 belongs to Class A, which side does the leaf 3 go on?

choices.text: On the left side of stem 7, because Class A is always on the left
On whichever side is designated for Class A in the key
On the right side, because 73 > 70
On both sides, to show the score belongs to the shared stem

hints.text: In a back-to-back stemplot, each group is assigned to one side of the shared stems.
There is no universal rule for which group goes on which side. The key or legend tells you which side represents which group.

solution_steps.text: In a back-to-back stemplot, the stems are shared in the center. One group's leaves extend to the left and the other's to the right.
The assignment of groups to sides is determined by whoever creates the display—there is no fixed rule. You must refer to the key.
The leaf 3 goes on whichever side is designated for Class A by the stemplot's key.

problems.question_html: On a standardized math test, Maria scored 72 in a class where the mean was 65 and the standard deviation was 5. What is Maria's z-score?

hints.text: Use the z-score formula: \(z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\).
Substitute: \(z = \frac{72 - 65}{5} = \frac{7}{5}\).

solution_steps.text: Identify the values: \(x = 72\), \(\bar{x} = 65\), \(s = 5\).
Apply the formula: \(z = \frac{72 - 65}{5} = \frac{7}{5} = 1.4\).
Maria's score is 1.4 standard deviations above the mean.

problems.question_html: A distribution of test scores has a mean of 100 and a standard deviation of 15. A student has a z-score of \(-1.2\). What is the student's raw score?

hints.text: Rearrange the z-score formula to solve for \(x\): \(x = \bar{x} + z \cdot s\).

solution_steps.text: Start with the z-score formula rearranged: \(x = \bar{x} + z \cdot s\).
The student's raw score is 82.

problems.question_html: A distribution of SAT Math scores has a mean of 528 and a standard deviation of 117. A distribution of ACT Math scores has a mean of 20.7 and a standard deviation of 5.4. A student scores 650 on the SAT Math and 27 on the ACT Math. Compute the z-score for the ACT Math score. Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Use the z-score formula with the ACT distribution parameters: \(z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\).
\(z = \frac{27 - 20.7}{5.4} = \frac{6.3}{5.4}\). Divide and round to two decimal places.

solution_steps.text: Identify ACT parameters: \(x = 27\), \(\bar{x} = 20.7\), \(s = 5.4\).
The ACT score of 27 is 1.17 standard deviations above the ACT mean.

problems.question_html: A distribution of employee salaries at Company A has a mean of $52,000 and a standard deviation of $8,000. At Company B, the mean salary is $60,000 with a standard deviation of $12,000. An employee at Company A earns $68,000. What salary at Company B would have the same relative standing? Enter as a whole number without the dollar sign.

hints.text: First compute the z-score for the Company A salary, then use that z-score to find the equivalent salary at Company B.

solution_steps.text: Set the Company B salary to have the same z-score: \(2.0 = \frac{x - 60{,}000}{12{,}000}\).

problems.question_html:
The parallel boxplots below show the distribution of daily step counts for three fitness groups during a 30-day challenge.

  • Group A: Min = 3,000, Q1 = 6,000, Median = 8,500, Q3 = 10,000, Max = 14,000
  • Group B: Min = 5,000, Q1 = 7,500, Median = 9,000, Q3 = 11,500, Max = 16,000 (outlier at 22,000)
  • Group C: Min = 2,000, Q1 = 4,000, Median = 5,500, Q3 = 7,000, Max = 9,000

Compare the three distributions in context. Be sure to address shape, center, spread, and any unusual features.
problems.correct_answer: Group B has the highest median daily step count (9,000) and the largest spread (IQR = 4,000), indicating that while Group B members generally walked the most, there was considerable variability among them. Group B also has a high outlier at 22,000 steps. Group A has a slightly lower median (8,500) but a similar IQR (4,000), suggesting comparable consistency. Group C has the lowest median (5,500) and the smallest IQR (3,000), meaning these members walked the least and were the most consistent. All three groups appear roughly symmetric based on the boxplots, though Group B's outlier suggests the distribution may have a right skew if we include that value.

hints.text: When comparing distributions with parallel boxplots, systematically address center (median), spread (IQR and range), and unusual features (outliers) for each group. Always write in context.
Compare medians: B (9,000) > A (8,500) > C (5,500). Compare IQRs: A and B (4,000 each) > C (3,000). Note Group B's outlier at 22,000 steps.

solution_steps.text: Center: Group B has the highest median daily step count at 9,000, followed by Group A at 8,500, and Group C at 5,500.
Spread: Groups A and B both have an IQR of 4,000 steps, while Group C has a smaller IQR of 3,000 steps, indicating more consistency in Group C.
Unusual features: Group B has an outlier at 22,000 steps, which is far above the upper fence. No outliers appear in Groups A or C.
Context: Group B members tended to walk the most steps per day but had an exceptionally active outlier. Group C members walked the fewest steps but were the most consistent.

diagram.alt_text: Three horizontal box plots: Group A (3K-14K), Group B (5K-16K with outlier at 22K), Group C (2K-9K)
diagram.caption: Parallel box plots of daily step counts for three fitness groups with outlier in Group B

problems.question_html:
Elena scored 82 on her chemistry midterm (class mean = 75, SD = 8) and 78 on her biology midterm (class mean = 71, SD = 5).

(a) Calculate Elena's z-score for each exam.

(b) On which exam did Elena perform better relative to her classmates? Justify your answer.

(c) If a third student scored exactly at the mean on both exams, what would their z-scores be? Explain what this means in context.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Chemistry z-score: z = (82 - 75)/8 = 0.875. Biology z-score: z = (78 - 71)/5 = 1.4. (b) Elena performed better relative to her classmates on the biology exam because her z-score of 1.4 is higher than her chemistry z-score of 0.875. This means she was 1.4 standard deviations above the biology mean but only 0.875 standard deviations above the chemistry mean. (c) A student who scored exactly at the mean on both exams would have z-scores of 0 for both. This means their performance was exactly average compared to their classmates on each exam.

hints.text: Use \(z = \frac{x - \bar{x}}{s}\) for each exam separately. The higher z-score indicates better relative performance.
Chemistry: \(z = \frac{82 - 75}{8}\). Biology: \(z = \frac{78 - 71}{5}\). Compare these z-scores. For part (c), what happens when \(x = \bar{x}\)?

solution_steps.text: (b) Elena performed better relative to her classmates on the biology exam. Her biology z-score of 1.4 means she was 1.4 SDs above the mean, compared to only 0.875 SDs above the mean in chemistry.
(c) When \(x = \bar{x}\), the z-score is \(\frac{\bar{x} - \bar{x}}{s} = 0\). A z-score of 0 means the student performed exactly at the class average on both exams.

diagrams.alt_text: Two horizontal box plots stacked vertically: Class A centered around 72 with smaller spread, Class B centered around 68 with larger spread and an outlier at 95
diagrams.caption: Side-by-side horizontal box plots comparing test scores for Class A and Class B, showing differences in center and spread

concepts.title: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection
concepts.content_html:
Investigative Questions and Data Collection

Statistics begins with a question. A good statistical investigative question is one that anticipates variability in the data and can be answered by collecting and analyzing data.

Components of a Good Investigative Question

A well-formed investigative question should:

  • Anticipate variability in the data (not have a single definitive answer)
  • Be answerable with data that can be collected
  • Be clear about the population or group of interest
  • Specify the variable(s) being measured

Example of a good investigative question: "How much sleep do students at Lincoln High School typically get on school nights?" This anticipates variability (different students sleep different amounts) and specifies the population (Lincoln High students) and variable (hours of sleep).

Example of a poor question: "How much sleep did I get last night?" This has a single definitive answer and does not anticipate variability.

Census vs. Sample

A census collects data from every individual in the population. A sample collects data from a subset of the population.

  • A census is often impractical (too expensive, too time-consuming, or the population is too large).
  • A well-designed sample can give reliable information about a population.

Observational Studies vs. Experiments

An observational study observes individuals and measures variables of interest but does not attempt to influence the responses. The researcher simply records what naturally occurs.

An experiment deliberately imposes some treatment on individuals in order to observe their responses. The researcher actively intervenes.

Key Takeaway: Only a well-designed experiment can establish a cause-and-effect relationship. Observational studies can only show associations (correlations), not causation, because lurking variables may be responsible for the observed relationship.
Common Mistake: Students often claim that an observational study that finds a strong association "proves" causation. Remember: association is not causation. Only experiments with random assignment can support causal conclusions.
concepts.content_raw: The Investigative Question Revisited and Data Collection

problem_sets.title: Practice: Investigative Questions and Data Collection

problems.question_html: A researcher wants to determine whether a new fertilizer increases tomato plant yield. She randomly assigns 40 tomato plants to receive the new fertilizer and 40 plants to receive the standard fertilizer, then compares the yields. What type of study is this?

choices.text: Observational study, because she is observing plant growth
Experiment, because she randomly assigned treatments to subjects
Census, because she is studying all of her plants
Survey, because she is collecting data from each plant

hints.text: The key distinction: does the researcher impose a treatment or simply observe what happens naturally?
The researcher actively assigned different fertilizers to different groups of plants. This imposition of treatment makes it an experiment.

solution_steps.text: The researcher deliberately imposed a treatment (new fertilizer vs. standard fertilizer) on the plants.
She randomly assigned plants to treatment groups.
Because a treatment was imposed with random assignment, this is an experiment, not an observational study.

problems.question_html: A health magazine reports that people who eat breakfast daily have lower BMIs than those who skip breakfast. The magazine concludes that eating breakfast causes lower BMI. What is the problem with this conclusion?

choices.text: The sample size was too small
This is an observational study, so we cannot conclude causation; lurking variables may explain the association
BMI is not a valid measurement
They should have used a census instead of a sample

hints.text: Was this an experiment (with random assignment to eat or skip breakfast) or an observational study (people chose their own habits)?
Since people self-selected whether to eat breakfast, this is an observational study. There could be lurking variables (e.g., health-conscious people may both eat breakfast and exercise more).

solution_steps.text: This is an observational study because researchers observed people's existing habits rather than assigning them to eat or skip breakfast.
Observational studies can show associations but cannot establish cause-and-effect because lurking variables may be present.
For example, people who eat breakfast might also exercise more, eat healthier overall, or have other habits that contribute to lower BMI.

problems.question_html: Which of the following questions is a well-formed statistical investigative question?

choices.text: What is the capital of France?
How many hours per week do college students at State University work at part-time jobs?
What grade did you get on the last test?
Is 7 a prime number?

hints.text: A statistical investigative question must anticipate variability in the data and involve data collection from a group.
The question about college students anticipates that different students work different amounts—this is variability. The other options have single definitive answers.

solution_steps.text: A statistical investigative question anticipates variability, specifies a population, and requires data collection.

"How many hours per week do college students at State University work at part-time jobs?" specifies the population (State U students), the variable (hours worked), and anticipates variability (different students work different amounts).
The other options either have a single answer (capital of France, prime number) or ask about one individual (your grade).

problems.question_html: A study found that counties with more churches tend to have higher crime rates. A reporter writes: "Churches cause crime." Which of the following best explains why this conclusion is invalid?

choices.text: The data must be wrong because churches promote good behavior
Population size is a lurking variable: larger counties have both more churches and more crime
Crime causes churches, not the other way around
The sample size of counties was too small

hints.text: Think about what else might vary along with both the number of churches and the amount of crime.
Larger populations have more of everything: more churches, more crime, more grocery stores. Population is a lurking variable (confounding variable) that explains the association.

solution_steps.text: This is an observational study, so causation cannot be established.
Population size is a lurking variable: counties with more people naturally have both more churches and more crime.
The association between churches and crime is explained by the confounding variable of population size, not by any causal relationship.

problems.question_html: A medical researcher examines hospital records and finds that patients who took aspirin daily had fewer heart attacks than those who did not. No treatments were assigned. What type of study is this? (Two words)
problems.correct_answer: observational study||observational

hints.text: Did the researcher assign patients to take aspirin or simply look at what already happened?
The researcher examined existing records without imposing any treatment. This is called an __________ study.

solution_steps.text: The researcher looked at existing hospital records and did not assign any treatments.
Because no treatment was imposed and the researcher simply observed existing data, this is an observational study.

problems.question_html: A school district wants to know the average commute time for all 5,000 of its students. They collect data from every single student. What is this type of data collection called? (One word)
problems.correct_answer: census

hints.text: The district is collecting data from every student, not just a subset.
When you collect data from the entire population (all 5,000 students), it is called a __________.

solution_steps.text: The district collected data from every one of its 5,000 students, not a sample.
Collecting data from the entire population is called a census.

problems.question_html: A researcher wants to determine if listening to classical music improves test scores. She allows students to choose whether to listen to classical music or silence while studying. Students who chose music scored higher on average. Is this sufficient evidence that classical music improves test scores? Explain why the study design limits the conclusion. (One word: experiment or observational)
problems.correct_answer: observational

hints.text: Who decided whether students listened to music—the researcher or the students themselves?
Because students self-selected into groups, no treatment was imposed by the researcher. This makes it an __________ study.

solution_steps.text: Students chose whether to listen to music or not. The researcher did not randomly assign the treatment.
Because subjects self-selected into groups, this is an observational study.
Students who chose music might differ in other ways (e.g., more motivated, better study habits), creating confounding variables. Causal conclusions are not justified.

problems.question_html: A pharmaceutical company wants to test whether a new drug reduces blood pressure. Participants are randomly assigned to receive either the drug or a placebo. Neither the participants nor the researchers know who receives which. What type of data collection is this? (One word)
problems.correct_answer: experiment

hints.text: The company is imposing a treatment (drug vs. placebo) on the participants.
Random assignment of treatments makes this an __________. The double-blind design is a feature of the experiment that reduces bias.

solution_steps.text: The pharmaceutical company randomly assigned participants to treatment groups (drug or placebo).
Because a treatment was deliberately imposed with random assignment, this is an experiment.
The double-blind design (neither participants nor researchers know assignments) helps reduce placebo effect and researcher bias.

problems.question_html:
A local news station wants to know whether voters in the city support a new tax for school funding. Consider the following two approaches:

Approach 1: The station calls every registered voter in the city and asks their opinion.

Approach 2: The station randomly selects 500 registered voters and calls them.

(a) Identify the type of data collection for each approach.

(b) Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of Approach 1 compared to Approach 2.

(c) Is either approach an experiment? Explain.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Approach 1 is a census because it attempts to reach every registered voter. Approach 2 is a sample survey because it selects a subset of 500 voters. (b) Advantage of Approach 1: It would give exact results for the entire population if every voter responds. Disadvantage: It is much more expensive and time-consuming, and achieving a 100% response rate is nearly impossible, leading to nonresponse bias. (c) Neither approach is an experiment because no treatment is being imposed. Both are observational in nature—they simply ask voters about their existing opinions.

hints.text: For part (a), does each approach collect data from every individual or just a subset? For part (c), remember that experiments impose treatments.
Approach 1 contacts ALL voters (census). Approach 2 contacts 500 (sample). Neither approach assigns a treatment—they just ask opinions, so neither is an experiment.

solution_steps.text: (a) Approach 1 is a census because it attempts to contact every registered voter. Approach 2 is a sample survey because it selects 500 voters from the population.

(b) Advantage of census: no sampling variability—if all respond, you know the true population proportion. Disadvantage: impractical, expensive, and nonresponse bias is likely since not all voters will answer.
(c) Neither is an experiment. No treatment is imposed; both approaches simply measure existing opinions. They are forms of observational data collection.

problems.question_html:
A university researcher reads that students who participate in study groups earn higher GPAs than students who study alone. She wants to determine whether study groups actually cause higher GPAs.

(a) Explain why the existing data cannot establish causation.

(b) Design an experiment that could establish whether study groups cause higher GPAs. Include: subjects, treatments, random assignment, and response variable.

(c) Identify one potential ethical concern with your experiment.
problems.correct_answer: (a) The existing data comes from an observational study where students self-selected into study groups or solo study. Students who join study groups may differ systematically from those who study alone (e.g., they may be more motivated, more social, or taking easier courses). These lurking variables could explain the GPA difference. (b) Experiment design: Recruit 200 student volunteers (subjects). Randomly assign 100 to mandatory study groups (treatment) and 100 to study alone (control). The response variable is GPA at the end of the semester. Random assignment ensures that lurking variables are roughly balanced between groups, allowing causal conclusions. (c) An ethical concern is that students assigned to study alone might be disadvantaged if study groups truly help. This could affect their grades and academic standing.

hints.text: For part (a), think about why students who voluntarily join study groups might be different in other ways. For part (b), the key element that allows causal conclusions is random assignment.

Lurking variables (motivation, course difficulty) confound the observational result. For the experiment, randomly assign students to study group vs. solo study and compare GPAs. Consider whether it's ethical to potentially disadvantage the control group.

solution_steps.text: (a) The existing data is observational: students chose their own study methods. Lurking variables such as motivation, prior academic ability, and course selection may confound the relationship. We cannot conclude causation from an observational study.

(b) Experiment: Recruit student volunteers and randomly assign them to either a study group condition or a solo study condition. Measure GPA at the end of the semester. Random assignment balances lurking variables between groups, so any GPA difference can be attributed to the study method.
(c) Ethical concern: If study groups truly do improve GPAs, then students assigned to study alone are being disadvantaged. Informed consent and the ability to withdraw are important safeguards.

concepts.title: Random Sampling
concepts.content_html:
Random Sampling Methods

To make valid inferences about a population, we need a representative sample. The best way to achieve this is through random sampling—using chance to select individuals so that every member of the population has a known probability of being selected.

Why Randomness Matters

Without randomness, our sample may be biased—it may systematically favor certain outcomes over others. Random sampling:

  • Eliminates selection bias
  • Allows us to generalize results to the population
  • Provides a basis for calculating margins of error and conducting inference

Simple Random Sample (SRS)

A simple random sample (SRS) of size \(n\) is selected so that every possible group of \(n\) individuals has an equal chance of being chosen. This is the gold standard of sampling.

How to select an SRS:

  1. Assign a number to every member of the population (the sampling frame).
  2. Use a random number generator or table of random digits to select \(n\) numbers.
  3. The individuals corresponding to those numbers form the sample.

Stratified Random Sampling

In a stratified random sample, the population is divided into homogeneous subgroups called strata (e.g., by grade level, gender, or income bracket). Then an SRS is taken within each stratum.

Advantage: Reduces variability by ensuring all subgroups are represented. Gives more precise estimates than an SRS of the same total size.

Cluster Sampling

In cluster sampling, the population is divided into groups called clusters (e.g., classrooms, city blocks, households). A random sample of clusters is selected, and then every individual within the chosen clusters is surveyed (census within clusters).

Advantage: More practical and cost-effective when the population is geographically spread out. Disadvantage: Less precise than SRS or stratified sampling because individuals within clusters tend to be similar.

Systematic Sampling

In systematic sampling, you select every \(k\)th individual from a list after a random starting point. For example, to sample 100 from a list of 2,000, you would pick every 20th name after a randomly chosen start.

Advantage: Easy to implement. Works well when the list has no hidden pattern.

Sampling With and Without Replacement

With replacement: An individual can be selected more than once. Each selection is independent. Without replacement: Once selected, an individual cannot be chosen again. Most real-world surveys sample without replacement.

Key Takeaway: Stratified sampling divides the population into groups and samples within each. Cluster sampling divides into groups and samples entire groups. Don't confuse the two!
Common Mistake: Students confuse stratified and cluster sampling. Remember: Stratified = sample within each stratum. Cluster = sample entire clusters.
concepts.content_raw: Random Sampling

problem_sets.title: Practice: Random Sampling

problems.question_html: A school principal wants to survey students about the cafeteria. She divides students by grade (9th, 10th, 11th, 12th), then randomly selects 25 students from each grade. What sampling method is this?

choices.text: Simple random sample
Stratified random sample
Cluster sample
Systematic sample

hints.text: The population was divided into subgroups (strata), and then a random sample was taken from each subgroup.
Dividing into grades (strata) and taking an SRS within each stratum is stratified random sampling. In cluster sampling, you would randomly select entire grades and survey everyone in them.

solution_steps.text: The principal divided students into strata based on grade level.
She then took a random sample of 25 students within each stratum.
This is a stratified random sample. It ensures representation from every grade level.

problems.question_html: A quality control manager inspects every 50th item coming off an assembly line, starting from a randomly selected item among the first 50. What sampling method is this?

choices.text: Simple random sample
Cluster sample
Stratified random sample
Systematic sample

hints.text: The manager selects items at regular intervals from the production line.
Selecting every \(k\)th individual after a random starting point is called systematic sampling.

solution_steps.text: The manager randomly selects a starting point and then picks every 50th item.
Selecting at regular intervals (every \(k\)th) after a random start is systematic sampling.

problems.question_html: A polling organization wants to estimate voter support for a ballot measure. They randomly select 200 registered voters from the complete voter registration list. Every set of 200 voters has an equal chance of being selected. What type of sample is this?

choices.text: Convenience sample
Simple random sample
Stratified random sample
Voluntary response sample

hints.text: The key phrase is that every group of 200 has an equal chance of being selected.
When every possible sample of size \(n\) from the population has an equal chance of being selected, this is the definition of a simple random sample (SRS).

solution_steps.text: The definition states that every set of 200 voters has an equal chance of being selected.
This is precisely the definition of a simple random sample (SRS): every possible sample of size \(n\) has the same probability of being chosen.

problems.question_html: A national health survey divides the U.S. into 3,000 geographic areas. The researchers randomly select 200 of these areas and then interview every household in the selected areas. Which type of sampling is being used?

choices.text: Stratified random sampling
Systematic sampling
Cluster sampling
Simple random sampling

hints.text: Are the geographic areas being used as strata (sample within each) or clusters (select entire areas)?
The researchers randomly selected entire geographic areas and surveyed everyone in them. This is cluster sampling, not stratified (which would sample within each area).

solution_steps.text: The geographic areas serve as clusters—naturally occurring groups.
The researchers randomly selected 200 clusters and then conducted a census within each.
This is cluster sampling. It is practical for geographically spread populations because interviewers only need to travel to 200 areas rather than the entire country.

problems.question_html: A researcher has a list of 800 employees at a company and wants to select a simple random sample of 40. She assigns each employee a number from 001 to 800 and uses a random number generator. How many employees are in her sampling frame?

hints.text: The sampling frame is the list of all individuals from which the sample is drawn.
She numbered all employees from 001 to 800. The sampling frame includes every individual who could potentially be selected.

solution_steps.text: The sampling frame is the complete list of all individuals who could be selected for the sample.
Since she assigned numbers 001 to 800 to all employees, the sampling frame contains 800 employees.

problems.question_html: A city has 120 elementary schools. A researcher randomly selects 10 schools and surveys every student in each of those 10 schools. What sampling method is this? (One word, all lowercase)
problems.correct_answer: cluster

hints.text: The researcher selected entire groups (schools) at random, then surveyed everyone within the selected groups.
When you randomly select groups and do a census within each selected group, that is __________ sampling.

solution_steps.text: The schools serve as naturally occurring groups (clusters).
The researcher randomly selected 10 clusters (schools) and surveyed every student in those clusters.
This is cluster sampling.

problems.question_html: A company has 3,000 employees. A researcher wants a sample of 150. He assigns each employee a number from 0001 to 3000 and uses a random number table. What is the value of \(k\) if he were to instead use systematic sampling? (Enter a whole number)

hints.text: In systematic sampling, you select every \(k\)th individual, where \(k = \frac{\text{population size}}{\text{sample size}}\).
\(k = \frac{3000}{150} = 20\). The researcher would pick a random start between 1 and 20, then select every 20th employee.

solution_steps.text: For systematic sampling, \(k = \frac{N}{n} = \frac{3000}{150} = 20\).
The researcher would randomly select a starting number between 1 and 20, then select every 20th employee after that.

problems.question_html: A university researcher wants to compare study habits across class years. She divides the 20,000 students into four groups: freshmen (6,000), sophomores (5,000), juniors (5,000), and seniors (4,000). She selects a random sample of 60 freshmen, 50 sophomores, 50 juniors, and 40 seniors (proportional to group sizes). What type of sampling is this? (One word, all lowercase)
problems.correct_answer: stratified

hints.text: The researcher divided the population into subgroups and then randomly sampled from within each subgroup.
The class years serve as strata. Taking a random sample within each stratum is __________ sampling.

solution_steps.text: The population was divided into four strata based on class year.
A random sample was drawn from each stratum, with sample sizes proportional to stratum sizes.
This is stratified random sampling. It guarantees representation from each class year.

problems.question_html:
A researcher wants to study the reading habits of high school students in a large urban district with 50 high schools. Describe how the researcher could use each of the following sampling methods to select students:

(a) Simple random sample

(b) Stratified random sample (strata: grade levels 9–12)

(c) Cluster sample (clusters: schools)

For each method, explain one advantage and one disadvantage compared to the other methods.
problems.correct_answer: (a) SRS: Obtain a list of all students in the district, assign each a number, and use a random number generator to select the sample. Advantage: every student has an equal chance of being selected, minimizing selection bias. Disadvantage: requires a complete list of all students across all 50 schools, which may be hard to obtain, and selected students are scattered across many schools, making data collection costly. (b) Stratified: Divide all students into four strata by grade level (9, 10, 11, 12). Take an SRS from each stratum. Advantage: guarantees representation from each grade, reducing variability and allowing grade-level comparisons. Disadvantage: still requires a complete list and students may be spread across many schools. (c) Cluster: Randomly select a subset of schools (e.g., 10 of the 50). Survey all students (or a random sample of students) in the selected schools. Advantage: much more practical and cost-effective because data collectors only visit a few schools. Disadvantage: less precise because students within a school tend to be similar, and some schools may have unusual reading habits.

hints.text: For each method, think about: How do you select? What are the practical considerations? How representative is the result?

SRS = random from entire list (precise but impractical for 50 schools). Stratified by grade = ensures grade representation (more precise). Cluster by school = select whole schools (practical but less precise).

solution_steps.text: (a) SRS: List all students across all 50 schools, assign numbers, use a random number generator. Advantage: unbiased. Disadvantage: impractical with students spread across 50 buildings.

(b) Stratified by grade: Separate students into four grade-level strata, then SRS within each. Advantage: guarantees each grade is represented and allows grade comparisons. Disadvantage: still requires a district-wide student list.

(c) Cluster by school: Randomly select schools, survey all students in chosen schools. Advantage: practical—only visit a few schools. Disadvantage: less precise because students within a school may share similar habits.

problems.question_html:
A market research firm has a list of 10,000 customers. They want to survey 500 customers about satisfaction with a new product.

(a) Describe how to select a simple random sample of 500 customers.

(b) The firm suspects satisfaction differs by region (East, Central, West). Explain why stratified random sampling by region would be preferable to an SRS.

(c) Explain the difference between sampling with replacement and without replacement. Which is typically used in practice and why?
problems.correct_answer: (a) Assign each of the 10,000 customers a unique number from 00001 to 10000. Use a random number generator to produce 500 distinct numbers in that range. The customers with those numbers form the sample. (b) If satisfaction varies by region, stratifying by region ensures each region is represented proportionally. This reduces the variability of the estimate compared to an SRS, which might by chance over- or under-represent certain regions. Stratified sampling gives more precise estimates when the strata differ from each other on the variable of interest. (c) Sampling with replacement means a selected individual can be chosen again in subsequent draws; each draw is independent. Sampling without replacement means once an individual is selected, they cannot be chosen again. In practice, sampling without replacement is used because it is more efficient (you never waste a selection on a repeat) and it reduces variability. When the population is much larger than the sample, the difference is negligible.

hints.text: For part (a), describe the mechanics of selecting an SRS. For part (b), think about what happens if regions have different satisfaction levels. For part (c), consider whether it makes sense to survey the same person twice.
SRS: number customers, use RNG. Stratified is better when the variable of interest differs across strata. Without replacement is standard because duplicates waste effort.

solution_steps.text: (a) Number all 10,000 customers (00001–10000). Use a random number generator to select 500 unique numbers. Contact those customers.
(b) If satisfaction varies by region, an SRS might by chance under-represent a region. Stratifying by region guarantees proportional representation and reduces variability in the overall estimate.

(c) With replacement: individuals can be selected more than once. Without replacement: once selected, an individual is removed from the pool. Without replacement is standard because it avoids duplicate responses and is more efficient.

concepts.title: Potential Problems with Sampling
concepts.content_html:
Potential Problems with Sampling

Even with the best sampling method, problems can arise that introduce bias into our results. Bias is a systematic tendency to over- or underestimate the true population parameter. A biased sampling method consistently misses the target in the same direction.

Types of Bias

1. Voluntary Response Bias

A voluntary response sample consists of people who choose to respond to a general appeal (e.g., online polls, call-in surveys, product review sites). These samples are biased because people with strong opinions (especially negative ones) are more likely to respond.

Example: A TV station asks viewers to call in and vote on whether a new law is fair. People with strong feelings about the law are most likely to call, so the results do not represent the general population.

2. Undercoverage

Undercoverage occurs when some members of the population are left out of the sampling frame (the list from which the sample is drawn). If the excluded group differs from the rest of the population, the results will be biased.

Example: A telephone survey that only calls landlines undercounts young adults, who primarily use cell phones.

3. Nonresponse Bias

Nonresponse bias occurs when selected individuals cannot be contacted or refuse to participate. If nonrespondents differ systematically from respondents, the sample results are biased.

Example: A mailed survey about income may have low response rates among very wealthy and very poor individuals, biasing the results toward middle-income respondents.

4. Response Bias (Question Wording Bias)

Response bias occurs when respondents give inaccurate answers due to the way questions are worded, the order of questions, the presence of an interviewer, or the desire to give socially acceptable answers.

Example: Asking "Don't you agree that we should protect the environment?" leads respondents toward "yes" because of the leading phrasing.

Reducing Bias

  • Use random sampling to avoid selection bias
  • Ensure the sampling frame covers the entire population (reduces undercoverage)
  • Follow up with nonrespondents and keep surveys short (reduces nonresponse)
  • Use neutral, clearly worded questions (reduces response bias)
  • Use anonymous surveys for sensitive topics
Key Takeaway: Bias is about the method, not the result. A biased method will consistently miss the target in one direction, no matter how large the sample. Increasing sample size does not fix bias.
Common Mistake: Students often think a larger sample fixes bias. It does not. A biased method with 10,000 respondents is still biased. Only changing the method can fix bias.
concepts.content_raw: Potential Problems with Sampling

problem_sets.title: Practice: Problems with Sampling

problems.question_html: A website asks visitors to rate their experience on a scale of 1 to 5 stars. The average rating is 1.8 stars. The company concludes that most customers are dissatisfied. What type of bias most likely affects this conclusion?

choices.text: Undercoverage, because not all customers visit the website
Voluntary response bias, because people with strong negative opinions are more likely to leave reviews
Nonresponse bias, because some customers refused to answer
Response bias, because the rating scale is confusing

hints.text: Were customers randomly selected to rate the website, or did they choose to leave a review on their own?
People self-selected to leave reviews. Those with strong opinions (especially negative ones) are most likely to volunteer their feedback. This is voluntary response bias.

solution_steps.text: The website allowed anyone to voluntarily leave a review—no random sampling was used.
People with strong opinions (particularly negative) are much more likely to take the time to leave a review.
This creates voluntary response bias, which likely overestimates dissatisfaction.

problems.question_html: A researcher mails a survey about health habits to 2,000 randomly selected adults. Only 300 respond. The researcher reports the results as representative of all adults. What type of bias is most concerning?

choices.text: Response bias due to question wording
Nonresponse bias, because the 300 who responded may differ systematically from the 1,700 who did not
Undercoverage, because not everyone in the population was mailed a survey
Voluntary response bias, because people chose to respond

hints.text: The initial selection was random (good!), but only 15% responded. What if the people who responded are different from those who didn't?

When a large fraction of selected individuals fail to respond, and those who respond may be systematically different from nonrespondents, this is nonresponse bias. Note: this is NOT voluntary response bias because the initial sample was randomly selected.

solution_steps.text: The sample was randomly selected (no selection bias in the design), but only 300 of 2,000 responded (15% response rate).
The 300 respondents may be systematically different from the 1,700 nonrespondents (e.g., healthier people might be more willing to discuss health habits).
This is nonresponse bias. The results from the 300 respondents may not represent all adults.

problems.question_html: A large online retailer asks all customers who make a purchase to complete a satisfaction survey. Only 8% do so. The company reports that 94% of customers are satisfied. Which TWO types of bias are most likely present?

choices.text: Undercoverage and response bias
Voluntary response bias and nonresponse bias
Nonresponse bias and undercoverage
Response bias and undercoverage

hints.text: Think about two things: (1) customers self-select whether to take the survey, and (2) only 8% responded.
Customers with very positive or very negative experiences are more likely to respond (voluntary response). The 92% who did not respond may have different opinions (nonresponse bias).

solution_steps.text: Customers chose whether to complete the survey—this is voluntary response bias. Satisfied customers may be more motivated to share positive feedback.
Only 8% of customers responded. The 92% who didn't respond may have different satisfaction levels, creating nonresponse bias.
Both biases likely inflate the reported satisfaction rate of 94%.

problems.question_html: A school survey about drug use is administered by having a teacher read questions aloud in class and collect written responses with students' names on them. What type of bias is most likely to result?

choices.text: Undercoverage, because absent students are missed
Response bias, because students may underreport drug use on a non-anonymous survey
Nonresponse bias, because some students may leave questions blank
Voluntary response bias, because students chose to attend school

hints.text: The survey is about a sensitive topic (drug use) and responses are not anonymous. How might this affect honesty?
Students may lie or underreport drug use because their names are on the survey and a teacher is present. This desire to give socially acceptable answers creates response bias.

solution_steps.text: Drug use is a sensitive topic. Students are unlikely to honestly report illegal behavior when their names are attached to the survey.
The presence of a teacher reading questions aloud and collecting named responses strongly encourages socially desirable answers.
This creates response bias—students will systematically underreport drug use, leading to an underestimate.

problems.question_html: A survey asks: "Do you agree that the government wastes too much of your hard-earned tax money?" This question is most likely to produce what type of bias? (Two words, all lowercase)
problems.correct_answer: response bias

hints.text: The question uses loaded language ("hard-earned," "wastes") that pushes respondents toward a particular answer.
When the wording of a question influences how people respond, the resulting inaccuracy is called __________ __________.

solution_steps.text: The question uses emotionally charged language ("wastes," "hard-earned") that nudges respondents toward agreeing.
This leading phrasing causes respondents to give inaccurate answers that don't reflect their true opinions.
This is response bias (specifically, question wording bias).

problems.question_html: A polling company surveys voters by calling numbers from the local phone book. This method fails to include people with unlisted numbers, cell-phone-only households, and people who have moved. What type of bias does this represent? (One word, all lowercase)
problems.correct_answer: undercoverage

hints.text: Some members of the population have no chance of being selected because they are not in the phone book.
When the sampling frame does not include all members of the population, the missing groups are "undercovered." This bias is called __________.

solution_steps.text: The phone book does not include cell-phone-only households, unlisted numbers, or people who recently moved.
These groups have zero probability of being selected, so the sampling frame does not cover the entire population.
This is undercoverage. If the excluded groups differ from included groups on the variable of interest, the results will be biased.

problems.question_html: A city wants to estimate the average household income. They survey residents at a shopping mall on a Wednesday afternoon. Identify the type of bias this introduces. (One word, all lowercase)
problems.correct_answer: undercoverage

hints.text: Think about who is at a mall on a Wednesday afternoon and who is missing from this sample.

People at the mall on a weekday afternoon are not representative of all residents. Working adults, low-income residents without transportation, and others are excluded from the sampling frame. This is __________.

solution_steps.text: The sampling frame effectively includes only people who shop at a particular mall on a weekday afternoon.
This excludes working adults, people without transportation, people in other parts of the city, etc.
Since large segments of the population cannot be reached, this is undercoverage (also considered a convenience sample). The results will not represent the city.

problems.question_html: A magazine survey asks readers: "Should the city build a new sports stadium using taxpayer money?" and provides a phone number to call with responses. 78% of callers say no. The magazine claims the city opposes the stadium. Identify the specific type of bias. (Two words, all lowercase)
problems.correct_answer: voluntary response||voluntary response bias

hints.text: Respondents chose to call in—they were not randomly selected.
People with strong opinions (especially those opposed to spending tax money) are most likely to call in. This self-selection is called __________ __________ bias.

solution_steps.text: The survey relied on readers voluntarily calling in—no random sampling was used.
People who feel strongly about the issue (particularly those opposed to taxpayer-funded stadiums) are most likely to make the effort to call.
This is voluntary response bias. The 78% opposition likely overestimates the true level of opposition in the city.

problems.question_html:
A state health department wants to estimate the percentage of residents who have been vaccinated against the flu. They plan to conduct a telephone survey.

(a) Describe a potential source of undercoverage in this survey and explain the likely direction of bias.

(b) Describe a potential source of nonresponse bias and explain the likely direction of bias.

(c) A survey question reads: "Given the proven effectiveness of flu vaccines, have you been vaccinated this year?" Explain why this question may lead to response bias and suggest a better wording.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Undercoverage: A telephone survey may miss residents without phones (homeless individuals, some elderly, certain low-income groups). These groups may have lower vaccination rates, so the survey would likely overestimate the vaccination rate. (b) Nonresponse bias: People who are busy or suspicious of phone surveys may not answer. If unvaccinated individuals are less health-conscious and also less likely to answer health-related surveys, the survey would again overestimate the vaccination rate. (c) The phrase "proven effectiveness" is leading—it suggests the vaccine is effective and implies the respondent should have been vaccinated. This may lead people to falsely claim they were vaccinated (response bias, overestimating the rate). Better wording: "Have you received a flu vaccine this year? Yes or No."

hints.text: For each type of bias, think about (1) who is affected, (2) how they differ from the general population on the variable of interest (vaccination), and (3) whether this causes an overestimate or underestimate.

Undercoverage: people without phones tend to be lower-income/less access to healthcare. Nonresponse: health-conscious people may be more likely to respond. Response bias: the leading phrase pressures a "yes" answer.

solution_steps.text: (a) Undercoverage: Residents without phone access (homeless, some elderly, very low-income) are excluded. These groups likely have lower vaccination rates, so the survey overestimates vaccination.

(b) Nonresponse: People who don't answer phone calls may differ from those who do. If unvaccinated individuals are less engaged with health matters and less likely to participate, the survey overestimates vaccination.
(c) "Given the proven effectiveness" is leading language that pressures respondents toward saying yes. Better: "Have you received a flu vaccine this year?" with a simple Yes/No response.

problems.question_html:
A student claims: "Our school's online poll received 2,000 responses about the new dress code. With such a large sample, the results must accurately represent student opinion."

(a) Explain why the student's reasoning is flawed.

(b) Identify the type of bias most likely present and explain its effect.

(c) Describe how the school could collect less biased data about student opinion on the dress code.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Large sample size does not eliminate bias. Bias is a property of the sampling method, not the sample size. A voluntary response sample of 2,000 is still biased—it just gives you a very precise wrong answer. (b) Voluntary response bias is most likely present. Students with the strongest opinions about the dress code (especially those who dislike it) are more likely to take the time to respond to an online poll. This probably overestimates opposition to the dress code. (c) The school should use random sampling: obtain a list of all students, assign numbers, and randomly select a sample of students to survey. This ensures every student has an equal chance of being selected and eliminates the self-selection problem.

hints.text: Does increasing sample size fix bias, or does it only reduce random sampling variability?

Bias \(
eq\) variability. A large biased sample gives a precise but inaccurate result. The online poll is a voluntary response sample. To fix it, use random selection.

solution_steps.text: (a) Sample size reduces variability (random error), not bias (systematic error). A biased method produces biased results regardless of how many people respond.
(b) The online poll is a voluntary response sample. Students with strong opinions, especially negative ones, are overrepresented. This likely exaggerates opposition to the dress code.
(c) Use random sampling: get a complete student list, randomly select a sample, and survey those students (with follow-ups to reduce nonresponse). This removes voluntary response bias.

concepts.title: Experimental Design
concepts.content_html:
Experimental Design

An experiment deliberately imposes treatments on experimental units to observe the effect on a response variable. Well-designed experiments allow researchers to establish cause-and-effect relationships.

Key Vocabulary

  • Experimental units: the individuals (people, animals, plots of land, etc.) on which the experiment is performed. When the units are people, they are called subjects.
  • Treatment: a specific condition applied to the experimental units. In a drug study, the treatments might be "Drug A" and "Placebo."
  • Response variable: the outcome measured on each unit after treatment is applied.
  • Explanatory variable (factor): the variable whose effect is being studied. Different values of the factor define the treatments.

Principles of Experimental Design

  1. Comparison: Compare the results of at least two treatments (or one treatment and a control). Without comparison, you cannot tell if the treatment had an effect.
  2. Random assignment: Assign experimental units to treatment groups at random. This balances lurking variables across groups so that any difference in outcomes can be attributed to the treatment.
  3. Replication: Use enough experimental units in each group to reduce the effects of chance variation. Replication does not mean repeating the experiment—it means having multiple units per treatment group.
  4. Direct control: Keep all other variables (besides the treatment) as similar as possible across groups (e.g., same environment, same time period).

Control Group and Placebo

A control group receives no treatment or a standard treatment for comparison. A placebo is a dummy treatment (e.g., a sugar pill) that has no therapeutic effect. Placebos control for the placebo effect—the tendency for people to improve simply because they believe they are receiving treatment.

Blinding

  • Single-blind: Either the subjects or the evaluators (but not both) do not know which treatment is being received.
  • Double-blind: Neither the subjects nor the evaluators know which treatment each subject receives. This prevents both the placebo effect and evaluator bias.

Confounding Variables

A confounding variable is a variable that is associated with both the explanatory variable and the response variable, making it impossible to determine which one is causing the observed effect. Random assignment helps reduce confounding.

Example: If all women receive Drug A and all men receive Drug B, gender is confounded with the drug. Any difference in outcomes could be due to the drug or to gender.

Blocking

Blocking is grouping experimental units that are similar in some way (the blocking variable) before random assignment. Within each block, units are randomly assigned to treatments. Blocking reduces variability and makes the experiment more sensitive to treatment differences.

Example: In an agricultural experiment testing fertilizers, you might block by field location (sunny vs. shady) because sunlight affects plant growth. Within each block, plots are randomly assigned to fertilizer treatments.

Matched Pairs Design

A matched pairs design is a special case of blocking with blocks of size 2. Each pair consists of two similar units (or the same unit measured twice).

  • Two matched subjects: Pair subjects by a key characteristic, then randomly assign one to treatment and one to control.
  • Same subject, two conditions: Each subject serves as their own control, receiving both treatments in random order.
Key Takeaway: The three essential features of a well-designed experiment are comparison, random assignment, and replication. Blocking is an additional technique that reduces variability but is not required for every experiment.
Common Mistake: Students confuse "replication" (using many units per group) with "repeating the experiment." On the AP exam, replication means having enough subjects in each treatment group, not running the whole experiment again.
concepts.content_raw: Experimental Design

problem_sets.title: Practice: Experimental Design

problems.question_html: A pharmaceutical company tests a new headache medication. They randomly assign 200 participants to receive either the new drug or a placebo. Neither the participants nor the doctors evaluating the results know who received which treatment. This is an example of a:

choices.text: Single-blind experiment
Double-blind experiment
Matched pairs design
Observational study

hints.text: How many groups are "blind" to the treatment assignments?
When both the subjects AND the evaluators are unaware of treatment assignments, the experiment is double-blind.

solution_steps.text: The participants do not know whether they received the drug or placebo (blind subjects).
The doctors evaluating the results also do not know who received which treatment (blind evaluators).
Since both groups are blinded, this is a double-blind experiment. This controls for both the placebo effect and evaluator bias.

problems.question_html: An agricultural researcher wants to test three different fertilizers on crop yield. She has 30 plots of land and randomly assigns 10 plots to each fertilizer. What are the experimental units in this experiment?

choices.text: The three fertilizers
The crop yields
The 30 plots of land
The researcher

hints.text: Experimental units are the individuals or objects to which the treatments are applied.
The fertilizer (treatment) is applied to the plots of land. The plots are the experimental units. Crop yield is the response variable.

solution_steps.text: Experimental units are the smallest entities to which a treatment is applied.
The fertilizers (treatments) are applied to the plots of land.
Therefore, the 30 plots of land are the experimental units. The fertilizers are the treatments, and crop yield is the response variable.

problems.question_html: A study is designed to test whether a new running shoe reduces injury rates in marathon runners. Researchers recruit 100 runners and block by weekly mileage (high vs. low). Within each block, runners are randomly assigned to wear the new shoe or a standard shoe. Which of the following best explains the purpose of blocking by weekly mileage?

choices.text: To ensure that high-mileage runners are in the treatment group
To eliminate mileage as a variable in the experiment
To reduce variability due to mileage differences and make it easier to detect a shoe effect
To increase the sample size of the experiment

hints.text: Blocking groups similar experimental units together. Why is this helpful?

High-mileage runners are more injury-prone regardless of shoe type. Blocking ensures each shoe group has a similar mix of mileage levels, reducing the "noise" from this variable and making the shoe effect easier to detect.

solution_steps.text: Weekly mileage affects injury risk: high-mileage runners are more injury-prone. This is a source of variability.
By blocking, we ensure each treatment group has a similar proportion of high- and low-mileage runners.
This reduces the variability within groups, making it easier to detect a genuine difference due to the shoe type.

problems.question_html: In a matched pairs design, a sleep researcher wants to test whether a white noise machine improves sleep quality. Each of 20 participants sleeps one week with the machine and one week without, in random order. Why is the order randomized?

choices.text: To increase the sample size
To control for order effects, so that going first or second does not confound the results
To ensure the study is double-blind
To create a control group

hints.text: What if everyone used the white noise machine in Week 1 and no machine in Week 2? What other factors might differ between the two weeks?

If all subjects used the machine first, any improvement could be due to novelty, learning effects, or seasonal changes rather than the machine. Randomizing the order eliminates order as a confounding variable.

solution_steps.text: In this matched pairs design, each subject experiences both conditions (machine and no machine).
If the order were the same for everyone, order effects (fatigue, novelty, seasonal changes) would be confounded with the treatment.
Randomizing the order ensures that order effects are balanced, so any observed difference can be attributed to the white noise machine.

problems.question_html: In a well-designed experiment, what is the primary purpose of random assignment?
problems.correct_answer: balance lurking variables||reduce confounding||control for confounding variables||balance confounding variables

hints.text: Random assignment does not eliminate lurking variables, but it does something important to them across groups.
Random assignment tends to distribute lurking variables evenly across treatment groups, so they cannot confound the results.

solution_steps.text: Random assignment ensures that lurking variables are roughly balanced across treatment groups.
This means any difference in the response variable can be attributed to the treatment rather than to a confounding variable.
The primary purpose is to balance lurking variables (reduce confounding) so that causal conclusions are valid.

problems.question_html: A researcher tests whether a new teaching method improves test scores. She uses her morning class (30 students) for the new method and her afternoon class (28 students) as the control. Identify the confounding variable in this design. (One word)
problems.correct_answer: time||class time||time of day

hints.text: What differs between the two groups besides the teaching method?
One class meets in the morning and the other in the afternoon. Time of day is confounded with the teaching method—any difference in scores could be due to when class meets rather than the method.

solution_steps.text: The morning class received the new method and the afternoon class was the control.

Time of day is confounded with the treatment. Students may perform differently at different times (alertness, fatigue), so any difference in scores could be due to time rather than the teaching method.
To fix this, the researcher should randomly assign individual students to treatment or control, regardless of class period.

problems.question_html: A clinical trial tests a new cholesterol medication. 150 volunteers are randomly assigned to three groups: Drug A, Drug B, and placebo. After 12 weeks, cholesterol levels are measured. How many treatments are in this experiment?

hints.text: A treatment is each specific condition applied to subjects. Count all distinct conditions, including the placebo.
The three treatments are: Drug A, Drug B, and placebo. The placebo counts as a treatment in the experimental design.

solution_steps.text: The three distinct conditions applied to subjects are Drug A, Drug B, and placebo.
In experimental design, the placebo is considered a treatment (the "control treatment").
There are 3 treatments in this experiment.

problems.question_html: A researcher wants to study the effect of background music on reading comprehension. She has 60 participants and plans to test three conditions: silence, classical music, and pop music. She knows that reading ability varies widely, so she first gives a reading pretest and classifies participants as high, medium, or low readers. Within each reading level, she randomly assigns equal numbers to the three music conditions. Name this experimental design technique. (One word, all lowercase)
problems.correct_answer: blocking

hints.text: The researcher grouped similar participants together before randomly assigning treatments within each group.
Grouping experimental units by a known source of variability (reading level) before random assignment is called __________.

solution_steps.text: The researcher identified reading ability as a source of variability that could mask the effect of music.
She grouped participants into blocks (high, medium, low readers) before randomly assigning treatments within each block.
This technique is called blocking. It reduces variability and makes it easier to detect the effect of background music.

problems.question_html:
A consumer products company wants to test whether a new laundry detergent removes stains better than the current formula. They have 60 identical white T-shirts.

(a) Identify the experimental units, treatments, and response variable.

(b) Describe a completely randomized design for this experiment.

(c) Explain why the company should use a control group and what that control group should receive.

(d) The company suspects that stain type matters (grass vs. grease vs. wine). Explain how they could use blocking to improve the experiment.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Experimental units: 60 white T-shirts. Treatments: new detergent and current detergent. Response variable: a measure of stain removal (e.g., stain remaining score rated by evaluators, or whiteness measured by a colorimeter). (b) Completely randomized design: Apply identical stains to all 60 shirts. Randomly assign 30 shirts to the new detergent and 30 to the current detergent. Wash all shirts under identical conditions (same water temperature, same cycle length). Measure stain removal for each shirt and compare the two groups. (c) The current detergent serves as the control group. Without comparison, the company cannot determine whether the new detergent is better. The control group receives the current detergent rather than no detergent, because the company wants to know if the new formula is an improvement over the existing product. (d) Blocking by stain type: Apply 20 grass stains, 20 grease stains, and 20 wine stains (one per shirt). Within each stain type block, randomly assign 10 shirts to the new detergent and 10 to the current detergent. This ensures each detergent is tested equally on each stain type and reduces the variability caused by differences in stain difficulty.

hints.text: For part (a), identify what receives the treatment, what the treatments are, and what is measured. For blocking, think about how stain type could confound the results if not controlled.
Units = shirts, treatments = new vs. current detergent, response = stain removal measure. For blocking: create blocks by stain type, randomly assign within each block.

solution_steps.text: (a) Experimental units: the 60 T-shirts. Treatments: new detergent vs. current detergent. Response variable: degree of stain removal (measured objectively).
(b) CRD: Stain all 60 shirts identically, randomly assign 30 to each detergent, wash under identical conditions, measure and compare stain removal.
(c) The control group receives the current detergent. This provides a baseline for comparison. Without it, we cannot determine whether the new detergent is better.

(d) Block by stain type: Create three blocks (grass, grease, wine) of 20 shirts each. Within each block, randomly assign 10 shirts to each detergent. This controls for stain difficulty and reduces variability.

problems.question_html:
A psychologist designs an experiment to test whether caffeine affects reaction time. She recruits 40 volunteers.

(a) Describe a completely randomized design for this experiment. Be specific about treatments, random assignment, and what is measured.

(b) Explain why a matched pairs design might be preferable. Describe how the psychologist could implement it.

(c) Identify one potential confounding variable in the completely randomized design and explain how the matched pairs design helps control for it.
problems.correct_answer: (a) CRD: Randomly assign 20 volunteers to receive caffeine (e.g., 200 mg caffeine pill) and 20 to receive a placebo (identical-looking pill with no caffeine). After a set time (e.g., 30 minutes), measure each volunteer's reaction time on a standardized test. Compare the mean reaction times of the two groups. (b) Matched pairs is preferable because reaction times vary greatly from person to person. In a matched pairs design, each volunteer serves as their own control: each person takes the caffeine on one day and the placebo on another day (order randomized). The difference in reaction time for each person is calculated, removing person-to-person variability. (c) In the CRD, baseline reaction time is a confounding variable—the caffeine group might by chance contain more naturally fast or slow reactors. The matched pairs design controls for this because each person is compared to themselves, eliminating individual differences as a source of variability.

hints.text: For the CRD, randomly assign subjects to two groups. For matched pairs, think about using each person as their own control. What advantage does this give?

CRD: random assignment to caffeine vs. placebo, measure reaction time. Matched pairs: each person receives both treatments in random order. This eliminates person-to-person variability in reaction time.

solution_steps.text: (a) CRD: Randomly assign 20 subjects to caffeine and 20 to placebo. After a waiting period, measure reaction time. Compare group means.

(b) Matched pairs: Each of the 40 volunteers participates twice—once with caffeine and once with placebo, in random order with a washout period. Calculate the difference in reaction time for each person.

(c) Confounding variable: individual differences in baseline reaction time. In the CRD, one group might have naturally faster reactors. Matched pairs eliminates this because each person serves as their own control.

concepts.title: Tabular and Graphical Representations for Two Categorical Variables
concepts.content_html:
Two-Way Tables and Graphical Displays for Two Categorical Variables

When we have data on two categorical variables measured on the same individuals, we organize the data in a two-way table (also called a contingency table). One variable defines the rows and the other defines the columns. Each cell contains the count (frequency) of individuals who fall into that combination of categories.

Anatomy of a Two-Way Table

Consider a survey of 400 high school students classified by grade level (Sophomore, Junior, Senior) and preferred social media platform (Instagram, TikTok, YouTube).

InstagramTikTokYouTubeTotal
Sophomore456035140
Junior504040130
Senior553045130
Total150130120400

The row variable is grade level and the column variable is preferred platform. The numbers along the right edge and bottom edge are called marginal totals (or marginal frequencies) because they appear in the margins of the table.

Graphical Displays

Side-by-side bar charts display bars for each category of one variable grouped by the categories of the other variable. They make it easy to compare raw counts or percentages across groups.

Segmented (stacked) bar charts stack the categories of one variable within a single bar for each category of the other variable. When the bars are scaled to 100%, they show the conditional distribution within each group and are ideal for comparing proportions.

Mosaic plots are like segmented bar charts, but the width of each bar is proportional to the number of individuals in that category. This means both the height and width carry information, giving a complete picture of counts and proportions simultaneously.

Key Idea: A segmented bar chart scaled to 100% is the best graphical tool for comparing conditional distributions across groups. If all the segments have roughly the same proportions, there is no association between the variables.
AP Exam Tip: When asked to "describe the association" between two categorical variables using a graph, always compare proportions (not counts) and state the direction: e.g., "Seniors had a higher proportion choosing Instagram than Sophomores did." Saying "Seniors chose Instagram more" without referencing proportions can lose points.
