problem_sets.title: Practice: Two-Way Tables and Displays

problems.question_html: A school surveyed 300 students about their favorite lunch option (Pizza, Salad, Sandwich) and recorded their grade level (9th, 10th, 11th, 12th). The results are displayed in a two-way table. What do the marginal totals in this table represent?

choices.text: The count of students in each cell of the table
The total count for each row or each column, shown at the edges of the table
The proportion of students who chose each lunch option
The average number of students per grade level

hints.text: Marginal totals get their name from where they appear in the table — think about the word "margin."
Marginal totals are the row totals and column totals that appear in the margins (edges) of the two-way table. They give the overall distribution of each individual variable.

solution_steps.text: In a two-way table, each cell contains the count for a specific combination of the two variables.

The marginal totals are the sums along each row and each column, written in the margins of the table. They represent the total count for each category of a single variable, ignoring the other variable.

problems.question_html: A researcher creates a 100%-segmented bar chart comparing exercise habits (Never, Sometimes, Regularly) across three age groups (18–29, 30–49, 50+). In the 18–29 group, the "Regularly" segment takes up 45% of the bar, while in the 50+ group it takes up 20%. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: More 18–29 year-olds exercise regularly than 50+ year-olds.
A higher proportion of 18–29 year-olds exercise regularly compared to 50+ year-olds.
The 18–29 group has more people than the 50+ group.
Exercise is the cause of age differences in the sample.

hints.text: A 100%-segmented bar chart shows proportions within each group, not raw counts. Can you compare counts from percentages alone?
Because the chart shows conditional percentages, we can only compare proportions, not raw counts. We cannot say more people exercise — only that a higher proportion does.

solution_steps.text: A 100%-segmented bar chart scales each bar to 100%, so the segments represent the conditional distribution (proportions) within each group.

45% of the 18–29 group exercises regularly versus 20% of the 50+ group. This tells us the proportion is higher, but since we do not know the group sizes, we cannot compare raw counts. The correct interpretation is about proportions.

problems.question_html:
A hospital tracked 600 patients by treatment type (Surgery, Medication, Physical Therapy) and recovery outcome (Full Recovery, Partial Recovery, No Improvement). The two-way table is shown below.

FullPartialNoneTotal
Surgery1106030200
Medication908050220
Physical Therapy707535180
Total270215115600

Which treatment group had the highest proportion of patients with a full recovery?

choices.text: Surgery, because 110 is the largest count in the Full Recovery column
Surgery, because \( 110/200 = 0.55 \) is the highest proportion of full recovery among the three groups
Medication, because it has the most total patients (220)
Physical Therapy, because \( 70/180 \approx 0.389 \) is the smallest group and therefore proportionally larger

hints.text: To compare groups fairly, compute the proportion of full recovery within each treatment group by dividing the Full Recovery count by the row total.
Surgery: \( 110/200 = 0.55 \). Medication: \( 90/220 \approx 0.409 \). Physical Therapy: \( 70/180 \approx 0.389 \). Surgery has the highest proportion.

solution_steps.text: Compute the conditional proportion of full recovery for each group: Surgery: \( 110/200 = 0.55 \), Medication: \( 90/220 \approx 0.409 \), Physical Therapy: \( 70/180 \approx 0.389 \).
Surgery has the highest proportion (0.55) of patients with a full recovery. Note: we compare proportions, not raw counts, to account for differing group sizes.

problems.question_html: When comparing the distributions of a categorical variable across groups, which type of graph is most appropriate for determining whether there is an association between the two categorical variables?

choices.text: A side-by-side bar chart of counts
A pie chart for each group
A 100%-segmented bar chart (or mosaic plot)
A histogram of frequencies

hints.text: Association between two categorical variables means the conditional distributions differ across groups. Which chart type directly shows conditional distributions?

A 100%-segmented bar chart scales each bar to the same height and shows the conditional distribution within each group. If the segment proportions differ noticeably across bars, there is evidence of association.

solution_steps.text: To detect association, we compare conditional distributions. A 100%-segmented bar chart makes this comparison visual: each bar shows the proportion breakdown within one group.

If the colored segments are roughly the same across all bars, there is no association. If they differ, there is an association. A mosaic plot serves the same purpose with added information about group sizes.

problems.question_html: A two-way table shows the results of a survey of 500 adults classified by region (East, West) and pet ownership (Dog, Cat, None). The East row has a total of 280 and the West row has a total of 220. The grand total is 500. How many rows and columns of data (excluding totals) does this table have?
problems.correct_answer: 2 rows and 3 columns||2 by 3||2x3

hints.text: Count the categories for each variable. The row variable (region) has how many categories? The column variable (pet ownership) has how many?
Region has 2 categories (East, West) → 2 rows. Pet ownership has 3 categories (Dog, Cat, None) → 3 columns. So the data portion is 2 rows and 3 columns.

solution_steps.text: The row variable is region with categories East and West, giving 2 rows of data.
The column variable is pet ownership with categories Dog, Cat, and None, giving 3 columns of data. The table is 2 × 3 (excluding totals).

problems.question_html: In a mosaic plot, the width of each vertical bar is proportional to what quantity?
problems.correct_answer: the number of individuals in that category||the count||the proportion||the frequency

hints.text: A mosaic plot differs from a standard segmented bar chart because the bars are not all the same width. What does a wider bar tell you?
In a mosaic plot, the width of each bar is proportional to the number (or proportion) of individuals in that column category. A wider bar means more individuals.

solution_steps.text: In a standard segmented bar chart, all bars have equal width. A mosaic plot adds information by varying the width.
The width of each bar in a mosaic plot is proportional to the count (or proportion) of individuals in that category of the variable displayed on the horizontal axis.

problems.question_html: A survey of 800 adults records gender (Male, Female) and voting preference (Candidate A, Candidate B, Undecided). The two-way table shows that 180 males prefer Candidate A, 120 males prefer Candidate B, and 100 males are Undecided. The total number of males surveyed is ________.

hints.text: The marginal total for males is the sum of all column entries in the Male row.
\( 180 + 120 + 100 = 400 \). The marginal total for the Male row is 400.

solution_steps.text: The Male row contains counts for each voting preference: Candidate A = 180, Candidate B = 120, Undecided = 100.
The marginal total for males is \( 180 + 120 + 100 = 400 \).

problems.question_html: A market researcher creates a side-by-side bar chart comparing smartphone brand preference (Apple, Samsung, Other) for three age groups (18–25, 26–40, 41+). The 18–25 group has 500 respondents and the 41+ group has 200. The chart shows that the bar for "Apple" in the 18–25 group is much taller than the bar for "Apple" in the 41+ group. A colleague concludes that a higher proportion of 18–25 year-olds prefer Apple. Explain why this conclusion may be incorrect based on the chart type used.
problems.correct_answer: side-by-side bar charts show counts not proportions||the bar heights show counts so a taller bar does not necessarily mean a higher proportion||different group sizes

hints.text: Think about what the heights of bars represent in a side-by-side bar chart. Are they showing counts or proportions?

A side-by-side bar chart typically displays counts (frequencies). Because the 18–25 group has 500 people and the 41+ group has only 200, a taller bar for Apple in the younger group could simply reflect more people overall, not a higher proportion.

solution_steps.text: Side-by-side bar charts display raw counts, not proportions. The height of each bar shows how many individuals selected that option.

Since the 18–25 group (500 people) is much larger than the 41+ group (200 people), the Apple bar could be taller simply because there are more people in the group. To compare proportions, we would need a 100%-segmented bar chart or compute conditional percentages.

problems.question_html:
A public health department collects data on smoking status (Smoker, Non-Smoker) and flu vaccination (Vaccinated, Not Vaccinated) for 1,000 adults. The two-way table is shown below.

VaccinatedNot VaccinatedTotal
Smoker80170250
Non-Smoker420330750
Total5005001000

(a) Calculate the proportion of smokers who are vaccinated and the proportion of non-smokers who are vaccinated.

(b) Based on these conditional proportions, is there evidence of an association between smoking status and vaccination status? Explain.

(c) Describe what a 100%-segmented bar chart of this data would look like and what it would reveal.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Proportion of smokers vaccinated = 80/250 = 0.32. Proportion of non-smokers vaccinated = 420/750 = 0.56. (b) Yes, there is evidence of association. The conditional proportion of being vaccinated differs between smokers (0.32) and non-smokers (0.56). Since these proportions are not approximately equal, vaccination status and smoking status appear to be associated. (c) The segmented bar chart would have two bars (one for Smoker, one for Non-Smoker), each scaled to 100%. The Smoker bar would show 32% Vaccinated and 68% Not Vaccinated. The Non-Smoker bar would show 56% Vaccinated and 44% Not Vaccinated. Because the segments differ in size across the two bars, the chart visually confirms an association.

hints.text: For part (a), compute conditional proportions by dividing the Vaccinated count in each row by that row's total. For part (b), if the proportions are different, it suggests association.

Smokers vaccinated: \( 80/250 = 0.32 \). Non-smokers vaccinated: \( 420/750 = 0.56 \). These differ substantially, indicating association. A 100%-segmented bar chart would show unequal segment proportions across bars.

solution_steps.text: Part (a): Conditional proportion of smokers vaccinated: \( 80/250 = 0.32 \). Conditional proportion of non-smokers vaccinated: \( 420/750 = 0.56 \).

Part (b): Since 0.32 \(
eq\) 0.56, the conditional distributions of vaccination status differ between smokers and non-smokers. This indicates an association between smoking status and vaccination status.

Part (c): A 100%-segmented bar chart would have two bars of equal height (100%). The Smoker bar would be 32% Vaccinated / 68% Not Vaccinated. The Non-Smoker bar would be 56% Vaccinated / 44% Not Vaccinated. The unequal segment sizes across the bars visually confirm the association.

problems.question_html:
A college admissions office tracks applicant data by intended major (STEM, Humanities, Business) and admission decision (Accepted, Waitlisted, Denied). The two-way table is below.

AcceptedWaitlistedDeniedTotal
STEM3001505501000
Humanities200100200500
Business250100400750
Total75035011502250

(a) Construct a side-by-side comparison of acceptance rates for each major. Which major has the highest acceptance rate?

(b) A mosaic plot is created with intended major on the horizontal axis and admission decision as the fill color. Describe what the widths of the three bars would look like and explain what they communicate.

(c) Explain why comparing raw acceptance counts (300, 200, 250) would be misleading when evaluating which major is "easiest" to get into.
problems.correct_answer: (a) STEM acceptance rate: 300/1000 = 0.30 (30%). Humanities: 200/500 = 0.40 (40%). Business: 250/750 = 0.333 (33.3%). Humanities has the highest acceptance rate. (b) The widths would be proportional to each major's total applicants: STEM would be the widest (1000/2250 ≈ 44.4%), Business medium (750/2250 ≈ 33.3%), and Humanities the narrowest (500/2250 ≈ 22.2%). The widths communicate the relative number of applicants in each major. (c) STEM has the highest raw count of acceptances (300) but the lowest acceptance rate (30%) because it also has the most applicants (1000). Comparing raw counts ignores the different group sizes and would incorrectly suggest STEM is easier to get into. Proportions must be compared instead.

hints.text: For part (a), divide the Accepted count by the Total for each major. For parts (b) and (c), remember that group sizes differ.

STEM: \( 300/1000 = 0.30 \), Humanities: \( 200/500 = 0.40 \), Business: \( 250/750 \approx 0.333 \). Humanities has the highest acceptance rate. In a mosaic plot, bar widths are proportional to group sizes.

solution_steps.text: Part (a): Acceptance rates — STEM: \( 300/1000 = 0.30 \), Humanities: \( 200/500 = 0.40 \), Business: \( 250/750 \approx 0.333 \). Humanities has the highest acceptance rate at 40%.

Part (b): In the mosaic plot, the bar widths are proportional to total applicants. STEM's bar is widest (1000 applicants), then Business (750), then Humanities (500). This shows that STEM attracts the most applicants.

Part (c): Raw counts are misleading because groups have different sizes. STEM has 300 acceptances but 1000 applicants (30% rate), while Humanities has only 200 acceptances but 500 applicants (40% rate). Comparing proportions gives the fair picture.

concepts.title: Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables
concepts.content_html:
Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables

Once data are organized in a two-way table, we summarize the relationship between two categorical variables using three types of relative frequencies.

Joint Relative Frequency

A joint relative frequency is the proportion of all individuals that fall into a specific combination of categories. It is calculated by dividing a cell count by the grand total.

\[ \text{Joint relative frequency} = \frac{\text{cell count}}{\text{grand total}} \]

For example, if 60 out of 400 surveyed students are Juniors who prefer TikTok, the joint relative frequency is \( 60/400 = 0.15 \), or 15%.

Marginal Relative Frequency

A marginal relative frequency is the proportion of all individuals that fall into a single category of one variable, regardless of the other variable. It uses a marginal total divided by the grand total.

\[ \text{Marginal relative frequency} = \frac{\text{row (or column) total}}{\text{grand total}} \]

If 130 out of 400 students are Juniors, the marginal relative frequency for Juniors is \( 130/400 = 0.325 \).

Conditional Relative Frequency

A conditional relative frequency gives the proportion of individuals in one category given that they are already in a specific category of the other variable. It divides a cell count by the relevant row total or column total.

\[ \text{Conditional relative frequency} = \frac{\text{cell count}}{\text{row total (or column total)}} \]

Among the 130 Juniors, if 40 prefer TikTok, the conditional relative frequency of TikTok given Junior is \( 40/130 \approx 0.308 \).

Association Between Variables

Two categorical variables are associated if the conditional distributions of one variable differ across categories of the other. If they are approximately the same, the variables are not associated (independent).

Key Idea: Joint = cell ÷ grand total. Marginal = row or column total ÷ grand total. Conditional = cell ÷ row total (or column total). Know which denominator to use!
AP Exam Tip: The most common mistake is confusing joint and conditional relative frequencies. If the question says "given that" or "among," you need a conditional relative frequency — divide by the row or column total, not the grand total.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Summary Statistics for Two Categorical Variables

problems.question_html: A survey of 500 college students recorded their year (Freshman, Sophomore, Junior, Senior) and whether they work a part-time job (Yes, No). The cell for "Sophomore and Yes" contains 65 students. What is the joint relative frequency of being a Sophomore who works part-time?

choices.text: \( 65/125 = 0.52 \), where 125 is the Sophomore row total
\( 65/210 = 0.31 \), where 210 is the Yes column total
\( 125/500 = 0.25 \), where 125 is the Sophomore row total

hints.text: Joint relative frequency always uses the grand total as the denominator. What is the grand total?
Joint relative frequency = cell count ÷ grand total = \( 65/500 = 0.13 \). The other answer choices use row or column totals, which would give conditional or marginal frequencies.

solution_steps.text: The joint relative frequency uses the cell count divided by the grand total.
Joint relative frequency = \( 65/500 = 0.13 \), or 13%. This means 13% of all surveyed students are Sophomores who work part-time.

problems.question_html: In a two-way table of 800 employees classified by department (Sales, Engineering, HR) and commute type (Car, Public Transit, Bike), the Engineering row total is 320. What is the marginal relative frequency of Engineering?

choices.text: It cannot be calculated without knowing the cell counts

hints.text: Marginal relative frequency uses the row total (or column total) divided by the grand total.
Marginal relative frequency of Engineering = row total ÷ grand total = \( 320/800 = 0.40 \). This means 40% of all employees are in Engineering.

solution_steps.text: Marginal relative frequency = row (or column) total ÷ grand total.
\( 320/800 = 0.40 \). 40% of employees are in the Engineering department.

problems.question_html:
The two-way table below shows data on transportation method (Bus, Car, Walk) and school type (Public, Private) for 1,000 students.

BusCarWalkTotal
Public280200120600
Private10022080400
Total3804202001000

What is the conditional relative frequency of taking the bus among Private school students?

hints.text: "Among Private school students" means we condition on the Private row. What is the Private row total?
Conditional on Private: \( 100/400 = 0.25 \). Option A uses grand total (joint frequency). Option B uses column total (wrong condition). Option D gives a marginal frequency.

solution_steps.text: We are conditioning on Private school students, so the denominator is the Private row total = 400.
Conditional relative frequency = \( 100/400 = 0.25 \), or 25% of Private school students take the bus.

problems.question_html:
Using the same transportation table from the previous problem, which statement provides the strongest evidence that transportation method and school type are associated?

BusCarWalkTotal
Public280200120600
Private10022080400
Total3804202001000

choices.text: More students attend Public school (600) than Private school (400).
The conditional distribution of transportation for Public students (46.7% Bus, 33.3% Car, 20% Walk) differs from that of Private students (25% Bus, 55% Car, 20% Walk).
Car is the most common transportation overall (420 students).
The joint relative frequency of Public and Bus is 0.28.

hints.text: Association means the conditional distribution of one variable changes depending on the category of the other variable.

Compare conditional distributions: Public: Bus 46.7%, Car 33.3%, Walk 20%. Private: Bus 25%, Car 55%, Walk 20%. The Bus and Car proportions differ substantially between school types, indicating association.

solution_steps.text: Association between categorical variables is detected by comparing conditional distributions across groups.

Public: \( 280/600 \approx 0.467 \) Bus, \( 200/600 \approx 0.333 \) Car, \( 120/600 = 0.20 \) Walk. Private: \( 100/400 = 0.25 \) Bus, \( 220/400 = 0.55 \) Car, \( 80/400 = 0.20 \) Walk. The distributions differ (especially Bus and Car), which is evidence of association.

problems.question_html: A two-way table shows data for 600 patients classified by blood type (A, B, AB, O) and Rh factor (Positive, Negative). The cell for "Type O and Positive" contains 246 patients, and the Type O row total is 280. What is the conditional relative frequency of being Rh Positive given blood Type O? Give your answer as a decimal rounded to three places.

hints.text: The phrase "given blood Type O" tells you to restrict to the Type O row. What is the denominator?
Conditional relative frequency = cell count ÷ row total = \( 246/280 \approx 0.879 \).

solution_steps.text: "Given Type O" means we condition on the Type O row, so the denominator is 280 (the Type O row total).
Conditional relative frequency = \( 246/280 \approx 0.879 \).

problems.question_html: A researcher examines the relationship between exercise frequency (Regular, Occasional, Never) and stress level (Low, Medium, High) for 400 adults. The cell for "Regular exercise and Low stress" contains 80 people. The grand total is 400. The joint relative frequency for this cell is ________.

hints.text: Joint relative frequency = cell count ÷ grand total.
\( 80/400 = 0.20 \). Twenty percent of all adults surveyed exercise regularly and have low stress.

solution_steps.text: Joint relative frequency = cell count ÷ grand total = \( 80/400 = 0.20 \).
This means 20% of all surveyed adults both exercise regularly and report low stress.

problems.question_html: In a study of 1,200 smartphone users classified by operating system (iOS, Android) and preferred payment method (Credit Card, Digital Wallet, Cash), the iOS column total is 500 and the cell for "iOS and Digital Wallet" is 175. What is the conditional relative frequency of using a Digital Wallet given iOS? Round to three decimal places.

hints.text: "Given iOS" means the denominator is the iOS column total, not the grand total.
\( 175/500 = 0.350 \). Among iOS users, 35% prefer Digital Wallet.

solution_steps.text: We condition on iOS, so the denominator is the iOS column total = 500.
Conditional relative frequency = \( 175/500 = 0.350 \).

problems.question_html: A two-way table of 900 survey respondents categorized by political affiliation (Democrat, Republican, Independent) and opinion on a policy (Support, Oppose) contains the following data: the marginal relative frequency for "Support" is 0.60. How many total respondents support the policy?

hints.text: Marginal relative frequency = column total ÷ grand total. You know the marginal relative frequency and the grand total — solve for the column total.
\( 0.60 = x/900 \), so \( x = 0.60 \times 900 = 540 \). 540 respondents support the policy.

solution_steps.text: Marginal relative frequency of Support = (Support column total) ÷ grand total.
\( 0.60 = x/900 \implies x = 540 \). There are 540 respondents who support the policy.

problems.question_html:
A health clinic records patient data by insurance type (Private, Medicaid, Uninsured) and visit outcome (Treated, Referred, Untreated). The two-way table is below.

TreatedReferredUntreatedTotal
Private1805020250
Medicaid200100100400
Uninsured6080110250
Total440230230900

(a) Calculate the joint relative frequency of being Uninsured and Untreated.

(b) Calculate the conditional relative frequency of being Untreated given that a patient is Uninsured.

(c) Compare the conditional distributions of visit outcome for Private and Uninsured patients. Is there evidence of an association between insurance type and visit outcome? Justify your answer using specific proportions.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Joint relative frequency = 110/900 ≈ 0.122 or about 12.2%. (b) Conditional P(Untreated | Uninsured) = 110/250 = 0.44 or 44%. (c) Private: Treated 180/250 = 72%, Referred 50/250 = 20%, Untreated 20/250 = 8%. Uninsured: Treated 60/250 = 24%, Referred 80/250 = 32%, Untreated 110/250 = 44%. Yes, there is strong evidence of association. Private patients are treated at a much higher rate (72% vs. 24%) and left untreated at a much lower rate (8% vs. 44%) compared to Uninsured patients.

hints.text: For (a), use cell ÷ grand total. For (b), use cell ÷ row total. For (c), compute the full conditional distribution for each group and compare.

(a) \( 110/900 \approx 0.122 \). (b) \( 110/250 = 0.44 \). (c) Private: 72% Treated, 20% Referred, 8% Untreated. Uninsured: 24% Treated, 32% Referred, 44% Untreated. The distributions differ dramatically.

solution_steps.text: Part (a): Joint relative frequency = cell count ÷ grand total = \( 110/900 \approx 0.122 \), or about 12.2%.
Part (b): Conditional relative frequency of Untreated given Uninsured = \( 110/250 = 0.44 \), or 44%.

Part (c): Private conditional distribution — Treated: \( 180/250 = 0.72 \), Referred: \( 50/250 = 0.20 \), Untreated: \( 20/250 = 0.08 \). Uninsured — Treated: \( 60/250 = 0.24 \), Referred: \( 80/250 = 0.32 \), Untreated: \( 110/250 = 0.44 \). These distributions are very different, providing strong evidence of association between insurance type and visit outcome.

problems.question_html:
A sports league records data on 500 athletes by sport (Basketball, Soccer, Swimming) and injury status this season (Injured, Not Injured). The table is below.

InjuredNot InjuredTotal
Basketball48112160
Soccer75125200
Swimming21119140
Total144356500

(a) Calculate the marginal relative frequency of being injured.

(b) For each sport, calculate the conditional relative frequency of being injured. Which sport has the highest injury rate?

(c) A reporter writes: "Soccer is the most dangerous sport because 75 soccer players were injured — the highest count of any sport." Explain why this reasoning is flawed and what the reporter should say instead.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Marginal relative frequency of injured = 144/500 = 0.288 or 28.8%. (b) Basketball: 48/160 = 0.30 (30%). Soccer: 75/200 = 0.375 (37.5%). Swimming: 21/140 = 0.15 (15%). Soccer has the highest injury rate. (c) The reporter's reasoning is flawed because Soccer also has the most athletes (200). The raw count of 75 is highest partly because Soccer has the largest group. The correct approach is to compare conditional proportions (injury rates). While Soccer does have the highest injury rate (37.5% vs. 30% for Basketball and 15% for Swimming), the conclusion should be based on proportions, not raw counts.

hints.text: For (a), use the Injured column total ÷ grand total. For (b), compute cell ÷ row total for each sport. For (c), think about why raw counts can be misleading when group sizes differ.

(a) \( 144/500 = 0.288 \). (b) Basketball: 30%, Soccer: 37.5%, Swimming: 15%. (c) Soccer has the most players (200), so a higher raw count does not necessarily mean a higher rate. Proportions must be compared.

solution_steps.text: Part (a): Marginal relative frequency of Injured = \( 144/500 = 0.288 \), or 28.8%.
Part (b): Basketball: \( 48/160 = 0.30 \) (30%). Soccer: \( 75/200 = 0.375 \) (37.5%). Swimming: \( 21/140 = 0.15 \) (15%). Soccer has the highest conditional injury rate.

Part (c): The reporter used raw counts instead of proportions. Soccer has 200 athletes — the largest group — so 75 injuries may be high partly due to group size. The valid comparison is injury rates: Soccer 37.5%, Basketball 30%, Swimming 15%. The conclusion about Soccer being highest happens to be correct, but the reasoning should cite proportions, not counts.

concepts.title: Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation
concepts.content_html:
Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation

Sometimes calculating a probability exactly is difficult or impossible. In those cases, we can estimate the probability using a simulation — a model that imitates a real process using random numbers.

Key Vocabulary

  • Outcome: A single result of a random process (e.g., rolling a 4 on a die).
  • Event: A collection of one or more outcomes (e.g., rolling an even number).
  • Trial: One repetition of the random process in a simulation.

Steps for Designing a Simulation

  1. Describe the outcomes of the random process and identify the event of interest.
  2. Assign digits (or use a random number generator) to represent outcomes, matching the known or assumed probabilities.
  3. Run many trials — perform the simulation a large number of times, recording the result of each trial.
  4. Summarize the results — calculate the proportion of trials in which the event of interest occurred. This proportion is the estimated probability.

Empirical vs. Theoretical Probability

Theoretical probability is calculated using mathematical reasoning (e.g., \( P(\text{heads}) = 0.5 \) for a fair coin). Empirical probability (also called experimental probability) is based on observed data from experiments or simulations:

\[ P(\text{event}) \approx \frac{\text{number of times event occurred}}{\text{total number of trials}} \]

The Law of Large Numbers

The Law of Large Numbers states that as the number of trials increases, the empirical probability of an event gets closer and closer to the true (theoretical) probability. This is why simulations with more trials produce better estimates.

For example, if you flip a fair coin 10 times, you might get 7 heads (empirical \( P = 0.70 \)). But if you flip it 10,000 times, the proportion of heads will be very close to 0.50.

Key Idea: The Law of Large Numbers guarantees that empirical probability converges to theoretical probability as the number of trials increases. More trials = better estimate. It does not say that short-term results will "balance out."
AP Exam Tip: When describing a simulation on the AP exam, you must clearly (1) state what each digit or random number represents, (2) explain what constitutes one trial, (3) state how many trials you will run, and (4) explain how to use the results to estimate the probability. Skipping any step will cost points.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Estimating Probabilities Using Simulation

problems.question_html: A teacher wants to estimate the probability that at least 2 of 5 randomly selected students share the same birth month. She uses a random number generator to assign each student a birth month (1–12) and runs 200 trials. In 78 of the trials, at least 2 students share a birth month. What is the estimated probability?

hints.text: The estimated probability is the proportion of trials in which the event of interest occurred.
Estimated probability = (number of trials with at least 2 shared months) ÷ (total trials) = \( 78/200 = 0.39 \).

solution_steps.text: The event of interest is "at least 2 of 5 students share a birth month." This occurred in 78 out of 200 trials.
Estimated probability = \( 78/200 = 0.39 \).

problems.question_html: A student flips a coin 20 times and gets 14 heads, giving an empirical probability of \( 0.70 \). She then flips the same coin 2,000 times and gets 1,024 heads. According to the Law of Large Numbers, which statement is true?

choices.text: The coin must be unfair because 14 out of 20 is far from 50%.
The proportion \( 1024/2000 = 0.512 \) is a better estimate of the true probability of heads than \( 14/20 = 0.70 \).
The next 20 flips are likely to have more tails to "balance out" the earlier run of heads.
With enough trials, the number of heads will exactly equal the number of tails.

hints.text: The Law of Large Numbers says the proportion (not the count) of successes approaches the true probability as trials increase.
With 2,000 flips, \( 1024/2000 = 0.512 \) is much closer to 0.50 than \( 14/20 = 0.70 \). The law does not promise "balancing out" or exact equality — only that the proportion converges.

solution_steps.text: The Law of Large Numbers states that as the number of trials increases, the empirical proportion approaches the true probability.
\( 1024/2000 = 0.512 \) is closer to 0.50 than \( 14/20 = 0.70 \). A common misconception is that future results will "balance out" past results — the law says nothing about that.

problems.question_html: A cereal company places one of 6 different toys (equally likely) in each box. You want to estimate the probability that you need to buy more than 10 boxes to collect all 6 toys. You design a simulation using a random number generator that produces integers 1–6. Which of the following correctly describes one trial of this simulation?

choices.text: Generate one random integer from 1 to 6.
Generate random integers from 1 to 6 until all six values (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) have appeared at least once. Record the total number of integers generated.
Generate 10 random integers from 1 to 6 and check if all 6 values appear.
Generate 6 random integers from 1 to 6 and check if they are all different.

hints.text: One trial should simulate the complete process of buying boxes until you have all 6 toys. Each random integer represents one box purchase.

A trial = keep generating random integers (each representing buying a box and getting a toy) until all 6 distinct values have appeared. Then record how many integers were needed. You check whether that number exceeds 10.

solution_steps.text: Each random integer (1–6) represents a box purchase with a random toy inside. One trial simulates the entire process of collecting all 6 toys.
Generate integers until all values 1–6 have appeared. Record the count. If the count > 10, the event of interest occurred. Repeat for many trials and find the proportion where count > 10.

problems.question_html: A student argues: "I flipped a fair coin 4 times and got 4 heads in a row. The next flip is more likely to be tails because the results need to even out." Which concept does this statement violate?

choices.text: The complement rule
The Law of Large Numbers
The addition rule
The empirical rule

hints.text: The student believes short-term results must "balance out." Which law is about long-run behavior and is often misunderstood this way?

This is the "gambler's fallacy" — a misunderstanding of the Law of Large Numbers. The law says the proportion approaches 0.5 over a very large number of trials, not that individual outcomes compensate for past results.

solution_steps.text: The student's error is the gambler's fallacy: believing that short-term results must "even out." Each coin flip is independent.

The Law of Large Numbers states that the proportion of heads approaches 0.5 over many trials, but this happens by dilution (new results swamping old ones), not by compensation. The 5th flip still has P(tails) = 0.5.

problems.question_html:
A simulation uses digits 0–9 to model a basketball player's free throws. The player makes 70% of free throws. Which digit assignment correctly represents the outcomes?

Enter your answer describing which digits represent a make and which represent a miss.
problems.correct_answer: 0-6 make 7-9 miss||0 to 6 make and 7 to 9 miss||digits 0-6 for make, 7-9 for miss

hints.text: There are 10 digits (0–9). You need 70% to represent a make. How many of the 10 digits is that?
70% of 10 digits = 7 digits for "make" and 3 digits for "miss." A common assignment: 0–6 = make (7 digits), 7–9 = miss (3 digits).

solution_steps.text: The player makes 70% of free throws, so 7 out of 10 digits should represent a make.
Assign digits 0–6 to represent a made free throw (7 digits = 70%) and digits 7–9 to represent a miss (3 digits = 30%).

problems.question_html: A researcher runs a simulation 500 times to estimate the probability of a certain event. The event occurs in 215 of the 500 trials. The estimated probability from this simulation is ________.

hints.text: Estimated probability = (number of successes) ÷ (number of trials).

solution_steps.text: Estimated (empirical) probability = number of times the event occurred ÷ total trials.

problems.question_html: A researcher simulates rolling two dice and recording their sum 1,000 times. In the simulation, a sum of 7 occurred 168 times. The theoretical probability of rolling a sum of 7 with two fair dice is \( 6/36 \). What is the estimated probability from the simulation, and how does it compare to the theoretical value? Round both to three decimal places.

hints.text: Estimated probability = successes ÷ trials = 168/1000. The theoretical value is 6/36 — simplify it.
Estimated: \( 168/1000 = 0.168 \). Theoretical: \( 6/36 \approx 0.167 \). They are very close, consistent with the Law of Large Numbers for 1,000 trials.

solution_steps.text: Estimated probability = \( 168/1000 = 0.168 \).
Theoretical probability = \( 6/36 = 1/6 \approx 0.167 \). The estimate (0.168) is very close to the theoretical value, as expected with 1,000 trials.

problems.question_html: A researcher wants to estimate the probability that a family with 4 children has exactly 2 boys (assuming each child is equally likely to be a boy or a girl). She assigns digits 0–4 to represent a boy and digits 5–9 to represent a girl. Explain why this digit assignment is incorrect and provide a correct assignment.
problems.correct_answer: 0-4 is 5 digits (50% not correct) should be 0-4 for boy means P(boy)=0.5 which is correct||wait 0-4 is 5 digits out of 10 so it is correct||the assignment is actually correct because 5/10 = 0.5

hints.text: Count how many digits are assigned to "boy" (0–4). Is this the right proportion for P(boy) = 0.5?
Digits 0–4 = 5 digits and digits 5–9 = 5 digits, so each outcome has probability 5/10 = 0.5. This assignment is actually correct! The question is testing whether you carefully count the digits.

solution_steps.text: Digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 = 5 digits for boy. Digits 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 = 5 digits for girl. Each has probability 5/10 = 0.5.
This assignment is actually correct because P(boy) = 5/10 = 0.5 and P(girl) = 5/10 = 0.5, matching the equally likely assumption. A careful reading shows the assignment is valid.

problems.question_html:
A weather forecaster wants to estimate the probability of rain on at least 3 out of the next 5 days. Historically, the probability of rain on any given day in this area during June is 0.40, and weather on different days can be considered independent.

(a) Describe a simulation using a random number table (digits 0–9) to estimate this probability. Clearly explain what digits represent rain, what constitutes one trial, and how to estimate the probability.

(b) The forecaster runs 250 trials and finds that rain occurred on at least 3 of 5 days in 83 trials. What is the estimated probability?

(c) Explain why running 2,500 trials instead of 250 would likely produce a better estimate.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Assign digits: 0–3 = rain (4 digits = 40%), 4–9 = no rain (6 digits = 60%). One trial = read 5 consecutive digits from the random number table. Each digit represents one day. Count how many of the 5 digits are 0–3 (rain days). Record whether that count is ≥ 3. Repeat for many trials. Estimated probability = (number of trials with ≥ 3 rain days) ÷ (total trials). (b) Estimated probability = 83/250 = 0.332. (c) The Law of Large Numbers states that as the number of trials increases, the empirical probability approaches the true probability. With 2,500 trials, random variation is reduced and the estimate is more precise than with only 250 trials.

hints.text: For part (a), P(rain) = 0.40, so assign 4 of the 10 digits (0–3) to rain. One trial uses 5 digits (one per day). For part (b), divide successes by trials.
(a) 0–3 = rain, 4–9 = no rain. Trial = 5 digits, count rain days, check if ≥ 3. (b) 83/250 = 0.332. (c) Law of Large Numbers: more trials → proportion closer to true probability.

solution_steps.text: Part (a): Since P(rain) = 0.40, assign 4 digits to rain: let 0, 1, 2, 3 = rain and 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 = no rain. One trial = read 5 consecutive single digits. Each digit is one day. Count how many are 0–3. If the count ≥ 3, the event occurred.
Part (b): Estimated probability = 83/250 = 0.332.

Part (c): By the Law of Large Numbers, the estimated probability converges to the true probability as the number of trials increases. With 2,500 trials (10× more), the estimate will have less variability and be closer to the true value.

problems.question_html:
A restaurant manager notices that about 15% of customers order dessert. She wants to estimate the probability that in a group of 8 customers, none of them orders dessert.

(a) Using a random number table with digits 00–99, describe how to assign numbers to represent ordering and not ordering dessert.

(b) Describe what constitutes one trial and what event you are tracking.

(c) The manager runs 400 trials and observes that zero dessert orders occurred in 109 trials. Calculate the estimated probability and compare it to the theoretical value \( (0.85)^8 \approx 0.2725 \).
problems.correct_answer: (a) Use two-digit numbers 00–99. Assign 00–14 to represent ordering dessert (15 numbers = 15%) and 15–99 to represent not ordering dessert (85 numbers = 85%). (b) One trial = read 8 two-digit numbers. Each number represents one customer. If all 8 numbers are in the range 15–99 (no dessert), the event occurred. (c) Estimated probability = 109/400 = 0.2725. Theoretical probability = (0.85)^8 ≈ 0.2725. The simulation estimate matches the theoretical value extremely well in this case.

hints.text: P(dessert) = 0.15, so you need 15% of two-digit numbers for dessert. Numbers 00–14 give you exactly 15 out of 100.
(a) 00–14 = dessert, 15–99 = no dessert. (b) Read 8 two-digit numbers; event = all 8 are 15–99. (c) 109/400 = 0.2725, matching (0.85)^8 ≈ 0.2725.

solution_steps.text: Part (a): Since P(dessert) = 0.15, assign two-digit numbers 00–14 (15 numbers out of 100) to "orders dessert" and 15–99 (85 numbers) to "does not order dessert."
Part (b): One trial = generate 8 two-digit random numbers (one per customer). Check whether all 8 are in the range 15–99 (meaning no one ordered dessert).

Part (c): Estimated probability = 109/400 = 0.2725. Theoretical: \( (0.85)^8 \approx 0.2725 \). The estimate matches the theoretical value closely, which is expected with a reasonably large number of trials.

concepts.title: Introduction to Probability
concepts.content_html:
Introduction to Probability

Probability is a number between 0 and 1 that describes the long-run proportion of times an outcome or event will occur. It provides the mathematical foundation for statistical inference.

Sample Space

The sample space \( S \) is the set of all possible outcomes of a random process. For example:

  • Flipping a coin: \( S = \{H, T\} \)
  • Rolling a die: \( S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} \)
  • Flipping two coins: \( S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\} \)

Events

An event is a subset of the sample space — one or more outcomes of interest. We often use capital letters like \( A \), \( B \), \( C \) to name events. For example, if we roll a die, the event "roll an even number" is \( A = \{2, 4, 6\} \).

Probability for Equally Likely Outcomes

When all outcomes in the sample space are equally likely, the probability of an event \( A \) is:

\[ P(A) = \frac{\text{number of outcomes in } A}{\text{total number of outcomes in } S} \]

For example, \( P(\text{even on a fair die}) = \frac{3}{6} = 0.5 \).

Probability Rules

  • Bound rule: For any event \( A \), \( 0 \leq P(A) \leq 1 \).
  • Certain event: \( P(S) = 1 \) — something in the sample space must happen.
  • Impossible event: \( P(\emptyset) = 0 \) — the probability of an impossible outcome is 0.

The Complement Rule

The complement of an event \( A \), written \( A' \) (or \( A^c \) or \( \bar{A} \)), is the event that \( A \) does not occur. It includes all outcomes in \( S \) that are not in \( A \).

\[ P(A') = 1 - P(A) \]

This is extremely useful when calculating \( P(A) \) directly is hard but \( P(A') \) is easy. For instance, to find the probability of getting at least one head in 3 flips, compute:

\[ P(\text{at least one head}) = 1 - P(\text{no heads}) = 1 - P(TTT) = 1 - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{7}{8} \]

Key Idea: The complement rule \( P(A') = 1 - P(A) \) is one of the most powerful tools in probability. Whenever a problem says "at least one," consider using the complement (none) to simplify the calculation.
AP Exam Tip: Probabilities must always be between 0 and 1 (inclusive). If your calculated probability is negative or greater than 1, you have made an error — go back and check your work. Also, the AP exam expects probability answers as decimals or fractions, not percentages, unless specifically requested.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Introduction to Probability

problems.question_html: A bag contains 5 red marbles, 3 blue marbles, and 2 green marbles. If one marble is drawn at random, what is the probability of drawing a blue marble?

hints.text: When all outcomes are equally likely, \( P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{favorable}}{\text{total}} \). How many total marbles are in the bag?
Total = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10 marbles. Blue = 3. So \( P(\text{blue}) = 3/10 \).

solution_steps.text: Total marbles = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10. Each marble is equally likely to be drawn.

problems.question_html: A spinner has four sections: Red (probability 0.35), Blue (probability 0.25), Green (probability 0.15), and Yellow. What is \( P(\text{Yellow}) \)?

hints.text: All probabilities in a sample space must sum to 1. Add the known probabilities and subtract from 1.

solution_steps.text: The sum of all probabilities in the sample space must equal 1.

problems.question_html: A medical test correctly identifies a disease 92% of the time when the disease is present. A patient tests positive. A statistician says that \( P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive test}) \) might be much lower than 0.92 if the disease is rare. This is because the probability 0.92 refers to:

choices.text: \( P(\text{disease}) \), the overall probability of having the disease
\( P(\text{positive test} \mid \text{disease}) \), the probability of testing positive given the disease is present
\( P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive test}) \), the probability of having the disease given a positive test
\( P(\text{positive test}) \), the overall probability of testing positive

hints.text: The test "correctly identifies the disease when it is present" — this means we are given that the disease is present (condition), and we ask about the test result.

"Correctly identifies a disease when present" means \( P(\text{positive} \mid \text{disease}) = 0.92 \). This is called sensitivity. It is NOT the same as \( P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive}) \) — confusing these is called the "prosecutor's fallacy."

solution_steps.text: The test correctly identifies the disease 92% of the time when the disease IS present. This is a conditional probability: \( P(\text{positive test} \mid \text{disease}) = 0.92 \).
This is NOT \( P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive test}) \). When the disease is rare, many false positives can occur, making \( P(\text{disease} \mid \text{positive}) \) much lower than 0.92.

problems.question_html: A game involves rolling a fair six-sided die. You win if you roll a number greater than 4. What is \( P(\text{not winning}) \)?

hints.text: First find \( P(\text{winning}) \) — winning means rolling a 5 or 6. Then use the complement.
\( P(\text{winning}) = P(5 \text{ or } 6) = 2/6 = 1/3 \). \( P(\text{not winning}) = 1 - 1/3 = 2/3 \).

solution_steps.text: Winning = rolling > 4, so winning outcomes = {5, 6}. \( P(\text{win}) = 2/6 = 1/3 \).
\( P(\text{not winning}) = 1 - 1/3 = 2/3 \approx 0.667 \).

problems.question_html: Two fair coins are flipped. The sample space is \( \{HH, HT, TH, TT\} \). What is \( P(\text{at least one head}) \)? Express your answer as a fraction or decimal.

hints.text: "At least one head" means one or more heads. You can count directly or use the complement: P(at least one head) = 1 − P(no heads).
P(no heads) = P(TT) = 1/4. So P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4 = 0.75.

solution_steps.text: The complement of "at least one head" is "no heads" = \( \{TT\} \). \( P(TT) = 1/4 \).
\( P(\text{at least one head}) = 1 - 1/4 = 3/4 = 0.75 \).

problems.question_html: A standard deck of 52 playing cards contains 4 aces. If a card is drawn at random, what is \( P(\text{not an ace}) \)? Express your answer as a fraction.

hints.text: Use the complement rule: \( P(\text{not ace}) = 1 - P(\text{ace}) \).

solution_steps.text: By the complement rule, \( P(\text{not ace}) = 1 - 1/13 = 12/13 \approx 0.923 \).

problems.question_html: A jar contains 8 red, 5 yellow, and 7 green candies. If one candy is drawn at random, what is \( P(\text{not green}) \)? Express your answer as a decimal.

hints.text: Total candies = 8 + 5 + 7 = 20. Find P(green) first, then use the complement.

solution_steps.text: Total = 8 + 5 + 7 = 20 candies. \( P(\text{green}) = 7/20 = 0.35 \).

problems.question_html: A password is created by choosing 3 digits (0–9), where each digit is chosen independently and uniformly at random. What is the total number of possible passwords (the size of the sample space)?

hints.text: Each position has 10 choices (0–9). Digits can repeat. Use the multiplication principle.
Sample space size = \( 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 10^3 = 1000 \).

solution_steps.text: Each of the 3 positions can be any digit from 0 to 9 (10 options), and digits can repeat.
By the multiplication principle, total passwords = \( 10 \times 10 \times 10 = 1000 \).

problems.question_html:
A bag contains tiles labeled with the letters A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H (8 tiles total). Two tiles are drawn at random without replacement.

(a) List the sample space for the first tile drawn. How many outcomes does it contain?

(b) After the first tile is drawn, how many outcomes are possible for the second tile?

(c) How many ordered pairs (first tile, second tile) are in the complete sample space?

(d) What is the probability that the two tiles drawn spell a two-letter combination that starts with a vowel (A or E)?
problems.correct_answer: (a) The sample space for the first tile is {A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H}, containing 8 outcomes. (b) After one tile is removed, 7 tiles remain, so there are 7 possible outcomes for the second draw. (c) Total ordered pairs = 8 × 7 = 56. (d) If the first tile is a vowel (A or E), there are 2 choices for the first tile and 7 remaining for the second, giving 2 × 7 = 14 favorable outcomes. P(starts with vowel) = 14/56 = 1/4 = 0.25.

hints.text: For without-replacement problems, the second draw has one fewer option. For part (d), count how many ordered pairs have a vowel in the first position.
(a) 8 outcomes. (b) 7 outcomes. (c) 8 × 7 = 56. (d) Vowels first: 2 × 7 = 14. P = 14/56 = 1/4.

solution_steps.text: Part (a): First tile sample space = {A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H}, which has 8 outcomes.
Part (b): Since one tile has been removed (without replacement), 7 tiles remain for the second draw.
Part (c): By the multiplication principle, total ordered pairs = 8 × 7 = 56.
Part (d): Vowels are A and E (2 vowels). Favorable outcomes = 2 choices for first tile × 7 for second = 14. \( P(\text{starts with vowel}) = 14/56 = 1/4 = 0.25 \).

problems.question_html:
At a state fair, a game involves spinning a wheel divided into 20 equal sections numbered 1 through 20. A player wins a prize if the wheel lands on a prime number.

(a) List all prime numbers from 1 to 20 and determine \( P(\text{prime}) \).

(b) What is \( P(\text{not prime}) \)? Show your work using the complement rule.

(c) A player spins the wheel 3 times. Using the complement approach, find the probability of landing on at least one prime number in 3 spins. Assume spins are independent. Express your answer as a decimal rounded to three places.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Primes from 1–20: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19. That is 8 primes. P(prime) = 8/20 = 0.4. (b) P(not prime) = 1 − P(prime) = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6. (c) P(no primes in 3 spins) = (0.6)^3 = 0.216. P(at least one prime) = 1 − 0.216 = 0.784.

hints.text: Remember that 1 is NOT a prime number. List primes carefully. For part (c), use the complement: P(at least one) = 1 − P(none).

solution_steps.text: Part (a): Primes between 1 and 20: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19. There are 8 primes. \( P(\text{prime}) = 8/20 = 2/5 = 0.4 \).
Part (b): By the complement rule, \( P(\text{not prime}) = 1 - P(\text{prime}) = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6 \).
Part (c): P(no primes in 3 independent spins) = \( (0.6)^3 = 0.216 \). P(at least one prime in 3 spins) = \( 1 - 0.216 = 0.784 \).

concepts.title: Mutually Exclusive Events
concepts.content_html:
Mutually Exclusive Events

Two events are mutually exclusive (also called disjoint) if they cannot occur at the same time. In set language, \( A \cap B = \emptyset \), so \( P(A \text{ and } B) = 0 \).

Examples of Mutually Exclusive Events

  • Rolling a 2 and rolling a 5 on a single die — the die shows exactly one face.
  • Drawing a heart and drawing a spade from a single card draw.
  • A randomly selected student being in Grade 9 and being in Grade 12.

Examples of Events That Are NOT Mutually Exclusive

  • Drawing a heart and drawing a queen — the queen of hearts satisfies both.
  • A student playing soccer and playing basketball — some students play both.

The Addition Rule for Mutually Exclusive Events

When two events \( A \) and \( B \) are mutually exclusive:

\[ P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) \]

This extends to any number of mutually exclusive events:

\[ P(A_1 \text{ or } A_2 \text{ or } \cdots \text{ or } A_k) = P(A_1) + P(A_2) + \cdots + P(A_k) \]

Worked Example

A bag contains 3 red, 5 blue, and 2 green marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is the probability that the marble is red or green?

Solution: Drawing a red marble and drawing a green marble are mutually exclusive (a single marble cannot be both colors).

\[ P(\text{red or green}) = P(\text{red}) + P(\text{green}) = \frac{3}{10} + \frac{2}{10} = \frac{5}{10} = 0.5 \]

Complement Rule Connection

The events \( A \) and \( A^C \) are always mutually exclusive, and they cover the entire sample space:

\[ P(A) + P(A^C) = 1 \quad \Rightarrow \quad P(A^C) = 1 - P(A) \]
Key Idea: Mutually exclusive means \( P(A \text{ and } B) = 0 \). You can only add probabilities directly when events are mutually exclusive. If they are not, you must subtract the overlap (the general addition rule from Topic 2.7).
AP Exam Trap: Students often confuse "mutually exclusive" with "independent." Two events that are mutually exclusive are actually dependent (if one occurs, the other cannot). The only exception is if one event has probability 0.
concepts.content_raw: Mutually Exclusive Events

problem_sets.title: Practice: Mutually Exclusive Events

problems.question_html: A standard deck of 52 cards is shuffled and one card is drawn. Let event \( A \) = drawing a king and event \( B \) = drawing a queen. Which statement is true?

choices.text: Events \( A \) and \( B \) are mutually exclusive because a single card cannot be both a king and a queen.
Events \( A \) and \( B \) are not mutually exclusive because both are face cards.
Events \( A \) and \( B \) are independent because the probability of one does not affect the other.
Events \( A \) and \( B \) are complementary because together they account for all face cards.

hints.text: Can a single card be a king and a queen at the same time?
No card is both a king and a queen, so \( P(A \text{ and } B) = 0 \). That is the definition of mutually exclusive.

solution_steps.text: A single card has exactly one rank. No card is simultaneously a king and a queen, so \( A \cap B = \emptyset \).
Since the events cannot occur together, they are mutually exclusive. Note: they are not complementary because other outcomes (aces, jacks, number cards) exist.

problems.question_html: A six-sided die is rolled once. Let event \( A \) = rolling an even number and event \( B \) = rolling a number greater than 4. Are events \( A \) and \( B \) mutually exclusive?

choices.text: Yes, because even numbers and numbers greater than 4 have nothing in common.
No, because the outcome 6 is both even and greater than 4.
Yes, because \( P(A) + P(B) = 1 \).
No, because all outcomes greater than 4 are odd.

hints.text: List the outcomes in each event. Event A = {2, 4, 6}. Event B = {5, 6}. Do they share any outcomes?
The outcome 6 appears in both events, so \( A \cap B = \{6\} \neq \emptyset \). The events are NOT mutually exclusive.

solution_steps.text: Event A (even) = {2, 4, 6}. Event B (greater than 4) = {5, 6}.
The intersection \( A \cap B = \{6\} \), which is not empty. Therefore the events are not mutually exclusive.

problems.question_html: In a quality-control process, manufactured items are classified as Grade A, Grade B, or Defective. The probabilities are \( P(A) = 0.70 \), \( P(B) = 0.22 \), and \( P(\text{Defective}) = 0.08 \). What is the probability that a randomly selected item is not Grade A?

hints.text: "Not Grade A" is the complement of Grade A. Use the complement rule.
\( P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A) = 1 - 0.70 = 0.30 \). Equivalently, \( P(B) + P(\text{Defective}) = 0.22 + 0.08 = 0.30 \).

solution_steps.text: Using the complement rule: \( P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A) = 1 - 0.70 = 0.30 \).
We can verify: since the three grades are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, \( P(B) + P(\text{Defective}) = 0.22 + 0.08 = 0.30 \). \checkmark

problems.question_html: Events \( A \) and \( B \) are mutually exclusive with \( P(A) = 0.3 \) and \( P(B) = 0.5 \). What is \( P(A \text{ or } B) \)?

hints.text: For mutually exclusive events, you can simply add the probabilities.
\( P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A) + P(B) = 0.3 + 0.5 = 0.8 \). The answer 0.15 would be \( P(A) \times P(B) \), which is the multiplication rule — not applicable here.

solution_steps.text: Since \( A \) and \( B \) are mutually exclusive, \( P(A \text{ and } B) = 0 \).

problems.question_html: A survey finds that 40% of customers prefer coffee, 35% prefer tea, and 25% prefer juice. Assuming each customer selects exactly one beverage, what is the probability that a randomly selected customer prefers coffee or tea? Give your answer as a decimal.

hints.text: Since each customer selects exactly one beverage, the three preferences are mutually exclusive events.
For mutually exclusive events: \( P(\text{coffee or tea}) = P(\text{coffee}) + P(\text{tea}) = 0.40 + 0.35 \).

solution_steps.text: Each customer picks exactly one beverage, so the events are mutually exclusive.
\( P(\text{coffee or tea}) = P(\text{coffee}) + P(\text{tea}) = 0.40 + 0.35 = 0.75 \).

problems.question_html: A bag contains 4 red, 6 blue, and 5 yellow marbles. One marble is drawn at random. What is \( P(\text{red or yellow}) \)? Express your answer as a fraction in lowest terms.

hints.text: A single marble has exactly one color, so drawing red and drawing yellow are mutually exclusive.
Total marbles = 15. \( P(\text{red or yellow}) = \frac{4}{15} + \frac{5}{15} = \frac{9}{15} = \frac{3}{5} \).

solution_steps.text: Total marbles = 4 + 6 + 5 = 15. The events are mutually exclusive (a marble is one color).
\( P(\text{red or yellow}) = \frac{4}{15} + \frac{5}{15} = \frac{9}{15} = \frac{3}{5} \).

problems.question_html: A spinner is divided into five colored sections. The probabilities are: Red = 0.15, Blue = 0.25, Green = 0.20, Yellow = 0.10, and Orange = 0.30. What is the probability that the spinner lands on a primary color (red, blue, or yellow)? Give your answer as a decimal.

hints.text: The spinner can land on only one section at a time, so the color events are mutually exclusive.
\( P(\text{primary}) = P(\text{red}) + P(\text{blue}) + P(\text{yellow}) = 0.15 + 0.25 + 0.10 = 0.50 \).

solution_steps.text: The primary colors on the spinner are red, blue, and yellow. The sections are mutually exclusive.

problems.question_html: Blood types O, A, B, and AB are mutually exclusive. In a certain population, \( P(O) = 0.44 \), \( P(A) = 0.42 \), and \( P(B) = 0.10 \). What is \( P(AB) \)?

hints.text: Since every person has exactly one blood type, the four probabilities must sum to 1.

solution_steps.text: The four blood types are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, so their probabilities sum to 1.

problems.question_html:
A weather forecaster says there is a 20% chance of rain, a 5% chance of snow, and rain and snow cannot occur simultaneously in this region during this season.

(a) Are the events "rain" and "snow" mutually exclusive? Justify your answer.

(b) Find \( P(\text{rain or snow}) \).

(c) Find \( P(\text{neither rain nor snow}) \).
problems.correct_answer: (a) Yes, the events are mutually exclusive because the problem states rain and snow cannot occur simultaneously, meaning P(rain and snow) = 0. (b) P(rain or snow) = P(rain) + P(snow) = 0.20 + 0.05 = 0.25. (c) P(neither) = 1 - P(rain or snow) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75.

hints.text: Mutually exclusive means the two events cannot happen at the same time. The problem explicitly tells you about this.
For part (c), use the complement rule: P(neither) = 1 - P(rain or snow).

solution_steps.text: (a) Yes, rain and snow are mutually exclusive because the problem states they cannot occur simultaneously: \( P(\text{rain and snow}) = 0 \).
(b) Since the events are mutually exclusive: \( P(\text{rain or snow}) = 0.20 + 0.05 = 0.25 \).
(c) \( P(\text{neither rain nor snow}) = 1 - P(\text{rain or snow}) = 1 - 0.25 = 0.75 \).

problems.question_html:
At a car dealership, vehicles are classified by type: sedan (S), SUV (U), or truck (T). The probability of selling a sedan is 0.45, and the probability of selling a truck is 0.20.

(a) Find the probability of selling an SUV. Show your work.

(b) A customer says they want "anything but a sedan." Find the probability that the next sale to this customer is an SUV or a truck.

(c) Are the events "selling a sedan" and "selling a truck" mutually exclusive? Are they independent? Explain both.
problems.correct_answer: (a) P(U) = 1 - P(S) - P(T) = 1 - 0.45 - 0.20 = 0.35. (b) P(SUV or truck) = 1 - P(sedan) = 1 - 0.45 = 0.55. Alternatively, 0.35 + 0.20 = 0.55. (c) They are mutually exclusive because a single sale is one vehicle type, so P(S and T) = 0. They are NOT independent because if one occurs the other cannot; P(S|T) = 0 which does not equal P(S) = 0.45.

hints.text: The three vehicle types are mutually exclusive and exhaustive — their probabilities must sum to 1.
For part (c), recall that mutually exclusive events with nonzero probabilities are always dependent, not independent.

solution_steps.text: (a) Since S, U, and T are mutually exclusive and exhaustive: \( P(U) = 1 - 0.45 - 0.20 = 0.35 \).

(c) Mutually exclusive: Yes, a single sale is exactly one type, so \( P(S \cap T) = 0 \). Independent: No. If the sale is a truck, the probability it is a sedan is 0, but \( P(S) = 0.45 \neq 0 \). So \( P(S|T) \neq P(S) \), meaning they are dependent.

concepts.title: Conditional Probability
concepts.content_html:
Conditional Probability

Conditional probability is the probability of one event occurring given that another event has already occurred (or is known to be true). We write this as \( P(A|B) \), read "the probability of \( A \) given \( B \)."

The Conditional Probability Formula

\[ P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}, \quad P(B) > 0 \]

This formula says: to find the probability of \( A \) given \( B \), restrict your attention to only the outcomes where \( B \) has occurred, then see how many of those also satisfy \( A \).

Reading Conditional Probability from Two-Way Tables

Two-way tables (also called contingency tables) are the most common way the AP exam tests conditional probability.

EmployedUnemployedTotal
College Degree42030450
No College Degree380170550
Total8002001000

Example: What is \( P(\text{Employed} | \text{College Degree}) \)?

Restrict to the "College Degree" row (total = 450). Of those, 420 are employed.

\[ P(\text{Employed} | \text{College Degree}) = \frac{420}{450} = \frac{14}{15} \approx 0.933 \]

Compare with: \( P(\text{Employed} | \text{No College Degree}) = \frac{380}{550} \approx 0.691 \). The conditional probabilities differ, suggesting the variables are associated.

Key Idea: When reading conditional probability from a two-way table, the "given" condition tells you which row or column total to use as the denominator. The numerator is the cell where both conditions meet.
AP Exam Trap: \( P(A|B) \) and \( P(B|A) \) are generally not the same! "The probability of being employed given a college degree" is different from "the probability of having a college degree given being employed." Always check which event is the given.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Conditional Probability

problems.question_html:
A survey of 500 adults produced the following two-way table:

Exercises RegularlyDoes Not ExerciseTotal
Under 40140110250
40 or Older90160250
Total230270500

What is \( P(\text{Exercises Regularly} | \text{Under 40}) \)?

hints.text: The given condition is "Under 40." Use the Under 40 row total as the denominator.
\( P(\text{Exercises} | \text{Under 40}) = \frac{140}{250} = 0.56 \). The denominator is 250 (all Under 40), not 230 (all who exercise).

solution_steps.text: The given condition is "Under 40," so restrict to that row. The row total is 250.
Of the 250 people under 40, 140 exercise regularly. \( P(\text{Exercises} | \text{Under 40}) = \frac{140}{250} = 0.56 \).

problems.question_html: Using the same table from Problem 1, what is \( P(\text{Under 40} | \text{Exercises Regularly}) \)?

hints.text: Now the given condition is "Exercises Regularly." Which total should be the denominator?
Restrict to the Exercises Regularly column (total = 230). Of those, 140 are under 40: \( \frac{140}{230} \approx 0.609 \).

solution_steps.text: The given condition is "Exercises Regularly," so use the column total 230 as the denominator.
\( P(\text{Under 40} | \text{Exercises}) = \frac{140}{230} \approx 0.609 \). Notice this differs from \( P(\text{Exercises} | \text{Under 40}) = 0.56 \).

problems.question_html:
A company surveys 600 employees about commuting method and department:

CarPublic TransitBike/WalkTotal
Engineering806060200
Marketing1105040200
Sales1304030200
Total320150130600

Find \( P(\text{Engineering} | \text{Bike/Walk}) \). Express your answer as a fraction.

hints.text: The given condition is "Bike/Walk." Find the Bike/Walk column total for the denominator.
Bike/Walk total = 130. Engineering who bike/walk = 60. \( P(\text{Eng} | \text{Bike/Walk}) = \frac{60}{130} \approx 0.462 \).

solution_steps.text: Given condition is Bike/Walk, so denominator = 130 (Bike/Walk column total).
Engineering employees who bike/walk = 60. \( P(\text{Eng} | \text{Bike/Walk}) = \frac{60}{130} \approx 0.462 \).

problems.question_html: If \( P(A|B) = 0.4 \) and \( P(B) = 0.25 \), what is \( P(A \cap B) \)?

hints.text: Rearrange the conditional probability formula to solve for \( P(A \cap B) \).
\( P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \Rightarrow P(A \cap B) = P(A|B) \cdot P(B) = 0.4 \times 0.25 = 0.10 \).

solution_steps.text: Rearranging: \( P(A \cap B) = P(A|B) \cdot P(B) \).

problems.question_html: A medical test for a disease has the following results among 10,000 patients: 200 have the disease and test positive, 50 have the disease and test negative, 300 do not have the disease but test positive, and 9,450 do not have the disease and test negative. What is \( P(\text{Disease} | \text{Positive Test}) \)? Round to three decimal places.

hints.text: First find the total number of positive tests. The given condition is "Positive Test," so that total is the denominator.
Total positive tests = 200 + 300 = 500. Of those, 200 have the disease. \( P(\text{Disease} | \text{Positive}) = \frac{200}{500} = 0.400 \).

solution_steps.text: Total who tested positive = 200 (true positive) + 300 (false positive) = 500.
\( P(\text{Disease} | \text{Positive}) = \frac{200}{500} = 0.400 \). This is called the positive predictive value.

problems.question_html: If \( P(A) = 0.6 \), \( P(B) = 0.5 \), and \( P(A \cap B) = 0.3 \), find \( P(A|B) \). Give your answer as a decimal.

hints.text: Apply the formula: \( P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \).
\( P(A|B) = \frac{0.3}{0.5} = 0.6 \). Interestingly, \( P(A|B) = P(A) \), which means A and B are independent.

solution_steps.text: Using the conditional probability formula: \( P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} = \frac{0.3}{0.5} = 0.6 \).
Note: Since \( P(A|B) = 0.6 = P(A) \), the events \( A \) and \( B \) are independent.

problems.question_html: In a class of 30 students, 18 play a sport and 12 are in the honor society. Seven students both play a sport and are in the honor society. If a student is selected at random from those who play a sport, what is the probability that the student is also in the honor society? Round to three decimal places.

hints.text: "From those who play a sport" means the given condition is playing a sport. Use 18 as the denominator.
\( P(\text{Honor} | \text{Sport}) = \frac{7}{18} \approx 0.389 \).

solution_steps.text: Given: play a sport. Denominator = 18 students who play a sport.
Of those 18, 7 are also in honor society. \( P(\text{Honor} | \text{Sport}) = \frac{7}{18} \approx 0.389 \).

hints.text: Use the definition directly: divide the joint probability by the probability of the given event.

problems.question_html:
The following two-way table shows the results of a drug trial with 400 patients:

ImprovedNo ChangeTotal
Drug14060200
Placebo80120200
Total220180400

(a) Find \( P(\text{Improved} | \text{Drug}) \).

(b) Find \( P(\text{Improved} | \text{Placebo}) \).

(c) Based on these conditional probabilities, does it appear that the drug is effective? Explain.
problems.correct_answer: (a) P(Improved | Drug) = 140/200 = 0.70. (b) P(Improved | Placebo) = 80/200 = 0.40. (c) Yes, the drug appears effective because patients who received the drug had a 70% improvement rate compared to only 40% for the placebo group. The 30 percentage-point difference suggests an association between taking the drug and improvement.

hints.text: For each conditional probability, restrict to the appropriate row and use the row total as the denominator.
Compare the two conditional probabilities. If they are substantially different, there is evidence of an association between treatment and outcome.

solution_steps.text: (a) Restrict to the Drug row (total 200). \( P(\text{Improved} | \text{Drug}) = \frac{140}{200} = 0.70 \).
(b) Restrict to the Placebo row (total 200). \( P(\text{Improved} | \text{Placebo}) = \frac{80}{200} = 0.40 \).

(c) The drug group has a much higher improvement rate (70% vs. 40%), a difference of 30 percentage points. This suggests the drug is effective, as there is an association between taking the drug and improved outcomes.

problems.question_html:
At a high school, 60% of students own a laptop and 45% of students own both a laptop and a tablet. A student is selected at random.

(a) Find \( P(\text{Tablet} | \text{Laptop}) \).

(b) If 70% of students own a tablet, find \( P(\text{Laptop} | \text{Tablet}) \).

(c) Explain why \( P(\text{Tablet} | \text{Laptop}) \neq P(\text{Laptop} | \text{Tablet}) \) in this case.
problems.correct_answer: (a) P(Tablet | Laptop) = P(Tablet and Laptop)/P(Laptop) = 0.45/0.60 = 0.75. (b) P(Laptop | Tablet) = P(Laptop and Tablet)/P(Tablet) = 0.45/0.70 = 9/14 ≈ 0.643. (c) The two conditional probabilities differ because the denominators (the given events) are different: P(Laptop) = 0.60 while P(Tablet) = 0.70. Conditional probability depends on which event is the given condition.

hints.text: Use \( P(A|B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)} \) for each part. Be careful about which event is the given.
In part (a) the denominator is P(Laptop) = 0.60. In part (b) the denominator is P(Tablet) = 0.70. The numerator P(both) = 0.45 is the same for both.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( P(\text{Tablet} | \text{Laptop}) = \frac{P(\text{Tablet} \cap \text{Laptop})}{P(\text{Laptop})} = \frac{0.45}{0.60} = 0.75 \).
(b) \( P(\text{Laptop} | \text{Tablet}) = \frac{P(\text{Laptop} \cap \text{Tablet})}{P(\text{Tablet})} = \frac{0.45}{0.70} = \frac{9}{14} \approx 0.643 \).

(c) The conditional probabilities differ because they have different denominators. \( P(\text{Tablet} | \text{Laptop}) \) restricts to laptop owners (60%), while \( P(\text{Laptop} | \text{Tablet}) \) restricts to tablet owners (70%). In general, \( P(A|B) \neq P(B|A) \) unless \( P(A) = P(B) \).

concepts.title: Independent Events and Unions of Events
concepts.content_html:
Independent Events and Unions of Events

This topic brings together three powerful probability rules that let you handle any combination of two events.

Independent Events

Events \( A \) and \( B \) are independent if knowing that one occurred does not change the probability of the other:

\[ P(A|B) = P(A) \quad \text{and equivalently} \quad P(B|A) = P(B) \]

Common real-world examples of independent events:

  • Flipping a coin and rolling a die (separate experiments)
  • Two different randomly selected people's blood types
  • Successive draws with replacement

Multiplication Rule for Independent Events

If \( A \) and \( B \) are independent:

\[ P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) \]

Example: The probability that a smoke detector works is 0.95. If two independent detectors are installed, \( P(\text{both work}) = 0.95 \times 0.95 = 0.9025 \).

General Multiplication Rule

For any two events (independent or not):

\[ P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B|A) \]

Example: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. \( P(\text{both red}) = \frac{5}{8} \cdot \frac{4}{7} = \frac{20}{56} = \frac{5}{14} \).

General Addition Rule (Union of Events)

For any two events:

\[ P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \]

We subtract \( P(A \cap B) \) because outcomes in both \( A \) and \( B \) would otherwise be counted twice.

Example: In a class, 70% play sports, 40% play music, and 25% do both. \( P(\text{sports or music}) = 0.70 + 0.40 - 0.25 = 0.85 \).

Key Idea: There are three common tests for independence. If any one holds, the events are independent:
(1) \( P(A|B) = P(A) \)
(2) \( P(B|A) = P(B) \)
(3) \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) \)
AP Exam Trap: "Mutually exclusive" and "independent" are not the same — and they cannot both be true (unless one event has probability 0). If \( A \) and \( B \) are mutually exclusive with \( P(A) > 0 \) and \( P(B) > 0 \), then \( P(A|B) = 0 \neq P(A) \), so they are dependent.
