problem_sets.title: Practice: Independent Events and Unions of Events

problems.question_html: A fair coin is flipped and a fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of getting heads on the coin and a 4 on the die?

choices.text: \( \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{6} \times 2 = \frac{1}{6} \)

hints.text: A coin flip and a die roll are independent events because neither outcome affects the other.
For independent events: \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12} \).

solution_steps.text: The coin and die are independent — the coin result has no effect on the die.
\( P(\text{heads and 4}) = P(\text{heads}) \cdot P(4) = \frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12} \).

problems.question_html: If \( P(A) = 0.3 \), \( P(B) = 0.6 \), and \( P(A \cap B) = 0.18 \), are events \( A \) and \( B \) independent?

choices.text: Yes, because \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) \).
No, because \( P(A \cap B) \neq 0 \).
Yes, because \( P(A) + P(B) < 1 \).
No, because \( P(A) \neq P(B) \).

hints.text: Check whether \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) \). If so, the events are independent.
\( P(A) \cdot P(B) = 0.3 \times 0.6 = 0.18 = P(A \cap B) \). The condition is satisfied, so yes, they are independent.

solution_steps.text: Check: \( P(A) \cdot P(B) = 0.3 \times 0.6 = 0.18 \).
Since \( P(A \cap B) = 0.18 = P(A) \cdot P(B) \), the events are independent.

problems.question_html: A factory has two independent machines. Machine A has a 0.02 probability of producing a defective item, and Machine B has a 0.03 probability. An item is produced by each machine. What is the probability that at least one item is defective?

hints.text: "At least one" problems are easiest with the complement: \( P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - P(\text{none}) \).
\( P(\text{neither defective}) = P(A \text{ good}) \cdot P(B \text{ good}) = 0.98 \times 0.97 = 0.9506 \). So \( P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.9506 = 0.0494 \).

solution_steps.text: Use the complement: \( P(\text{at least one defective}) = 1 - P(\text{no defectives}) \).
Since the machines are independent: \( P(\text{no defectives}) = 0.98 \times 0.97 = 0.9506 \).
\( P(\text{at least one defective}) = 1 - 0.9506 = 0.0494 \).

problems.question_html: If \( P(A) = 0.5 \), \( P(B) = 0.4 \), and \( A \) and \( B \) are independent, what is \( P(A \cup B) \)?

hints.text: First use independence to find \( P(A \cap B) \), then apply the general addition rule.

solution_steps.text: Since independent: \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B) = 0.5 \times 0.4 = 0.20 \).
General addition rule: \( P(A \cup B) = 0.5 + 0.4 - 0.20 = 0.70 \).

problems.question_html: In a class, 55% of students own a dog and 30% own a cat. If 10% own both a dog and a cat, what is \( P(\text{dog or cat}) \)? Give your answer as a decimal.

hints.text: Use the general addition rule: \( P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \).

solution_steps.text: Apply the general addition rule: \( P(D \cup C) = P(D) + P(C) - P(D \cap C) \).
\( P(D \cup C) = 0.55 + 0.30 - 0.10 = 0.75 \). So 75% of students own at least one pet.

problems.question_html: A bag contains 6 red and 4 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both marbles are red? Express your answer as a fraction in lowest terms.

hints.text: Without replacement means the draws are dependent. Use the general multiplication rule: \( P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B|A) \).
\( P(\text{both red}) = \frac{6}{10} \cdot \frac{5}{9} = \frac{30}{90} = \frac{1}{3} \).

solution_steps.text: First draw: \( P(\text{red}_1) = \frac{6}{10} \). After removing one red marble, 5 red and 4 blue remain.
Second draw given first was red: \( P(\text{red}_2 | \text{red}_1) = \frac{5}{9} \). So \( P(\text{both red}) = \frac{6}{10} \cdot \frac{5}{9} = \frac{30}{90} = \frac{1}{3} \).

problems.question_html: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. Let \( A \) = drawing a face card (J, Q, K) and \( B \) = drawing a heart. Find \( P(A \cup B) \). Express your answer as a fraction with denominator 52.

hints.text: Find \( P(A) \), \( P(B) \), and \( P(A \cap B) \) — the face cards that are hearts (J, Q, K of hearts).

solution_steps.text: There are 12 face cards, 13 hearts, and 3 cards that are both (J, Q, K of hearts).

problems.question_html: A drawer contains 10 socks: 4 black and 6 white. Two socks are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both socks are black? Express your answer as a fraction in lowest terms.

hints.text: Without replacement makes the draws dependent. Use the general multiplication rule.
\( P(\text{both black}) = \frac{4}{10} \cdot \frac{3}{9} = \frac{12}{90} = \frac{2}{15} \).

solution_steps.text: \( P(\text{black}_1) = \frac{4}{10} \). After removing one black sock: \( P(\text{black}_2 | \text{black}_1) = \frac{3}{9} \).
\( P(\text{both black}) = \frac{4}{10} \cdot \frac{3}{9} = \frac{12}{90} = \frac{2}{15} \approx 0.133 \).

problems.question_html:
A fire station has three independent alarm systems. The probabilities that each system functions during an emergency are 0.95, 0.90, and 0.85, respectively.

(a) Find the probability that all three systems function during an emergency.

(b) Find the probability that at least one system functions during an emergency.

(c) A city regulation requires that the probability of at least one alarm functioning be at least 0.999. Does this station meet the requirement? Justify your answer.
problems.correct_answer: (a) P(all 3 work) = 0.95 × 0.90 × 0.85 = 0.72675. (b) P(at least one works) = 1 - P(none work) = 1 - (0.05)(0.10)(0.15) = 1 - 0.00075 = 0.99925. (c) No, 0.99925 < 0.999. The station does not meet the requirement.

hints.text: For part (b), use the complement: "at least one works" = 1 - "none work". The probability a system fails is 1 minus its success probability.
P(none work) = (1-0.95)(1-0.90)(1-0.85) = 0.05 × 0.10 × 0.15. Compare the result of 1 minus this to 0.999.

solution_steps.text: (a) Since independent: \( P(\text{all work}) = 0.95 \times 0.90 \times 0.85 = 0.72675 \).
(c) Since \( 0.99925 < 0.999 \), the station does not meet the regulation. The probability of at least one alarm functioning falls short by 0.00025.

problems.question_html:
Events \( C \) and \( D \) satisfy \( P(C) = 0.6 \), \( P(D) = 0.3 \), and \( P(C \cup D) = 0.72 \).

(a) Find \( P(C \cap D) \).

(b) Determine whether \( C \) and \( D \) are independent. Justify your answer.

(c) Find \( P(C|D) \) and verify it is consistent with your answer in part (b).
problems.correct_answer: (a) P(C ∩ D) = P(C) + P(D) - P(C ∪ D) = 0.6 + 0.3 - 0.72 = 0.18. (b) P(C)·P(D) = 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.18 = P(C ∩ D), so the events are independent. (c) P(C|D) = P(C ∩ D)/P(D) = 0.18/0.3 = 0.6 = P(C). Since P(C|D) = P(C), this confirms independence.

hints.text: Rearrange the general addition rule to isolate \( P(C \cap D) \).
\( P(C \cap D) = P(C) + P(D) - P(C \cup D) = 0.6 + 0.3 - 0.72 = 0.18 \). Compare this with \( P(C) \cdot P(D) \) to check independence.

solution_steps.text: (a) Rearranging the addition rule: \( P(C \cap D) = P(C) + P(D) - P(C \cup D) = 0.6 + 0.3 - 0.72 = 0.18 \).
(b) Check: \( P(C) \cdot P(D) = 0.6 \times 0.3 = 0.18 = P(C \cap D) \). Since the multiplication rule for independence holds, \( C \) and \( D \) are independent.
(c) \( P(C|D) = \frac{0.18}{0.3} = 0.6 = P(C) \). Since conditioning on \( D \) does not change the probability of \( C \), this confirms independence.

concepts.title: Introduction to Random Variables and Probability Distributions
concepts.content_html:
Introduction to Random Variables and Probability Distributions

A random variable is a variable whose numerical value is determined by the outcome of a chance process. We typically use capital letters (\( X \), \( Y \)) for random variables.

Discrete vs. Continuous Random Variables

A discrete random variable takes a countable number of values (often whole numbers). Examples:

  • The number of heads in 10 coin flips (\( X = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, 10 \))
  • The number of defective items in a shipment
  • The number of customers arriving per hour

A continuous random variable takes any value in an interval. Examples:

  • The exact weight of a randomly selected apple
  • The time until the next earthquake
  • A person's exact blood pressure

Probability Distribution of a Discrete Random Variable

A probability distribution lists every possible value of the random variable along with its probability. It can be displayed as a table or a histogram.

Example: Let \( X \) = number of goals scored by a soccer team per game.

\( x \)01234
\( P(X=x) \)0.180.340.270.150.06

Requirements for a Valid Probability Distribution

  1. Every probability must satisfy \( 0 \le P(X = x) \le 1 \).
  2. The sum of all probabilities must equal 1: \( \sum P(X = x) = 1 \).

Check for the example above: \( 0.18 + 0.34 + 0.27 + 0.15 + 0.06 = 1.00 \). \checkmark

Finding Probabilities from a Distribution

From the table above:

  • \( P(X \ge 2) = P(2) + P(3) + P(4) = 0.27 + 0.15 + 0.06 = 0.48 \)
  • \( P(X < 2) = P(0) + P(1) = 0.18 + 0.34 = 0.52 \)
  • \( P(1 \le X \le 3) = P(1) + P(2) + P(3) = 0.34 + 0.27 + 0.15 = 0.76 \)
Key Idea: A probability distribution is like a population distribution — it describes the long-run behavior of a random variable. The histogram of a discrete probability distribution shows the values on the x-axis and probabilities on the y-axis.
AP Exam Trap: When a problem asks for \( P(X > 3) \), do not include \( P(X = 3) \). Pay careful attention to strict inequality (\( > \), \( < \)) versus inclusive inequality (\( \ge \), \( \le \)). For discrete random variables, \( P(X > 3) \neq P(X \ge 3) \).

problem_sets.title: Practice: Random Variables and Probability Distributions

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a discrete random variable?

choices.text: The exact time a student spends on homework
The number of text messages a teenager sends in a day
The weight of a randomly selected newborn
The distance a javelin is thrown

hints.text: A discrete random variable takes countable values — typically whole numbers you can list.
Number of text messages is countable (0, 1, 2, 3, ...). Time, weight, and distance are continuous because they can take any value in an interval.

solution_steps.text: A discrete random variable takes countable values. The number of text messages can be 0, 1, 2, 3, ... — a countable set.
Time, weight, and distance are continuous because they can take any value within a range (e.g., 3.217 hours, 7.84 lbs).

problems.question_html:
The following table shows the probability distribution of \( X \), the number of pets owned by a randomly selected household:

\( x \)0123
\( P(X=x) \)0.300.400.20\( k \)

What is the value of \( k \)?

hints.text: All probabilities in a valid distribution must sum to exactly 1.

solution_steps.text: The probabilities must sum to 1: \( 0.30 + 0.40 + 0.20 + k = 1 \).
\( 0.90 + k = 1 \Rightarrow k = 0.10 \).

problems.question_html: Which of the following is not a valid probability distribution?

hints.text: Check two conditions: (1) every probability is between 0 and 1, and (2) all probabilities sum to 1.
Option B sums to \( 0.4 + 0.4 + 0.3 = 1.1 \neq 1 \), violating the sum requirement.

solution_steps.text: Check sums: A = 1.0 \checkmark, B = 1.1 \times, C = 1.0 \checkmark, D = 1.0 \checkmark.
Option B has probabilities summing to 1.1, which exceeds 1. This is not a valid probability distribution.

problems.question_html: A random variable \( X \) represents the number of heads when a fair coin is tossed 3 times. Which choice correctly gives \( P(X = 2) \)?

hints.text: List all 8 equally likely outcomes (HHH, HHT, HTH, ...) and count how many have exactly 2 heads.
The outcomes with exactly 2 heads are: HHT, HTH, THH — that's 3 out of 8 total. \( P(X=2) = \frac{3}{8} \).

solution_steps.text: With 3 fair coin tosses, there are \( 2^3 = 8 \) equally likely outcomes.
Outcomes with exactly 2 heads: HHT, HTH, THH — 3 outcomes. \( P(X=2) = \frac{3}{8} \).

problems.question_html: Using the completed probability distribution from Problem 2 (with \( k = 0.10 \)), find \( P(X \ge 2) \). Give your answer as a decimal.

hints.text: \( P(X \ge 2) \) means the probability that \( X \) is 2 or more. Add the appropriate probabilities.

solution_steps.text: \( P(X \ge 2) \) includes \( X = 2 \) and \( X = 3 \).

problems.question_html:
A discrete random variable \( Y \) has the following partial distribution:

\( y \)12345
\( P(Y=y) \)0.100.250.300.200.15

Find \( P(2 \le Y \le 4) \). Give your answer as a decimal.

hints.text: The inequality is inclusive (\( \le \)), so include \( Y = 2 \), \( Y = 3 \), and \( Y = 4 \).

solution_steps.text: \( P(2 \le Y \le 4) \) includes \( Y = 2, 3, 4 \).

problems.question_html:
The random variable \( W \) has the probability distribution shown below. Find \( P(W > 2) \). Give your answer as a decimal.

\( w \)12345
\( P(W=w) \)0.050.200.350.250.15

hints.text: \( P(W > 2) \) means strictly greater than 2. Do NOT include \( W = 2 \).

solution_steps.text: \( P(W > 2) \) excludes \( W = 2 \). Include only \( W = 3, 4, 5 \).

problems.question_html:
A discrete random variable \( X \) has the probability distribution:

\( x \)0123
\( P(X=x) \)0.1\( a \)0.30.2

Find the value of \( a \) and then compute \( P(X < 2) \). Give \( P(X < 2) \) as a decimal.

hints.text: First find \( a \) using the requirement that all probabilities sum to 1. Then \( P(X < 2) = P(X=0) + P(X=1) \).

problems.question_html:
A game costs $2 to play. You roll a fair six-sided die. If you roll a 6, you win $10 (net gain $8). If you roll a 1, you win $4 (net gain $2). Otherwise, you win nothing (net gain −$2).

(a) Define a random variable \( X \) for the net gain and construct its probability distribution table.

(b) Verify that your distribution is valid.

(c) Find \( P(X \ge 0) \) — the probability of not losing money.

hints.text: List all possible net gains. Rolling a 6 gives +$8, rolling a 1 gives +$2, rolling 2–5 gives −$2.
There are 3 possible values of X. Find the probability of each die outcome: P(6) = 1/6, P(1) = 1/6, P(2,3,4,5) = 4/6.

solution_steps.text: (a) Let \( X \) = net gain. Possible values: \( X = 8 \) (roll 6), \( X = 2 \) (roll 1), \( X = -2 \) (roll 2, 3, 4, 5). Distribution: \( P(X=8) = \frac{1}{6} \), \( P(X=2) = \frac{1}{6} \), \( P(X=-2) = \frac{4}{6} = \frac{2}{3} \).
(b) All probabilities are between 0 and 1. \( \frac{1}{6} + \frac{1}{6} + \frac{4}{6} = \frac{6}{6} = 1 \). Valid \checkmark

problems.question_html:
A quality-control inspector examines items from an assembly line. Let \( X \) = the number of defective items found in a random sample of 4 items. The probability distribution of \( X \) is:

\( x \)01234
\( P(X=x) \)0.65610.29160.04860.00360.0001

(a) Verify that this is a valid probability distribution.

(b) Find \( P(X \ge 1) \) — the probability of finding at least one defective item.

(c) Interpret \( P(X \ge 1) \) in the context of quality control.
problems.correct_answer: (a) All probabilities are between 0 and 1. Sum = 0.6561 + 0.2916 + 0.0486 + 0.0036 + 0.0001 = 1.0000. Valid. (b) P(X ≥ 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - 0.6561 = 0.3439. (c) There is about a 34.4% chance that a random sample of 4 items will contain at least one defective item. This means roughly 1 in 3 samples will trigger further inspection.

hints.text: For part (b), the complement approach is fastest: P(at least 1) = 1 - P(none).
P(X = 0) = 0.6561. So P(X ≥ 1) = 1 - 0.6561 = 0.3439. For part (c), interpret in context of the quality-control setting.

solution_steps.text: (a) Check: all probabilities are between 0 and 1 \checkmark. Sum: \( 0.6561 + 0.2916 + 0.0486 + 0.0036 + 0.0001 = 1.0000 \) \checkmark. Valid distribution.

(c) There is approximately a 34.4% probability that a random sample of 4 items from the assembly line will contain at least one defective item. The inspector should expect to find defects in roughly one out of every three samples.

concepts.title: Parameters of Random Variables
concepts.content_html:
Parameters of Random Variables

When we have a discrete random variable \( X \), we can calculate numerical summaries that describe its probability distribution. These summaries—the expected value (mean) and standard deviation—are called parameters because they describe the entire distribution, not just a sample.

Expected Value (Mean) of a Discrete Random Variable

The expected value of a discrete random variable \( X \) is the long-run average value of \( X \) over many repetitions. It is calculated as:

\[ \mu_X = E(X) = \sum x_i \cdot P(x_i) \]

This is a weighted average of the possible values, where each value is weighted by its probability.

Worked Example: Insurance Policy

An insurance company sells a one-year policy for $250. The policy pays $10,000 for a major claim (probability 0.005), $1,000 for a minor claim (probability 0.08), and $0 otherwise.

Let \( X \) = the company’s profit on a single policy.

Outcome\( x_i \) (Profit)\( P(x_i) \)
Major claim\( 250 - 10{,}000 = -9{,}750 \)0.005
Minor claim\( 250 - 1{,}000 = -750 \)0.08
No claim\( 250 \)0.915
\[ E(X) = (-9750)(0.005) + (-750)(0.08) + (250)(0.915) \]\[ E(X) = -48.75 + (-60) + 228.75 = 120 \]

The company expects to profit $120 per policy on average over the long run.

Standard Deviation of a Discrete Random Variable

The variance measures the average squared deviation from the mean:

\[ \text{Var}(X) = \sigma_X^2 = \sum (x_i - \mu_X)^2 \cdot P(x_i) \]

The standard deviation is the square root of the variance:

\[ \sigma_X = \sqrt{\sum (x_i - \mu_X)^2 \cdot P(x_i)} \]

Continuing the insurance example with \( \mu_X = 120 \):

\[ \sigma_X^2 = (-9750 - 120)^2(0.005) + (-750 - 120)^2(0.08) + (250 - 120)^2(0.915) \]\[ = (9870)^2(0.005) + (870)^2(0.08) + (130)^2(0.915) \]\[ = 487,084.50 + 60,552.00 + 15,463.50 = 563,100 \]\[ \sigma_X = \sqrt{563,100} \approx 750.40 \]

Linear Transformations of a Random Variable

If \( Y = aX + b \), where \( a \) and \( b \) are constants:

\[ E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b \]\[ \text{SD}(aX + b) = |a| \cdot \text{SD}(X) \]
Key Idea: Adding a constant shifts the mean but does not change the spread. Multiplying by a constant scales both the mean and the standard deviation.

Combining Independent Random Variables

If \( X \) and \( Y \) are independent random variables:

\[ E(X + Y) = E(X) + E(Y) \]\[ E(X - Y) = E(X) - E(Y) \]\[ \text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) \]\[ \text{Var}(X - Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) \]
AP Trap: Variances always add, even when subtracting random variables! The most common mistake on the AP exam is subtracting variances when computing \( \text{Var}(X - Y) \). Remember: variability never cancels out.
Key Idea: Means add or subtract as expected, but standard deviations do not add. You must work with variances, then take the square root at the end.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Parameters of Random Variables

problems.question_html: A game at a charity fundraiser costs $5 to play. The player spins a wheel and wins $20 with probability 0.10, $5 with probability 0.25, or $0 with probability 0.65. Let \( X \) = the player’s net gain (winnings minus cost). What is \( E(X) \)?

hints.text: First find the net gain for each outcome: subtract the $5 cost from each prize. Then compute \( E(X) = \sum x_i \cdot P(x_i) \).

solution_steps.text: Identify the net gain for each outcome: Win $20 → net = $20 - $5 = $15; Win $5 → net = $5 - $5 = $0; Win $0 → net = $0 - $5 = -$5.
Calculate expected value: \( E(X) = 15(0.10) + 0(0.25) + (-5)(0.65) = 1.50 + 0 - 3.25 = -1.75 \). The expected net gain is \(-\$1.75\).

problems.question_html: A discrete random variable \( X \) has mean \( \mu_X = 8 \) and standard deviation \( \sigma_X = 3 \). Define \( Y = 4X - 5 \). What are the mean and standard deviation of \( Y \)?

hints.text: Use the linear transformation rules: \( E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b \) and \( \text{SD}(aX + b) = |a| \cdot \text{SD}(X) \).
\( \mu_Y = 4(8) - 5 = 32 - 5 = 27 \). \( \sigma_Y = |4|(3) = 12 \). The additive constant does not affect the standard deviation.

solution_steps.text: Apply the mean transformation: \( \mu_Y = 4\mu_X - 5 = 4(8) - 5 = 27 \).
Apply the SD transformation: \( \sigma_Y = |4| \cdot \sigma_X = 4(3) = 12 \). Adding or subtracting a constant does not change the spread.

problems.question_html: A small bakery tracks daily revenue \( R \) and daily costs \( C \), where \( R \) and \( C \) are independent random variables with \( E(R) = 800 \), \( \text{SD}(R) = 120 \), \( E(C) = 500 \), and \( \text{SD}(C) = 80 \). Let \( P = R - C \) represent daily profit. What is \( E(P) \) and what is \( \text{SD}(P) \)?

hints.text: Expected value of a difference: \( E(R - C) = E(R) - E(C) \). For standard deviation, remember that variances add even when subtracting.

problems.question_html:
A discrete random variable \( X \) has the following probability distribution:

\( x \)0123
\( P(x) \)0.100.400.300.20

Calculate \( \text{Var}(X) \). Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: First find \( E(X) \), then use \( \text{Var}(X) = \sum (x_i - \mu)^2 \cdot P(x_i) \).

problems.question_html:
A delivery service finds that the number of packages delivered per hour follows the distribution below.

\( x \)10152025
\( P(x) \)0.200.350.300.15

Calculate the expected number of packages delivered per hour.

hints.text: Multiply each value by its probability and add the results: \( E(X) = \sum x_i \cdot P(x_i) \).

solution_steps.text: Apply the expected value formula: \( E(X) = 10(0.20) + 15(0.35) + 20(0.30) + 25(0.15) \).
\( E(X) = 2.00 + 5.25 + 6.00 + 3.75 = 17.00 \). The expected number of packages delivered per hour is 17.

problems.question_html: Independent random variables \( A \) and \( B \) have means \( \mu_A = 50 \) and \( \mu_B = 30 \), and standard deviations \( \sigma_A = 4 \) and \( \sigma_B = 3 \). What is the standard deviation of \( A - B \)?

hints.text: When combining independent random variables, variances always add—even when subtracting. Find \( \text{Var}(A - B) \) first, then take the square root.
\( \text{Var}(A - B) = \text{Var}(A) + \text{Var}(B) = 16 + 9 = 25 \). So \( \sigma_{A-B} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \).

solution_steps.text: For independent RVs, \( \text{Var}(A - B) = \text{Var}(A) + \text{Var}(B) = 4^2 + 3^2 = 16 + 9 = 25 \).
\( \sigma_{A-B} = \sqrt{25} = 5 \). Remember: variances add even when subtracting random variables.

problems.question_html: A factory produces light bulbs with a lifespan described by a random variable \( L \) with \( E(L) = 1200 \) hours and \( \text{SD}(L) = 100 \) hours. Each bulb is sold for a price (in dollars) given by \( P = 0.02L + 1 \). What is the expected selling price in dollars?

hints.text: Use linear transformation rules: \( E(aL + b) = aE(L) + b \) and \( \text{SD}(aL + b) = |a| \cdot \text{SD}(L) \).

solution_steps.text: Apply mean transformation: \( E(P) = 0.02(1200) + 1 = 25 \) dollars.
Apply SD transformation: \( \text{SD}(P) = |0.02|(100) = 2 \) dollars. The constant +1 does not affect spread.

problems.question_html: At a medical clinic, the waiting time \( W \) (in minutes) has \( E(W) = 22 \) and \( \text{SD}(W) = 8 \). The consultation time \( C \) has \( E(C) = 15 \) and \( \text{SD}(C) = 5 \). Assume \( W \) and \( C \) are independent. Let \( T = W + C \) be the total time. Calculate \( \text{SD}(T) \) to two decimal places.

hints.text: For independent random variables, \( \text{Var}(W + C) = \text{Var}(W) + \text{Var}(C) \). Then take the square root.

solution_steps.text: \( \text{Var}(T) = \text{Var}(W) + \text{Var}(C) = 64 + 25 = 89 \).
\( \text{SD}(T) = \sqrt{89} \approx 9.43 \) minutes.

problems.question_html:
A landscaping company charges customers based on lawn area. The revenue \( R \) per job has \( E(R) = 150 \) and \( \text{SD}(R) = 40 \), while the cost \( C \) per job has \( E(C) = 90 \) and \( \text{SD}(C) = 25 \). Revenue and cost are independent.

(a) Find the expected profit \( E(R - C) \) per job.

(b) Find the standard deviation of profit per job.

(c) The company adds a flat $20 fuel surcharge to each job. How does this affect the expected profit and the standard deviation of profit?
problems.correct_answer: (a) E(R - C) = 150 - 90 = $60. (b) Var(R - C) = 40^2 + 25^2 = 1600 + 625 = 2225. SD = sqrt(2225) ≈ $47.17. (c) With the $20 surcharge, the new revenue is R + 20. E(R + 20 - C) = 150 + 20 - 90 = $80. Adding a constant shifts the mean by $20 but does not change the spread, so SD remains ≈ $47.17.

hints.text: For parts (a) and (b), use combining rules for independent RVs. For part (c), the surcharge is a constant—how does adding a constant affect mean and SD?

Part (a): \( E(R - C) = 150 - 90 = 60 \). Part (b): Variances add: \( 40^2 + 25^2 = 2225 \), so \( \text{SD} = \sqrt{2225} \approx 47.17 \). Part (c): Adding $20 shifts the mean to $80 but SD stays the same at $47.17.

solution_steps.text: (b) \( \text{Var}(R - C) = \text{Var}(R) + \text{Var}(C) = 1600 + 625 = 2225 \). \( \text{SD}(R - C) = \sqrt{2225} \approx 47.17 \) dollars.

(c) New profit = \( (R + 20) - C \). \( E = 150 + 20 - 90 = 80 \). Adding a constant shifts the mean by $20 but does not change the variance or standard deviation. \( \text{SD} \) remains \( \approx 47.17 \).

problems.question_html:
A carnival game involves two independent spins. Spin 1 gives a score \( S_1 \) with \( E(S_1) = 5 \) and \( \text{SD}(S_1) = 2 \). Spin 2 gives a score \( S_2 \) with \( E(S_2) = 3 \) and \( \text{SD}(S_2) = 1.5 \). The total score is \( T = 2S_1 + S_2 \) and you win a prize if \( T > 18 \).

(a) Calculate \( E(T) \) and \( \text{SD}(T) \).

(b) Explain why we cannot simply find \( P(T > 18) \) without knowing the shape of the distribution of \( T \).
problems.correct_answer: (a) E(T) = 2E(S1) + E(S2) = 2(5) + 3 = 13. Var(T) = 4·Var(S1) + Var(S2) = 4(4) + 2.25 = 18.25. SD(T) = sqrt(18.25) ≈ 4.27. (b) Without knowing the shape of the distribution of T, we cannot calculate exact probabilities. If T were normally distributed, we could use z-scores, but we have not been told the distribution is normal. The mean and SD alone do not determine probabilities for arbitrary distributions.

hints.text: For part (a), treat \( 2S_1 \) as a linear transformation, then combine with \( S_2 \). Remember \( \text{Var}(aX) = a^2 \text{Var}(X) \).

\( E(T) = 2(5) + 3 = 13 \). \( \text{Var}(T) = 2^2(2^2) + 1.5^2 = 16 + 2.25 = 18.25 \). \( \text{SD}(T) \approx 4.27 \). For part (b), we need the shape of the distribution to calculate probabilities, not just the mean and SD.

solution_steps.text: (b) Knowing only the mean and standard deviation is not enough to calculate \( P(T > 18) \). We would need to know the shape (e.g., normal) of the distribution to convert to a z-score and use a table. Without that information, we can only describe center and spread.

concepts.title: The Binomial Distribution
concepts.content_html:
The Binomial Distribution

A binomial setting arises when we perform a fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of success. The number of successes is a binomial random variable.

The BINS Conditions

A random variable \( X \) has a binomial distribution if all four conditions are met:

  • Binary: Each trial has exactly two outcomes (success/failure).
  • Independent: The result of one trial does not affect another.
  • Number fixed: The number of trials \( n \) is fixed in advance.
  • Same probability: The probability of success \( p \) is the same for each trial.

We write \( X \sim B(n, p) \).

The Binomial Probability Formula

The probability of getting exactly \( k \) successes in \( n \) trials is:

\[ P(X = k) = \binom{n}{k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k} \]

where \( \binom{n}{k} = \frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} \) is the binomial coefficient (the number of ways to choose which \( k \) trials are successes).

Worked Example: Manufacturing Quality

A factory produces circuit boards with a 3% defect rate. In a random sample of 10 boards, what is the probability that exactly 2 are defective?

Check BINS: Binary (defective or not), Independent (assuming large production run), Number fixed (\( n = 10 \)), Same probability (\( p = 0.03 \)).

\[ P(X = 2) = \binom{10}{2}(0.03)^2(0.97)^8 \]\[ = 45 \times 0.0009 \times 0.7837 = 45 \times 0.000705 \approx 0.0317 \]

Mean and Standard Deviation of a Binomial Distribution

For \( X \sim B(n, p) \):

\[ \mu_X = np \]\[ \sigma_X = \sqrt{np(1-p)} \]

Example

If \( n = 100 \) and \( p = 0.25 \), then \( \mu = 100(0.25) = 25 \) and \( \sigma = \sqrt{100(0.25)(0.75)} = \sqrt{18.75} \approx 4.33 \).

Key Idea: The binomial formula gives the probability of exactly \( k \) successes. For "at least" or "at most" questions, you need to sum multiple binomial probabilities or use the complement rule.
AP Trap: Before using the binomial model, always verify all four BINS conditions. A common error is assuming independence when sampling without replacement from a small population. The 10% condition states that sampling without replacement is approximately independent if the sample is less than 10% of the population.
Key Idea: On the AP exam, you can use calculator notation like binompdf(n, p, k) and binomcdf(n, p, k) as long as you state the parameters. You do not need to show every term of the formula.
concepts.content_raw: The Binomial Distribution

problem_sets.title: Practice: The Binomial Distribution

problems.question_html: A pharmaceutical company tests a new allergy medication. Each patient independently has a 0.70 probability of experiencing symptom relief. In a clinical trial of 8 patients, what is the probability that exactly 6 experience relief?

hints.text: Verify BINS: Binary (relief or not), Independent (given), Number fixed (n = 8), Same probability (p = 0.70). Then apply \( P(X = 6) = \binom{8}{6}(0.70)^6(0.30)^2 \).

solution_steps.text: Check BINS conditions: Binary (relief/no relief), Independent (stated), n = 8 fixed, p = 0.70 constant. \( X \sim B(8, 0.70) \).

problems.question_html: Which of the following scenarios does not satisfy the conditions for a binomial distribution?

choices.text: Rolling a die 20 times and counting the number of sixes
Selecting 5 cards from a standard deck without replacement and counting the number of hearts
Flipping a coin 50 times and counting the number of heads
Surveying 100 randomly selected adults and asking if they support a policy (yes/no)

hints.text: Check each scenario for the BINS conditions. Look for a case where independence or constant probability is violated.

Drawing cards without replacement changes the probability of success on each draw and violates independence. For example, if the first card is a heart, the probability of a heart on the second draw changes from 13/52 to 12/51.

solution_steps.text: Check each scenario against BINS. Drawing 5 cards without replacement from a 52-card deck violates both Independence (outcomes change based on prior draws) and Same probability (the probability of drawing a heart changes after each card is removed).

Note: If the sample were less than 10% of the population (the 10% condition), we could approximate with binomial. But 5 out of 52 is about 9.6%, which is borderline—and the question says "without replacement" explicitly, highlighting the violation.

problems.question_html: A basketball player makes 80% of her free throws. She shoots 10 free throws in a game. What is the probability that she makes at least 9 of them?

hints.text: "At least 9" means \( P(X \geq 9) = P(X = 9) + P(X = 10) \). Calculate each term using the binomial formula.

problems.question_html: An airline knows that 5% of passengers do not show up for their flight. The airline sells 200 tickets for a plane with 195 seats. What is the expected number of no-shows and the standard deviation?

choices.text: \( \mu = 10, \; \sigma \approx 3.08 \)
\( \mu = 190, \; \sigma \approx 3.08 \)
\( \mu = 5, \; \sigma \approx 3.08 \)

hints.text: Let \( X \) = number of no-shows. \( X \sim B(200, 0.05) \). Use \( \mu = np \) and \( \sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} \).

problems.question_html: A multiple-choice quiz has 12 questions, each with 5 answer choices. A student guesses randomly on every question. What is the expected number of questions the student answers correctly?

hints.text: For a binomial distribution, the expected value is \( \mu = np \). What are \( n \) and \( p \) here?

solution_steps.text: This is binomial with \( n = 12 \) and \( p = 0.20 \) (1 correct out of 5 choices).
\( \mu = np = 12(0.20) = 2.4 \). The student expects to get 2.4 questions correct on average.

problems.question_html: A quality inspector checks 15 items from a production line where 10% of items are defective. Calculate the standard deviation of the number of defective items. Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Use the binomial standard deviation formula: \( \sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} \).

solution_steps.text: \( X \sim B(15, 0.10) \). \( \sigma = \sqrt{np(1-p)} = \sqrt{15 \times 0.10 \times 0.90} \).
\( \sigma = \sqrt{1.35} \approx 1.1619 \).

problems.question_html: A seed company advertises a 90% germination rate. A gardener plants 25 seeds. What is the probability that all 25 seeds germinate? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: This is \( P(X = 25) \) where \( X \sim B(25, 0.90) \). Use the formula with \( k = n = 25 \).

solution_steps.text: \( (0.90)^{25} \approx 0.0718 \). There is about a 7.2% chance all seeds germinate.

problems.question_html: In a survey, 60% of voters favor a ballot measure. A pollster randomly contacts 20 voters. What is the probability that fewer than 10 favor the measure? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: "Fewer than 10" means \( P(X \leq 9) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + \cdots + P(X = 9) \). Use binomcdf(20, 0.60, 9) on a calculator.
Using a calculator: binomcdf(20, 0.60, 9) \( \approx 0.1275 \).

solution_steps.text: Using calculator: binomcdf(20, 0.60, 9) \( \approx 0.1275 \).

problems.question_html:
A tire manufacturer claims that 95% of its tires last at least 40,000 miles. A consumer group tests 12 randomly selected tires.

(a) Verify that this is a binomial setting by checking all four conditions.

(b) Find the probability that at most 10 of the 12 tires meet the claim.

(c) If only 9 of the 12 tires lasted at least 40,000 miles, would this be surprising if the manufacturer’s claim is true? Justify using a probability calculation.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Binary: each tire either lasts 40,000+ miles or not. Independent: tires are randomly selected, and assuming the sample is less than 10% of all tires produced (10% condition). Number fixed: n = 12. Same probability: p = 0.95 for each tire. (b) P(X ≤ 10) = 1 - P(X = 11) - P(X = 12). P(X = 12) = (0.95)^12 ≈ 0.5404. P(X = 11) = C(12,11)(0.95)^11(0.05)^1 = 12(0.5688)(0.05) ≈ 0.3413. P(X ≤ 10) = 1 - 0.5404 - 0.3413 = 0.1184. (c) P(X ≤ 9) = 1 - P(X=12) - P(X=11) - P(X=10). P(X=10) = C(12,10)(0.95)^10(0.05)^2 = 66(0.5987)(0.0025) ≈ 0.0988. P(X ≤ 9) ≈ 1 - 0.5404 - 0.3413 - 0.0988 = 0.0196. Since P(X ≤ 9) ≈ 0.02, this would be surprising (less than 5% probability) if the claim is true.

hints.text: For part (a), explicitly address each letter of BINS. For parts (b) and (c), use the complement approach: \( P(X \leq k) = 1 - P(X > k) \).
\( X \sim B(12, 0.95) \). For part (b), compute \( P(X = 12) + P(X = 11) \) and subtract from 1. For part (c), compare \( P(X \leq 9) \) to 0.05 to determine if the result is surprising.

solution_steps.text: (a) B: Each tire either meets the 40,000-mile claim or does not. I: Tires are randomly selected; assuming sample < 10% of production (10% condition met). N: \( n = 12 \) fixed. S: \( p = 0.95 \) for each tire.

(c) \( P(X \leq 9) \approx 0.0196 \). Since this probability is less than 0.05, getting only 9 out of 12 would be surprisingly low if the 95% claim is true. This provides evidence against the manufacturer’s claim.

problems.question_html:
A medical screening test correctly identifies a condition 85% of the time (sensitivity). A clinic screens 20 patients who are known to have the condition.

(a) What is the probability that the test correctly identifies at least 18 of the 20 patients?

(b) The clinic is considering requiring two consecutive positive tests for a diagnosis. If the tests are independent, what is the probability that a patient with the condition tests positive on both tests?

(c) Explain why repeating the test changes the effective sensitivity and discuss the tradeoff.
problems.correct_answer: (a) X ~ B(20, 0.85). P(X ≥ 18) = P(X=18) + P(X=19) + P(X=20). P(X=20) = (0.85)^20 ≈ 0.0388. P(X=19) = C(20,19)(0.85)^19(0.15)^1 = 20(0.0456)(0.15) ≈ 0.1368. P(X=18) = C(20,18)(0.85)^18(0.15)^2 = 190(0.0536)(0.0225) ≈ 0.2293. P(X ≥ 18) ≈ 0.0388 + 0.1368 + 0.2293 = 0.4049. (b) P(both positive) = 0.85 × 0.85 = 0.7225. (c) Requiring two positive tests reduces the effective sensitivity from 85% to 72.25%. This means more patients with the condition will be missed (false negatives increase). The tradeoff is that requiring two tests typically reduces false positives (increases specificity), but at the cost of missing more true cases.

hints.text: For part (a), compute \( P(X = 18) + P(X = 19) + P(X = 20) \) using the binomial formula. For part (b), use the multiplication rule for independent events.

Part (a): \( P(X \geq 18) \approx 0.4049 \). Part (b): \( 0.85^2 = 0.7225 \). Part (c): The effective sensitivity drops from 85% to 72.25%, meaning more true cases are missed, but false positives would be reduced.

solution_steps.text: (b) For independent tests: \( P(\text{both positive}) = 0.85 \times 0.85 = 0.7225 \).

(c) Requiring two consecutive positive tests lowers the effective sensitivity from 85% to 72.25%. More patients with the condition will be missed (more false negatives). The benefit is fewer false positives (higher specificity), but the tradeoff is that the test becomes less effective at detecting true cases.

concepts.title: The Normal Distribution
concepts.content_html:
The Normal Distribution

The normal distribution is a continuous probability distribution described by its mean \( \mu \) and standard deviation \( \sigma \). Its graph is the familiar symmetric, bell-shaped curve. We write \( X \sim N(\mu, \sigma) \).

Properties of the Normal Distribution

  • Symmetric about the mean \( \mu \).
  • Mean = median = mode.
  • The total area under the curve equals 1.
  • The curve extends infinitely in both directions but never touches the horizontal axis.
  • The inflection points occur at \( \mu \pm \sigma \).

The Empirical Rule (68–95–99.7 Rule)

For any normal distribution:

  • About 68% of observations fall within \( \mu \pm 1\sigma \).
  • About 95% of observations fall within \( \mu \pm 2\sigma \).
  • About 99.7% of observations fall within \( \mu \pm 3\sigma \).

Z-Scores

A z-score tells us how many standard deviations a value is from the mean:

\[ z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \]

The standard normal distribution has \( \mu = 0 \) and \( \sigma = 1 \), written \( Z \sim N(0, 1) \).

Worked Example: SAT Scores

SAT math scores are approximately normal with \( \mu = 528 \) and \( \sigma = 117 \). What proportion of students score above 700?

\[ z = \frac{700 - 528}{117} = \frac{172}{117} \approx 1.47 \]

Using the z-table: \( P(Z < 1.47) = 0.9292 \).

\[ P(X > 700) = 1 - 0.9292 = 0.0708 \]

About 7.08% of students score above 700.

Finding Values from Percentiles

To find the value \( x \) at a given percentile, use the inverse process:

\[ x = \mu + z \cdot \sigma \]

For example, what SAT score marks the 90th percentile? From the z-table, the z-score for 0.90 is approximately 1.28.

\[ x = 528 + 1.28(117) = 528 + 149.76 \approx 678 \]
Key Idea: The z-score converts any normal distribution question into a standard normal question. Always draw a sketch, shade the region of interest, then convert to z and use the table or calculator.
AP Trap: The z-table gives the area to the left of a z-score (i.e., \( P(Z < z) \)). For "greater than" questions, remember to subtract from 1. For "between" questions, find both areas and subtract.
AP Trap: On free-response questions, you must show your work. State the distribution, draw a picture if possible, show the z-score calculation, and give the probability in context. Simply writing an answer from a calculator without showing z or stating the distribution will lose credit.

problem_sets.title: Practice: The Normal Distribution

problems.question_html: The weights of cereal boxes filled by a machine are normally distributed with \( \mu = 16.2 \) oz and \( \sigma = 0.4 \) oz. Using the empirical rule, approximately what percentage of boxes weigh between 15.4 oz and 17.0 oz?

hints.text: How many standard deviations are 15.4 and 17.0 from the mean of 16.2?
\( 16.2 - 15.4 = 0.8 = 2(0.4) = 2\sigma \). \( 17.0 - 16.2 = 0.8 = 2\sigma \). The range is \( \mu \pm 2\sigma \), which captures about 95% of the data.

solution_steps.text: By the empirical rule, about 95% of observations in a normal distribution fall within \( \mu \pm 2\sigma \).

problems.question_html: The heights of adult women in a city are normally distributed with mean \( \mu = 64.5 \) inches and standard deviation \( \sigma = 2.8 \) inches. What proportion of women are taller than 70.1 inches?

hints.text: Convert to a z-score: \( z = \frac{70.1 - 64.5}{2.8} \). Then find the area to the right of that z-score.

solution_steps.text: \( P(X > 70.1) = P(Z > 2.00) = 1 - 0.9772 = 0.0228 \). About 2.28% of women are taller than 70.1 inches.

problems.question_html: The amount of coffee dispensed by a vending machine is normally distributed with \( \mu = 8.0 \) oz and \( \sigma = 0.3 \) oz. A cup overflows if the machine dispenses more than 8.5 oz. What is the probability that a randomly selected cup overflows?

hints.text: Find the z-score for 8.5 oz and look up the area to the right.

problems.question_html: ACT composite scores are approximately normally distributed with \( \mu = 21 \) and \( \sigma = 5.2 \). A student wants to score in the top 10%. What is the minimum score needed? Round to the nearest whole number.

hints.text: Top 10% means the 90th percentile. Find the z-score for 0.90 and convert back to the original scale using \( x = \mu + z\sigma \).
The z-score for the 90th percentile is approximately 1.282. \( x = 21 + 1.282(5.2) = 21 + 6.67 = 27.67 \). Rounding up to the nearest whole number gives 28.

solution_steps.text: The 90th percentile corresponds to \( z \approx 1.282 \).
\( x = \mu + z\sigma = 21 + 1.282(5.2) = 21 + 6.67 \approx 27.67 \). Rounding to the nearest whole number: 28.

problems.question_html: The time to complete a standardized test is normally distributed with \( \mu = 52 \) minutes and \( \sigma = 8 \) minutes. What is the z-score of a student who finishes in 40 minutes?

hints.text: Use the z-score formula: \( z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma} \).
\( z = \frac{40 - 52}{8} = \frac{-12}{8} = -1.5 \). The student is 1.5 standard deviations below the mean.

solution_steps.text: A z-score of \(-1.5\) means the student finished 1.5 standard deviations faster than the average.

problems.question_html: Battery lifetimes are normally distributed with \( \mu = 500 \) hours and \( \sigma = 40 \) hours. What proportion of batteries last between 460 and 540 hours? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Convert both boundaries to z-scores and find the area between them.

problems.question_html: IQ scores are normally distributed with \( \mu = 100 \) and \( \sigma = 15 \). What IQ score marks the 25th percentile? Round to one decimal place.

hints.text: Find the z-score corresponding to a cumulative probability of 0.25 and convert to the original scale.
The z-score for the 25th percentile is approximately \(-0.674\). \( x = 100 + (-0.674)(15) = 100 - 10.11 = 89.9 \).

solution_steps.text: From the z-table, \( P(Z < -0.674) \approx 0.25 \), so \( z \approx -0.674 \).

problems.question_html: The diameter of bolts produced by a machine is normally distributed with \( \mu = 10.00 \) mm and \( \sigma = 0.05 \) mm. Bolts are rejected if their diameter is less than 9.90 mm or greater than 10.10 mm. What proportion of bolts are rejected? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Find the z-scores for both limits: \( z_1 = \frac{9.90 - 10.00}{0.05} \) and \( z_2 = \frac{10.10 - 10.00}{0.05} \). Rejected bolts are in both tails.

solution_steps.text: \( P(\text{rejected}) = P(Z < -2) + P(Z > 2) = 0.0228 + 0.0228 = 0.0456 \). About 4.56% of bolts are rejected.

problems.question_html:
A college admissions office reports that the GPAs of admitted students are normally distributed with \( \mu = 3.65 \) and \( \sigma = 0.25 \).

(a) What proportion of admitted students have a GPA above 3.90?

(b) What GPA separates the bottom 5% of admitted students from the rest?

(c) A student with a GPA of 3.15 applies. How unusual is this GPA among admitted students? Use a z-score and probability to justify your answer.
problems.correct_answer: (a) z = (3.90 - 3.65)/0.25 = 1.00. P(X > 3.90) = P(Z > 1.00) = 1 - 0.8413 = 0.1587. About 15.87% of admitted students have a GPA above 3.90. (b) The 5th percentile has z ≈ -1.645. x = 3.65 + (-1.645)(0.25) = 3.65 - 0.411 = 3.239. A GPA of about 3.24 separates the bottom 5%. (c) z = (3.15 - 3.65)/0.25 = -2.00. P(Z < -2.00) = 0.0228. A GPA of 3.15 is 2 standard deviations below the mean, and only about 2.28% of admitted students have a GPA this low or lower. This is quite unusual.

hints.text: For each part, convert between x-values and z-scores. Part (a) is a "greater than" problem. Part (b) requires working backward from a percentile. Part (c) asks you to interpret a z-score in context.
(a) \( z = 1.00 \), area to right = 0.1587. (b) 5th percentile \( z \approx -1.645 \), so \( x \approx 3.24 \). (c) \( z = -2.00 \), \( P(Z < -2) = 0.0228 \), which is very unusual.

solution_steps.text: (c) \( z = \frac{3.15 - 3.65}{0.25} = -2.00 \). \( P(Z < -2.00) = 0.0228 \). Only about 2.3% of admitted students have a GPA this low. This is quite unusual—the student’s GPA is well below typical admitted students.

problems.question_html:
A food packaging company fills bags of chips. The weight of chips per bag is normally distributed with \( \mu = 10.5 \) oz and \( \sigma = 0.4 \) oz. The company labels the bags as "10 oz."

(a) What proportion of bags contain less than the labeled amount?

(b) The company wants to reduce the proportion of underfilled bags to at most 1%. Without changing \( \sigma \), what should the new mean weight be?

(c) Alternatively, if the company keeps \( \mu = 10.5 \) oz, what maximum value of \( \sigma \) would ensure that at most 1% of bags are underfilled?

hints.text: Part (a): find \( P(X < 10) \). Parts (b) and (c): set up the equation so that the z-score for \( x = 10 \) equals \(-2.326\) (the 1st percentile z-score).

concepts.title: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem
concepts.content_html:
Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

When we take a random sample from a population and compute a statistic (like the sample mean \( \bar{x} \) or sample proportion \( \hat{p} \)), that statistic varies from sample to sample. The distribution of all possible values of the statistic is called the sampling distribution.

Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean \( \bar{x} \)

If we take random samples of size \( n \) from a population with mean \( \mu \) and standard deviation \( \sigma \):

\[ \mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu \]\[ \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \]

The quantity \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} \) is called the standard error of the mean. It decreases as \( n \) increases, meaning larger samples give more precise estimates.

The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

The Central Limit Theorem states:

  • If the population is normal, then \( \bar{x} \) is normal for any sample size.
  • If the population is not normal, then \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal when \( n \) is sufficiently large (typically \( n \geq 30 \)).

In either case: \( \bar{x} \sim N\left(\mu, \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\right) \) (exactly or approximately).

Worked Example: Grocery Checkout Times

Checkout times at a grocery store have \( \mu = 6.5 \) minutes and \( \sigma = 2.4 \) minutes (right-skewed distribution). For a random sample of \( n = 36 \) customers, what is the probability that the sample mean checkout time is less than 6 minutes?

Since \( n = 36 \geq 30 \), the CLT tells us \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal.

\[ \mu_{\bar{x}} = 6.5, \quad \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{2.4}{\sqrt{36}} = 0.4 \]\[ z = \frac{6.0 - 6.5}{0.4} = -1.25 \]\[ P(\bar{x} < 6.0) = P(Z < -1.25) = 0.1056 \]

Sampling Distribution of the Sample Proportion \( \hat{p} \)

If we take random samples of size \( n \) from a population where the true proportion is \( p \):

\[ \mu_{\hat{p}} = p \]\[ \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \]

The sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) is approximately normal when:

  • \( np \geq 10 \) (at least 10 expected successes)
  • \( n(1-p) \geq 10 \) (at least 10 expected failures)

This is called the Large Counts condition.

Worked Example: Voter Poll

Suppose 55% of voters in a state support a ballot measure (\( p = 0.55 \)). A pollster surveys \( n = 200 \) randomly selected voters. What is the probability that the sample proportion is less than 0.50?

Check conditions: \( np = 200(0.55) = 110 \geq 10 \) and \( n(1-p) = 200(0.45) = 90 \geq 10 \). ✓

\[ \mu_{\hat{p}} = 0.55, \quad \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.55(0.45)}{200}} = \sqrt{0.0012375} \approx 0.0352 \]\[ z = \frac{0.50 - 0.55}{0.0352} \approx -1.42 \]\[ P(\hat{p} < 0.50) = P(Z < -1.42) \approx 0.0778 \]
Key Idea: The sampling distribution describes the behavior of a statistic, not individual observations. The standard error shrinks by \( \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \), so quadrupling the sample size cuts the standard error in half.
AP Trap: You must check conditions before using the normal approximation. For means, state that the population is normal or that \( n \geq 30 \) (CLT). For proportions, verify \( np \geq 10 \) and \( n(1-p) \geq 10 \). Forgetting conditions costs points on the AP exam.
AP Trap: Do not confuse the standard deviation of individual observations (\( \sigma \)) with the standard error of the mean (\( \sigma / \sqrt{n} \)). On the exam, if a question asks about a single observation, use \( \sigma \). If it asks about a sample mean, use \( \sigma / \sqrt{n} \).
Key Idea: The 10% condition: If sampling without replacement, the sample should be less than 10% of the population to treat observations as independent. Always state this condition on the AP exam.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

problems.question_html: The amount of soda in cans filled at a bottling plant has \( \mu = 12.05 \) oz and \( \sigma = 0.10 \) oz. An inspector takes a random sample of \( n = 25 \) cans. What is the standard error of the sample mean?

hints.text: The standard error of the sample mean is \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \).

solution_steps.text: \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{0.10}{\sqrt{25}} = \frac{0.10}{5} = 0.02 \) oz.
The standard error (0.02 oz) is much smaller than the individual SD (0.10 oz), reflecting the increased precision from averaging 25 observations.

problems.question_html: A population has a strongly right-skewed distribution with \( \mu = 45 \) and \( \sigma = 12 \). Which of the following is true about the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) for samples of size \( n = 50 \)?

choices.text: It will be right-skewed with mean 45 and SD 12.
It will be approximately normal with mean 45 and SD 12.
It will be approximately normal with mean 45 and SD \( \approx 1.70 \).
It will be right-skewed with mean 45 and SD \( \approx 1.70 \).

hints.text: The Central Limit Theorem tells us the shape of the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) when \( n \) is large enough. What is the threshold?

Since \( n = 50 \geq 30 \), the CLT applies: \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal regardless of the population shape. \( \mu_{\bar{x}} = 45 \) and \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{12}{\sqrt{50}} \approx 1.70 \).

solution_steps.text: By the CLT, since \( n = 50 \geq 30 \), the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal even though the population is right-skewed.

problems.question_html: In a large city, 72% of residents have high-speed internet. A researcher takes a random sample of \( n = 150 \) residents. What is the probability that the sample proportion \( \hat{p} \) is between 0.68 and 0.76?

hints.text: Find \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} \), convert both boundaries to z-scores, and find the area between them.

problems.question_html: A machine fills bottles with a mean of \( \mu = 500 \) mL and \( \sigma = 8 \) mL. The quality control manager takes a sample of \( n = 16 \) bottles. Assuming the population is normally distributed, what is the probability that the sample mean is within 3 mL of the population mean?

hints.text: "Within 3 mL of the mean" means \( P(497 < \bar{x} < 503) \). Since the population is normal, \( \bar{x} \) is exactly normal for any \( n \).

solution_steps.text: Population is normal, so \( \bar{x} \sim N(500, 2) \) where \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 8/\sqrt{16} = 2 \).

problems.question_html: A large university reports that 35% of students commute to campus. A researcher surveys a random sample of \( n = 120 \) students. What is the standard error of the sample proportion \( \hat{p} \)? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Use \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \). First verify the Large Counts condition.

solution_steps.text: Check conditions: \( np = 42 \geq 10 \), \( n(1-p) = 78 \geq 10 \). Large Counts condition met.

problems.question_html: The time customers spend at an ATM has \( \mu = 3.5 \) minutes and \( \sigma = 1.8 \) minutes. For a random sample of \( n = 64 \) transactions, what is the probability that the sample mean is greater than 4.0 minutes? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Since \( n = 64 \geq 30 \), the CLT applies. Find \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} \), compute the z-score for 4.0, and find the area to the right.

solution_steps.text: By CLT (\( n = 64 \geq 30 \)): \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal. \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{1.8}{8} = 0.225 \).

problems.question_html: A state health department knows that 18% of adults smoke. In a random sample of \( n = 400 \) adults, what is the probability that fewer than 15% of the sample are smokers? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Check the Large Counts condition, find \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} \), compute the z-score for 0.15, and find the area to the left.

problems.question_html: Daily revenue at a restaurant has \( \mu = \$2{,}800 \) and \( \sigma = \$450 \). Over a random sample of \( n = 9 \) days (from a normally distributed population), what is the probability that the average daily revenue exceeds \$3{,}100? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Since the population is normal, the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) is normal for any \( n \). Find \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} \) and compute the z-score.

solution_steps.text: Population is normal, so \( \bar{x} \sim N(2800, 150) \) where \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 450/3 = 150 \).

problems.question_html:
A national poll finds that 62% of Americans support renewable energy subsidies. A news organization surveys \( n = 500 \) randomly selected Americans.

(a) Describe the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \). State and verify all necessary conditions.

(b) What is the probability that the poll finds less than 60% support?

(c) How large a sample would be needed so that the standard error of \( \hat{p} \) is at most 0.01?
problems.correct_answer: (a) Conditions: Random sample (stated). 10% condition: 500 < 10% of all Americans (yes). Large Counts: np = 500(0.62) = 310 ≥ 10 and n(1-p) = 500(0.38) = 190 ≥ 10. The sampling distribution of p-hat is approximately normal with mean 0.62 and standard error sqrt(0.62 × 0.38 / 500) = sqrt(0.0004712) ≈ 0.02171. (b) z = (0.60 - 0.62)/0.02171 ≈ -0.92. P(Z < -0.92) ≈ 0.1788. (c) Set sqrt(p(1-p)/n) ≤ 0.01. 0.62(0.38)/n ≤ 0.0001. n ≥ 0.2356/0.0001 = 2356. Need n ≥ 2356.

hints.text: For part (a), state all three conditions (Random, 10%, Large Counts) and give the mean and standard error. For part (c), solve \( \sqrt{p(1-p)/n} \leq 0.01 \) for \( n \).

solution_steps.text: (a) Random: stated. 10% condition: 500 is less than 10% of all Americans. Large Counts: \( np = 310 \geq 10 \), \( n(1-p) = 190 \geq 10 \). \( \hat{p} \) is approximately \( N(0.62, 0.02171) \).
(c) \( \sqrt{\frac{0.62(0.38)}{n}} \leq 0.01 \implies \frac{0.2356}{n} \leq 0.0001 \implies n \geq 2356 \). The organization needs at least 2,356 respondents.

problems.question_html:
A factory produces bolts whose lengths are normally distributed with \( \mu = 5.00 \) cm and \( \sigma = 0.08 \) cm. Bolts are packaged in boxes of 4.

(a) What is the probability that a single randomly selected bolt has a length greater than 5.10 cm?

(b) What is the probability that the mean length of the 4 bolts in a box exceeds 5.10 cm?

(c) Explain why the answer to part (b) is smaller than the answer to part (a).
problems.correct_answer: (a) z = (5.10 - 5.00)/0.08 = 1.25. P(X > 5.10) = P(Z > 1.25) = 1 - 0.8944 = 0.1056. (b) Since the population is normal, the sampling distribution of x-bar is normal with mean 5.00 and sigma-xbar = 0.08/sqrt(4) = 0.04. z = (5.10 - 5.00)/0.04 = 2.50. P(x-bar > 5.10) = P(Z > 2.50) = 1 - 0.9938 = 0.0062. (c) The mean of 4 bolts has a smaller standard deviation (0.04 vs. 0.08) than an individual bolt. Extreme values in individual bolts tend to cancel out when averaged, making it much less likely for the mean of 4 bolts to be far from 5.00 cm. Averaging reduces variability, so the probability of an extreme sample mean is smaller than for a single observation.

hints.text: Part (a) asks about a single bolt (use \( \sigma \)). Part (b) asks about the mean of 4 bolts (use \( \sigma / \sqrt{n} \)). Part (c): compare the two standard deviations.

(a) \( z = 1.25 \), \( P = 0.1056 \). (b) \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 0.04 \), \( z = 2.50 \), \( P = 0.0062 \). (c) Averaging reduces variability, so extreme sample means are less likely than extreme individual values.

solution_steps.text: (c) The standard error of the mean (0.04) is half the individual SD (0.08). Averaging reduces variability because extreme values in individual observations tend to cancel. This makes it much less likely for the sample mean to be far from \( \mu \).

concepts.title: Estimators
concepts.content_html:
Estimators

In statistics, we rarely know the true value of a population parameter. Instead, we use sample data to calculate a statistic that serves as our best guess — an estimator — of the unknown parameter.

Point Estimators

A point estimator is a single value computed from sample data that estimates a population parameter. The two most common point estimators on the AP exam are:

  • The sample proportion \( \hat{p} \) estimates the population proportion \( p \).
  • The sample mean \( \bar{x} \) estimates the population mean \( \mu \).

Unbiased Estimators

An estimator is unbiased if the mean of its sampling distribution equals the true parameter value. In other words, if we could take every possible sample of size \( n \) and compute the statistic for each, the average of all those statistics would equal the parameter.

Formally:

\[ E(\hat{p}) = p \quad \text{and} \quad E(\bar{x}) = \mu \]

Being unbiased means the estimator does not systematically overestimate or underestimate the parameter. Individual samples will give values above or below the true parameter, but on average, the estimator hits the target.

Variability of Estimators

Even an unbiased estimator varies from sample to sample. The variability (or spread) of an estimator describes how much the statistic fluctuates across repeated samples.

  • Larger sample sizes produce estimators with less variability — the statistic clusters more tightly around the true parameter.
  • Smaller sample sizes produce estimators with more variability — the statistic is more spread out.

An ideal estimator is both unbiased (centered on the parameter) and has low variability (tightly clustered).

Worked Example

A polling company surveys 400 randomly selected voters and finds that 52% support a ballot measure. Here:

  • The population parameter is \( p \) = the true proportion of all voters who support the measure (unknown).
  • The point estimator is \( \hat{p} = 0.52 \), computed from the sample.
  • \( \hat{p} \) is unbiased because \( E(\hat{p}) = p \).
Key Idea: A statistic is unbiased if its sampling distribution is centered at the true parameter. Unbiased does NOT mean the statistic equals the parameter for any single sample — it means it equals the parameter on average over many samples.
AP Trap: Students often confuse "unbiased" with "accurate for my sample." A single \( \hat{p} \) can be far from \( p \) and the estimator is still unbiased. Bias is a property of the method, not of a single result.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Estimators

problems.question_html: A researcher surveys 500 randomly selected adults and finds that 62% own a pet. Which of the following best describes \( \hat{p} = 0.62 \)?

choices.text: It is the population proportion of adults who own a pet.
It is a point estimator of the population proportion of adults who own a pet.
It is the parameter of interest for the study.
It is the exact proportion of all adults who own a pet.

hints.text: A statistic computed from a sample is used to estimate a population parameter. What do we call such a statistic?
\( \hat{p} = 0.62 \) is a sample proportion — a point estimator of the unknown population proportion \( p \).

solution_steps.text: The value 0.62 was calculated from a sample of 500 adults, so it is a statistic, not a parameter.
Since \( \hat{p} \) provides a single value to estimate the population proportion \( p \), it is called a point estimator of \( p \).

problems.question_html: Which of the following statements correctly describes an unbiased estimator?

choices.text: The estimator always equals the population parameter.
The mean of the estimator's sampling distribution equals the population parameter.
The estimator has the smallest possible variability among all estimators.
The estimator produces the same value for every sample of the same size.

hints.text: Think about what happens when we take many, many samples and compute the estimator each time. What does "unbiased" say about the average of all those values?
An estimator is unbiased when \( E(\text{statistic}) = \text{parameter} \). The center of the sampling distribution equals the true value.

solution_steps.text: An estimator is unbiased if the expected value (mean) of its sampling distribution equals the population parameter.
This does NOT mean it always equals the parameter — individual samples will vary. It means on average, across all possible samples, it equals the parameter.

problems.question_html: Two researchers each estimate the mean household income in a city. Researcher A uses a random sample of \( n = 50 \) and Researcher B uses a random sample of \( n = 500 \). Both use \( \bar{x} \) as their estimator. Which of the following statements is true?

choices.text: Researcher A's estimator has less variability because smaller samples are more consistent.
Both estimators have the same variability because both are unbiased.
Researcher B's estimator has less variability because larger samples produce statistics closer to the parameter.
Neither estimator's variability can be compared without knowing \( \mu \).

hints.text: Think about how sample size affects the spread of the sampling distribution.
Larger samples reduce variability. The sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) with \( n = 500 \) is narrower than with \( n = 50 \).

solution_steps.text: The variability of \( \bar{x} \) depends on \( n \). The standard deviation of the sampling distribution is \( \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \), which decreases as \( n \) increases.
Since \( n = 500 > n = 50 \), Researcher B's estimator has less variability — it is more tightly clustered around \( \mu \).

problems.question_html: A survey methodology systematically overestimates voter support for a candidate by 3 percentage points on average. Which term best describes this estimator?

choices.text: Unbiased with high variability
Biased
Unbiased with low variability
Precise but not accurate

hints.text: If the estimator systematically overestimates, does its sampling distribution center on the true parameter?
A systematic overestimate of 3 points means the expected value of the estimator is \( p + 0.03 \), not \( p \). The estimator is biased.

solution_steps.text: If the estimator overestimates by 3 points on average, then \( E(\hat{p}) = p + 0.03 \neq p \).
Since the sampling distribution is not centered on the true parameter, the estimator is biased.

problems.question_html: A quality control inspector takes a random sample of 80 widgets and finds a defect rate of \( \hat{p} = 0.045 \). The true defect rate for the production line is \( p = 0.045 \). The inspector concludes that \( \hat{p} \) is unbiased because it equaled \( p \) in this sample. Is this conclusion valid? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: no

hints.text: Bias is a property of the estimation method across many samples, not a property of a single sample result.
One sample matching the parameter is coincidence. Unbiasedness means the average of the statistic over ALL possible samples equals the parameter.

solution_steps.text: The conclusion is not valid. The fact that \( \hat{p} = p \) in one sample does not prove unbiasedness.
Unbiasedness is a property of the estimator across all possible samples: \( E(\hat{p}) = p \). A single match could be coincidence.

problems.question_html:
A researcher takes a random sample of 50 students and calculates \( \bar{x} = 72.3 \) as an estimate of the population mean test score \( \mu \). What type of estimator is \( \bar{x} = 72.3 \)?

Enter: point estimator or interval estimator.
problems.correct_answer: point estimator||point

hints.text: Consider whether \( \bar{x} = 72.3 \) gives a single value or a range of values.
A single number used to estimate a parameter is called a point estimator. A range (like a confidence interval) would be an interval estimator.

solution_steps.text: \( \bar{x} = 72.3 \) is a single numerical value used to estimate the population mean \( \mu \).
A single value that estimates a parameter is called a point estimator.

problems.question_html: In a random sample of 200 households, 134 have internet access. Calculate the point estimate \( \hat{p} \) for the proportion of all households with internet access. Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: The sample proportion is calculated as \( \hat{p} = \frac{\text{number of successes}}{\text{sample size}} \).

solution_steps.text: The point estimator for a proportion is \( \hat{p} = \frac{x}{n} \), where \( x \) is the number of successes and \( n \) is the sample size.

problems.question_html: If \( \bar{x} \) is an unbiased estimator of \( \mu \), what is the value of \( E(\bar{x}) \)? Enter your answer using the appropriate Greek letter or symbol.
problems.correct_answer: μ||mu||\mu

hints.text: Unbiased means the expected value of the estimator equals the parameter it estimates.
Since \( \bar{x} \) estimates \( \mu \) and is unbiased, \( E(\bar{x}) = \mu \).

solution_steps.text: By definition, an estimator is unbiased if \( E(\text{estimator}) = \text{parameter} \).
Since \( \bar{x} \) is an unbiased estimator of \( \mu \), we have \( E(\bar{x}) = \mu \).

problems.question_html:
A consumer advocacy group wants to estimate the proportion of defective batteries in a large shipment. A random sample of 300 batteries is tested and 18 are found to be defective.

(a) Identify the population parameter of interest and define it in context.

(b) Calculate the point estimate of the parameter.

(c) Explain what it means for \( \hat{p} \) to be an unbiased estimator of \( p \) in this context.

(d) If the sample size were increased to 1,000, describe how this would affect the variability of the point estimator. Explain why.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) The parameter of interest is p = the true proportion of all batteries in the shipment that are defective.
(b) The point estimate is p-hat = 18/300 = 0.06.
(c) If we were to take many, many random samples of 300 batteries from this shipment and compute p-hat for each, the mean of all those p-hat values would equal the true proportion p. The estimator does not systematically overestimate or underestimate the defect rate.
(d) Increasing the sample size from 300 to 1,000 would decrease the variability of p-hat. With a larger sample, the sampling distribution becomes narrower, meaning p-hat values from repeated samples would cluster more tightly around the true value p. This is because the standard deviation of the sampling distribution is sqrt(p(1-p)/n), which decreases as n increases.

hints.text: For part (a), define the parameter using context — what population and what characteristic? For part (b), use \( \hat{p} = x/n \).

For part (c), explain unbiasedness as a long-run property — over many samples, the average \( \hat{p} \) equals \( p \). For part (d), relate sample size to the formula \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{p(1-p)/n} \).

solution_steps.text: (a) The parameter is \( p \) = the true proportion of all batteries in the shipment that are defective.

(c) \( \hat{p} \) is unbiased means that if we took every possible random sample of size 300 from the shipment, the average of all the \( \hat{p} \) values would equal \( p \). On average, \( \hat{p} \) neither overestimates nor underestimates the true defect rate.

(d) Increasing the sample size to 1,000 would decrease the variability of \( \hat{p} \). The standard deviation of the sampling distribution is \( \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \), which gets smaller as \( n \) increases, so the point estimates would be more tightly clustered around \( p \).

problems.question_html:
A political pollster uses two different sampling methods to estimate the proportion \( p \) of voters who support a proposed tax increase.

  • Method A: Randomly selects 250 registered voters from the voter rolls and calls them. This method produces an unbiased estimator with standard deviation 0.031.
  • Method B: Posts an online poll on a news website. Respondents self-select to participate (\( n = 2{,}000 \)). Research has shown this method systematically overestimates support by about 5 percentage points.

(a) Define the parameter of interest in context.

(b) Identify which method produces an unbiased estimator and explain why.

(c) Method B has a larger sample size. A colleague argues this makes Method B more reliable. Evaluate this argument.

(d) Describe the ideal properties of a point estimator and explain which method comes closer to meeting them.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) The parameter of interest is p = the true proportion of all registered voters who support the proposed tax increase.
(b) Method A produces an unbiased estimator because it uses random selection, so E(p-hat_A) = p. Method B is biased because self-selection and the online format systematically overestimate support by about 5 points, so E(p-hat_B) = p + 0.05 \(
eq\) p.
(c) The colleague's argument is not valid. Although Method B has a larger sample size (n = 2,000 vs 250), which reduces variability, it is biased — it systematically overestimates by 5 points. A larger sample does not fix bias; it just produces more precise but consistently wrong estimates. Low variability without unbiasedness is like a marksman who always hits the same wrong spot.
(d) An ideal estimator is both unbiased (centered on the true parameter) and has low variability (estimates cluster tightly around the center). Method A is unbiased but has moderate variability (SD = 0.031). Method B has lower variability due to larger n, but is biased. Method A is the better choice because bias cannot be reduced by increasing sample size, whereas variability can be reduced by sampling more individuals using Method A's random sampling approach.

hints.text: For part (b), think about what random sampling guarantees versus what self-selection introduces. For part (c), consider whether a large sample size can fix a fundamental flaw in the sampling method.

Bias is a systematic error that does not decrease with larger sample size. Variability decreases with larger \( n \), but only matters if the estimator is also unbiased. An estimator that is precise but wrong is not useful.

solution_steps.text: (a) The parameter is \( p \) = the true proportion of all registered voters who support the proposed tax increase.
(b) Method A is unbiased because random selection ensures \( E(\hat{p}_A) = p \). Method B is biased because self-selection systematically overestimates, so \( E(\hat{p}_B) = p + 0.05 \neq p \).

(c) The argument is invalid. A larger sample size reduces variability but does not eliminate bias. Method B's estimates are more precise (less spread out) but consistently wrong (centered at \( p + 0.05 \)). Precision without accuracy is misleading.

(d) An ideal estimator is unbiased (centered on \( p \)) with low variability (tight clustering). Method A meets the unbiasedness criterion; its variability could be reduced by increasing the sample size. Method B fails the unbiasedness criterion, making it the inferior method overall.

concepts.title: Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions
concepts.content_html:
Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions

When we take a random sample and compute \( \hat{p} \), we get one number. But if we took a different random sample of the same size, we would get a different \( \hat{p} \). The sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) describes all possible values of \( \hat{p} \) and how often each would occur across all possible random samples of size \( n \).

Center (Mean)

The mean of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) equals the true population proportion:

\[ \mu_{\hat{p}} = p \]

This confirms that \( \hat{p} \) is an unbiased estimator of \( p \).

Spread (Standard Deviation)

The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) is:

\[ \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \]

This formula requires that the sample is drawn from an effectively infinite population (or that we sample with replacement). In practice, we check the 10% condition.

The 10% Condition

The standard deviation formula above is valid when the sample is no more than 10% of the population:

\[ n \leq 0.10N \]

When sampling without replacement from a finite population, observations are not independent. However, if the sample is small relative to the population (less than 10%), the dependence is negligible and we can treat the observations as approximately independent.

Shape: The Large Counts Condition

The sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) is approximately Normal when both:

\[ np \geq 10 \quad \text{and} \quad n(1 - p) \geq 10 \]

These are called the Large Counts conditions. They ensure there are enough expected successes and failures for the Normal approximation to be reasonable.

Putting It Together

When the conditions are met:

\[ \hat{p} \sim N\left(p, \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}\right) \]

We can then use Normal calculations (z-scores) to find probabilities involving \( \hat{p} \).

Worked Example

Suppose 30% of all adults exercise regularly (\( p = 0.30 \)). A researcher takes a random sample of \( n = 200 \) adults.

Check conditions:

  • 10% condition: The population of all adults is well over 2,000, so \( 200 \leq 0.10N \). ✓
  • Large Counts: \( np = 200(0.30) = 60 \geq 10 \) ✓ and \( n(1-p) = 200(0.70) = 140 \geq 10 \) ✓

Sampling distribution:

\[ \mu_{\hat{p}} = 0.30 \]\[ \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.30(0.70)}{200}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.21}{200}} = \sqrt{0.00105} \approx 0.0324 \]

So \( \hat{p} \) is approximately \( N(0.30, 0.0324) \).

Key Idea: The sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) has three key features: it is centered at \( p \) (unbiased), its spread decreases as \( n \) increases, and its shape is approximately Normal when the Large Counts condition is satisfied.
AP Trap: On the AP exam, you MUST check the Large Counts condition using \( np \) and \( n(1-p) \) (with the true \( p \)) for sampling distribution problems. When constructing confidence intervals (Topic 3.3), you switch to \( n\hat{p} \) and \( n(1-\hat{p}) \). Know the difference!
