problem_sets.title: Practice: Sampling Distributions for Sample Proportions

problems.question_html: In a large city, 40% of residents commute by public transit. A random sample of 150 residents is selected. What is the mean of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \)?

hints.text: The mean of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) equals the population proportion \( p \).
\( \mu_{\hat{p}} = p = 0.40 \). The mean of the sampling distribution always equals the parameter, confirming that \( \hat{p} \) is unbiased.

solution_steps.text: The mean of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) is \( \mu_{\hat{p}} = p \).
Since \( p = 0.40 \), we have \( \mu_{\hat{p}} = 0.40 \).

problems.question_html: It is known that 15% of a population carries a certain genetic marker. A researcher plans to take a random sample of 40 individuals. Which condition for using a Normal model for the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) is not met?

choices.text: The 10% condition
The Large Counts condition: \( np \geq 10 \)
The Large Counts condition: \( n(1-p) \geq 10 \)
Both Large Counts conditions are met; all conditions are satisfied.

hints.text: Calculate \( np \) and \( n(1-p) \) separately and check if each is at least 10.
\( np = 40(0.15) = 6 < 10 \). The expected number of successes is too small. The Large Counts condition for successes is not met.

solution_steps.text: Since \( np = 6 < 10 \), the Large Counts condition is not met for successes. The Normal approximation is not appropriate.

problems.question_html: A factory produces computer chips with a known defect rate of \( p = 0.08 \). A quality inspector takes a random sample of 300 chips from a day's production of 10,000 chips. What is the probability that the sample proportion of defective chips exceeds 0.10?

hints.text: First verify the conditions, then find \( \mu_{\hat{p}} \) and \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} \), compute the z-score for 0.10, and look up the probability.

problems.question_html: Suppose \( p = 0.60 \) and \( n = 50 \). Which of the following correctly describes the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \)?

choices.text: Approximately Normal with mean 0.60 and standard deviation 0.0693
Approximately Normal with mean 0.60 and standard deviation 0.0048
Skewed right with mean 0.60
Approximately Normal with mean 30 and standard deviation 3.46

hints.text: Check the Large Counts condition first, then calculate \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} \).
\( np = 30 \geq 10 \) ✓, \( n(1-p) = 20 \geq 10 \) ✓, so approximately Normal. \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.60(0.40)}{50}} = \sqrt{0.0048} \approx 0.0693 \).

solution_steps.text: Large Counts: \( np = 50(0.60) = 30 \geq 10 \) ✓ and \( n(1-p) = 50(0.40) = 20 \geq 10 \) ✓. Shape is approximately Normal.
The sampling distribution is approximately \( N(0.60, 0.0693) \).

problems.question_html: A survey finds that 25% of all households in a large country have solar panels. A random sample of \( n = 100 \) households is selected. Calculate the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \). Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Use the formula \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \).

solution_steps.text: Apply the formula: \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.25 \times 0.75}{100}} \).

problems.question_html: A school district has 800 students. A researcher takes a random sample of 120 students. Is the 10% condition satisfied? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: no

hints.text: The 10% condition requires \( n \leq 0.10N \). Calculate 10% of the population size.
\( 0.10 \times 800 = 80 \). Since \( n = 120 > 80 \), the sample is more than 10% of the population. The condition is not satisfied.

solution_steps.text: The 10% condition requires \( n \leq 0.10N \). Here \( 0.10 \times 800 = 80 \).
Since \( 120 > 80 \), the sample is more than 10% of the population, so the condition is NOT met.

problems.question_html: A national study reports that 72% of high school seniors plan to attend college. A counselor takes a random sample of 250 seniors from across the state (population well over 100,000). Calculate \( np \) for the Large Counts condition.

hints.text: Multiply the sample size by the population proportion: \( np = n \times p \).
\( np = 250 \times 0.72 = 180 \). Since \( 180 \geq 10 \), this part of the Large Counts condition is satisfied.

solution_steps.text: Since \( 180 \geq 10 \), the Large Counts condition for successes is met.

problems.question_html: If the population proportion is \( p = 0.45 \) and the sample size is \( n = 80 \), calculate \( n(1-p) \).

hints.text: Calculate \( 1 - p \) first, then multiply by \( n \).

solution_steps.text: Since \( 44 \geq 10 \), this part of the Large Counts condition is satisfied.

problems.question_html:
A national poll reports that 55% of adults support expanding renewable energy subsidies. A local news station wants to check whether their viewing area differs from the national figure. They take a simple random sample of 400 adults from their viewing area (population approximately 500,000).

(a) State the population parameter of interest and define it in context.

(b) Verify that the conditions for the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) to be approximately Normal are met.

(c) Describe the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \), including shape, center, and spread.

(d) Find the probability that the sample proportion \( \hat{p} \) is less than 0.50. Show your work.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) The parameter of interest is p = the true proportion of all adults in the viewing area who support expanding renewable energy subsidies.
(b) Random: The sample is a simple random sample. ✓
10% condition: n = 400 ≤ 0.10(500,000) = 50,000. ✓
Large Counts: np = 400(0.55) = 220 ≥ 10 ✓ and n(1-p) = 400(0.45) = 180 ≥ 10 ✓.
All conditions are met.
(c) The sampling distribution of p-hat is approximately Normal with mean μ_p-hat = 0.55 and standard deviation σ_p-hat = sqrt(0.55 × 0.45 / 400) = sqrt(0.00061875) ≈ 0.0249.
(d) z = (0.50 - 0.55) / 0.0249 = -0.05 / 0.0249 ≈ -2.01. P(p-hat < 0.50) = P(Z < -2.01) ≈ 0.0222. There is about a 2.2% chance of getting a sample proportion below 0.50 if the true proportion is 0.55.

hints.text: For part (b), check three conditions: random sampling, 10% condition, and Large Counts. For part (d), convert to a z-score using the mean and SD you found.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( p \) = the true proportion of all adults in the viewing area who support expanding renewable energy subsidies.
(c) Shape: approximately Normal (conditions met). Center: \( \mu_{\hat{p}} = 0.55 \). Spread: \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.55(0.45)}{400}} = \sqrt{0.00061875} \approx 0.0249 \).

problems.question_html:
A medical researcher knows that 12% of adults in a large country have Type 2 diabetes. She takes a simple random sample of 500 adults for a health study.

(a) Verify that the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \) is approximately Normal.

(b) Calculate the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p} \).

(c) Find the probability that the sample proportion is between 0.09 and 0.15.

(d) The researcher's colleague takes a different random sample of only 60 adults. Without doing calculations, explain how the colleague's sampling distribution would differ in shape, center, and spread.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Random: SRS stated ✓. 10% condition: The country is large, so 500 is well under 10% of the population ✓. Large Counts: np = 500(0.12) = 60 ≥ 10 ✓ and n(1-p) = 500(0.88) = 440 ≥ 10 ✓. The sampling distribution is approximately Normal.
(b) Mean: μ_p-hat = p = 0.12. SD: σ_p-hat = sqrt(0.12 × 0.88 / 500) = sqrt(0.0002112) ≈ 0.01453.
(c) z_lower = (0.09 - 0.12)/0.01453 ≈ -2.07. z_upper = (0.15 - 0.12)/0.01453 ≈ 2.07. P(-2.07 < Z < 2.07) = P(Z < 2.07) - P(Z < -2.07) ≈ 0.9808 - 0.0192 = 0.9616. About 96.2% probability.
(d) Center: The mean would still be 0.12 (p-hat is still unbiased regardless of sample size). Spread: The standard deviation would be larger because n is smaller — sqrt(0.12 × 0.88 / 60) ≈ 0.0420, nearly three times as large. Shape: np = 60(0.12) = 7.2 < 10, so the Large Counts condition is NOT met. The sampling distribution would be right-skewed rather than approximately Normal.

hints.text: For part (c), convert both boundary values to z-scores and find the area between them. For part (d), think about what happens to each of the three properties (shape, center, spread) as \( n \) decreases.
\( \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{0.12(0.88)/500} \approx 0.01453 \). For the colleague's sample: \( np = 60(0.12) = 7.2 < 10 \), so Large Counts fails — the shape would not be Normal.

solution_steps.text: (a) Random ✓. 10% condition: \( 500 \leq 0.10N \) for a large country ✓. Large Counts: \( np = 60 \geq 10 \) ✓, \( n(1-p) = 440 \geq 10 \) ✓. Approximately Normal.

(d) Center: still \( 0.12 \) (unbiased). Spread: larger — \( \sigma_{\hat{p}} = \sqrt{0.12(0.88)/60} \approx 0.042 \). Shape: \( np = 7.2 < 10 \), so Large Counts fails; the distribution would be right-skewed, not Normal.

concepts.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion
concepts.content_html:
Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter based on sample data. For a population proportion \( p \), the confidence interval takes the form:

\[ \hat{p} \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}} \]

where \( \hat{p} \) is the sample proportion, \( n \) is the sample size, and \( z^* \) is the critical value corresponding to the desired confidence level.

Common Critical Values

Confidence Level\( z^* \)
90%1.645
95%1.960
99%2.576

The Margin of Error

The margin of error (ME) is the amount added and subtracted from \( \hat{p} \):

\[ ME = z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}} \]

A smaller margin of error gives a more precise estimate. The margin of error decreases when:

  • The sample size \( n \) increases
  • The confidence level decreases (smaller \( z^* \))

Conditions for the Confidence Interval

Before constructing a confidence interval for \( p \), you must verify three conditions:

  1. Random: The data come from a random sample or randomized experiment.
  2. 10% condition (Independence): \( n \leq 0.10N \), where \( N \) is the population size.
  3. Large Counts: \( n\hat{p} \geq 10 \) and \( n(1 - \hat{p}) \geq 10 \).
AP Trap: For confidence intervals, the Large Counts condition uses \( \hat{p} \) (the sample proportion), NOT \( p \) (the population proportion). This is because we don't know \( p \) — that's what we're trying to estimate! Compare this to Topic 3.2 where we used \( p \) because it was known.

Interpreting a Confidence Interval

The correct interpretation follows a specific template:

"We are [C]% confident that the true proportion of [context] is between [lower bound] and [upper bound]."

This means: if we repeated this sampling procedure many times and constructed a confidence interval each time, approximately C% of those intervals would contain the true proportion \( p \).

AP Trap: NEVER say "there is a [C]% probability that \( p \) is in the interval." The parameter \( p \) is fixed — it either is or isn't in the interval. The confidence level describes the procedure, not the probability for a specific interval.

Worked Example

A consumer group surveys 600 randomly selected shoppers and finds that 408 prefer online shopping. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion of shoppers who prefer online shopping.

Step 1: Calculate \( \hat{p} \)

\[ \hat{p} = \frac{408}{600} = 0.68 \]

Step 2: Check conditions

  • Random: stated ✓
  • 10% condition: 600 is less than 10% of all shoppers ✓
  • Large Counts: \( 600(0.68) = 408 \geq 10 \) ✓ and \( 600(0.32) = 192 \geq 10 \) ✓

Step 3: Calculate the interval

\[ ME = 1.960 \sqrt{\frac{0.68(0.32)}{600}} = 1.960 \sqrt{0.000363} = 1.960(0.01905) \approx 0.0373 \]\[ 0.68 \pm 0.0373 = (0.6427, 0.7173) \]

Step 4: Interpret

We are 95% confident that the true proportion of all shoppers who prefer online shopping is between 0.643 and 0.717.

Key Idea: The confidence interval formula is \( \text{point estimate} \pm \text{margin of error} \). The margin of error captures the uncertainty due to sampling variability. Wider intervals (higher confidence or smaller \( n \)) mean more certainty but less precision.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

problems.question_html: A random sample of 250 college students reveals that 175 use a budgeting app. What is the margin of error for a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion of college students who use a budgeting app?

hints.text: First find \( \hat{p} = 175/250 \), then use \( ME = z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} \) with \( z^* = 1.960 \).

solution_steps.text: The margin of error is approximately 0.0569.

problems.question_html: Which of the following is the correct interpretation of a 90% confidence interval of (0.42, 0.58) for the proportion of voters who support a bond measure?

choices.text: There is a 90% probability that the true proportion is between 0.42 and 0.58.
90% of all voters support the bond measure at a rate between 42% and 58%.
We are 90% confident that the true proportion of voters who support the bond measure is between 0.42 and 0.58.
In 90% of all samples, exactly 50% of voters will support the bond measure.

hints.text: The correct interpretation uses the phrase "we are [C]% confident" and references the true proportion in context.
Never say "there is a 90% probability." The parameter is fixed. We say "we are 90% confident" because the method captures the true proportion 90% of the time across many samples.

solution_steps.text: The correct interpretation is: "We are 90% confident that the true proportion of voters who support the bond measure is between 0.42 and 0.58."
This means if we repeated the procedure many times, about 90% of the resulting intervals would capture the true proportion \( p \).

problems.question_html: A health organization surveys 1,200 randomly selected adults and finds that 324 have been vaccinated against the flu this season. Which of the following is the 95% confidence interval for the true proportion of adults vaccinated?

hints.text: Calculate \( \hat{p} = 324/1200 \), then the margin of error using \( z^* = 1.960 \).

solution_steps.text: Check conditions: Random ✓. 10% ✓ (adult population far exceeds 12,000). Large Counts: \( 1200(0.27) = 324 \geq 10 \) ✓, \( 1200(0.73) = 876 \geq 10 \) ✓.

problems.question_html: A researcher wants a 95% confidence interval for a proportion with a margin of error no larger than 0.03. Using a planning value of \( \hat{p} = 0.5 \), what is the minimum sample size needed?

choices.text: 1,068 (round up to 1,068)

hints.text: Set up the equation \( ME = z^*\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} \leq 0.03 \) and solve for \( n \).

solution_steps.text: Round up: \( n = 1{,}068 \). Always round up for sample size to ensure the margin of error does not exceed the target.

problems.question_html: A researcher constructs a 95% confidence interval and gets (0.31, 0.45). What is the point estimate \( \hat{p} \)?

hints.text: The point estimate is the center of the confidence interval. How do you find the center of two numbers?

solution_steps.text: The point estimate \( \hat{p} \) is the midpoint of the confidence interval.

problems.question_html: What is the critical value \( z^* \) used for a 99% confidence interval?

hints.text: For a 99% confidence interval, the critical value leaves 0.5% in each tail of the standard Normal distribution.
The common critical values are: 90% → 1.645, 95% → 1.960, 99% → 2.576.

solution_steps.text: A 99% confidence level means 1% total is in the tails, so 0.5% in each tail.
The z-value that leaves 0.005 in the upper tail is \( z^* = 2.576 \).

problems.question_html: A confidence interval for a proportion is (0.52, 0.68). Calculate the margin of error.

hints.text: The margin of error is the distance from the point estimate to either endpoint of the interval.

solution_steps.text: The margin of error is half the width of the confidence interval.

problems.question_html: In the confidence interval formula \( \hat{p} \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}} \), the expression \( \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p})}{n}} \) is called the __________.
problems.correct_answer: standard error||SE

hints.text: This expression estimates the standard deviation of \( \hat{p} \) using sample data. What is the name for an estimated standard deviation?
When we replace the parameter \( p \) with the statistic \( \hat{p} \) in the standard deviation formula, the result is called the standard error.

solution_steps.text: The standard deviation of \( \hat{p} \) is \( \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \), which uses the unknown \( p \).
When we substitute \( \hat{p} \) for \( p \), we get \( \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}} \), which is called the standard error (SE).

problems.question_html:
A city council wants to estimate the proportion of residents who support building a new community center. A simple random sample of 500 residents is surveyed, and 320 express support. The population of the city is 85,000.

(a) State the parameter of interest in context.

(b) Check all conditions for constructing a one-sample \( z \)-interval for \( p \).

(c) Construct a 95% confidence interval for \( p \). Show all work.

(d) Interpret the interval in context.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) p = the true proportion of all residents of the city who support building a new community center.
(b) Random: The sample is a simple random sample ✓. 10% condition: n = 500 ≤ 0.10(85,000) = 8,500 ✓. Large Counts: n*p-hat = 500(0.64) = 320 ≥ 10 ✓ and n(1 - p-hat) = 500(0.36) = 180 ≥ 10 ✓. All conditions are met.
(c) p-hat = 320/500 = 0.64. SE = sqrt(0.64 × 0.36 / 500) = sqrt(0.0004608) ≈ 0.02147. ME = 1.960 × 0.02147 ≈ 0.04208. CI: 0.64 ± 0.042 = (0.598, 0.682).
(d) We are 95% confident that the true proportion of all city residents who support building a new community center is between 0.598 and 0.682.

hints.text: Follow the 4-step process: State the parameter, Plan (check conditions), Do (compute the interval), Conclude (interpret in context).

solution_steps.text: State: \( p \) = the true proportion of all city residents who support building a new community center.
Conclude: We are 95% confident that the true proportion of all city residents who support building a new community center is between 0.598 and 0.682.

problems.question_html:
A pharmaceutical company tests a new allergy medication. In a random sample of 800 allergy sufferers, 592 report symptom relief after taking the medication.

(a) Construct a 90% confidence interval for the true proportion of allergy sufferers who would experience relief.

(b) The company's competitor claims that their existing medication provides relief for 70% of users. Based on your confidence interval, is there evidence that the new medication has a different relief rate? Explain.

(c) If the company wanted a 99% confidence interval instead, how would the interval change? Explain without recalculating.

(d) How large a sample would be needed to estimate the relief rate within \( \pm 0.02 \) at 95% confidence, using the current \( \hat{p} \) as a planning value?
problems.correct_answer:
(a) State: p = the true proportion of all allergy sufferers who experience relief from the new medication.
Plan: Random ✓. 10%: 800 is well under 10% of all allergy sufferers ✓. Large Counts: 800(0.74) = 592 ≥ 10 ✓, 800(0.26) = 208 ≥ 10 ✓.
Do: p-hat = 592/800 = 0.74. SE = sqrt(0.74 × 0.26 / 800) = sqrt(0.0002405) ≈ 0.01551. ME = 1.645 × 0.01551 ≈ 0.02551. CI: (0.74 - 0.0255, 0.74 + 0.0255) = (0.7145, 0.7655).
Conclude: We are 90% confident that the true proportion of allergy sufferers who experience relief is between 0.715 and 0.766.
(b) The competitor's claim of 0.70 is NOT in the 90% CI (0.715, 0.766). Since 0.70 falls below the interval, there is convincing evidence that the new medication's relief rate differs from (and appears higher than) 70%.
(c) A 99% CI uses a larger z* (2.576 instead of 1.645), so the margin of error would increase. The interval would be wider, providing less precision but more confidence.
(d) n = (z*/ME)^2 × p-hat(1-p-hat) = (1.960/0.02)^2 × 0.74 × 0.26 = 9604 × 0.1924 ≈ 1847.8. Round up to n = 1,848.

hints.text: For part (a), use \( z^* = 1.645 \) for a 90% interval. For part (b), check whether 0.70 falls inside your interval.
\( \hat{p} = 0.74 \). \( SE \approx 0.01551 \). 90% CI: \( (0.715, 0.766) \). Since 0.70 is below this interval, there is evidence the new medication differs from the competitor's 70% rate.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( \hat{p} = 592/800 = 0.74 \). Conditions: Random ✓, 10% ✓, Large Counts: \( 592 \geq 10 \) and \( 208 \geq 10 \) ✓.
(b) The claimed value 0.70 is not in (0.715, 0.766), so there is convincing evidence that the new medication's relief rate differs from 70%.
(c) A 99% interval would use \( z^* = 2.576 \), which increases the margin of error. The interval would be wider.

concepts.title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval
concepts.content_html:
Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

Once we have a confidence interval, we can use it to evaluate claims about a population proportion. The logic is straightforward:

The Decision Rule

  • If the claimed value of \( p \) falls inside the confidence interval, the sample data is consistent with the claim. We do not have convincing evidence against it.
  • If the claimed value of \( p \) falls outside the confidence interval, we have convincing evidence against the claim at the corresponding confidence level.

Why This Works

A confidence interval contains all plausible values of the parameter given the observed data. If a claimed value is plausible (inside the interval), we cannot reject it. If it is implausible (outside the interval), we have evidence it is wrong.

Worked Example 1: Claim Supported

A company claims that 80% of its customers are satisfied. A 95% confidence interval from a random sample is (0.76, 0.84). Since 0.80 is inside the interval, the data is consistent with the company's claim. We do not have convincing evidence that the true satisfaction rate differs from 80%.

Worked Example 2: Claim Contradicted

A politician claims that a majority (more than 50%) of voters support a policy. A 95% confidence interval is (0.43, 0.51). Since every value below 0.50 is plausible and 0.50 itself is barely inside the interval, the data does not provide convincing evidence that a majority supports the policy. Many plausible values of \( p \) are below 0.50.

Connecting to Hypothesis Tests

There is a direct link between confidence intervals and two-sided hypothesis tests:

  • A 95% confidence interval that does not contain \( p_0 \) corresponds to rejecting \( H_0: p = p_0 \) at the \( \alpha = 0.05 \) level.
  • A 95% confidence interval that does contain \( p_0 \) corresponds to failing to reject \( H_0 \) at \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
Key Idea: A confidence interval provides a range of plausible values. If a claimed parameter value is in the interval, the data does not contradict the claim. If it is outside the interval, the data provides evidence against the claim.
AP Trap: "Consistent with the claim" does NOT mean "proves the claim is true." The confidence interval shows the data is compatible with the claim, but many other values are also plausible. Similarly, failing to reject a claim is not the same as accepting it.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval

problems.question_html: A manufacturer claims that 90% of its light bulbs last at least 1,000 hours. A consumer group constructs a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion and gets (0.84, 0.91). Which conclusion is most appropriate?

choices.text: The data proves the manufacturer's claim is true.
The data provides convincing evidence that the true proportion is less than 0.90.
The data is consistent with the manufacturer's claim because 0.90 is within the confidence interval.
The data is inconsistent with any claim because the interval is too wide.

hints.text: Check whether the claimed value of 0.90 falls inside or outside the interval (0.84, 0.91).
Since 0.90 is inside (0.84, 0.91), the data is consistent with the claim. We do not have convincing evidence against it.

solution_steps.text: The claimed value is \( p = 0.90 \). The 95% confidence interval is (0.84, 0.91).
Since 0.90 falls within the interval, the data is consistent with the manufacturer's claim. Note: this does not prove the claim — it simply means the data does not contradict it.

problems.question_html: A school board claims that at least 75% of parents support a new homework policy. A 95% confidence interval for the true proportion of supportive parents is (0.68, 0.73). What can be concluded?

choices.text: The data supports the school board's claim because the interval is close to 0.75.
The data provides convincing evidence that the true proportion is less than 0.75, contradicting the claim.
Nothing can be concluded because the interval does not include exactly 0.75.
The claim is proven false because \( \hat{p} < 0.75 \).

hints.text: The claim is that \( p \geq 0.75 \). Check whether 0.75 (or any value ≥ 0.75) is in the interval.
The entire interval (0.68, 0.73) is below 0.75. Since no plausible value reaches 0.75, there is convincing evidence against the claim.

solution_steps.text: The claim is \( p \geq 0.75 \). The 95% CI is (0.68, 0.73).
The upper bound of the interval (0.73) is below the claimed value (0.75). Every plausible value of \( p \) is below 0.75, so there is convincing evidence that the true proportion is less than 75%.

problems.question_html: A nonprofit claims that 1 in 3 households in a region donate to charity. A researcher constructs a 95% confidence interval and gets (0.28, 0.36). Which of the following is the best conclusion?

choices.text: The claim is proven true because \( \frac{1}{3} \approx 0.333 \) is near the center of the interval.
The data is consistent with the claim because \( 0.333 \) is within the interval, but many other values are also plausible.
The data disproves the claim because the interval includes values other than \( 0.333 \).
No conclusion is possible because the interval is too wide.

hints.text: Check if \( 1/3 \approx 0.333 \) falls inside the interval (0.28, 0.36).

\( 0.333 \) is inside the interval, so the data is consistent with the claim. However, the interval also includes values as low as 0.28 and as high as 0.36, so the claim is not proven — it is merely plausible.

solution_steps.text: The claim is \( p = 1/3 \approx 0.333 \). The 95% CI is (0.28, 0.36).

Since 0.333 is inside the interval, the data is consistent with the claim. However, many other values (from 0.28 to 0.36) are also plausible. The confidence interval does not prove the claim — it shows the claim is one of many plausible values.

problems.question_html: Two competing claims are made about the proportion of registered voters who favor stricter gun laws: Claim A says \( p = 0.60 \) and Claim B says \( p = 0.50 \). A 95% confidence interval from a random sample is (0.53, 0.61). Which claims are consistent with the data?

choices.text: Only Claim A
Only Claim B
Both Claim A and Claim B
Claim A is consistent with the data; Claim B is not.

hints.text: Check whether each claimed value (0.60 and 0.50) falls inside the interval (0.53, 0.61).
\( 0.60 \) is inside (0.53, 0.61) ✓. \( 0.50 \) is outside (below 0.53) ✗. So Claim A is consistent with the data, but Claim B is not.

solution_steps.text: Check Claim A: \( 0.60 \) is in (0.53, 0.61) ✓ — consistent.
Check Claim B: \( 0.50 < 0.53 \), so 0.50 is outside the interval ✗ — there is convincing evidence against this claim.
Claim A is consistent with the data; Claim B is not supported.

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for the proportion of adults who exercise daily is (0.22, 0.34). A health official claims that exactly 25% of adults exercise daily. Based on this interval, is the claim plausible? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: yes

hints.text: Check whether 0.25 falls inside the interval (0.22, 0.34).
Since 0.25 is between 0.22 and 0.34, it is within the confidence interval. The claim is plausible — the data is consistent with it.

solution_steps.text: The claimed value is \( p = 0.25 \). The 95% CI is (0.22, 0.34).
Since \( 0.22 < 0.25 < 0.34 \), the claimed value is inside the interval. The data is consistent with the claim, so yes, it is plausible.

problems.question_html: A 99% confidence interval for the proportion of students who prefer online classes is (0.55, 0.67). A dean claims that fewer than half of students prefer online classes. Does the interval support the dean's claim? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: no

hints.text: The dean claims \( p < 0.50 \). Is any value below 0.50 in the interval?
The entire interval (0.55, 0.67) is above 0.50. No plausible value is below 0.50, so the data contradicts the dean's claim.

solution_steps.text: The dean claims \( p < 0.50 \). The 99% CI is (0.55, 0.67).

The lower bound (0.55) is above 0.50, so all plausible values of \( p \) exceed 0.50. The data does not support the dean's claim — in fact, it provides convincing evidence that a majority prefers online classes.

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for the proportion of households with at least one pet is (0.61, 0.69). Is the value \( p = 0.70 \) plausible based on this interval? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: no

hints.text: Is 0.70 between 0.61 and 0.69?
\( 0.70 > 0.69 \), so 0.70 is outside the upper bound of the confidence interval. It is not a plausible value.

solution_steps.text: The 95% CI is (0.61, 0.69). The value 0.70 is above the upper bound.
Since 0.70 is outside the interval, it is not a plausible value for \( p \). There is convincing evidence that the true proportion is less than 0.70.

problems.question_html: A 90% confidence interval for the proportion of commuters who carpool is (0.14, 0.22). Would a 95% confidence interval computed from the same data be more likely or less likely to contain the value \( p = 0.12 \)? Enter more likely or less likely.
problems.correct_answer: more likely

hints.text: How does the width of the interval change as the confidence level increases?
A 95% CI is wider than a 90% CI (larger \( z^* \)). A wider interval is more likely to include values near the edges, like 0.12, which is just below the current lower bound of 0.14.

solution_steps.text: A 95% confidence interval uses a larger critical value (\( z^* = 1.960 \) vs \( 1.645 \)), producing a wider interval.
Since \( p = 0.12 \) is just below the 90% CI lower bound of 0.14, the wider 95% interval is more likely to extend far enough to include 0.12.

problems.question_html:
A marketing team claims that at least 40% of consumers recognize their brand. To test this, they commission a survey of 600 randomly selected consumers from their target market (population over 2 million). The survey finds that 222 consumers recognize the brand.

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true proportion of consumers who recognize the brand.

(b) Based on the confidence interval, is the marketing team's claim justified? Explain your reasoning.

(c) A rival company claims that fewer than 35% of consumers recognize the brand. Does the confidence interval provide evidence for or against this claim?

(d) Explain why "the data is consistent with the claim" is a different statement than "the data proves the claim."
problems.correct_answer:
(a) State: p = the true proportion of all consumers in the target market who recognize the brand.
Plan: Random ✓. 10%: 600 ≤ 0.10(2,000,000) ✓. Large Counts: 600(0.37) = 222 ≥ 10 ✓, 600(0.63) = 378 ≥ 10 ✓.
Do: p-hat = 222/600 = 0.37. SE = sqrt(0.37 × 0.63 / 600) ≈ 0.01971. ME = 1.960 × 0.01971 ≈ 0.03863. CI: (0.37 - 0.039, 0.37 + 0.039) = (0.331, 0.409).
Conclude: We are 95% confident the true proportion is between 0.331 and 0.409.
(b) The claim is p ≥ 0.40. The CI is (0.331, 0.409). While 0.40 is inside the interval (so the claim is plausible), most of the interval falls below 0.40. The claim is not well-supported — the data is only barely consistent with it, and values below 0.40 are also highly plausible.
(c) The rival claims p < 0.35. Since the interval includes values both below and above 0.35 (0.331 to 0.409), we do not have convincing evidence for or against this claim at the 95% level. The value 0.35 is plausible.
(d) "Consistent with the claim" means the claimed value is one of many plausible values in the CI. It does not rule out other values. "Proves the claim" would mean we know the exact parameter value, which a CI cannot do — it only narrows the range of plausible values.

hints.text: For part (a), compute \( \hat{p} = 222/600 \) and build the interval. For parts (b) and (c), check whether each claimed value falls inside or outside.
\( \hat{p} = 0.37 \). 95% CI: (0.331, 0.409). For part (b), 0.40 is in the interval but near the upper end. For part (c), 0.35 is also in the interval.

solution_steps.text: (b) The claim \( p \geq 0.40 \) is barely plausible — 0.40 is in the interval, but most plausible values are below 0.40. The claim is not strongly supported.
(c) The rival's claim \( p < 0.35 \) is also not conclusively supported or refuted. The value 0.35 is inside the interval, so we do not have convincing evidence that \( p < 0.35 \).
(d) "Consistent" means the claimed value is plausible (inside the CI), but so are many other values. A CI cannot prove a specific value — it only identifies a range of plausible values.

problems.question_html:
A national education report claims that 65% of high school students feel prepared for college. A state education board suspects the proportion in their state is different. They survey 450 randomly selected high school seniors in the state and construct a 95% confidence interval of (0.58, 0.66).

(a) State the claim being evaluated and the parameter in context.

(b) Does the confidence interval provide convincing evidence that the proportion in this state differs from the national claim of 0.65? Explain.

(c) Suppose the confidence interval had been (0.58, 0.63) instead. Would your conclusion change? Explain.

(d) A colleague suggests using a 99% confidence interval to make a stronger case. Explain why a higher confidence level does not necessarily produce stronger evidence against a claim.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) The claim is that p = 0.65, where p = the true proportion of all high school seniors in the state who feel prepared for college.
(b) The 95% CI is (0.58, 0.66). Since 0.65 is inside this interval, the data is consistent with the national claim. There is not convincing evidence that the state proportion differs from 0.65.
(c) If the CI were (0.58, 0.63), then 0.65 would fall outside (above) the interval. We would then have convincing evidence that the proportion in this state is less than the national figure of 0.65. Yes, the conclusion would change.
(d) A 99% CI is wider than a 95% CI. A wider interval is MORE likely to contain the claimed value, making it HARDER to find evidence against the claim. Higher confidence means a wider net — you include more values as plausible, reducing the chance of catching a difference. Stronger evidence comes from larger samples (narrower intervals), not higher confidence levels.

hints.text: For part (b), check if 0.65 is in (0.58, 0.66). For part (c), check if 0.65 is in (0.58, 0.63). For part (d), think about what happens to the interval width as confidence increases.
0.65 is in (0.58, 0.66) → consistent. 0.65 is NOT in (0.58, 0.63) → evidence against. A 99% CI is wider, making it harder to exclude any particular value.

solution_steps.text: (a) Claim: \( p = 0.65 \). Parameter: \( p \) = the true proportion of all high school seniors in the state who feel prepared for college.
(b) \( 0.65 \in (0.58, 0.66) \), so the data is consistent with the claim. No convincing evidence of a difference.
(c) \( 0.65 \notin (0.58, 0.63) \), so there would be convincing evidence that the state proportion is less than 0.65. The conclusion changes.

(d) A 99% CI is wider (larger \( z^* \)), so it includes more values as plausible. This makes it harder to exclude a claimed value. Higher confidence does not mean stronger evidence — it means a wider range of plausible values.

concepts.title: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion
concepts.content_html:
Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

A significance test (hypothesis test) is a formal procedure for using sample data to decide between two competing claims about a population parameter.

The Hypotheses

Every significance test starts with two hypotheses:

  • Null hypothesis \( H_0 \): A statement of "no change" or "no difference." For a proportion, it takes the form \( H_0: p = p_0 \), where \( p_0 \) is the claimed value.
  • Alternative hypothesis \( H_a \): The claim we are looking for evidence to support. It takes one of three forms:
\[ H_a: p < p_0 \quad \text{(one-sided, left)} \]\[ H_a: p > p_0 \quad \text{(one-sided, right)} \]\[ H_a: p \neq p_0 \quad \text{(two-sided)} \]

Choosing One-Sided vs. Two-Sided

  • Use a one-sided alternative when you have a specific direction in mind before seeing the data. For example, "we suspect the proportion has increased" → \( H_a: p > p_0 \).
  • Use a two-sided alternative when you want to detect a difference in either direction. For example, "we want to know if the proportion has changed" → \( H_a: p \neq p_0 \).

The Significance Level \( \alpha \)

The significance level \( \alpha \) is the threshold for deciding when the evidence is strong enough to reject \( H_0 \). Common values are \( \alpha = 0.05 \) and \( \alpha = 0.01 \).

\( \alpha \) represents the probability of making a Type I error — rejecting \( H_0 \) when it is actually true (a false positive). A smaller \( \alpha \) means stricter evidence is required.

Important Rules for Writing Hypotheses

  1. Hypotheses are always about the population parameter \( p \), never about the sample statistic \( \hat{p} \).
  2. The null hypothesis always uses \( = \) (not \( \leq \) or \( \geq \)).
  3. Define the parameter in context before writing the hypotheses.

Worked Example

A hospital administrator believes that more than 20% of emergency room visits are for non-urgent conditions. She plans to test this using a random sample of ER records.

Define the parameter: Let \( p \) = the true proportion of all ER visits at this hospital that are for non-urgent conditions.

Write the hypotheses:

\[ H_0: p = 0.20 \]\[ H_a: p > 0.20 \]

This is a one-sided (right-tailed) test because the administrator suspects the proportion is greater than 20%.

Choose \( \alpha \): Use \( \alpha = 0.05 \) unless otherwise specified.

Key Idea: The alternative hypothesis reflects the research question — what you're trying to find evidence for. The null hypothesis is the status quo that you assume is true unless the data convinces you otherwise.
AP Trap: Never write hypotheses using \( \hat{p} \). Hypotheses are about the population parameter \( p \), not the sample statistic. Also, the null hypothesis must include \( = \), even for one-sided tests. Writing \( H_0: p \geq 0.20 \) is incorrect on the AP exam.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Setting Up a Test for a Population Proportion

problems.question_html: A car manufacturer claims that no more than 5% of its vehicles have a certain defect. A consumer group suspects the defect rate is higher and wants to test the claim. Which hypotheses should the consumer group use?

hints.text: The consumer group suspects the rate is higher than 5%. Which direction does the alternative hypothesis point?
Since the group suspects \( p > 0.05 \), use a one-sided right alternative: \( H_0: p = 0.05 \), \( H_a: p > 0.05 \). Never use \( \hat{p} \) in hypotheses.

solution_steps.text: The consumer group suspects the defect rate is higher than claimed, so they want evidence for \( p > 0.05 \).
The hypotheses are \( H_0: p = 0.05 \) and \( H_a: p > 0.05 \). This is a one-sided (right) test. Note: hypotheses use \( p \), not \( \hat{p} \).

problems.question_html: A school district claims that 70% of students graduate on time. A researcher wants to determine if the true rate is different from 70%. Which alternative hypothesis is appropriate?

hints.text: The researcher wants to know if the rate is "different" — not specifically higher or lower. What type of alternative does this require?
"Different from 70%" means the rate could be higher or lower, so use a two-sided alternative: \( H_a: p \neq 0.70 \).

solution_steps.text: The researcher wants to detect a difference in either direction (higher or lower than 70%).
This calls for a two-sided alternative: \( H_a: p \neq 0.70 \).

problems.question_html: A restaurant chain claims that 85% of customers are satisfied with their dining experience. A franchise owner believes the satisfaction rate at her location is lower. She surveys 200 randomly selected customers. Which of the following correctly states the hypotheses?

choices.text: \( H_0: p = 0.85 \), \( H_a: p \neq 0.85 \) where \( p \) is the true proportion of all customers at this franchise who are satisfied
\( H_0: \hat{p} = 0.85 \), \( H_a: \hat{p} < 0.85 \) where \( \hat{p} \) is the sample proportion who are satisfied
\( H_0: p = 0.85 \), \( H_a: p < 0.85 \) where \( p \) is the true proportion of all customers at this franchise who are satisfied
\( H_0: p \geq 0.85 \), \( H_a: p < 0.85 \) where \( p \) is the true proportion of all customers at this franchise who are satisfied

hints.text: The owner believes satisfaction is lower, so which direction should the alternative point? Also, remember: hypotheses use \( p \), not \( \hat{p} \).
Since the owner suspects \( p < 0.85 \), the alternative is left-tailed. The null must use \( = \), not \( \geq \). Hypotheses are about \( p \), not \( \hat{p} \).

solution_steps.text: The owner suspects satisfaction is lower, so \( H_a: p < 0.85 \).
The null is always \( H_0: p = 0.85 \) (with equals). The parameter must be \( p \) (population proportion), not \( \hat{p} \).
The correct answer defines the parameter in context and uses proper notation.

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a consequence of using a smaller significance level \( \alpha \)?

choices.text: It becomes easier to reject \( H_0 \).
The probability of a Type I error increases.
Stronger evidence is needed to reject \( H_0 \).
The probability of a Type II error decreases.

hints.text: A smaller \( \alpha \) means a stricter threshold. What does that imply about the evidence needed?
A smaller \( \alpha \) (e.g., 0.01 instead of 0.05) requires more extreme results to reject \( H_0 \). It reduces Type I error risk but increases Type II error risk (failing to detect a real effect).

solution_steps.text: A smaller \( \alpha \) makes the rejection threshold stricter — the p-value must be very small to reject \( H_0 \).
This means stronger evidence is needed. The tradeoff is that a smaller \( \alpha \) increases the chance of a Type II error (failing to reject a false \( H_0 \)).

problems.question_html: In a hypothesis test, the null hypothesis \( H_0 \) always uses which mathematical symbol?
problems.correct_answer: =||equals

hints.text: The null hypothesis states a specific value for the parameter. What symbol indicates a specific value?
The null hypothesis always takes the form \( H_0: p = p_0 \). It uses the equals sign, never \( < \), \( > \), or \( \neq \).

solution_steps.text: The null hypothesis is a statement of "no effect" or "no difference" and specifies a single value for the parameter.
It always uses the equals sign: \( H_0: p = p_0 \).

problems.question_html: A significance level of \( \alpha = 0.01 \) means there is a ___% chance of rejecting \( H_0 \) when it is actually true.

hints.text: Convert \( \alpha = 0.01 \) to a percentage.
\( \alpha = 0.01 = 1\% \). This is the probability of a Type I error — incorrectly rejecting a true \( H_0 \).

solution_steps.text: The significance level \( \alpha \) is the probability of committing a Type I error.
\( \alpha = 0.01 = 1\% \), so there is a 1% chance of rejecting \( H_0 \) when it is true.

problems.question_html: A medical study wants to test whether a new vaccine is effective. Historical data shows the infection rate without the vaccine is 12%. The researchers believe the vaccine will reduce the infection rate. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses using proper notation. Use the format: H0: p = [value], Ha: p [symbol] [value].

hints.text: The researchers believe the vaccine will reduce the infection rate below 12%. Which direction does this suggest?
The null is the status quo: \( H_0: p = 0.12 \). The alternative reflects the belief that the rate is lower: \( H_a: p < 0.12 \).

solution_steps.text: The status quo (no vaccine effect) is \( p = 0.12 \), so \( H_0: p = 0.12 \).
The researchers believe the vaccine reduces the rate, so \( H_a: p < 0.12 \). This is a one-sided (left) test.

problems.question_html: A test is conducted at the \( \alpha = 0.05 \) significance level. The probability of rejecting \( H_0 \) when \( H_0 \) is actually true is called a Type ____ error.
problems.correct_answer: I||1||Type I

hints.text: There are two types of errors in hypothesis testing. Which type involves incorrectly rejecting a true null hypothesis?
A Type I error is rejecting \( H_0 \) when it is true (false positive). Its probability equals \( \alpha \). A Type II error is failing to reject \( H_0 \) when it is false (false negative).

solution_steps.text: Rejecting \( H_0 \) when it is true is a Type I error.
The probability of a Type I error equals the significance level: \( P(\text{Type I error}) = \alpha = 0.05 \).

problems.question_html:
A state environmental agency reports that 45% of lakes in the state meet water quality standards. An environmental group believes that recent industrial activity has decreased this proportion. They plan to test their belief using a random sample of 150 lakes.

(a) Define the parameter of interest in context.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses using appropriate notation.

(c) The group decides to use \( \alpha = 0.05 \). Explain what this significance level means in the context of this test.

(d) Describe what a Type I error and a Type II error would mean in this context, and discuss the consequences of each.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Let p = the true proportion of all lakes in the state that currently meet water quality standards.
(b) H0: p = 0.45 (the proportion of lakes meeting standards has not changed). Ha: p < 0.45 (the proportion has decreased due to industrial activity).
(c) Using α = 0.05 means that if the true proportion really is 0.45 (H0 is true), there is a 5% chance we would incorrectly conclude that the proportion has decreased. We are willing to accept a 5% risk of a false alarm.
(d) Type I error: Concluding that the proportion of lakes meeting standards has decreased (rejecting H0) when in reality it has not changed from 0.45. Consequence: The agency might unnecessarily impose costly regulations on industries or divert resources to address a problem that doesn't exist.
Type II error: Failing to conclude that the proportion has decreased (not rejecting H0) when in reality it has decreased below 0.45. Consequence: Real environmental degradation goes undetected, and no corrective action is taken, potentially harming ecosystems and public health.

hints.text: For part (b), the group believes the proportion has decreased, so the alternative should point left. For part (d), think about real-world consequences of each type of mistake.
Type I = false alarm (conclude decrease when none occurred). Type II = missed detection (fail to detect a real decrease). Consider who is harmed by each mistake.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( p \) = the true proportion of all lakes in the state that currently meet water quality standards.
(b) \( H_0: p = 0.45 \). \( H_a: p < 0.45 \). One-sided left because the group suspects a decrease.
(c) \( \alpha = 0.05 \) means a 5% risk of concluding the proportion has decreased when it actually hasn't. We accept this small risk of a false positive.

(d) Type I error: Concluding lakes have degraded when they haven't → unnecessary regulations and wasted resources. Type II error: Failing to detect actual degradation → environmental harm continues unchecked.

problems.question_html:
A large university reports that 60% of its students complete their degree within four years. A new academic advisor program has been implemented, and the administration wants to know if the four-year completion rate has changed.

(a) Define the parameter and state the hypotheses for this test.

(b) Explain why a two-sided test is more appropriate than a one-sided test here.

(c) The administration decides to use \( \alpha = 0.01 \) instead of the more common \( \alpha = 0.05 \). Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of using the smaller significance level.

(d) A sample of 350 recent students is selected and 228 completed their degree within four years. Without performing the full test, explain how you would set up the test statistic and what the next steps would be.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Let p = the true proportion of all students at this university who complete their degree within four years after the advisor program was implemented.
H0: p = 0.60 (the completion rate has not changed).
Ha: p \(
eq\) 0.60 (the completion rate has changed).
(b) A two-sided test is appropriate because the administration wants to know if the rate has changed — it could have increased (the program helped) or decreased (the program was counterproductive or other factors caused a decline). They have no prior reason to predict a specific direction.
(c) Advantage: Using α = 0.01 reduces the probability of a Type I error from 5% to 1%, meaning the administration is less likely to falsely conclude the rate has changed when it hasn't. This is important for a university making policy decisions.
Disadvantage: A smaller α makes it harder to reject H0, increasing the probability of a Type II error. The administration might fail to detect a real change in the completion rate, missing the chance to scale up a successful program or fix a failing one.
(d) The test statistic would be z = (p-hat - p0) / sqrt(p0(1-p0)/n). Here p-hat = 228/350 ≈ 0.6514, p0 = 0.60, n = 350. After computing z, we would find the two-sided p-value = 2 × P(Z > |z|) and compare it to α = 0.01. If the p-value < 0.01, reject H0; otherwise, fail to reject.

hints.text: For part (b), the key question is: does the administration expect the program to help, hurt, or simply want to detect any change? For part (d), recall the z-test statistic formula for proportions.
Two-sided is appropriate because change could go either direction. The test statistic is \( z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}} \). \( \hat{p} = 228/350 \approx 0.651 \).

solution_steps.text: (a) \( p \) = true proportion completing in 4 years after the program. \( H_0: p = 0.60 \), \( H_a: p \neq 0.60 \).
(b) Two-sided because the administration wants to detect any change — the program could have helped or been counterproductive. No prior directional belief.
(c) Advantage: lower Type I error risk (1% vs 5%). Disadvantage: higher Type II error risk — harder to detect a real change.
(d) \( z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}} = \frac{0.651 - 0.60}{\sqrt{0.60(0.40)/350}} \). Compute \( z \), find two-sided p-value \( = 2P(Z > |z|) \), and compare to \( \alpha = 0.01 \).

concepts.title: p-Values
concepts.content_html:
p-Values

A p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme as, or more extreme than, the one actually observed, assuming the null hypothesis \( H_0 \) is true.

What the p-Value Tells Us

The p-value measures how surprising the sample result is under the assumption that \( H_0 \) is true. A small p-value means the observed data would be unlikely if \( H_0 \) were true, providing evidence against \( H_0 \).

  • Small p-value (e.g., \( p < 0.05 \)): The observed result is unlikely under \( H_0 \). We have convincing evidence against \( H_0 \).
  • Large p-value (e.g., \( p > 0.05 \)): The observed result is not unusual under \( H_0 \). We do not have convincing evidence against \( H_0 \).

Significance Level \( \alpha \)

Before conducting a test, we choose a significance level \( \alpha \) (commonly 0.05). This is the threshold for deciding whether the p-value is small enough to reject \( H_0 \).

  • If \( p\text{-value} \leq \alpha \): Reject \( H_0 \). We have statistically significant evidence against \( H_0 \).
  • If \( p\text{-value} > \alpha \): Fail to reject \( H_0 \). We do not have sufficient evidence against \( H_0 \).

Direction of p-Values

The direction depends on the alternative hypothesis:

  • One-sided (right) \( H_a: p > p_0 \): p-value = \( P(z \geq z_{\text{obs}}) \)
  • One-sided (left) \( H_a: p < p_0 \): p-value = \( P(z \leq z_{\text{obs}}) \)
  • Two-sided \( H_a: p \neq p_0 \): p-value = \( 2 \cdot P(z \geq |z_{\text{obs}}|) \)

Worked Example

A company claims that 40% of customers prefer Brand A. A researcher surveys 150 customers and finds 72 prefer Brand A (\( \hat{p} = 0.48 \)). She tests \( H_0: p = 0.40 \) vs. \( H_a: p > 0.40 \).

The test statistic is \( z = \dfrac{0.48 - 0.40}{\sqrt{\frac{0.40(0.60)}{150}}} = \dfrac{0.08}{0.04} = 2.00 \).

Using a z-table, \( P(z \geq 2.00) = 0.0228 \). Since \( 0.0228 < 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that more than 40% of customers prefer Brand A.

Key Idea: The p-value is a conditional probability — it tells you how likely the observed data (or more extreme) would be if \( H_0 \) were true. It does NOT tell you the probability that \( H_0 \) is true or false.
AP Exam Trap: A common wrong answer choice states "the p-value is the probability that the null hypothesis is true." This is incorrect. The p-value assumes \( H_0 \) is true and measures how extreme the data are under that assumption. Never interpret it as the probability of \( H_0 \) being true.
concepts.content_raw: p-Values

problem_sets.title: Practice: p-Values

problems.question_html: A researcher tests \( H_0: p = 0.50 \) vs. \( H_a: p > 0.50 \) and obtains a test statistic of \( z = 1.85 \). Using a standard normal table, \( P(Z > 1.85) = 0.0322 \). At the \( \alpha = 0.05 \) significance level, what is the correct conclusion?

choices.text: Fail to reject \( H_0 \) because \( 0.0322 < 0.05 \).
Reject \( H_0 \) because \( 0.0322 < 0.05 \). There is convincing evidence that the true proportion is greater than 0.50.
Reject \( H_0 \) because there is a 3.22% chance that \( H_0 \) is true.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \) because we need the p-value to be less than 0.01 to reject.

hints.text: Compare the p-value to the significance level \( \alpha \). If the p-value is less than or equal to \( \alpha \), reject \( H_0 \).
Since \( 0.0322 < 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). Be careful: the p-value is NOT the probability that \( H_0 \) is true.

solution_steps.text: The p-value is 0.0322. The significance level is \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
Since \( 0.0322 < 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence at the 5% level that the true proportion is greater than 0.50.

problems.question_html: Which of the following is a correct interpretation of a p-value of 0.03?

choices.text: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true.
There is a 3% probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.
If the null hypothesis is true, there is a 3% probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme as or more extreme than the one observed.
There is a 97% probability that the alternative hypothesis is true.

hints.text: Remember that the p-value is a conditional probability calculated under the assumption that \( H_0 \) is true.
The p-value is \( P(\text{data as extreme or more extreme} \mid H_0 \text{ is true}) \). It is not the probability that \( H_0 \) or \( H_a \) is true.

solution_steps.text: A p-value is the probability of observing data as extreme as or more extreme than the observed data, assuming \( H_0 \) is true.
A p-value of 0.03 means: if \( H_0 \) is true, there is a 3% chance of getting results this extreme or more extreme. It does NOT tell us the probability that \( H_0 \) or \( H_a \) is true.

problems.question_html: A political analyst tests whether support for a policy differs from 50%. She surveys 400 registered voters and finds 218 in favor (\( \hat{p} = 0.545 \)). The test statistic is \( z = 1.80 \) and the p-value for the two-sided test is 0.0718. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), what is the correct conclusion?

choices.text: Reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that support differs from 50%.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is not convincing evidence that support differs from 50%.
Reject \( H_0 \). The sample proportion is clearly not 0.50.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that support is exactly 50%.

hints.text: Compare the p-value of 0.0718 to \( \alpha = 0.05 \). Which is larger?
Since \( 0.0718 > 0.05 \), we fail to reject \( H_0 \). Note: failing to reject does NOT mean we proved \( H_0 \) is true — it means we lack convincing evidence against it.

solution_steps.text: The p-value is 0.0718 and \( \alpha = 0.05 \). Since \( 0.0718 > 0.05 \), we fail to reject \( H_0 \).
Conclusion: We do not have convincing evidence that the true proportion of registered voters who support the policy differs from 50%. Note we do NOT say that support is exactly 50%.

problems.question_html: A quality control manager tests \( H_0: p = 0.02 \) vs. \( H_a: p > 0.02 \) (the defect rate has increased). She obtains a p-value of 0.08. At \( \alpha = 0.10 \), what is the correct conclusion?

choices.text: Fail to reject \( H_0 \) because \( 0.08 > 0.05 \).
Reject \( H_0 \). At the 10% significance level, there is convincing evidence that the defect rate has increased.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \). The defect rate is definitely still 2%.
Reject \( H_0 \) because the p-value proves the defect rate increased.

hints.text: Pay close attention to the significance level given in this problem. It is not the usual 0.05.
Since \( 0.08 < 0.10 \), we reject \( H_0 \) at the \( \alpha = 0.10 \) level. The conclusion must reference the context (defect rate).

solution_steps.text: Compare the p-value to the given significance level: \( 0.08 < 0.10 \), so we reject \( H_0 \).
At the 10% significance level, there is convincing evidence that the defect rate has increased above 2%. Note: this would NOT be significant at \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

problems.question_html: A significance test yields a p-value of 0.042. If the significance level is \( \alpha = 0.05 \), is the result statistically significant? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: yes||Yes||YES

hints.text: A result is statistically significant when the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level \( \alpha \).
Since \( 0.042 < 0.05 \), the result is statistically significant. We reject \( H_0 \).

solution_steps.text: Compare the p-value to \( \alpha \): \( 0.042 \leq 0.05 \).
Since the p-value is less than \( \alpha \), the result is statistically significant. Answer: yes.

problems.question_html: A researcher tests \( H_0: p = 0.30 \) vs. \( H_a: p \neq 0.30 \) and obtains \( z = -2.10 \). Using \( P(Z < -2.10) = 0.0179 \), what is the p-value for this two-sided test? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: For a two-sided test, the p-value accounts for extreme values in both tails of the distribution.
For a two-sided test, double the one-tail probability: \( p\text{-value} = 2 \times 0.0179 = 0.0358 \).

solution_steps.text: For a two-sided test (\( H_a: p \neq p_0 \)), the p-value is \( 2 \times P(Z \leq -|z|) \).

problems.question_html: A doctor tests a new drug and obtains a p-value of 0.001. She concludes there is a 99.9% probability that the drug works. Is her interpretation correct? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: no||No||NO

hints.text: Think carefully about what the p-value actually measures. Does it tell us the probability that a hypothesis is true or false?
The p-value is NOT \( 1 - P(H_0 \text{ is true}) \). It is the probability of getting data this extreme assuming \( H_0 \) is true. Her interpretation is incorrect.

solution_steps.text: A p-value of 0.001 means: if the drug has no effect (\( H_0 \) true), there is only a 0.1% chance of seeing results this extreme.
It does NOT mean there is a 99.9% probability the drug works. The p-value is not \( 1 - P(H_0) \). Her interpretation is incorrect. Answer: no.

problems.question_html: A test of \( H_0: p = 0.65 \) vs. \( H_a: p < 0.65 \) produces \( z = -1.50 \). Using \( P(Z < -1.50) = 0.0668 \), what is the p-value? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Look at the direction of the alternative hypothesis. Is this a one-sided or two-sided test?
Since \( H_a: p < 0.65 \) is one-sided (left), the p-value is simply \( P(Z \leq z_{\text{obs}}) = P(Z \leq -1.50) = 0.0668 \). No doubling needed.

solution_steps.text: The alternative hypothesis is \( H_a: p < 0.65 \), which is a left-tailed (one-sided) test.
For a left-tailed test, the p-value = \( P(Z \leq z_{\text{obs}}) = P(Z \leq -1.50) = 0.0668 \).

problems.question_html:
A pharmaceutical company claims that at least 80% of patients respond positively to a new medication. A clinical trial with 250 patients finds that 188 respond positively (\( \hat{p} = 0.752 \)).

(a) State the null and alternative hypotheses.

(b) The test statistic is \( z = -1.90 \) and the p-value is 0.0287. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), state the conclusion in context.

(c) Explain what the p-value of 0.0287 means in the context of this study.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) H_0: p = 0.80 (the true proportion of patients who respond positively is 0.80). H_a: p < 0.80 (the true proportion of patients who respond positively is less than 0.80).

(b) Since the p-value (0.0287) is less than alpha = 0.05, we reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of patients who respond positively to the new medication is less than 80%.

(c) If the true proportion of patients who respond positively is 0.80, there is a 2.87% probability of obtaining a sample proportion of 0.752 or lower (as extreme as or more extreme than observed) by chance alone.

hints.text: For part (a), consider what the company claims and what the researcher is trying to show. For part (c), remember the p-value is a conditional probability assuming \( H_0 \) is true.

The company claims \( p \geq 0.80 \), so the test checks if the proportion is less than 0.80: \( H_a: p < 0.80 \). The p-value interpretation must reference the specific context (patients, medication, proportion).

solution_steps.text:
(a) The company claims at least 80% respond positively. We test whether the true proportion is less than 80%.
\( H_0: p = 0.80 \) vs. \( H_a: p < 0.80 \), where \( p \) is the true proportion of patients who respond positively.

(b) Since \( p\text{-value} = 0.0287 < \alpha = 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of patients who respond positively to the medication is less than 80%.
(c) If the true proportion of patients who respond positively is 0.80, there is a 2.87% probability of observing a sample proportion of 0.752 or lower in a random sample of 250 patients.

problems.question_html:
An education researcher believes that fewer than 60% of high school seniors in a district are proficient in reading. She randomly samples 300 seniors and finds 165 are proficient (\( \hat{p} = 0.55 \)).

(a) State the hypotheses for this test.

(b) The test statistic is \( z = -1.77 \) and the p-value is 0.0384. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), draw a conclusion in context.

(c) Would the conclusion change if the significance level were \( \alpha = 0.01 \)? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) H_0: p = 0.60 (the true proportion of high school seniors in the district who are proficient in reading is 0.60). H_a: p < 0.60 (the true proportion is less than 0.60).

(b) Since the p-value (0.0384) is less than alpha = 0.05, we reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of high school seniors in the district who are proficient in reading is less than 60%.

(c) Yes, the conclusion would change. Since 0.0384 > 0.01, we would fail to reject H_0 at the alpha = 0.01 level. We would not have convincing evidence at the 1% significance level that the true proportion is less than 60%.

hints.text: The researcher 'believes fewer than 60%' — this tells you the direction of the alternative hypothesis. For part (c), compare the same p-value to a different \( \alpha \).
Since the researcher suspects \( p < 0.60 \), this is a left-tailed test. For part (c), \( 0.0384 > 0.01 \), so the result is not significant at \( \alpha = 0.01 \).

solution_steps.text: (a) \( H_0: p = 0.60 \) vs. \( H_a: p < 0.60 \), where \( p \) is the true proportion of high school seniors in the district who are proficient in reading.
(b) Since \( 0.0384 < 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that fewer than 60% of high school seniors in the district are proficient in reading.
(c) At \( \alpha = 0.01 \), since \( 0.0384 > 0.01 \), we would fail to reject \( H_0 \). The conclusion changes: we would not have convincing evidence at the 1% level.

concepts.title: Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion
concepts.content_html:
Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion

A one-sample z-test for a proportion is used to test a claim about a single population proportion \( p \). The test follows the four-step process: State, Plan, Do, Conclude.

Step 1: State

Define the parameter and state the hypotheses:

  • \( H_0: p = p_0 \) (null hypothesis — the claimed value)
  • \( H_a: p < p_0 \), \( H_a: p > p_0 \), or \( H_a: p \neq p_0 \)

Also state the significance level \( \alpha \).

Step 2: Plan

Identify the test (one-sample z-test for \( p \)) and verify the conditions:

  • Random: The data come from a random sample or randomized experiment.
  • 10% Condition: The sample size is less than 10% of the population (\( n < 0.10N \)) to ensure independence.
  • Large Counts: \( np_0 \geq 10 \) and \( n(1 - p_0) \geq 10 \). Use \( p_0 \) (not \( \hat{p} \)) for the check because we assume \( H_0 \) is true.

Step 3: Do

Calculate the test statistic and p-value.

\[ z = \frac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\dfrac{p_0(1 - p_0)}{n}}} \]

The denominator uses \( p_0 \) because, under \( H_0 \), the true proportion is \( p_0 \).

Then find the p-value based on the direction of \( H_a \).

Step 4: Conclude

Compare the p-value to \( \alpha \) and state the conclusion in context:

  • If \( p\text{-value} \leq \alpha \): "Because the p-value of ___ is less than \( \alpha = \) ___, we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that [context]."
  • If \( p\text{-value} > \alpha \): "Because the p-value of ___ is greater than \( \alpha = \) ___, we fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is not convincing evidence that [context]."

Worked Example

A local news station claims that 55% of residents support a new park. A community group suspects the true proportion is lower. They randomly survey 200 residents and find 98 in favor (\( \hat{p} = 0.49 \)). Test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

State: \( H_0: p = 0.55 \), \( H_a: p < 0.55 \), where \( p \) = true proportion of residents who support the new park. \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

Plan: One-sample z-test for \( p \). Random: stated random sample. 10%: 200 is less than 10% of all residents. Large Counts: \( 200(0.55) = 110 \geq 10 \) and \( 200(0.45) = 90 \geq 10 \). ✓

Do: \( z = \dfrac{0.49 - 0.55}{\sqrt{\frac{0.55(0.45)}{200}}} = \dfrac{-0.06}{0.0352} = -1.71 \). p-value = \( P(Z \leq -1.71) = 0.0436 \).

Conclude: Because the p-value of 0.0436 is less than \( \alpha = 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of residents who support the new park is less than 55%.

Key Idea: In the Large Counts condition for a significance test, always use \( p_0 \) (the null hypothesis value), NOT \( \hat{p} \). This is different from confidence intervals, which use \( \hat{p} \).
AP Exam Trap: Students frequently lose points by (1) forgetting to check all three conditions, (2) using \( \hat{p} \) instead of \( p_0 \) in the standard error or Large Counts check, or (3) failing to state the conclusion in context. Always follow all four steps completely.
