problem_sets.title: Practice: Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion

problems.question_html: An app developer claims that 70% of users rate the app 4 stars or higher. A tech blogger suspects the proportion is different and randomly surveys 500 users, finding that 325 gave 4+ stars (\( \hat{p} = 0.65 \)). What is the appropriate alternative hypothesis?

hints.text: The blogger suspects the proportion 'is different' — not specifically higher or lower. What kind of test does this suggest?
'Different from' indicates a two-sided test: \( H_a: p \neq 0.70 \). Also note that hypotheses are always about the population parameter \( p \), never about \( \hat{p} \).

solution_steps.text: The blogger suspects the true proportion is 'different' from 70%, without specifying a direction.
This calls for a two-sided test: \( H_a: p \neq 0.70 \). Hypotheses are always about the population parameter \( p \), not the sample statistic \( \hat{p} \).

problems.question_html: A factory claims that 5% of its products are defective. A quality inspector randomly selects 300 items and finds 24 defective (\( \hat{p} = 0.08 \)). When checking the Large Counts condition for a significance test of \( H_0: p = 0.05 \), which values should be used?

hints.text: For a significance test, the Large Counts condition uses the null hypothesis value \( p_0 \), not the sample proportion \( \hat{p} \).

solution_steps.text: For a significance test, the Large Counts condition uses \( p_0 \) (the null value), not \( \hat{p} \).
Check \( np_0 = 300(0.05) = 15 \geq 10 \) and \( n(1 - p_0) = 300(0.95) = 285 \geq 10 \). Both conditions are satisfied.

problems.question_html: A marketing team claims that 30% of online shoppers use mobile devices to complete purchases. A random sample of 400 shoppers reveals 140 used a mobile device (\( \hat{p} = 0.35 \)). The test statistic is \( z = 2.18 \) and the p-value is 0.0146. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), which statement is the best conclusion?

choices.text: Reject \( H_0 \). We have proven that more than 30% of online shoppers use mobile devices.
Reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of online shoppers who use mobile devices to complete purchases is greater than 0.30.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \). The difference could be due to chance.
Reject \( H_0 \). The probability that 30% of shoppers use mobile devices is only 1.46%.

hints.text: Since \( 0.0146 < 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). Look for the answer that states the conclusion in context without overstating what the test proves.
We never say a hypothesis test "proves" something — we say there is "convincing evidence." Also, the p-value is NOT the probability that \( H_0 \) is true.

solution_steps.text: Since \( p\text{-value} = 0.0146 < \alpha = 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \).

The correct conclusion: There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of online shoppers who use mobile devices to complete purchases is greater than 0.30. We never claim to have "proven" anything, and the p-value is not the probability that \( H_0 \) is true.

problems.question_html: A national survey from last year found that 62% of adults exercise regularly. A health organization wants to test whether this proportion has changed. They randomly survey 800 adults and find 520 exercise regularly (\( \hat{p} = 0.65 \)). The test produces \( z = 1.75 \). For the two-sided test \( H_a: p \neq 0.62 \), the p-value is 0.0802. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), what is the correct conclusion?

choices.text: Reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence the proportion has changed.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is not convincing evidence that the true proportion of adults who exercise regularly has changed from 0.62.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \). The proportion is still exactly 0.62.
Reject \( H_0 \) because \( \hat{p} = 0.65 \neq 0.62 \).

hints.text: Compare the p-value to \( \alpha \). Remember that failing to reject \( H_0 \) does not prove \( H_0 \) is true.
Since \( 0.0802 > 0.05 \), we fail to reject \( H_0 \). We say there is not convincing evidence, but we do NOT claim \( p \) is exactly 0.62.

solution_steps.text: The p-value is 0.0802, which is greater than \( \alpha = 0.05 \), so we fail to reject \( H_0 \).
We do not have convincing evidence that the true proportion of adults who exercise regularly has changed from 0.62. Failing to reject does not mean the proportion is exactly 0.62.

problems.question_html: A researcher tests \( H_0: p = 0.40 \) vs. \( H_a: p > 0.40 \) using a random sample of 150 individuals. She finds \( \hat{p} = 0.47 \). What is the test statistic \( z \)? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Use the formula \( z = \dfrac{\hat{p} - p_0}{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}} \). Remember to use \( p_0 = 0.40 \) in the denominator.

problems.question_html: A school board claims that 85% of parents support a new schedule. A teacher randomly surveys 200 parents and finds 158 in favor (\( \hat{p} = 0.79 \)). She tests \( H_0: p = 0.85 \) vs. \( H_a: p < 0.85 \). Calculate the test statistic \( z \). Round to two decimal places.

solution_steps.text: Standard error: \( \sqrt{\dfrac{0.85(0.15)}{200}} = \sqrt{0.0006375} \approx 0.02525 \).

problems.question_html: A nutrition study tests \( H_0: p = 0.25 \) vs. \( H_a: p > 0.25 \) using \( n = 180 \) and \( \hat{p} = 0.31 \). What is the standard error used in the test statistic? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: The standard error for a one-sample z-test for proportions uses \( p_0 \), not \( \hat{p} \): \( SE = \sqrt{\dfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}} \).

solution_steps.text: For a significance test, the standard error uses \( p_0 \): \( SE = \sqrt{\dfrac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}} \).

problems.question_html: In a hypothesis test for a proportion with \( n = 50 \) and \( p_0 = 0.10 \), is the Large Counts condition satisfied? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: no||No||NO

hints.text: Check both \( np_0 \geq 10 \) and \( n(1-p_0) \geq 10 \). Both must hold.
\( np_0 = 50(0.10) = 5 \), which is less than 10. The Large Counts condition is not satisfied.

solution_steps.text: Since \( np_0 = 5 < 10 \), the Large Counts condition is NOT satisfied. Answer: no.

problems.question_html: A consumer advocacy group believes that fewer than 90% of a company's orders are delivered on time. They randomly select 250 recent orders and find that 212 were delivered on time (\( \hat{p} = 0.848 \)). Conduct a full significance test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \). Follow the State, Plan, Do, Conclude framework.
problems.correct_answer:
State: H_0: p = 0.90 vs. H_a: p < 0.90, where p is the true proportion of orders delivered on time. Alpha = 0.05.

Plan: One-sample z-test for p. Random: stated random sample. 10%: 250 is less than 10% of all orders. Large Counts: 250(0.90) = 225 >= 10 and 250(0.10) = 25 >= 10. Conditions met.

Do: z = (0.848 - 0.90) / sqrt(0.90 * 0.10 / 250) = -0.052 / sqrt(0.00036) = -0.052 / 0.01897 = -2.74. p-value = P(Z <= -2.74) = 0.0031.

Conclude: Because the p-value of 0.0031 is less than alpha = 0.05, we reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of the company's orders delivered on time is less than 90%.

hints.text: Follow all four steps. In State, define \( p \) in context. In Plan, check all three conditions using \( p_0 = 0.90 \).
SE = \( \sqrt{0.90 \times 0.10 / 250} \approx 0.01897 \). The test statistic is \( z = (0.848 - 0.90)/0.01897 \approx -2.74 \). This gives a very small p-value.

solution_steps.text: State: \( H_0: p = 0.90 \) vs. \( H_a: p < 0.90 \), where \( p \) is the true proportion of the company's orders that are delivered on time. \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

Plan: One-sample z-test for \( p \). Random: random sample stated. 10%: \( 250 < 0.10N \) (assuming thousands of orders). Large Counts: \( 250(0.90) = 225 \geq 10 \) ✓ and \( 250(0.10) = 25 \geq 10 \) ✓.

Conclude: Because the p-value of 0.0031 is less than \( \alpha = 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the true proportion of the company's orders delivered on time is less than 90%.

problems.question_html: An A/B testing team at a tech company runs an experiment. The current website has a 12% click-through rate. They redesign the landing page and want to test if the new design has a higher click-through rate. Out of 600 randomly assigned visitors to the new page, 84 clicked through (\( \hat{p} = 0.14 \)). Conduct a complete significance test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
problems.correct_answer:
State: H_0: p = 0.12 vs. H_a: p > 0.12, where p is the true click-through rate for the new landing page design. Alpha = 0.05.

Plan: One-sample z-test for p. Random: visitors were randomly assigned. 10%: 600 is less than 10% of all potential visitors. Large Counts: 600(0.12) = 72 >= 10 and 600(0.88) = 528 >= 10. Conditions met.

Do: z = (0.14 - 0.12) / sqrt(0.12 * 0.88 / 600) = 0.02 / sqrt(0.000176) = 0.02 / 0.01327 = 1.51. p-value = P(Z >= 1.51) = 0.0655.

Conclude: Because the p-value of 0.0655 is greater than alpha = 0.05, we fail to reject H_0. There is not convincing evidence that the new landing page design has a higher click-through rate than 12%.

hints.text: The company wants to know if the new design is better (higher rate), so this is a one-sided test with \( H_a: p > 0.12 \).
SE = \( \sqrt{0.12 \times 0.88 / 600} \approx 0.01327 \). \( z = 0.02/0.01327 \approx 1.51 \). The p-value = \( P(Z \geq 1.51) \approx 0.0655 \), which is greater than 0.05.

solution_steps.text: State: \( H_0: p = 0.12 \) vs. \( H_a: p > 0.12 \), where \( p \) is the true click-through rate for the new landing page. \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
Plan: One-sample z-test for \( p \). Random: random assignment stated. 10%: 600 < 10% of all visitors. Large Counts: \( 600(0.12) = 72 \geq 10 \) ✓ and \( 600(0.88) = 528 \geq 10 \) ✓.

Conclude: Because the p-value of 0.0655 is greater than \( \alpha = 0.05 \), we fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is not convincing evidence that the new landing page design has a click-through rate higher than 12%.

concepts.title: Potential Errors When Performing Tests
concepts.content_html:
Potential Errors When Performing Tests

When we make a decision in a hypothesis test (reject or fail to reject \( H_0 \)), we might be wrong. There are two types of errors we can make.

Type I and Type II Errors

\( H_0 \) is True\( H_0 \) is False
Reject \( H_0 \)Type I ErrorCorrect Decision
Fail to Reject \( H_0 \)Correct DecisionType II Error
  • Type I Error: Rejecting \( H_0 \) when \( H_0 \) is actually true (a "false positive"). The probability of a Type I error equals the significance level: \( P(\text{Type I}) = \alpha \).
  • Type II Error: Failing to reject \( H_0 \) when \( H_0 \) is actually false (a "false negative"). The probability of a Type II error is denoted \( \beta \).

Power of a Test

The power of a test is the probability of correctly rejecting \( H_0 \) when \( H_0 \) is false:

\[ \text{Power} = 1 - \beta \]

Higher power means the test is better at detecting a real effect.

Factors That Affect Power

  • Sample size (\( n \)): Increasing \( n \) increases power. Larger samples give more precise estimates.
  • Significance level (\( \alpha \)): Increasing \( \alpha \) increases power (but also increases the risk of Type I error).
  • True parameter value: The farther the true value is from \( p_0 \), the greater the power. Larger effects are easier to detect.
  • Variability: Less variability in the population leads to greater power.

Consequences in Context

Always describe errors in context. For example, if testing whether a new drug is effective:

  • Type I Error: Concluding the drug is effective when it actually is not (could lead to patients taking an ineffective drug).
  • Type II Error: Concluding there is not enough evidence the drug is effective when it actually is (patients miss out on a beneficial treatment).
Key Idea: There is a tradeoff between Type I and Type II errors. Decreasing \( \alpha \) (making it harder to reject \( H_0 \)) reduces the chance of a Type I error but increases the chance of a Type II error (and reduces power). The only way to reduce both simultaneously is to increase the sample size.
AP Exam Trap: When asked to describe a Type I or Type II error, you must describe it in context. Simply saying "reject \( H_0 \) when it's true" without connecting it to the scenario will lose credit. Also, never say "accept \( H_0 \)" — the correct language is "fail to reject \( H_0 \)."
concepts.content_raw: Potential Errors When Performing Tests

problem_sets.title: Practice: Potential Errors When Performing Tests

problems.question_html: A hospital tests whether a new screening method detects a disease more accurately than the current method (\( H_0 \): the new method is not more accurate). They reject \( H_0 \) and adopt the new method. If \( H_0 \) is actually true, what type of error has been made?

choices.text: Type I error — they concluded the new method is more accurate when it actually is not.
Type II error — they concluded the new method is more accurate when it actually is not.
Type I error — they failed to adopt a method that actually works better.
No error was made because they rejected \( H_0 \).

hints.text: A Type I error occurs when you reject \( H_0 \) but \( H_0 \) is actually true. A Type II error occurs when you fail to reject \( H_0 \) but \( H_0 \) is actually false.
They rejected \( H_0 \) (adopted the new method), but \( H_0 \) is true (the new method is not better). This is a Type I error — a false positive.

solution_steps.text: The hospital rejected \( H_0 \) (concluded the new method is more accurate).
But \( H_0 \) is actually true (the new method is not more accurate). Rejecting a true \( H_0 \) is a Type I error.

problems.question_html: A drug company tests \( H_0: \) the drug is not effective vs. \( H_a: \) the drug is effective. They fail to reject \( H_0 \), but the drug actually is effective. Which type of error occurred, and what is one potential consequence?

choices.text: Type I error — the company may waste money developing an ineffective drug.
Type II error — patients may miss out on an effective treatment that is not brought to market.
Type I error — patients may miss out on an effective treatment.
Type II error — the company may waste money marketing an ineffective drug.

hints.text: They failed to reject \( H_0 \) (concluded not enough evidence the drug works), but the drug actually is effective. Which type of error matches this scenario?
Failing to reject a false \( H_0 \) is a Type II error. The consequence: an effective drug is not brought to market, so patients miss a beneficial treatment.

solution_steps.text: The company failed to reject \( H_0 \), but \( H_0 \) is false (the drug is effective). This is a Type II error.
Consequence: The effective drug may not be developed or marketed, causing patients to miss out on a beneficial treatment.

problems.question_html: A researcher wants to increase the power of a hypothesis test. Which of the following changes would increase power?

choices.text: Decrease the sample size.
Decrease the significance level from 0.05 to 0.01.
Increase the sample size.
Use a two-sided test instead of a one-sided test.

hints.text: Think about what makes a test better at detecting a real effect. Consider how sample size, significance level, and test direction each affect the ability to reject a false \( H_0 \).

Increasing the sample size gives more precise estimates, making it easier to detect a real difference. Decreasing \( \alpha \) and using two-sided tests both reduce power. Decreasing \( n \) also reduces power.

solution_steps.text: Power is increased by: (1) increasing sample size, (2) increasing \( \alpha \), (3) the true parameter being farther from \( p_0 \), (4) less variability.
Increasing the sample size increases power. Decreasing \( \alpha \) or \( n \), or switching to a two-sided test, would decrease power.

problems.question_html: A city tests whether a new traffic signal reduces the proportion of accidents at an intersection (\( H_0: p = 0.15 \), \( H_a: p < 0.15 \)). They use \( \alpha = 0.05 \). Describe a Type II error and a consequence in this context.

choices.text: A Type II error would be concluding the signal reduces accidents when it actually doesn't, wasting city funds.
A Type II error would be failing to conclude the signal reduces accidents when it actually does, leading the city to remove an effective signal.
A Type II error would be concluding the accident rate is exactly 15%.
A Type II error would be using the wrong significance level.

hints.text: A Type II error means failing to reject \( H_0 \) when \( H_0 \) is actually false. In this context, what would it mean if \( H_0 \) is false (the signal does reduce accidents) but we fail to reject?

If the signal truly reduces accidents (\( H_0 \) is false) but we fail to reject \( H_0 \), we would incorrectly conclude there isn't enough evidence it helps. The city might then remove an effective signal.

solution_steps.text: A Type II error: failing to reject \( H_0 \) when \( H_0 \) is false. Here, \( H_0 \) is false means the signal really does reduce the accident rate below 15%.
If we fail to reject \( H_0 \), we conclude there is not convincing evidence the signal reduces accidents — even though it does. The city might remove the signal, losing its safety benefit.

problems.question_html: If a significance test uses \( \alpha = 0.01 \), what is the probability of making a Type I error (assuming \( H_0 \) is true)? Enter as a decimal.

hints.text: The probability of a Type I error is directly related to a specific value chosen before the test is conducted.
The probability of a Type I error equals the significance level \( \alpha \). So \( P(\text{Type I error}) = 0.01 \).

solution_steps.text: By definition, \( P(\text{Type I error}) = \alpha \).
Since \( \alpha = 0.01 \), the probability of a Type I error is 0.01.

problems.question_html: A test has power 0.85. What is the probability of making a Type II error? Enter as a decimal.

hints.text: Power and the probability of a Type II error are complementary. How are they related?
Power = \( 1 - \beta \), so \( \beta = 1 - \text{Power} = 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 \).

solution_steps.text: Power = \( 1 - \beta \), where \( \beta = P(\text{Type II error}) \).
\( \beta = 1 - 0.85 = 0.15 \). The probability of a Type II error is 0.15.

problems.question_html: A researcher uses \( \alpha = 0.05 \) and obtains a power of 0.70. What is the probability of a Type II error (\( \beta \))? Enter as a decimal.

hints.text: Recall the relationship between power and \( \beta \): Power = \( 1 - \beta \).

solution_steps.text: The probability of a Type II error is 0.30.

problems.question_html: Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) when sample size is held constant?
problems.correct_answer: inverse||inversely related||inversely||tradeoff||trade-off

hints.text: Think about what happens when you make it harder to reject \( H_0 \) (smaller \( \alpha \)). Does that make it easier or harder to detect a real effect?

When \( \alpha \) decreases, we require stronger evidence to reject \( H_0 \), so we are more likely to fail to reject a false \( H_0 \) (\( \beta \) increases). They have an inverse (tradeoff) relationship.

solution_steps.text: When sample size is fixed, decreasing \( \alpha \) increases \( \beta \), and vice versa.
\( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) have an inverse (tradeoff) relationship when \( n \) is constant. The only way to decrease both is to increase the sample size.

problems.question_html:
A school district tests whether a new reading program increases the proportion of students reading at grade level (\( H_0: p = 0.65 \) vs. \( H_a: p > 0.65 \)). The test uses \( \alpha = 0.05 \) with \( n = 200 \) students.

(a) Describe a Type I error in the context of this study and give a potential consequence.

(b) Describe a Type II error in context and give a potential consequence.

(c) The district is considering increasing the sample size to 500. How would this affect the power of the test? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Type I error: The district concludes that the new reading program increases the proportion of students reading at grade level when it actually does not. Consequence: The district spends money implementing an ineffective program, diverting resources from other initiatives.

(b) Type II error: The district fails to find convincing evidence that the reading program increases the proportion of students reading at grade level when it actually does. Consequence: An effective program is abandoned, and students miss out on its benefits.

(c) Increasing the sample size from 200 to 500 would increase the power of the test. A larger sample provides a more precise estimate of the true proportion, making it easier to detect a real increase in reading proficiency if one exists. The standard error decreases, which makes it more likely to get a large enough test statistic to reject H_0 when H_0 is false.

hints.text: For parts (a) and (b), first identify what each error type means (reject true \( H_0 \) vs. fail to reject false \( H_0 \)), then translate into the specific context of the reading program.

Type I: conclude program works when it doesn't (waste resources on ineffective program). Type II: conclude not enough evidence program works when it does (miss beneficial program). Larger \( n \) reduces SE and increases power.

solution_steps.text: (a) Type I error: Concluding the new reading program increases the proportion reading at grade level when it actually does not. Consequence: Resources wasted on an ineffective program.
(b) Type II error: Failing to find convincing evidence that the program works when it actually does increase reading proficiency. Consequence: An effective program is not adopted, harming students.
(c) Increasing \( n \) from 200 to 500 increases power. The larger sample reduces the standard error, making the test more sensitive to detecting a true increase in the proportion.

problems.question_html:
A medical researcher tests a new vaccine (\( H_0: p = 0.50 \) vs. \( H_a: p > 0.50 \), where \( p \) is the proportion of patients who recover). The test uses \( \alpha = 0.01 \) and has power 0.60 when the true proportion is 0.60.

(a) What is the probability of a Type I error? Explain in context.

(b) What is the probability of a Type II error when \( p = 0.60 \)? Explain in context.

(c) The researcher considers changing \( \alpha \) to 0.05 (keeping \( n \) constant). How does this affect the probability of each type of error?
problems.correct_answer:
(a) P(Type I error) = alpha = 0.01. In context: There is a 1% probability that the researcher will conclude the vaccine has a recovery rate above 50% when the true recovery rate is actually 50%.

(b) P(Type II error) = beta = 1 - Power = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40. In context: If the true recovery rate is 60%, there is a 40% probability that the test will fail to detect that the vaccine is better than the 50% baseline.

(c) Increasing alpha from 0.01 to 0.05 increases the probability of a Type I error from 0.01 to 0.05 (easier to reject H_0, so more likely to reject a true H_0). However, it decreases the probability of a Type II error (increases power) because the rejection region is larger, making it easier to detect a real effect.

hints.text: For (a), recall that \( P(\text{Type I}) = \alpha \). For (b), use \( \beta = 1 - \text{Power} \). For (c), think about the tradeoff between the two error types.
\( P(\text{Type I}) = 0.01 \). \( \beta = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 \). Increasing \( \alpha \) to 0.05 increases Type I error probability but decreases Type II error probability (increases power).

solution_steps.text: (a) \( P(\text{Type I error}) = \alpha = 0.01 \). In context: There is a 1% chance of concluding the vaccine recovery rate exceeds 50% when it actually equals 50%.
(b) \( P(\text{Type II error}) = 1 - 0.60 = 0.40 \). In context: If the true recovery rate is 60%, there is a 40% chance the test will fail to detect the improvement.

(c) Changing \( \alpha \) from 0.01 to 0.05 increases \( P(\text{Type I error}) \) from 0.01 to 0.05, but decreases \( P(\text{Type II error}) \) (increases power) because it is easier to reject \( H_0 \).

concepts.title: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions
concepts.content_html:
Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions

When comparing two populations, we often want to estimate or test claims about the difference between two proportions, \( p_1 - p_2 \). To do this, we need to understand the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \).

Shape, Center, and Spread

If two independent random samples are taken from two populations with true proportions \( p_1 \) and \( p_2 \):

  • Shape: Approximately normal if the Large Counts condition is met for both samples.
  • Center (Mean): \[ \mu_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} = p_1 - p_2 \] The sampling distribution is centered at the true difference in population proportions.
  • Spread (Standard Deviation): \[ \sigma_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}} \] The variances add because the samples are independent.

Conditions

For the sampling distribution to be approximately normal:

  • Random: Both samples are random samples or come from randomized experiments.
  • Independent: The two samples are independent of each other, and within each sample, the 10% condition holds (\( n_1 < 0.10N_1 \) and \( n_2 < 0.10N_2 \)).
  • Large Counts: For both samples: \( n_1 p_1 \geq 10 \), \( n_1(1-p_1) \geq 10 \), \( n_2 p_2 \geq 10 \), and \( n_2(1-p_2) \geq 10 \).

Why Variances Add

A key property: when two random variables are independent, the variance of their difference equals the sum of their individual variances:

\[ \text{Var}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \text{Var}(\hat{p}_1) + \text{Var}(\hat{p}_2) \]

This is why we add the fractions under the square root, never subtract them.

Worked Example

A researcher compares two cities. In City A, 60% of residents recycle (\( p_1 = 0.60 \), \( n_1 = 200 \)). In City B, 45% recycle (\( p_2 = 0.45 \), \( n_2 = 250 \)).

Mean: \( \mu_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} = 0.60 - 0.45 = 0.15 \).

Standard deviation: \( \sigma_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.60(0.40)}{200} + \dfrac{0.45(0.55)}{250}} = \sqrt{0.0012 + 0.00099} = \sqrt{0.00219} \approx 0.0468 \).

Large Counts: \( 200(0.60) = 120 \), \( 200(0.40) = 80 \), \( 250(0.45) = 112.5 \), \( 250(0.55) = 137.5 \) — all \( \geq 10 \) ✓. The sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \) is approximately \( N(0.15, 0.0468) \).

Key Idea: The standard deviation formula adds the variance components, even though we are looking at a difference. This is because independent sources of variability always combine by addition, regardless of whether you add or subtract the random variables.
AP Exam Trap: Students often mistakenly subtract the variance terms when computing \( \sigma_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} \). Remember: for independent random variables, variances always ADD, whether you are computing the variance of a sum or a difference.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Sample Proportions

problems.question_html: When computing the standard deviation of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \), why do we add the variance terms rather than subtract them?

choices.text: Because the samples come from different populations.
Because independent sources of variability always combine by addition, whether computing a sum or a difference of random variables.
Because we want the standard deviation to be as large as possible.
Because subtracting would give a negative variance, which is impossible.

hints.text: Think about the mathematical property of variance for independent random variables: \( \text{Var}(X - Y) = ? \)
For independent random variables, \( \text{Var}(X - Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) \). Variability in a difference comes from variability in both components, so they always add.

solution_steps.text: For independent random variables \( X \) and \( Y \): \( \text{Var}(X \pm Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) \).
The variability in a difference comes from uncertainty in both variables. Independent sources of variability always combine by addition.

problems.question_html: Which set of conditions must be verified to use the normal model for \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \)?

choices.text: Random samples, 10% condition for one sample, and Large Counts for one sample.
Random samples, 10% condition for both samples, and Large Counts for both samples.
Random samples and \( n_1 + n_2 \geq 30 \).
Independent samples and \( n_1 = n_2 \).

hints.text: Since we are working with two separate samples, think about which conditions must hold for each individual sample.
All three conditions (Random, 10%, Large Counts) must be checked for both samples independently.

solution_steps.text: For the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \) to be approximately normal, we need conditions met for both samples.

Conditions: (1) Both samples are random, (2) 10% condition holds for both (\( n_1 < 0.10N_1 \) and \( n_2 < 0.10N_2 \)), and (3) Large Counts for both (\( n_1p_1 \geq 10 \), \( n_1(1-p_1) \geq 10 \), \( n_2p_2 \geq 10 \), \( n_2(1-p_2) \geq 10 \)).

problems.question_html: In a study comparing two schools, School A has \( p_1 = 0.72 \) (proportion meeting fitness standards) with \( n_1 = 180 \), and School B has \( p_2 = 0.58 \) with \( n_2 = 220 \). Find the probability that \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > 0.20 \). Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: First find the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution, then standardize to find the z-score for 0.20.

problems.question_html: A political pollster samples \( n_1 = 500 \) voters from State A and \( n_2 = 400 \) voters from State B. In State A, 55% support a ballot measure (\( p_1 = 0.55 \)); in State B, 48% support it (\( p_2 = 0.48 \)). What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \)? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Use the formula \( \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}} \). Compute each fraction separately, then add and take the square root.

problems.question_html: Two independent random samples are taken: \( n_1 = 100 \) from Population 1 (\( p_1 = 0.70 \)) and \( n_2 = 150 \) from Population 2 (\( p_2 = 0.55 \)). What is the mean of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \)?

hints.text: The mean of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \) equals the true difference in population proportions.

solution_steps.text: The mean of the sampling distribution is \( \mu_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} = p_1 - p_2 \).

problems.question_html: Suppose \( p_1 = 0.35 \), \( n_1 = 120 \), \( p_2 = 0.35 \), \( n_2 = 150 \). What is the mean of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \)?

hints.text: The mean of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \) is \( p_1 - p_2 \). What happens when both proportions are the same?
\( \mu = p_1 - p_2 = 0.35 - 0.35 = 0 \). When the population proportions are equal, the sampling distribution is centered at 0.

solution_steps.text: When both population proportions are equal, the sampling distribution of their difference is centered at 0.

problems.question_html: Two independent random samples are taken: \( n_1 = 200 \) from Population 1 (\( p_1 = 0.50 \)) and \( n_2 = 300 \) from Population 2 (\( p_2 = 0.40 \)). What is the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \)? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Use the formula \( \sigma_{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \dfrac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}} \). Remember, the variances are added.

problems.question_html: Two independent samples have \( n_1 = 80 \), \( p_1 = 0.90 \), \( n_2 = 60 \), \( p_2 = 0.85 \). Is the Large Counts condition satisfied for both samples? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: no||No||NO

hints.text: Check all four values: \( n_1 p_1 \), \( n_1(1-p_1) \), \( n_2 p_2 \), \( n_2(1-p_2) \). All must be at least 10.
\( n_1 p_1 = 72 \) ✓, \( n_1(1-p_1) = 8 \) ✗ (less than 10). The condition fails for sample 1. Answer: no.

solution_steps.text: Since \( n_1(1-p_1) = 8 < 10 \), the Large Counts condition is NOT satisfied. Answer: no.

problems.question_html:
A medical researcher compares recovery rates for two treatments. Treatment A is given to 300 patients in Hospital 1 (\( p_1 = 0.78 \)), and Treatment B is given to 350 patients in Hospital 2 (\( p_2 = 0.71 \)).

(a) Find the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \).

(b) Verify the conditions for using a normal model.

(c) Find the probability that \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < 0 \) (i.e., Treatment B appears better in the sample). Round to four decimal places.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Mean: mu = p_1 - p_2 = 0.78 - 0.71 = 0.07. Standard deviation: sigma = sqrt(0.78*0.22/300 + 0.71*0.29/350) = sqrt(0.000572 + 0.000588) = sqrt(0.001160) ≈ 0.03406.

(b) Random: Assume patients were randomly assigned or randomly sampled. 10%: 300 < 10% of all potential patients for Treatment A, and 350 < 10% for Treatment B. Large Counts: 300(0.78) = 234 >= 10, 300(0.22) = 66 >= 10, 350(0.71) = 248.5 >= 10, 350(0.29) = 101.5 >= 10. All conditions met.

(c) z = (0 - 0.07)/0.03406 = -2.056. P(Z < -2.056) ≈ 0.0199.

hints.text: For part (a), use the standard formulas. For part (c), standardize 0 using the mean and SD you found, then use the z-table.

solution_steps.text: (b) Random: assumed. 10%: both sample sizes are less than 10% of their populations. Large Counts: \( 300(0.78) = 234 \), \( 300(0.22) = 66 \), \( 350(0.71) = 248.5 \), \( 350(0.29) = 101.5 \) — all \( \geq 10 \) ✓.

(c) \( z = \frac{0 - 0.07}{0.03406} \approx -2.06 \). \( P(Z < -2.06) \approx 0.0197 \). There is about a 2% chance that Treatment B would appear better in the sample when Treatment A actually has a higher recovery rate.

problems.question_html:
An education study compares graduation rates at two types of schools. Type 1 schools have \( p_1 = 0.88 \) with \( n_1 = 400 \), and Type 2 schools have \( p_2 = 0.82 \) with \( n_2 = 350 \).

(a) Describe the sampling distribution of \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \) (shape, center, spread).

(b) What is the probability that \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \) is between 0.03 and 0.09?

hints.text: For part (a), compute the mean and SD, then check Large Counts to confirm normality. For part (b), convert both bounds to z-scores.
Mean = 0.06, SD ≈ 0.02619. For part (b), both z-scores are \( \pm 1.15 \). Use the z-table to find the area between them.

concepts.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
concepts.content_html:
Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

To estimate the difference between two population proportions \( p_1 - p_2 \), we construct a two-sample z-interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \).

Formula

\[ (\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z^* \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}} \]

where \( z^* \) is the critical value for the desired confidence level (e.g., \( z^* = 1.96 \) for 95% confidence).

Common Critical Values

  • 90% confidence: \( z^* = 1.645 \)
  • 95% confidence: \( z^* = 1.960 \)
  • 99% confidence: \( z^* = 2.576 \)

Conditions

Before constructing the interval, verify:

  • Random: Both samples are random samples or from randomized experiments.
  • 10% Condition: \( n_1 < 0.10N_1 \) and \( n_2 < 0.10N_2 \).
  • Large Counts: \( n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10 \), \( n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10 \), \( n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10 \), \( n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10 \). (Use \( \hat{p} \) for confidence intervals, not \( p_0 \).)

Interpretation

"We are [C]% confident that the true difference in proportions (\( p_1 - p_2 \)) is between [lower bound] and [upper bound]."

Always state this in context, referencing the specific populations and variable.

Does the Interval Contain 0?

  • If the interval contains 0: There is no convincing evidence that the two proportions differ.
  • If the interval is entirely positive: There is convincing evidence that \( p_1 > p_2 \).
  • If the interval is entirely negative: There is convincing evidence that \( p_1 < p_2 \).

Worked Example

A study compares the proportion of students who pass a standardized test at two schools. School A: 120 out of 200 pass (\( \hat{p}_1 = 0.60 \)). School B: 90 out of 180 pass (\( \hat{p}_2 = 0.50 \)). Construct a 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \).

Conditions: Random samples assumed. 10%: both \( n < 0.10N \). Large Counts: \( 200(0.60) = 120 \), \( 200(0.40) = 80 \), \( 180(0.50) = 90 \), \( 180(0.50) = 90 \) — all \( \geq 10 \) ✓.

Point estimate: \( 0.60 - 0.50 = 0.10 \).

Standard error: \( SE = \sqrt{\dfrac{0.60(0.40)}{200} + \dfrac{0.50(0.50)}{180}} = \sqrt{0.0012 + 0.001389} = \sqrt{0.002589} \approx 0.05088 \).

Margin of error: \( 1.96 \times 0.05088 \approx 0.0997 \).

Interval: \( 0.10 \pm 0.0997 = (0.0003, 0.1997) \).

Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true difference in pass rates (School A minus School B) is between 0.0003 and 0.1997. Since the interval does not contain 0, there is convincing evidence that School A has a higher pass rate.

Key Idea: For confidence intervals involving proportions, use \( \hat{p}_1 \) and \( \hat{p}_2 \) (the sample proportions) in both the standard error formula and the Large Counts check. This is different from hypothesis tests, which use \( p_0 \).
AP Exam Trap: When interpreting a confidence interval, never say "there is a 95% probability that the true difference is in this interval." Once the interval is constructed, the true difference either is or isn't in it. Say "we are 95% confident." Also, always check whether 0 is in the interval to determine if the difference is statistically significant.

problems.question_html: Which critical value \( z^* \) is used for a 99% confidence interval?

hints.text: The common critical values to memorize are: 90% → 1.645, 95% → 1.960, 99% → ?
For 99% confidence, \( z^* = 2.576 \). This leaves 0.5% in each tail of the normal distribution.

solution_steps.text: For a 99% confidence interval, we need the z-value that captures the middle 99% of the standard normal distribution.

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) is \( (0.03, 0.15) \). Which of the following is a correct interpretation?

choices.text: There is a 95% probability that \( p_1 - p_2 \) is between 0.03 and 0.15.
We are 95% confident that the true difference in population proportions \( p_1 - p_2 \) is between 0.03 and 0.15.
95% of all samples will produce a difference between 0.03 and 0.15.
The probability that \( p_1 > p_2 \) is 0.95.

hints.text: Remember the correct language for confidence intervals: "we are [C]% confident" rather than "there is a [C]% probability."
The correct interpretation is: "We are 95% confident that the true difference in population proportions is between 0.03 and 0.15." We do not say probability because the true value is fixed.

solution_steps.text: A confidence interval interpretation uses "we are [C]% confident," not "there is a [C]% probability."
Correct: We are 95% confident that the true difference in population proportions \( p_1 - p_2 \) is between 0.03 and 0.15.

problems.question_html: An A/B test compares two website designs. Design A: 84 out of 600 visitors clicked (\( \hat{p}_1 = 0.14 \)). Design B: 54 out of 500 visitors clicked (\( \hat{p}_2 = 0.108 \)). Calculate the 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \). Which interval is correct?

hints.text: First compute the point estimate \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \), then the standard error, then apply \( \pm 1.96 \times SE \).

solution_steps.text: Since the interval contains 0, there is not convincing evidence at the 95% level that the two designs have different click-through rates.

problems.question_html: A political poll compares support for a candidate in two regions. Region 1: 280 out of 500 support (\( \hat{p}_1 = 0.56 \)). Region 2: 210 out of 450 support (\( \hat{p}_2 = 0.467 \)). A 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) is \( (0.030, 0.156) \). What can we conclude?

choices.text: There is not convincing evidence that support differs between the two regions because the interval is narrow.

We are 95% confident that the true difference in support (Region 1 minus Region 2) is between 0.030 and 0.156. Since the interval does not contain 0, there is convincing evidence that support is higher in Region 1.
There is a 95% probability that more people in Region 1 support the candidate.
Exactly 9.3% more people in Region 1 support the candidate.

hints.text: Check whether 0 is in the interval. Also remember the correct language for confidence interval interpretations.
The interval \( (0.030, 0.156) \) is entirely positive and does not contain 0. This means there is convincing evidence that \( p_1 > p_2 \) — support is higher in Region 1.

solution_steps.text: The interval \( (0.030, 0.156) \) does not contain 0, and all values are positive.
We are 95% confident that the true difference (Region 1 - Region 2) is between 0.030 and 0.156. Since the entire interval is positive, there is convincing evidence that support is higher in Region 1.

problems.question_html: A researcher constructs a 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) and gets \( (0.02, 0.14) \). What is the point estimate \( \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \)?

hints.text: The point estimate is the center of the confidence interval.

solution_steps.text: The point estimate is the midpoint of the confidence interval.

problems.question_html: A 90% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) is \( (-0.08, 0.04) \). Does this interval provide convincing evidence that the two population proportions are different? Enter yes or no.
problems.correct_answer: no||No||NO

hints.text: Check whether the confidence interval contains 0. If 0 is a plausible value for the difference, what does that tell us?
The interval \( (-0.08, 0.04) \) contains 0, which means 0 is a plausible value for \( p_1 - p_2 \). There is NOT convincing evidence that the proportions differ.

solution_steps.text: The interval \( (-0.08, 0.04) \) includes 0.
Since 0 is in the interval, it is plausible that \( p_1 = p_2 \). There is not convincing evidence the proportions are different. Answer: no.

problems.question_html: In a study, \( \hat{p}_1 = 0.64 \) (\( n_1 = 250 \)) and \( \hat{p}_2 = 0.58 \) (\( n_2 = 300 \)). Calculate the standard error for the confidence interval of \( p_1 - p_2 \). Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: For a confidence interval, use \( \hat{p}_1 \) and \( \hat{p}_2 \) (not \( p_0 \)) in the standard error formula.

problems.question_html: A study finds \( \hat{p}_1 = 0.45 \) (\( n_1 = 200 \)) and \( \hat{p}_2 = 0.38 \) (\( n_2 = 250 \)). What is the margin of error for a 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \)? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Margin of error = \( z^* \times SE \), where \( z^* = 1.96 \) for 95% confidence.

problems.question_html: A medical study compares the effectiveness of two treatments. Treatment A: 156 out of 240 patients improved (\( \hat{p}_1 = 0.65 \)). Treatment B: 110 out of 200 patients improved (\( \hat{p}_2 = 0.55 \)). Construct a 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) using the full four-step process (State, Plan, Do, Conclude).
problems.correct_answer:
State: We want to estimate p_1 - p_2, where p_1 is the true proportion of patients who improve with Treatment A and p_2 is the true proportion who improve with Treatment B, at 95% confidence.

Plan: Two-sample z-interval for p_1 - p_2. Random: Assume patients were randomly assigned to treatments. 10%: 240 and 200 are each less than 10% of all potential patients. Large Counts: 240(0.65) = 156 >= 10, 240(0.35) = 84 >= 10, 200(0.55) = 110 >= 10, 200(0.45) = 90 >= 10. All conditions met.

Do: Point estimate = 0.65 - 0.55 = 0.10. SE = sqrt(0.65*0.35/240 + 0.55*0.45/200) = sqrt(0.000948 + 0.001238) = sqrt(0.002186) ≈ 0.04675. ME = 1.96 * 0.04675 ≈ 0.0916. Interval: 0.10 ± 0.0916 = (0.0084, 0.1916).

Conclude: We are 95% confident that the true difference in improvement rates (Treatment A minus Treatment B) is between 0.008 and 0.192. Since the interval does not contain 0, there is convincing evidence that Treatment A has a higher improvement rate than Treatment B.

hints.text: Follow the four-step process. In Plan, check all three conditions using \( \hat{p}_1 \) and \( \hat{p}_2 \) for the Large Counts check (not \( p_0 \) — this is a confidence interval, not a test).

SE = \( \sqrt{0.65 \times 0.35/240 + 0.55 \times 0.45/200} \approx 0.04675 \). ME = \( 1.96 \times 0.04675 \approx 0.0916 \). Point estimate = 0.10. Interval ≈ (0.008, 0.192). Since 0 is not in the interval, there is evidence Treatment A is better.

solution_steps.text: State: Estimate \( p_1 - p_2 \), where \( p_1 \) = true proportion improved with Treatment A and \( p_2 \) = true proportion improved with Treatment B. Confidence level: 95%.
Plan: Two-sample z-interval. Random: assumed random assignment. 10%: both \( n < 0.10N \). Large Counts: \( 156 \geq 10 \), \( 84 \geq 10 \), \( 110 \geq 10 \), \( 90 \geq 10 \) ✓.

Conclude: We are 95% confident that the true difference in improvement rates (Treatment A minus Treatment B) is between 0.008 and 0.192. Since 0 is not in the interval, there is convincing evidence that Treatment A is more effective.

problems.question_html:
An education researcher compares pass rates on a state exam. Urban schools: 432 out of 600 students passed (\( \hat{p}_1 = 0.72 \)). Rural schools: 351 out of 500 students passed (\( \hat{p}_2 = 0.702 \)).

(a) Construct a 90% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \). Show your work.

(b) Based on the interval, is there convincing evidence that pass rates differ between urban and rural schools? Explain.

(c) How would the interval change if a 99% confidence level were used instead? Explain without calculating.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Point estimate: 0.72 - 0.702 = 0.018. SE = sqrt(0.72*0.28/600 + 0.702*0.298/500) = sqrt(0.000336 + 0.000419) = sqrt(0.000755) ≈ 0.02748. For 90% confidence, z* = 1.645. ME = 1.645 * 0.02748 ≈ 0.0452. Interval: 0.018 ± 0.0452 = (-0.027, 0.063).

(b) The interval (-0.027, 0.063) contains 0, so there is not convincing evidence at the 90% confidence level that the pass rates differ between urban and rural schools.

(c) Using a 99% confidence level would produce a wider interval because z* increases from 1.645 to 2.576. The larger margin of error means a wider range of plausible values for p_1 - p_2. The interval would still contain 0 (and be even wider), so the conclusion would remain the same.

hints.text: For 90% confidence, use \( z^* = 1.645 \). For part (b), check if 0 is in the interval. For part (c), think about how \( z^* \) affects the width.

SE ≈ 0.02748. ME = \( 1.645 \times 0.02748 \approx 0.0452 \). Interval: \( (-0.027, 0.063) \). Since 0 is in the interval, no convincing evidence of a difference. A 99% interval would be wider (larger \( z^* \)).

solution_steps.text: (b) The interval \( (-0.027, 0.063) \) contains 0. There is not convincing evidence that pass rates differ between urban and rural schools at the 90% confidence level.
(c) A 99% confidence interval would be wider because \( z^* = 2.576 > 1.645 \), increasing the margin of error. The interval would still contain 0, so the conclusion would not change.

concepts.title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
concepts.content_html:
Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

Once you have constructed a confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \), the next step is to use it to justify a claim about whether the two population proportions differ. The key question is simple: does the interval contain 0?

The Decision Rule

A confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) gives a range of plausible values for the true difference between the two population proportions.

  • If 0 is inside the interval, then 0 is a plausible value for \( p_1 - p_2 \). We do not have convincing evidence that the two population proportions differ.
  • If 0 is not inside the interval, then 0 is not a plausible value. We do have convincing evidence that the two population proportions differ.

Direction of the Difference

When 0 is not in the interval, the direction tells us which proportion is larger:

  • If the entire interval is positive (e.g., \( (0.03, 0.15) \)), then \( p_1 > p_2 \).
  • If the entire interval is negative (e.g., \( (-0.12, -0.02) \)), then \( p_1 < p_2 \).

Worked Example

A 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of adults who exercise regularly (Group 1: suburban, Group 2: urban) is \( (0.04, 0.18) \).

Interpretation: Because the interval does not contain 0 and is entirely positive, there is convincing evidence that the proportion of suburban adults who exercise regularly is greater than the proportion of urban adults who exercise regularly.

Key Idea: A confidence interval that does not contain 0 provides the same conclusion as a two-sided hypothesis test that rejects \( H_0 \) at the corresponding significance level. A 95% CI corresponds to \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
AP Exam Trap: Students often say "the proportions are different" without specifying direction. When the entire interval is above or below 0, always state which proportion is larger and reference the context.

Confidence Level and Width

Higher confidence levels produce wider intervals. A wider interval is more likely to contain 0, making it harder to conclude there is a difference. This mirrors the idea that higher confidence levels require stronger evidence to reject \( H_0 \).

problem_sets.title: Practice: Justifying Claims from Confidence Intervals for Two Proportions

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of patients who recover within one week (new drug minus standard drug) is \( (0.05, 0.21) \). Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: There is no convincing evidence of a difference between the two drugs.
There is convincing evidence that the new drug has a higher recovery rate than the standard drug.
There is convincing evidence that the standard drug has a higher recovery rate than the new drug.
The drugs are equally effective because both proportions are positive.

hints.text: Check whether 0 is inside or outside the interval, and note the sign of both endpoints.
The interval \( (0.05, 0.21) \) is entirely positive and does not contain 0, so the new drug proportion is plausibly higher than the standard drug proportion.

solution_steps.text: The interval is \( (0.05, 0.21) \). Since 0 is not in this interval, we have convincing evidence that the true difference \( p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \).
Both endpoints are positive, meaning the new drug's recovery proportion is higher. We conclude there is convincing evidence that the new drug has a higher recovery rate.

problems.question_html: A 90% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \), where \( p_1 \) is the proportion of teens who prefer streaming and \( p_2 \) is the proportion of adults who prefer streaming, is \( (-0.03, 0.11) \). What can we conclude?

choices.text: There is convincing evidence that teens prefer streaming more than adults.
There is convincing evidence that adults prefer streaming more than teens.
There is no convincing evidence of a difference between the proportions of teens and adults who prefer streaming.
The interval proves that \( p_1 = p_2 \).

hints.text: Does the interval contain 0? If so, 0 is a plausible value for the difference.
The interval \( (-0.03, 0.11) \) contains 0, so we cannot conclude the proportions differ. But note: we have not proved they are equal — we simply lack convincing evidence.

solution_steps.text: The interval \( (-0.03, 0.11) \) includes 0, so 0 is a plausible value for \( p_1 - p_2 \).
Since 0 is plausible, we do not have convincing evidence that the proportions differ. We cannot say the interval "proves" equality — it only means we lack evidence to claim a difference.

problems.question_html: A marketing firm constructs a 95% confidence interval for the difference in click-through rates (email campaign A minus email campaign B) and obtains \( (-0.15, -0.03) \). Which interpretation is most appropriate?

choices.text: Campaign A has a higher click-through rate than Campaign B.
Campaign B has a higher click-through rate than Campaign A.
There is no difference in click-through rates between the two campaigns.
The difference in click-through rates is exactly \(-0.09\).

hints.text: The interval is entirely negative. What does a negative value of \( p_A - p_B \) mean?
If \( p_A - p_B < 0 \), then \( p_A < p_B \), meaning Campaign B has the higher click-through rate.

solution_steps.text: The interval \( (-0.15, -0.03) \) does not contain 0 and is entirely negative.
Since the difference is A minus B and is negative, \( p_A < p_B \). Campaign B has a higher click-through rate.

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of college graduates who own homes (millennials minus baby boomers at the same age) is \( (-0.22, -0.08) \). A newspaper headline reads: "Millennials lag behind boomers in homeownership." Is this headline supported by the interval?

choices.text: No, because the interval contains 0.
No, because confidence intervals cannot support directional claims.
Yes, because the entire interval is negative, indicating the millennial proportion is lower.
Yes, because the interval is wide enough to be meaningful.

hints.text: The difference is defined as millennials minus boomers. If this difference is entirely negative, what does that tell you?
A negative interval for (millennials minus boomers) means the millennial proportion is lower — they "lag behind." The headline is supported.

solution_steps.text: The interval \( (-0.22, -0.08) \) is entirely negative and does not contain 0.
Since the difference is millennials minus boomers, a negative difference means the millennial homeownership proportion is lower. The headline is supported by the data.

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of customers who return a product (online minus in-store) is \( (0.02, 0.10) \). Does this interval provide convincing evidence of a difference? State the direction.
problems.correct_answer: yes, online is higher||yes, online return rate is higher||yes online higher

hints.text: Check whether 0 is in the interval, then look at whether both endpoints are positive or negative.
The interval \( (0.02, 0.10) \) does not contain 0 and is entirely positive. Since the difference is defined as online minus in-store, the online return rate is higher.

solution_steps.text: The interval \( (0.02, 0.10) \) does not contain 0, so there is convincing evidence of a difference.
Both endpoints are positive, and the difference is defined as online minus in-store, so the online return proportion is higher than the in-store return proportion.

problems.question_html: A 99% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) is \( (-0.08, 0.02) \). A researcher claims that \( p_1 < p_2 \). Is this claim supported by the interval? Answer "yes" or "no" and briefly explain.
problems.correct_answer: no||no, the interval contains 0

hints.text: For the claim \( p_1 < p_2 \) to be supported, the entire interval would need to be negative (below 0).
The interval \( (-0.08, 0.02) \) contains 0, so we do not have convincing evidence that \( p_1 \neq p_2 \), let alone that \( p_1 < p_2 \).

solution_steps.text: The interval \( (-0.08, 0.02) \) contains 0, which means 0 is a plausible value for the difference.
Since the interval is not entirely negative, the claim that \( p_1 < p_2 \) is not supported. We lack convincing evidence of any difference.

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) is \( (0.01, 0.09) \). A corresponding 99% confidence interval would be wider. Is it possible that the 99% interval could contain 0? Answer "yes" or "no."
problems.correct_answer: yes

hints.text: A 99% confidence interval is wider than a 95% interval. Could the lower endpoint shift below 0?
The 95% lower bound is 0.01, very close to 0. A wider 99% interval could extend below 0, so yes, it is possible the 99% interval contains 0.

solution_steps.text: A 99% CI uses a larger critical value (\( z^* \approx 2.576 \) vs. \( z^* \approx 1.96 \)), producing a wider interval.
The 95% lower bound is only 0.01 above 0. The increased width of the 99% interval could push the lower bound below 0. So yes, it is possible.

problems.question_html: A researcher obtains a 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of voters favoring a policy (rural minus urban): \( (-0.05, 0.05) \). The researcher concludes "the proportions are equal." Identify the error in this reasoning.
problems.correct_answer: the interval shows no convincing evidence of a difference, not that the proportions are equal||lack of evidence is not proof of equality||cannot prove equality

hints.text: There is an important distinction between "no evidence of a difference" and "proof that there is no difference."

A confidence interval that contains 0 means 0 is plausible, but so are other values in the interval. We cannot conclude the proportions are exactly equal — only that we lack convincing evidence of a difference.

solution_steps.text: The interval \( (-0.05, 0.05) \) contains 0, so 0 is a plausible value for the difference.

However, every value from \(-0.05\) to \(0.05\) is also plausible. Failing to find evidence of a difference is not the same as proving the proportions are equal. The correct conclusion is that there is no convincing evidence of a difference.

problems.question_html:
A clinical trial compares a new treatment to a placebo for reducing symptoms. A 95% confidence interval for the difference in the proportion of patients who improve (treatment minus placebo) is \( (0.08, 0.24) \).

(a) Does this interval provide convincing evidence that the treatment is more effective than the placebo? Explain.

(b) A second study with a larger sample yields a 95% CI of \( (0.10, 0.16) \). Compare the two intervals and explain what the narrower interval tells us.

(c) If the FDA requires that the treatment improve recovery rates by at least 0.15 compared to the placebo, does the second interval support this requirement? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Yes. The interval (0.08, 0.24) does not contain 0 and is entirely positive, providing convincing evidence that the treatment proportion is higher than the placebo proportion.

(b) The second interval (0.10, 0.16) is narrower because of the larger sample size. It gives a more precise estimate of the true difference. Both intervals suggest the treatment is more effective, but the second study pins the improvement to between 10 and 16 percentage points.

(c) No. The interval (0.10, 0.16) includes values below 0.15 (such as 0.10 through 0.14). Since 0.15 is inside the interval, we cannot conclude that the true difference is at least 0.15.

hints.text: For part (a), check if 0 is in the interval. For part (b), think about how sample size affects interval width. For part (c), check if 0.15 is inside or outside the interval.

Part (c) is tricky: the FDA benchmark is 0.15, not 0. Check whether 0.15 is a plausible value in the second interval. Since the interval includes values both above and below 0.15, we cannot confirm the benchmark is met.

solution_steps.text: (a) The interval \( (0.08, 0.24) \) does not contain 0. Both endpoints are positive, so there is convincing evidence that the treatment has a higher improvement rate than the placebo.
(b) The second interval \( (0.10, 0.16) \) is narrower, reflecting the larger sample size, which reduces the standard error. It provides a more precise estimate of the true difference.
(c) The value 0.15 falls inside the interval \( (0.10, 0.16) \), meaning the true difference could plausibly be less than 0.15. We cannot conclude that the treatment meets the FDA's 0.15 benchmark.

problems.question_html:
An education researcher studies whether an after-school tutoring program increases the proportion of students passing a standardized test. A random sample of 150 students receives tutoring (Group 1) and 150 students do not (Group 2). The 95% confidence interval for \( p_1 - p_2 \) is \( (0.03, 0.19) \).

(a) Interpret this confidence interval in context.

(b) Based on this interval, is there convincing evidence that the tutoring program increases the pass rate? Justify your answer.

(c) The school board says the program is only worth funding if it increases the pass rate by more than 10 percentage points. Does this interval address the school board's question? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) We are 95% confident that the true difference in the proportion of students who pass (tutored minus not tutored) is between 0.03 and 0.19.

(b) Yes. The interval does not contain 0 and is entirely positive, providing convincing evidence that the tutoring program increases the proportion of students who pass.

(c) The interval does not fully address the board's question. The interval (0.03, 0.19) contains values both above and below 0.10, so we cannot conclude that the true improvement exceeds 10 percentage points. The data are consistent with improvements as small as 3 percentage points.

hints.text: For the interpretation, use the template: "We are [confidence level]% confident that the true [parameter in context] is between [lower] and [upper]."

For part (c), the school board's threshold is 0.10. Check whether 0.10 is inside the interval. Since the interval includes values below 0.10, we cannot be confident the improvement exceeds 10 percentage points.

solution_steps.text: (a) We are 95% confident that the true difference in the proportion of students who pass the standardized test (tutored minus not tutored) is between 0.03 and 0.19.
(b) Since the interval does not contain 0 and is entirely positive, there is convincing evidence that the tutoring program increases the pass rate.

(c) The threshold of 0.10 is inside the interval \( (0.03, 0.19) \), meaning the true difference could be less than 0.10. We cannot conclude the improvement exceeds the school board's 10-percentage-point threshold.

concepts.title: Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
concepts.content_html:
Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

A two-proportion z-test determines whether there is convincing evidence that two population proportions differ. Before performing calculations, we must correctly set up the hypotheses and identify the key components.

The Hypotheses

The null hypothesis always states that there is no difference:

\[ H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \quad \text{(equivalently, } p_1 = p_2\text{)} \]

The alternative hypothesis depends on the research question:

  • Two-sided: \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \) (the proportions differ)
  • One-sided (greater): \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0 \) (proportion 1 is larger)
  • One-sided (less): \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0 \) (proportion 1 is smaller)

The Pooled Proportion

Under \( H_0 \), we assume \( p_1 = p_2 \), so we combine the two samples to get a single estimate of the common proportion:

\[ \hat{p}_c = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2} \]

where \( x_1 \) and \( x_2 \) are the number of successes in each sample. This pooled proportion is used in the standard error for the test (but not for a confidence interval).

Worked Example

A pharmaceutical company tests whether a new antibiotic has a different cure rate than the standard antibiotic. Of 200 patients on the new drug, 172 are cured. Of 200 patients on the standard drug, 158 are cured.

Setup:

  • \( p_1 \) = true cure rate of new drug; \( p_2 \) = true cure rate of standard drug
  • \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \)
  • \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \) (two-sided, since we want to detect any difference)
  • \( \hat{p}_1 = 172/200 = 0.86 \), \( \hat{p}_2 = 158/200 = 0.79 \)
  • \( \hat{p}_c = \frac{172 + 158}{200 + 200} = \frac{330}{400} = 0.825 \)
Key Idea: The pooled proportion \( \hat{p}_c \) is used only in hypothesis testing, never in confidence intervals. For confidence intervals, use the individual sample proportions \( \hat{p}_1 \) and \( \hat{p}_2 \) separately.
AP Exam Trap: When writing hypotheses, always define \( p_1 \) and \( p_2 \) in context (e.g., "\( p_1 \) = true proportion of patients cured by the new drug"). The AP rubric deducts points for undefined parameters.

Choosing One-Sided vs. Two-Sided

Use a one-sided test only when the research question, stated before seeing the data, asks specifically whether one proportion is larger. If the question just asks whether they differ, use a two-sided test.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Setting Up a Two-Proportion z-Test

problems.question_html: A researcher wants to test whether the proportion of high school seniors who plan to attend college differs between rural and urban schools. Which set of hypotheses is appropriate?

hints.text: Hypotheses should use population parameters (\( p \)), not sample statistics (\( \hat{p} \)). The word "differs" suggests a two-sided test.
The null always states no difference: \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \). "Differs" implies \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \) (two-sided).

solution_steps.text: Hypotheses must be about population parameters \( p_1 \) and \( p_2 \), not sample statistics.
The word "differs" does not specify a direction, so the test is two-sided: \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \), \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \).

problems.question_html: An A/B test compares two website designs. Design A was shown to 500 visitors, and 85 made a purchase. Design B was shown to 600 visitors, and 78 made a purchase. The company wants to know if Design A has a higher purchase rate. Which is the correct alternative hypothesis?

choices.text: \( H_a: p_A - p_B \neq 0 \)
\( H_a: \hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B > 0 \)

hints.text: The company specifically asks if Design A has a higher rate. This indicates a one-sided (greater) test.
"Higher" for Design A means \( p_A > p_B \), or equivalently \( p_A - p_B > 0 \). Use population parameters, not sample statistics.

solution_steps.text: The company wants to test if Design A's purchase rate is higher than Design B's.
This is a one-sided test: \( H_a: p_A - p_B > 0 \). The alternative uses population parameters \( p \), not \( \hat{p} \).

problems.question_html: A consumer group surveys 800 adults: 420 out of 500 smartphone users and 210 out of 300 non-smartphone users say they read news daily. The group wants to test whether the proportion who read news daily differs between smartphone users and non-smartphone users. What is the pooled proportion \( \hat{p}_c \)?

hints.text: The pooled proportion combines the total successes over total sample size, not the average of two proportions.
\( \hat{p}_c = \frac{420 + 210}{500 + 300} = \frac{630}{800} = 0.7875 \). Note that averaging the two sample proportions gives an incorrect answer when sample sizes differ.

solution_steps.text: The pooled proportion is \( \hat{p}_c = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2} \), where we combine all successes and all observations.
\( \hat{p}_c = \frac{420 + 210}{500 + 300} = \frac{630}{800} = 0.7875 \). Averaging the individual proportions would be incorrect because the sample sizes differ.

problems.question_html: A school district wants to test whether the proportion of students passing a math exam is higher at School A than at School B. A teacher writes: \( H_0: \hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B = 0 \), \( H_a: \hat{p}_A - \hat{p}_B > 0 \). Identify the error.

choices.text: The alternative should be two-sided.
The hypotheses should use population parameters \( p_A \) and \( p_B \), not sample statistics \( \hat{p}_A \) and \( \hat{p}_B \).
The null hypothesis should be \( H_0: p_A - p_B > 0 \).
There is no error; the hypotheses are correctly stated.

hints.text: Look carefully at the notation. Are hypotheses about sample statistics or population parameters?
Hypotheses are always about population parameters (\( p \)), never sample statistics (\( \hat{p} \)). The direction is fine since the question asks about "higher."

solution_steps.text: The teacher used \( \hat{p} \) (sample proportions) instead of \( p \) (population parameters).
Hypotheses must refer to population parameters. The correct version is \( H_0: p_A - p_B = 0 \), \( H_a: p_A - p_B > 0 \).

problems.question_html: In a study, 45 out of 300 men and 60 out of 350 women reported experiencing migraines regularly. Calculate the pooled proportion \( \hat{p}_c \). Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: The pooled proportion combines both samples: \( \hat{p}_c = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2} \).

problems.question_html: A study tests whether a new vaccine has a lower infection rate than a placebo. Of 400 vaccine recipients, 12 became infected. Of 400 placebo recipients, 28 became infected. Define the parameters and state the null and alternative hypotheses using \( p_1 \) for the vaccine group.

hints.text: The research question asks if the vaccine has a lower infection rate. This determines the direction of the alternative.
With \( p_1 \) = vaccine infection rate and \( p_2 \) = placebo infection rate, "lower" means \( p_1 < p_2 \), so \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0 \).

solution_steps.text: Define: \( p_1 \) = true proportion of vaccine recipients who become infected; \( p_2 \) = true proportion of placebo recipients who become infected.
Hypotheses: \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \); \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0 \) (one-sided, testing if the vaccine group has a lower infection rate).

problems.question_html: In a study, 120 out of 400 adults under 30 and 90 out of 350 adults 30 and older support a policy. Calculate the pooled proportion \( \hat{p}_c \). Round to four decimal places.

A political analyst wants to know if the proportion of voters who support a candidate is lower among women than among men. Among 600 women surveyed, 252 support the candidate. Among 550 men surveyed, 264 support the candidate. Define parameters, state hypotheses, and compute the pooled proportion.

hints.text: Define \( p_1 \) for women and \( p_2 \) for men. "Lower among women" tells you the direction for \( H_a \). Then calculate \( \hat{p}_c \).

solution_steps.text: Let \( p_1 \) = true proportion of women who support the candidate, \( p_2 \) = true proportion of men who support the candidate.
\( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \); \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0 \) (one-sided, testing if women's support is lower).

problems.question_html:
A health organization conducts a study comparing smoking rates in two cities. In City X, 84 out of 600 adults smoke. In City Y, 108 out of 750 adults smoke. The organization wants to test whether the smoking rates differ.

(a) Define the population parameters.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses.

(c) Calculate the pooled proportion and explain why pooling is appropriate here.

(d) Explain why a one-sided test would not be appropriate for this study.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Let p_1 = true proportion of adults in City X who smoke. Let p_2 = true proportion of adults in City Y who smoke.

(b) H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 (no difference in smoking rates). H_a: p_1 - p_2 \(
eq\) 0 (the smoking rates differ).

(c) p_c = (84 + 108)/(600 + 750) = 192/1350 ≈ 0.1422. Pooling is appropriate because under H_0 we assume p_1 = p_2, so combining the samples gives the best single estimate of this common proportion.

(d) The research question asks whether the rates "differ," with no prior suspicion about which city has the higher rate. A one-sided test requires a directional claim made before seeing the data, which is not the case here.

hints.text: For part (c), remember that pooling is justified by the assumption of H_0, which says the two proportions are equal.
For part (d), the key point is that one-sided tests require a directional hypothesis stated before data collection. "Differ" implies no predetermined direction.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( p_1 \) = true proportion of adults in City X who smoke; \( p_2 \) = true proportion of adults in City Y who smoke.
(b) \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \); \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \). The word "differ" calls for a two-sided test.

(c) \( \hat{p}_c = \frac{84 + 108}{600 + 750} = \frac{192}{1350} \approx 0.1422 \). Pooling is appropriate because \( H_0 \) assumes the proportions are equal, so combining gives the best estimate of the shared proportion.
(d) A one-sided test requires a directional hypothesis stated before seeing data. The study only asks whether the rates differ, with no prior belief about which city has a higher rate.

problems.question_html:
A tech company runs an A/B test to see if changing a button color from blue (Group A, \( n_A = 1{,}200 \)) to green (Group B, \( n_B = 1{,}000 \)) increases the click rate. Group A had 180 clicks and Group B had 170 clicks.

(a) Define parameters and state the hypotheses. Explain why this is a one-sided test.

(b) Calculate \( \hat{p}_A \), \( \hat{p}_B \), and the pooled proportion \( \hat{p}_c \).

(c) A colleague suggests using \( \hat{p}_c \) to build a confidence interval. Explain why this is incorrect.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Let p_A = true click rate with blue button; p_B = true click rate with green button. H_0: p_B - p_A = 0; H_a: p_B - p_A > 0. This is one-sided because the company specifically wants to test if the green button increases clicks.

(b) p-hat_A = 180/1200 = 0.15; p-hat_B = 170/1000 = 0.17; p_c = (180 + 170)/(1200 + 1000) = 350/2200 ≈ 0.1591.

(c) The pooled proportion assumes H_0 is true (p_1 = p_2) and is used only in hypothesis testing. For a confidence interval, we do not assume the proportions are equal, so we use the individual sample proportions in the standard error formula.

hints.text: The company wants to know if the green button "increases" the click rate — this is directional, so one-sided.
For part (c), the pooled proportion is valid only under the null hypothesis assumption. A confidence interval estimates the actual difference without assuming it is zero.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( p_A \) = true click rate for blue button; \( p_B \) = true click rate for green button. \( H_0: p_B - p_A = 0 \); \( H_a: p_B - p_A > 0 \). One-sided because the question asks specifically about an increase.
(c) The pooled proportion assumes \( H_0: p_1 = p_2 \) is true. Confidence intervals do not assume this, so they use individual \( \hat{p}_1 \) and \( \hat{p}_2 \) in the standard error formula.

concepts.title: Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions
concepts.content_html:
Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions

The two-proportion z-test follows the standard four-step inference framework: State, Plan, Do, Conclude. This topic focuses on checking conditions, computing the test statistic, finding the p-value, and writing a conclusion in context.

The Test Statistic

Under \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \), the test statistic is:

\[ z = \frac{(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) - 0}{\sqrt{\hat{p}_c(1 - \hat{p}_c)\left(\dfrac{1}{n_1} + \dfrac{1}{n_2}\right)}} \]

where \( \hat{p}_c = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{n_1 + n_2} \) is the pooled proportion.

Conditions (Plan Step)

All three conditions must be checked for both samples:

  1. Random: Both samples must be randomly selected or randomly assigned.
  2. 10% Condition: \( n_1 \leq 10\% \) of population 1, and \( n_2 \leq 10\% \) of population 2. (Not needed for experiments.)
  3. Large Counts: Using the pooled proportion: \( n_1 \hat{p}_c \geq 10 \), \( n_1(1 - \hat{p}_c) \geq 10 \), \( n_2 \hat{p}_c \geq 10 \), \( n_2(1 - \hat{p}_c) \geq 10 \).

Worked Example (Full 4-Step Process)

A school district tests whether a new reading program improves literacy. In a randomized experiment, 64 out of 200 students using the new program pass a literacy test, while 42 out of 200 students using the traditional program pass.

State: \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \); \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0 \), where \( p_1 \) = true pass rate with new program and \( p_2 \) = true pass rate with traditional. \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

Plan:

  • Random: Students were randomly assigned to programs. \(\checkmark\)
  • 10%: Not needed for an experiment. \(\checkmark\)
  • Large Counts: \( \hat{p}_c = 106/400 = 0.265 \). Check: \( 200(0.265) = 53 \geq 10 \), \( 200(0.735) = 147 \geq 10 \). \(\checkmark\) (same for both groups since \( n_1 = n_2 \))

Do:

\[ z = \frac{(0.32 - 0.21) - 0}{\sqrt{0.265(0.735)\left(\frac{1}{200} + \frac{1}{200}\right)}} = \frac{0.11}{\sqrt{0.265 \times 0.735 \times 0.01}} = \frac{0.11}{0.04413} \approx 2.49 \]

P-value: \( P(z > 2.49) \approx 0.0064 \).

Conclude: Since the p-value (0.0064) is less than \( \alpha = 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the new reading program results in a higher pass rate than the traditional program.

Key Idea: In the Large Counts condition for a two-proportion z-test, use the pooled proportion \( \hat{p}_c \), not the individual sample proportions. This is because the null hypothesis assumes the proportions are equal.
AP Exam Trap: Many students lose points by not checking conditions for both samples. You must verify Random, 10%, and Large Counts for each group separately. Also, always use \( \hat{p}_c \) (not \( \hat{p}_1 \) or \( \hat{p}_2 \)) in the Large Counts check.
