problem_sets.title: Practice: Two-Proportion z-Test

problems.question_html: In a randomized experiment, 78 out of 250 participants in Group 1 succeed and 54 out of 250 in Group 2 succeed. The pooled proportion is \( \hat{p}_c = 0.264 \). Which value is closest to the test statistic for \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0 \)?

choices.text: \( z \approx 1.22 \)
\( z \approx 2.42 \)
\( z \approx 3.06 \)
\( z \approx 0.96 \)

hints.text: Use \( z = \frac{\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2}{\sqrt{\hat{p}_c(1-\hat{p}_c)(1/n_1 + 1/n_2)}} \). First compute \( \hat{p}_1 = 78/250 \) and \( \hat{p}_2 = 54/250 \).

problems.question_html: When checking the Large Counts condition for a two-proportion z-test, a student uses \( n_1 \hat{p}_1 \geq 10 \) and \( n_1(1 - \hat{p}_1) \geq 10 \) instead of using \( \hat{p}_c \). What is wrong with this approach?

choices.text: Nothing — using individual sample proportions is always acceptable.
The 10% condition should be checked instead of Large Counts.
Under \( H_0 \), we assume the proportions are equal, so the pooled proportion \( \hat{p}_c \) should be used for the Large Counts check.
The Large Counts condition only needs to be checked for one sample.

hints.text: Think about what the null hypothesis assumes. If \( H_0 \) says \( p_1 = p_2 \), what should be used to estimate this common proportion?
Since \( H_0 \) assumes a common proportion, we use the pooled estimate \( \hat{p}_c \) for all calculations under the null, including the Large Counts condition.

solution_steps.text: The null hypothesis assumes \( p_1 = p_2 \). Under this assumption, the best estimate of the common proportion is \( \hat{p}_c \).
Therefore, the Large Counts condition should use \( \hat{p}_c \): check \( n_1 \hat{p}_c \geq 10 \), \( n_1(1 - \hat{p}_c) \geq 10 \), and similarly for \( n_2 \).

problems.question_html: A researcher tests whether a new fertilizer increases the proportion of seeds that germinate compared to a standard fertilizer. In a randomized experiment, 156 out of 200 seeds with the new fertilizer germinated, versus 138 out of 200 with the standard. Which condition is not required to check for this experiment?

choices.text: Random assignment
Large Counts using \( \hat{p}_c \)
10% condition
Independence within each group

hints.text: The 10% condition is about sampling without replacement from a finite population. Does this apply to experiments?
In a randomized experiment, subjects are assigned to treatments — they are not sampled from a population. The 10% condition is not needed.

solution_steps.text: The 10% condition applies when sampling from a finite population to ensure approximate independence.
In a randomized experiment, treatments are assigned, not sampled. The 10% condition is not required.

problems.question_html: A poll finds that 320 out of 800 Democrats and 280 out of 750 Republicans support a policy. A two-sided test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) gives \( z = 1.03 \). The p-value is 0.3030. Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: Reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence of a difference in support between Democrats and Republicans.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is not convincing evidence of a difference in support between Democrats and Republicans.
Accept \( H_0 \). The proportions are equal.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \). The proportions are proven to be equal.

hints.text: Compare the p-value to \( \alpha \). Remember: we never "accept" \( H_0 \) or "prove" equality.
0.3030 > 0.05, so we fail to reject \( H_0 \). The correct language is "there is not convincing evidence of a difference" — we do not say the proportions are equal.

solution_steps.text: The p-value (0.3030) exceeds \( \alpha = 0.05 \), so we fail to reject \( H_0 \).
We conclude there is not convincing evidence of a difference. We never say "accept \( H_0 \)" or that the proportions are proven equal.

problems.question_html: A two-proportion z-test yields \( z = -1.85 \) for a two-sided test. Using a standard normal table, the area to the left of \( -1.85 \) is 0.0322. What is the p-value?

hints.text: For a two-sided test, the p-value accounts for both tails of the distribution.

solution_steps.text: For a two-sided test, the p-value is twice the tail area: \( 2 \times 0.0322 = 0.0644 \).
Since \( 0.0644 > 0.05 \), we would fail to reject \( H_0 \) at \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

problems.question_html: A one-sided two-proportion z-test yields \( z = 2.10 \) with \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0 \). The area to the right of 2.10 in the standard normal distribution is 0.0179. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), what is the conclusion?
problems.correct_answer: reject H0||reject the null hypothesis||reject

hints.text: Compare the p-value to \( \alpha \). If p-value < \( \alpha \), reject \( H_0 \).
P-value = 0.0179 < 0.05 = \( \alpha \). We reject \( H_0 \) and conclude there is convincing evidence that \( p_1 > p_2 \).

solution_steps.text: The p-value for this one-sided test is 0.0179.
Since 0.0179 < 0.05, we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that \( p_1 > p_2 \).

problems.question_html: In a study, 90 out of 300 patients taking Drug A and 75 out of 300 patients taking Drug B experience side effects. Compute the z-test statistic for \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \). Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: First find \( \hat{p}_c = (90 + 75)/(300 + 300) \), then compute the standard error and test statistic.

problems.question_html: A survey asks 500 adults under 40 and 500 adults 40+ whether they support a ban on single-use plastics. Of the younger group, 310 support it; of the older group, 275 support it. Compute the z-test statistic for \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \). Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Find \( \hat{p}_c \) first, then the SE, then \( z \).

problems.question_html:
A medical researcher conducts a randomized controlled trial comparing a new therapy to standard care. Of 180 patients receiving the new therapy, 99 show improvement. Of 180 patients receiving standard care, 72 show improvement. Perform a complete two-proportion z-test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) to determine whether the new therapy has a higher improvement rate.

Use the four-step process: State, Plan, Do, Conclude.
problems.correct_answer:
STATE: H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 where p_1 = true improvement rate for new therapy and p_2 = true improvement rate for standard care. H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0. α = 0.05.

PLAN: Random — patients were randomly assigned to treatments. ✓ 10% — not needed for a randomized experiment. ✓ Large Counts — p_c = (99+72)/(180+180) = 171/360 = 0.475. n_1·p_c = 180(0.475) = 85.5 ≥ 10 ✓; n_1(1-p_c) = 180(0.525) = 94.5 ≥ 10 ✓; n_2·p_c = 85.5 ≥ 10 ✓; n_2(1-p_c) = 94.5 ≥ 10 ✓.

DO: p-hat_1 = 99/180 = 0.55, p-hat_2 = 72/180 = 0.40. SE = sqrt(0.475 × 0.525 × (1/180 + 1/180)) = sqrt(0.249375 × 0.01111) = sqrt(0.002771) ≈ 0.05264. z = (0.55 - 0.40)/0.05264 ≈ 2.85. P-value = P(z > 2.85) ≈ 0.0022.

CONCLUDE: Since the p-value (0.0022) < α (0.05), we reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that the new therapy has a higher improvement rate than standard care.

hints.text: Remember to define parameters in context, check all three conditions (Random, 10%, Large Counts), compute the test statistic using the pooled proportion, and write the conclusion in context.
This is a randomized experiment, so the 10% condition is not needed. Use \( \hat{p}_c = 171/360 = 0.475 \) for the Large Counts check and the SE calculation.

solution_steps.text: STATE: Let \( p_1 \) = true improvement rate for new therapy, \( p_2 \) = true improvement rate for standard care. \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \); \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0 \). \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

PLAN: Random — patients were randomly assigned. \(\checkmark\) 10% — not needed for an experiment. Large Counts: \( \hat{p}_c = 171/360 = 0.475 \). All four products (\( 180 \times 0.475 = 85.5 \), \( 180 \times 0.525 = 94.5 \)) are \( \geq 10 \). \(\checkmark\)
CONCLUDE: Since p-value (0.0022) < \( \alpha \) (0.05), reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the new therapy has a higher improvement rate than standard care.

problems.question_html:
A consumer advocacy group surveys shoppers at two grocery chains. At Chain A, 216 out of 600 shoppers say they are "very satisfied." At Chain B, 195 out of 500 shoppers say the same. The group obtained both samples using random selection from membership lists.

Perform a complete two-proportion z-test at \( \alpha = 0.01 \) to determine whether there is a difference in the proportions of satisfied shoppers. Use State, Plan, Do, Conclude.
problems.correct_answer:
STATE: p_1 = true proportion of Chain A shoppers who are very satisfied. p_2 = true proportion of Chain B shoppers who are very satisfied. H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0; H_a: p_1 - p_2 \(
eq\) 0. α = 0.01.

PLAN: Random — both samples were randomly selected from membership lists. ✓ 10% — 600 is less than 10% of all Chain A shoppers, and 500 is less than 10% of all Chain B shoppers (assuming large chains). ✓ Large Counts: p_c = (216+195)/(600+500) = 411/1100 ≈ 0.3736. 600(0.3736)=224.2 ≥ 10; 600(0.6264)=375.8 ≥ 10; 500(0.3736)=186.8 ≥ 10; 500(0.6264)=313.2 ≥ 10. ✓

DO: p-hat_1 = 216/600 = 0.36, p-hat_2 = 195/500 = 0.39. SE = sqrt(0.3736 × 0.6264 × (1/600 + 1/500)) = sqrt(0.2340 × 0.003667) = sqrt(0.000858) ≈ 0.02929. z = (0.36 - 0.39)/0.02929 = -0.03/0.02929 ≈ -1.02. P-value = 2 × P(z < -1.02) ≈ 2 × 0.1539 = 0.3078.

CONCLUDE: Since the p-value (0.3078) > α (0.01), we fail to reject H_0. There is not convincing evidence of a difference in the proportions of shoppers who are very satisfied between Chain A and Chain B.

hints.text: This is a two-sided test since the question asks about "a difference" (no direction specified). Remember to double the tail area for the p-value.
\( \hat{p}_c = 411/1100 \approx 0.3736 \). The difference \( 0.36 - 0.39 = -0.03 \) is small. With the SE around 0.029, \( z \approx -1.02 \), which gives a large p-value.

solution_steps.text: STATE: \( p_1 \) = true proportion of Chain A shoppers who are very satisfied; \( p_2 \) = same for Chain B. \( H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \); \( H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0 \). \( \alpha = 0.01 \).

PLAN: Random \(\checkmark\) (random selection from membership lists). 10% \(\checkmark\) (both samples are less than 10% of all shoppers at large chains). Large Counts: \( \hat{p}_c = 411/1100 \approx 0.3736 \). All four products exceed 10. \(\checkmark\)
CONCLUDE: Since 0.3078 > 0.01, fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is not convincing evidence of a difference in satisfaction proportions between the two chains.

concepts.title: Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
concepts.content_html:
Setting Up a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

Chi-square tests extend the comparison of proportions to situations with more than two categories or more than two groups. There are two types, distinguished by study design:

Test for Homogeneity

Used when we have two or more independent samples (populations) and want to test whether the distribution of a categorical variable is the same across all populations.

Example: Are the distributions of political party affiliation (Democrat, Republican, Independent) the same for three age groups?

Test for Independence

Used when we have one sample from one population and want to test whether two categorical variables are associated (not independent).

Example: Is there an association between gender and preferred mode of transportation among U.S. adults?

Hypotheses

Homogeneity:

  • \( H_0 \): The distribution of [variable] is the same across all populations.
  • \( H_a \): The distribution of [variable] is not the same across all populations.

Independence:

  • \( H_0 \): [Variable 1] and [Variable 2] are independent in the population.
  • \( H_a \): [Variable 1] and [Variable 2] are not independent (they are associated).

Expected Counts

For each cell in the two-way table:

\[ E = \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{table total}} \]

Expected counts represent what we would observe if the null hypothesis were true.

The Chi-Square Statistic

\[ \chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E} \]

where \( O \) = observed count and \( E \) = expected count. The sum is taken over all cells in the table.

Degrees of Freedom

\[ df = (r - 1)(c - 1) \]

where \( r \) = number of rows and \( c \) = number of columns.

Worked Example

A researcher surveys 400 adults about their preferred news source (TV, Online, Print) in two cities:

TVOnlinePrintTotal
City A809030200
City B6011030200
Total14020060400

Expected count for City A, TV: \( E = \frac{200 \times 140}{400} = 70 \).

Expected count for City A, Online: \( E = \frac{200 \times 200}{400} = 100 \).

This is a test for homogeneity (two separate populations: City A and City B).

\( df = (2-1)(3-1) = 2 \).

Key Idea: Homogeneity and independence tests use the same formula and the same mechanics. The difference is in the study design: homogeneity compares distributions across pre-defined populations, while independence tests for an association within one population.
AP Exam Trap: Many students confuse homogeneity and independence. Ask: "Were multiple populations sampled separately (homogeneity), or was one population sampled and two variables recorded (independence)?" The AP exam will test your ability to distinguish them.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Chi-Square Test Setup

problems.question_html: A researcher randomly selects 300 adults from a city and records their education level (high school, bachelor's, graduate) and exercise frequency (daily, weekly, rarely). Which test is appropriate?

choices.text: Chi-square test for homogeneity
Chi-square test for independence
Two-proportion z-test
Chi-square goodness-of-fit test

hints.text: How many populations were sampled? Were two variables measured on each individual from a single sample?
One sample of 300 adults was drawn, and two categorical variables (education level, exercise frequency) were recorded. This calls for a chi-square test for independence.

solution_steps.text: A single sample of 300 adults was selected from one population, and two categorical variables were recorded for each.
This is a test for independence: we test whether education level and exercise frequency are associated.

problems.question_html: A marketing firm surveys 200 customers from Brand X and 250 customers from Brand Y about their satisfaction (satisfied, neutral, dissatisfied). Which test is appropriate?

choices.text: Chi-square test for independence
Chi-square test for homogeneity
One-proportion z-test
Two-proportion z-test

hints.text: Were separate samples drawn from distinct populations, or was one sample drawn and two variables measured?
Two separate populations (Brand X customers and Brand Y customers) were sampled independently. We compare the distribution of satisfaction across these populations — this is a test for homogeneity.

solution_steps.text: Two independent samples were drawn from two populations (Brand X and Brand Y customers).
We want to know if the distribution of satisfaction is the same across the two brands. This is a chi-square test for homogeneity.

Consider the following two-way table of observed counts:

Prefer APrefer BNo Preference
Group 1405010
Group 2304525

What is the expected count for the cell (Group 2, No Preference)?

problems.question_html: A study examines whether the distribution of beverage preferences (coffee, tea, juice, water) is the same for three age groups (18–30, 31–50, 51+). Samples of 150 are drawn from each age group. State the null and alternative hypotheses.

choices.text: \( H_0 \): Age group and beverage preference are independent. \( H_a \): They are not independent.
\( H_0 \): The distribution of beverage preference is the same for all three age groups. \( H_a \): The distribution is not the same for all three age groups.
\( H_0 \): \( p_1 = p_2 = p_3 \). \( H_a \): At least one \( p_i \) differs.
\( H_0 \): The proportions are equal. \( H_a \): The proportions are not equal.

hints.text: Separate samples were drawn from three populations. Is this homogeneity or independence?
Three separate samples (one per age group) means this is a test for homogeneity. The hypotheses compare distributions, not just single proportions.

solution_steps.text: Three independent samples from three populations indicate a test for homogeneity.
\( H_0 \): The distribution of beverage preference is the same across all three age groups. \( H_a \): The distribution is not the same for all three age groups.

problems.question_html: A two-way table has 3 rows and 4 columns. What are the degrees of freedom for the chi-square test?

hints.text: Use the formula \( df = (r-1)(c-1) \).

solution_steps.text: Apply the formula: \( df = (r-1)(c-1) = (3-1)(4-1) = 6 \).

problems.question_html: In a two-way table, one cell has a row total of 120, a column total of 80, and a table total of 400. What is the expected count for this cell?

hints.text: Use \( E = \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{table total}} \).

problems.question_html: A two-way table has observed count \( O = 30 \) and expected count \( E = 22 \) in one cell. What is this cell's contribution to the chi-square statistic? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Each cell's contribution is \( \frac{(O - E)^2}{E} \).

problems.question_html: A researcher collects data from 500 employees at a single company and records their department (Sales, Engineering, HR) and job satisfaction (High, Medium, Low). The degrees of freedom for the chi-square test are:

hints.text: Count the rows and columns. \( df = (r-1)(c-1) \).
3 departments (rows) and 3 satisfaction levels (columns): \( df = (3-1)(3-1) = 4 \). This is a test for independence (one sample from one company).

solution_steps.text: The table is 3 rows by 3 columns. \( df = (3-1)(3-1) = 2 \times 2 = 4 \).

problems.question_html:
A school district wants to know if the distribution of students' post-graduation plans (4-year college, community college, workforce, military) is the same across three high schools. Random samples of 100 seniors are taken from each school.

(a) Identify whether this is a test for homogeneity or independence. Justify your answer.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses in context.

(c) Determine the degrees of freedom.

(d) One cell has row total 100, column total 90, and table total 300. Calculate the expected count and explain what it represents.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) This is a test for homogeneity. Three separate random samples were drawn from three distinct populations (seniors at each of the three high schools). We are comparing the distribution of post-graduation plans across these populations.

(b) H_0: The distribution of post-graduation plans is the same across all three high schools. H_a: The distribution of post-graduation plans is not the same across all three high schools.

(c) df = (3-1)(4-1) = 2 × 3 = 6.

(d) E = (100 × 90)/300 = 30. This expected count represents the number of students in that cell we would expect to observe if the distribution of post-graduation plans were truly the same across all three schools.

hints.text: Were separate samples drawn from distinct groups, or was one sample drawn and two variables measured?
Three separate samples of 100 from three schools means homogeneity. The table is 3 rows (schools) by 4 columns (plans), so \( df = (3-1)(4-1) = 6 \).

solution_steps.text: (a) Test for homogeneity — three independent samples were drawn from three populations (one per school).
(b) \( H_0 \): The distribution of post-graduation plans is the same across all three schools. \( H_a \): The distribution is not the same across all three schools.
(d) \( E = \frac{100 \times 90}{300} = 30 \). This is the expected number of students in that cell if the null hypothesis (same distribution across schools) is true.

problems.question_html:
A health survey records the smoking status (current, former, never) and exercise level (active, moderate, sedentary) for 1,200 randomly selected adults. The data are shown below:

ActiveModerateSedentaryTotal
Current4080120240
Former100140120360
Never200220180600
Total3404404201200

(a) Is this a test for homogeneity or independence? Explain.

(b) State the hypotheses.

(c) Calculate the expected count for the cell (Current smoker, Active). Show your work.

(d) Calculate the degrees of freedom and explain what they represent.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) This is a test for independence. One sample of 1,200 adults was drawn from a single population, and two categorical variables (smoking status and exercise level) were recorded for each person.

(b) H_0: Smoking status and exercise level are independent in the population of adults. H_a: Smoking status and exercise level are not independent (they are associated).

(c) E = (row total × column total)/table total = (240 × 340)/1200 = 81600/1200 = 68. If smoking status and exercise level were independent, we would expect 68 current smokers to be active.

(d) df = (3-1)(3-1) = 4. The degrees of freedom represent the number of cells whose values can vary freely once the row and column totals are fixed.

hints.text: One sample of 1,200 was drawn, and two variables were measured. This points to independence, not homogeneity.
For the expected count: \( E = \frac{240 \times 340}{1200} = 68 \). Degrees of freedom: \( (3-1)(3-1) = 4 \).

solution_steps.text: (a) One sample from one population with two variables recorded — this is a test for independence.
(b) \( H_0 \): Smoking status and exercise level are independent. \( H_a \): They are not independent (associated).
(d) \( df = (3-1)(3-1) = 4 \). These represent the number of cell values that can vary freely given fixed margins.

concepts.title: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence
concepts.content_html:
Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

After setting up the hypotheses and computing expected counts, we check conditions, calculate the chi-square statistic, find the p-value, and write a conclusion in context.

Conditions

  1. Random: Data come from a random sample or random assignment.
  2. 10% Condition: The sample is less than 10% of the population (for surveys; not needed for experiments).
  3. Large Counts: All expected counts are at least 5. (Note: this is \( \geq 5 \), not \( \geq 10 \) as in proportion tests.)

Computing the Chi-Square Statistic

\[ \chi^2 = \sum \frac{(O - E)^2}{E} \]

Each cell contributes one term to the sum. Larger values of \( \chi^2 \) provide stronger evidence against \( H_0 \).

P-Value and Conclusion

The chi-square test is always a right-tail test. Use the chi-square distribution with \( df = (r-1)(c-1) \) to find the p-value.

  • If p-value \( < \alpha \): reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence of an association (independence test) or that the distributions differ (homogeneity test).
  • If p-value \( \geq \alpha \): fail to reject \( H_0 \). No convincing evidence.

Follow-Up Analysis

After finding a significant result, examine which cells contributed most to the chi-square statistic. The cells with the largest \( \frac{(O-E)^2}{E} \) values drove the result. Describe how the observed count differs from the expected count (more than expected or fewer than expected) for those cells.

Worked Example

A researcher tests whether the distribution of exercise habits (daily, weekly, rarely) is the same for three regions. The chi-square statistic is \( \chi^2 = 14.8 \) with \( df = 4 \).

Using a chi-square table: for \( df = 4 \), \( \chi^2 = 13.28 \) gives p-value = 0.01 and \( \chi^2 = 14.86 \) gives p-value = 0.005. Since \( 13.28 < 14.8 < 14.86 \), the p-value is between 0.005 and 0.01.

At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), the p-value is less than 0.05, so we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the distribution of exercise habits is not the same across the three regions.

Key Idea: The chi-square test is always right-tailed. A large \( \chi^2 \) value means the observed data deviate substantially from what we would expect under \( H_0 \). There is no "left tail" rejection region for chi-square.
AP Exam Trap: For follow-up analysis, the AP exam often asks you to identify which cells contributed most to \( \chi^2 \) and describe the pattern. Simply stating "the test was significant" is not enough — you must explain where the differences are and in what direction (observed > expected or observed < expected).

Important Distinction from Proportion Tests

The Large Counts condition for chi-square requires all expected counts \( \geq 5 \) (not 10). This is a common source of confusion. Also, chi-square tests use expected counts, while proportion tests use \( n\hat{p}_c \) and \( n(1 - \hat{p}_c) \).
concepts.content_raw: Carrying Out a Chi-Square Test for Homogeneity or Independence

problem_sets.title: Practice: Carrying Out Chi-Square Tests

problems.question_html: A chi-square test for independence with \( df = 6 \) yields \( \chi^2 = 18.3 \). Using a chi-square table, the critical value for \( \alpha = 0.01 \) with \( df = 6 \) is 16.812. What is the decision?

choices.text: Fail to reject \( H_0 \) because \( \chi^2 < 16.812 \).
Reject \( H_0 \) because \( \chi^2 = 18.3 > 16.812 \), so the p-value < 0.01.
Reject \( H_0 \) only if \( \alpha = 0.05 \), not at \( \alpha = 0.01 \).
Cannot determine without the exact p-value.

hints.text: For a right-tail test, if the test statistic exceeds the critical value, the p-value is less than \( \alpha \).
\( 18.3 > 16.812 \), so the p-value < 0.01. We reject \( H_0 \) at the 0.01 significance level.

solution_steps.text: The chi-square test is right-tailed. Since \( \chi^2 = 18.3 > 16.812 \) (the critical value for \( \alpha = 0.01 \)), the p-value is less than 0.01.
We reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence of an association (or that the distributions differ).

problems.question_html: Which condition for a chi-square test is different from the conditions for a two-proportion z-test?

choices.text: The Random condition
The 10% condition
The Large Counts condition — chi-square requires all expected counts \( \geq 5 \), not \( \geq 10 \)
All conditions are identical for both tests

hints.text: Think about the threshold in the Large Counts condition. Is it the same for both types of tests?
For proportion z-tests, each expected count (\( n\hat{p}_c \) and \( n(1-\hat{p}_c) \)) must be \( \geq 10 \). For chi-square, each expected cell count must be \( \geq 5 \).

solution_steps.text: The Random and 10% conditions are similar for both tests.
The Large Counts condition differs: z-tests require \( \geq 10 \) for each count; chi-square tests require all expected counts \( \geq 5 \).

problems.question_html: A researcher finds \( \chi^2 = 3.2 \) with \( df = 2 \) in a test for independence. Using a chi-square table, the critical value at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) for \( df = 2 \) is 5.991. What is the conclusion?

choices.text: Reject \( H_0 \); the variables are associated.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \); the variables are proven independent.
Fail to reject \( H_0 \); there is not convincing evidence of an association.
Reject \( H_0 \); the p-value is less than 0.05.

hints.text: Compare the test statistic to the critical value. If \( \chi^2 \) is less than the critical value, the p-value exceeds \( \alpha \).
\( 3.2 < 5.991 \), so the p-value > 0.05. We fail to reject \( H_0 \). We do not say the variables are "proven independent" — only that we lack evidence of an association.

solution_steps.text: We fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is not convincing evidence that the two variables are associated.

problems.question_html: A chi-square test for homogeneity comparing the distribution of transportation mode (car, bus, bike) across 4 neighborhoods yields \( \chi^2 = 22.5 \). The table has 4 rows and 3 columns. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), the critical value for \( df = 6 \) is 12.592. What is the decision, and what does it mean in context?

choices.text: Fail to reject \( H_0 \); the distribution of transportation mode is the same across all neighborhoods.
Reject \( H_0 \); there is convincing evidence that the distribution of transportation mode is not the same across all four neighborhoods.
Reject \( H_0 \); there is convincing evidence that transportation mode and neighborhood are independent.
Cannot determine without knowing expected counts.

hints.text: Compare \( \chi^2 = 22.5 \) to the critical value 12.592. This is a test for homogeneity, so the conclusion should reference distributions.
\( 22.5 > 12.592 \), so we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the distribution of transportation mode is not the same across the four neighborhoods.

solution_steps.text: \( \chi^2 = 22.5 > 12.592 \), so the p-value < 0.05. We reject \( H_0 \).
Conclusion: There is convincing evidence that the distribution of transportation mode is not the same across all four neighborhoods.

problems.question_html: A chi-square test for homogeneity has \( df = 4 \) and \( \chi^2 = 9.49 \). The p-value is approximately 0.05. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), should we reject \( H_0 \)? Answer "yes" or "no."
problems.correct_answer: no||no, p-value is not less than alpha

hints.text: We reject \( H_0 \) when the p-value is less than \( \alpha \), not equal to it.
The p-value \( \approx 0.05 \) is not strictly less than \( \alpha = 0.05 \). We fail to reject \( H_0 \). (Borderline cases like this are typically reported as "fail to reject" on the AP exam.)

solution_steps.text: The rejection rule is p-value < \( \alpha \). Since the p-value \( \approx 0.05 \) is not strictly less than 0.05, we fail to reject \( H_0 \).

problems.question_html: In a chi-square test, one cell has \( O = 15 \) and \( E = 25 \). Another cell has \( O = 42 \) and \( E = 38 \). Which cell contributes more to the chi-square statistic?
problems.correct_answer: the first cell||cell 1||O=15 E=25

hints.text: Compute \( (O-E)^2/E \) for each cell and compare.
Cell 1: \( (15-25)^2/25 = 100/25 = 4.00 \). Cell 2: \( (42-38)^2/38 = 16/38 \approx 0.42 \). The first cell contributes much more.

solution_steps.text: Cell 2: \( \frac{(42-38)^2}{38} = \frac{16}{38} \approx 0.42 \). The first cell contributes more to \( \chi^2 \) (4.00 vs. 0.42).

problems.question_html: A chi-square test yields \( \chi^2 = 11.07 \) with \( df = 3 \). Using a chi-square table, the p-value for \( \chi^2 = 11.07 \) with \( df = 3 \) falls between which two values? (Reference: for \( df = 3 \), \( \chi^2 = 9.348 \) gives p = 0.025 and \( \chi^2 = 11.345 \) gives p = 0.01.)

hints.text: Locate \( \chi^2 = 11.07 \) relative to the table values. If it falls between two \( \chi^2 \) values, the p-value falls between the corresponding probabilities.
\( 9.348 < 11.07 < 11.345 \), so the p-value is between 0.01 and 0.025.

solution_steps.text: Since \( 9.348 < 11.07 < 11.345 \) for \( df = 3 \), the p-value is between 0.01 and 0.025.

problems.question_html: After a significant chi-square test, a student says: "The chi-square test tells us exactly which groups differ." Is this statement correct? Explain what additional analysis is needed.
problems.correct_answer: incorrect, need to examine individual cell contributions||no, must look at which cells contributed most to chi-square

hints.text: A significant chi-square test tells you that at least one cell deviates from expectation, but not which specific cells.

The statement is incorrect. A significant \( \chi^2 \) only says the overall pattern differs from what \( H_0 \) predicts. To determine where the differences are, examine each cell's contribution \( (O-E)^2/E \) and note which cells have the largest values.

solution_steps.text: The statement is incorrect. A significant chi-square result only tells us that, overall, the observed counts differ from expected counts.
To identify where the differences are, we must examine each cell's individual contribution \( (O-E)^2/E \) and describe whether the observed count was larger or smaller than expected.

problems.question_html:
A university surveys 600 randomly selected students about their class year (Freshman, Sophomore, Junior, Senior) and preferred study location (Library, Dorm, Cafe). The data are:

LibraryDormCafeTotal
Freshman507030150
Sophomore455550150
Junior605040150
Senior654540150
Total220220160600

(a) Is this a test for homogeneity or independence? Explain.

(b) State the hypotheses.

(c) Calculate the expected count for Freshman/Library and check the Large Counts condition.

(d) The chi-square statistic is \( \chi^2 = 15.45 \). Using \( df = 6 \) and a critical value of 12.592 at \( \alpha = 0.05 \), state your conclusion in context.

(e) The cell (Freshman, Dorm) has the largest contribution of 3.03. Describe what this means.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) This is a test for independence. One sample of 600 students was drawn from a single population (the university), and two categorical variables (class year and study location) were recorded.

(b) H_0: Class year and preferred study location are independent. H_a: Class year and preferred study location are not independent (they are associated).

(c) E(Freshman, Library) = (150 × 220)/600 = 33000/600 = 55. To check Large Counts, we need all expected counts ≥ 5. The smallest expected count is (150 × 160)/600 = 40, so all expected counts ≥ 5. ✓

(d) df = (4-1)(3-1) = 6. Since χ² = 15.45 > 12.592, the p-value < 0.05. We reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that class year and preferred study location are associated among students at this university.

(e) The Freshman/Dorm cell has the largest contribution (3.03), meaning freshmen chose dorm studying more often than would be expected if class year and study location were independent. This cell is a major driver of the significant result.

hints.text: One sample, two variables measured = independence test. For the expected count, use \( E = \frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{table total}} \).
For part (e), the Freshman/Dorm observed count is 70 and the expected is \( 150 \times 220/600 = 55 \). Since \( O > E \), freshmen chose the dorm more often than expected under independence.

solution_steps.text: (a) One sample of 600 students, two variables recorded. This is a test for independence.
(b) \( H_0 \): Class year and study location are independent. \( H_a \): They are not independent.
(c) \( E = \frac{150 \times 220}{600} = 55 \). The smallest expected count is \( \frac{150 \times 160}{600} = 40 \geq 5 \). Large Counts satisfied.
(d) \( \chi^2 = 15.45 > 12.592 \), so p-value < 0.05. Reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that class year and study location are associated.
(e) The Freshman/Dorm cell contributed most (3.03). The observed count (70) exceeds the expected count (55), indicating freshmen disproportionately prefer studying in dorms.

problems.question_html:
A public health study examines whether the distribution of vaccination status (fully vaccinated, partially vaccinated, unvaccinated) is the same across three regions. Random samples of 200 adults are drawn from each region. The data are:

FullyPartiallyUnvaccinatedTotal
Region A1403525200
Region B1205030200
Region C1005545200
Total360140100600

Perform a complete chi-square test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) using State, Plan, Do, Conclude. Then identify which cell contributes the most to \( \chi^2 \) and interpret what that means.
problems.correct_answer:
STATE: H_0: The distribution of vaccination status is the same across all three regions. H_a: The distribution of vaccination status is not the same across all three regions. α = 0.05.

PLAN: Random — random samples from each region. ✓ 10% — 200 is less than 10% of adults in each region. ✓ Large Counts — Expected counts: E = (row total × col total)/600. Smallest expected = (200 × 100)/600 = 33.33 ≥ 5. ✓

Expected counts table:
          Fully    Partially  Unvaccinated
Region A: 120       46.67      33.33
Region B: 120       46.67      33.33
Region C: 120       46.67      33.33

DO: χ² = (140-120)²/120 + (35-46.67)²/46.67 + (25-33.33)²/33.33 + (120-120)²/120 + (50-46.67)²/46.67 + (30-33.33)²/33.33 + (100-120)²/120 + (55-46.67)²/46.67 + (45-33.33)²/33.33
= 3.333 + 2.912 + 2.083 + 0 + 0.238 + 0.333 + 3.333 + 1.487 + 4.083
= 17.80 (approximately).

df = (3-1)(3-1) = 4. For df = 4, χ² = 17.80 far exceeds the critical value 9.488 at α = 0.05, so p-value < 0.005.

CONCLUDE: Since p-value < 0.05, reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that the distribution of vaccination status is not the same across the three regions.

FOLLOW-UP: The cell (Region C, Unvaccinated) contributes the most (4.083). The observed count (45) is much higher than expected (33.33), meaning Region C has a disproportionately high rate of unvaccinated adults compared to what we would expect if all regions had the same distribution.

hints.text: Since equal sample sizes are drawn from three regions, this is a test for homogeneity. Expected counts all equal \( \frac{200 \times \text{column total}}{600} \).
Compute all 9 expected counts (they will be the same across rows since each row total is 200). Then sum all 9 contributions \( (O-E)^2/E \). Look for the cell with the largest value.

solution_steps.text: STATE: \( H_0 \): The distribution of vaccination status is the same across all three regions. \( H_a \): Not the same. \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
PLAN: Random \(\checkmark\), 10% \(\checkmark\), Large Counts: smallest expected count = \( 200 \times 100/600 = 33.33 \geq 5 \) \(\checkmark\).

DO: Expected counts for each region: Fully = 120, Partially = 46.67, Unvaccinated = 33.33. \( \chi^2 \approx 3.33 + 2.91 + 2.08 + 0 + 0.24 + 0.33 + 3.33 + 1.49 + 4.08 \approx 17.80 \). \( df = 4 \). P-value < 0.005.
CONCLUDE: Since p-value < 0.05, reject \( H_0 \). Convincing evidence that vaccination status distributions differ across regions.
FOLLOW-UP: The (Region C, Unvaccinated) cell contributes most (4.08). Region C has more unvaccinated adults (45) than expected (33.33), indicating a disproportionately high unvaccinated rate.

topics.name: Unit 4: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
topics.description: Apply inference methods to quantitative data. Construct confidence intervals and perform hypothesis tests for one population mean, matched pairs, and the difference between two population means using t-procedures.

concepts.title: Sampling Distributions for Sample Means
concepts.content_html:
Sampling Distributions for Sample Means

When we take a random sample of size \( n \) from a population and compute the sample mean \( \bar{x} \), the value we get varies from sample to sample. The sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) describes all possible values of the sample mean and how often they occur.

Mean and Standard Deviation of \( \bar{x} \)

If the population has mean \( \mu \) and standard deviation \( \sigma \), then for random samples of size \( n \):

\[ \mu_{\bar{x}} = \mu \]\[ \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \]

The quantity \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} \) is called the standard error of the sample mean. Notice that as \( n \) increases, the standard error decreases — larger samples give more precise estimates.

Shape: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)

The Central Limit Theorem is one of the most important results in statistics:

  • If the population is normally distributed, then \( \bar{x} \) is normally distributed for any sample size.
  • If the population is not normal, the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal when \( n \geq 30 \).

This means we can use Normal probability calculations for \( \bar{x} \) whenever one of these conditions is met.

The 10% Condition

The formula \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \) is exactly correct only for sampling with replacement. When sampling without replacement (as we almost always do), the formula is approximately correct as long as the sample is no more than 10% of the population:

\[ n \leq 0.10 N \]

This is called the 10% condition. It ensures that removing sampled individuals doesn't noticeably change the population.

Worked Example

The weights of adult male Labrador Retrievers are normally distributed with \( \mu = 70 \) lb and \( \sigma = 6 \) lb. A veterinary clinic randomly selects 9 adult male Labs. Find the probability that the sample mean weight exceeds 74 lb.

Step 1: Identify the sampling distribution. Since the population is normal, \( \bar{x} \) is normal with:

\[ \mu_{\bar{x}} = 70, \quad \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{6}{\sqrt{9}} = 2 \]

Step 2: Standardize.

\[ z = \frac{74 - 70}{2} = 2.00 \]

Step 3: Find the probability.

\[ P(\bar{x} > 74) = P(z > 2.00) = 1 - 0.9772 = 0.0228 \]
Key Idea: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution (\( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma / \sqrt{n} \)) shrinks as \( n \) grows. This is why larger samples produce more reliable estimates.
AP Exam Trap: Don't confuse \( \sigma \) (population SD) with \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} \) (standard error of the mean). When a problem asks about the probability of a sample mean, you must divide \( \sigma \) by \( \sqrt{n} \). Using \( \sigma \) alone answers a question about an individual, not a mean.
concepts.content_raw: Sampling Distributions for Sample Means

problem_sets.title: Practice: Sampling Distributions for Sample Means

problems.question_html: The distribution of battery lifetimes for a certain brand is approximately normal with \( \mu = 500 \) hours and \( \sigma = 40 \) hours. A quality control technician randomly selects 16 batteries. What is the standard deviation (standard error) of the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \)?

choices.text: 2.5 hours
10 hours
40 hours
100 hours

hints.text: Use the formula for the standard error of the sample mean: \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma / \sqrt{n} \).

solution_steps.text: The standard error of \( \bar{x} \) is \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma / \sqrt{n} \).

problems.question_html: The mean commute time for employees at a large company is \( \mu = 35 \) minutes with \( \sigma = 12 \) minutes. The distribution of commute times is right-skewed. Which statement best describes the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) for random samples of size \( n = 50 \)?

choices.text: Right-skewed with mean 35 and standard deviation 12
Approximately normal with mean 35 and standard deviation 12
Approximately normal with mean 35 and standard deviation 1.697
Right-skewed with mean 35 and standard deviation 1.697

hints.text: Think about the Central Limit Theorem. What does it say about the shape of the sampling distribution when \( n \) is large?
Since \( n = 50 \geq 30 \), the CLT says the sampling distribution is approximately normal. The mean is \( \mu = 35 \) and the SE is \( 12/\sqrt{50} \approx 1.697 \).

solution_steps.text: The population is right-skewed, but \( n = 50 \geq 30 \), so by the Central Limit Theorem, the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal.
Mean: \( \mu_{\bar{x}} = 35 \). Standard error: \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 12/\sqrt{50} \approx 1.697 \) minutes.

problems.question_html: A factory produces cereal boxes with a mean fill of \( \mu = 16.0 \) oz and \( \sigma = 0.5 \) oz (normally distributed). An inspector samples 25 boxes. What is the probability that the sample mean is between 15.8 and 16.2 oz?

hints.text: Find \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} \), then convert both boundaries to z-scores.

problems.question_html: A researcher draws random samples of size \( n \) from a population with \( \sigma = 20 \). She wants \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} \leq 2 \). What is the minimum sample size \( n \)?

hints.text: Set up the inequality \( \sigma / \sqrt{n} \leq 2 \) and solve for \( n \).
\( 20/\sqrt{n} \leq 2 \Rightarrow \sqrt{n} \geq 10 \Rightarrow n \geq 100 \).

solution_steps.text: We need \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma/\sqrt{n} \leq 2 \).
\( 20/\sqrt{n} \leq 2 \Rightarrow \sqrt{n} \geq 10 \Rightarrow n \geq 100 \). The minimum sample size is 100.

problems.question_html: A population has mean \( \mu = 80 \) and standard deviation \( \sigma = 15 \). A random sample of \( n = 25 \) is drawn from a population of \( N = 200 \). Calculate \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} \).

hints.text: First check the 10% condition: is \( n \leq 0.10 N \)?

\( 25 \leq 0.10(200) = 20 \)? No — 25 > 20, so the 10% condition is violated. However, the AP exam typically still uses \( \sigma / \sqrt{n} \) and notes the condition failure separately. \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 15/\sqrt{25} = 3 \).

solution_steps.text: Apply the standard error formula: \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \sigma / \sqrt{n} = 15 / \sqrt{25} = 15 / 5 = 3 \).
Note: The 10% condition (\( 25 \leq 20 \)) is not met, so this formula is only an approximation. On the AP exam, you would note this condition is not satisfied.

problems.question_html: The scores on a standardized fitness test are normally distributed with \( \mu = 72 \) and \( \sigma = 8 \). A trainer randomly selects 4 clients. Find \( P(\bar{x} > 76) \). Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Since the population is normal, \( \bar{x} \) is normal for any \( n \). Find the standard error and then standardize.

solution_steps.text: The population is normal, so \( \bar{x} \) is normal with \( \mu_{\bar{x}} = 72 \) and \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 8/\sqrt{4} = 4 \).

problems.question_html: A nutritionist measures daily sodium intake (in mg) for a sample of 36 adults. The population has \( \mu = 3400 \) mg and \( \sigma = 600 \) mg, and the distribution is strongly right-skewed. What is \( P(\bar{x} < 3200) \)? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Even though the population is skewed, can you apply the CLT? Check whether \( n \geq 30 \).

solution_steps.text: Since \( n = 36 \geq 30 \), the CLT tells us \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal with \( \mu_{\bar{x}} = 3400 \) and \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 600/\sqrt{36} = 100 \).

problems.question_html: Household monthly electricity usage is approximately normal with \( \mu = 900 \) kWh and \( \sigma = 150 \) kWh. A utility company samples 9 households. Find the probability that the sample mean is within 100 kWh of the population mean. Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: "Within 100 kWh of the mean" means \( 800 < \bar{x} < 1000 \). Find the SE and standardize both endpoints.

solution_steps.text: "Within 100 kWh" means \( 800 < \bar{x} < 1000 \).

problems.question_html:
A medical researcher measures resting heart rates in a large population with \( \mu = 72 \) bpm and \( \sigma = 9 \) bpm (approximately normal). She takes a random sample of \( n = 36 \) patients and finds \( \bar{x} = 75 \) bpm.

(a) Describe the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \).

(b) Find the probability of obtaining a sample mean of 75 or higher.

(c) Based on your answer to (b), is this result unusual? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Since the population is approximately normal, the sampling distribution of x-bar is normal with mean mu_x-bar = 72 bpm and standard error sigma_x-bar = 9/sqrt(36) = 1.5 bpm.

(b) z = (75 - 72)/1.5 = 2.00. P(x-bar >= 75) = P(z >= 2.00) = 1 - 0.9772 = 0.0228.

(c) Yes, this result is unusual. There is only about a 2.28% chance of getting a sample mean of 75 bpm or higher if the true population mean is 72 bpm. This suggests that the sample may have come from a population with a higher mean resting heart rate.

hints.text: For part (a), state the shape, center, and spread of the sampling distribution. For parts (b) and (c), use z-scores.
SE = 9/sqrt(36) = 1.5. z = (75-72)/1.5 = 2.00. Use the z-table: P(z > 2) = 0.0228. Events with probability below 5% are generally considered unusual.

solution_steps.text: (a) Shape: Normal (population is approximately normal). Center: \( \mu_{\bar{x}} = 72 \) bpm. Spread: \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 9/\sqrt{36} = 1.5 \) bpm.

(c) Yes, this is unusual. There is only a 2.28% probability of observing a sample mean this high or higher if \( \mu = 72 \). This provides evidence that the true mean for this group may exceed 72 bpm.

problems.question_html:
A large university reports that the amount of student loan debt for graduating seniors has a mean of \( \mu = \$28{,}500 \) and standard deviation \( \sigma = \$6{,}000 \). The distribution is right-skewed. A financial aid office randomly samples 100 seniors from a class of 4,200.

(a) Verify that the conditions for applying the Central Limit Theorem are met.

(b) Describe the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \).

(c) Find the probability that the sample mean debt is less than \$27,500.
problems.correct_answer:
State: We want to find the probability that the sample mean student loan debt for 100 seniors is less than $27,500.

Plan: Check conditions for CLT. (1) Random: The sample is randomly selected. (2) 10% condition: 100 <= 0.10(4200) = 420. Check. (3) Large sample: n = 100 >= 30, so the CLT applies even though the population is right-skewed.

Do: The sampling distribution of x-bar is approximately normal with mean mu_x-bar = 28500 and SE = 6000/sqrt(100) = 600. z = (27500 - 28500)/600 = -1.67. P(x-bar < 27500) = P(z < -1.67) = 0.0475.

Conclude: There is approximately a 4.75% probability that a random sample of 100 graduating seniors would have a mean student loan debt less than $27,500.

hints.text: For part (a), check three conditions: Random, 10%, and Normal/Large Sample. For parts (b) and (c), apply the CLT to find the sampling distribution and compute a z-score.

solution_steps.text: (a) Random: The sample is randomly selected (stated). 10% condition: \( 100 \leq 0.10 \times 4200 = 420 \). \(\checkmark\) Normal/Large Sample: \( n = 100 \geq 30 \), so the CLT applies despite the right-skewed population.
(b) The sampling distribution of \( \bar{x} \) is approximately normal with \( \mu_{\bar{x}} = 28500 \) and \( \sigma_{\bar{x}} = 6000/\sqrt{100} = 600 \).
There is approximately a 4.75% chance that a random sample of 100 seniors would have a mean debt below $27,500.

concepts.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Mean Difference
concepts.content_html:
Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Mean Difference

When the population standard deviation \( \sigma \) is unknown (which is almost always the case in practice), we estimate it with the sample standard deviation \( s \) and use the t-distribution instead of the normal distribution.

The One-Sample t-Interval

A confidence interval for a population mean \( \mu \) is:

\[ \bar{x} \pm t^* \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \]

where:

  • \( \bar{x} \) is the sample mean (point estimate)
  • \( t^* \) is the critical value from the t-distribution with \( df = n - 1 \)
  • \( s / \sqrt{n} \) is the standard error of \( \bar{x} \)
  • \( t^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n} \) is the margin of error

The t-Distribution

The t-distribution is symmetric and bell-shaped like the normal distribution, but has heavier tails. This means t-intervals are wider than z-intervals, reflecting the extra uncertainty from estimating \( \sigma \) with \( s \). As \( df \) increases, the t-distribution approaches the standard normal.

Conditions for a t-Interval

  1. Random: The data come from a random sample or randomized experiment.
  2. 10% Condition: \( n \leq 0.10N \) (when sampling without replacement).
  3. Normal/Large Sample: The population is approximately normal, OR \( n \geq 30 \) with no strong skewness or outliers. For \( 15 \leq n < 30 \), the data should show no strong skewness or outliers.

Matched-Pairs Design

In a matched-pairs study, each subject provides two measurements (before/after, or paired with a match). We compute the differences \( d = x_1 - x_2 \) for each pair and then construct a one-sample t-interval for \( \mu_d \) using the differences.

\[ \bar{d} \pm t^* \frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}} \]

Worked Example

A random sample of 20 students has mean study time \( \bar{x} = 14.5 \) hours/week with \( s = 3.8 \) hours. Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true mean study time.

Conditions: Random sample (stated), assume the school has at least 200 students (10%), and \( n = 20 \) with no mention of extreme skewness — proceed with caution.

Calculation: \( df = 19 \), \( t^* = 2.093 \) (from t-table at 95%).

\[ 14.5 \pm 2.093 \cdot \frac{3.8}{\sqrt{20}} = 14.5 \pm 2.093 \cdot 0.8497 = 14.5 \pm 1.778 \]\[ (12.722, \; 16.278) \]

Interpretation: We are 95% confident that the true mean weekly study time for all students at this school is between 12.72 and 16.28 hours.

Key Idea: A confidence interval has the form: point estimate \( \pm \) margin of error. The margin of error is \( t^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n} \). Increasing the confidence level or decreasing \( n \) makes the interval wider.
AP Exam Trap: The interpretation must say "We are C% confident that the true population mean is between [lower] and [upper]." Do NOT say "There is a C% probability that \( \mu \) is in the interval." The parameter is fixed; it's the method that succeeds C% of the time.
concepts.content_raw: Constructing a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Mean Difference

problem_sets.title: Practice: Constructing a CI for a Population Mean

problems.question_html: A random sample of 25 patients at a clinic has a mean wait time of \( \bar{x} = 22.4 \) minutes with \( s = 6.0 \) minutes. What are the degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-interval?

hints.text: Degrees of freedom for a one-sample t-procedure: \( df = n - 1 \).

solution_steps.text: For a one-sample t-interval, \( df = n - 1 = 25 - 1 = 24 \).

problems.question_html: A researcher surveys a random sample of 40 teachers and finds their mean annual spending on classroom supplies is \( \bar{x} = \$485 \) with \( s = \$120 \). She constructs a 90% confidence interval. Using \( t^* = 1.685 \) (df = 39), what is the margin of error? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Margin of error = \( t^* \cdot s / \sqrt{n} \).

solution_steps.text: Standard error: \( s/\sqrt{n} = 120/\sqrt{40} \approx 18.974 \).
Margin of error: \( t^* \cdot SE = 1.685 \times 18.974 \approx \$31.96 \).

problems.question_html: Which of the following will decrease the width of a confidence interval for \( \mu \)?

choices.text: Increasing the confidence level from 90% to 99%
Increasing the sample size from 30 to 120
Increasing the sample standard deviation
Decreasing the sample size from 100 to 25

hints.text: Width = \( 2 \times t^* \times s / \sqrt{n} \). Which changes make this smaller?
Increasing \( n \) decreases \( s/\sqrt{n} \), making the interval narrower. Higher confidence level increases \( t^* \), making it wider.

solution_steps.text: Width = \( 2 \cdot t^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n} \). Increasing \( n \) from 30 to 120 reduces the standard error by a factor of 2, making the interval narrower.
The other options either increase the width (higher confidence, larger \( s \), smaller \( n \)).

problems.question_html: A nutritionist collects a random sample of 15 adults and records their daily vitamin C intake (in mg). The sample yields \( \bar{x} = 82 \) mg and \( s = 18 \) mg. A dotplot of the data shows no outliers and approximate symmetry. Using \( t^* = 2.145 \) (df = 14), construct a 95% confidence interval. Which interval is correct?

hints.text: Compute SE = \( s/\sqrt{n} \) and then ME = \( t^* \times \text{SE} \).

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for the mean weight of cereal boxes is \( (15.72, 16.28) \) oz. What is the point estimate \( \bar{x} \)?

hints.text: The point estimate is the midpoint of the confidence interval.

solution_steps.text: The point estimate is the center of the interval: \( \bar{x} = (15.72 + 16.28)/2 = 16.00 \) oz.

problems.question_html: A fitness trainer measures the resting heart rate of a random sample of 12 clients: \( \bar{x} = 68.3 \) bpm, \( s = 5.1 \) bpm. Using \( t^* = 2.201 \) (df = 11, 95% confidence), compute the lower bound of the confidence interval. Round to one decimal place.

hints.text: Lower bound = \( \bar{x} - t^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n} \).

solution_steps.text: Lower bound = \( 68.3 - 3.24 = 65.06 \approx 65.1 \) bpm.

problems.question_html: In a matched-pairs study, 10 runners have their mile times recorded before and after a training program. The mean difference (before \( - \) after) is \( \bar{d} = 0.45 \) minutes with \( s_d = 0.30 \) minutes. Using \( t^* = 2.262 \) (df = 9, 95%), compute the margin of error. Round to three decimal places.

hints.text: For matched pairs, use the differences. ME = \( t^* \times s_d / \sqrt{n} \).

solution_steps.text: ME = \( 2.262 \times 0.09487 \approx 0.215 \) minutes.

problems.question_html: A sample of 50 manufactured bolts has a mean diameter of \( \bar{x} = 10.02 \) mm and \( s = 0.08 \) mm. Construct a 99% confidence interval using \( t^* = 2.680 \) (df = 49). Give the upper bound, rounded to three decimal places.

hints.text: Upper bound = \( \bar{x} + t^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n} \).

problems.question_html:
A medical researcher wants to estimate the mean systolic blood pressure of adults with hypertension. She takes a random sample of 30 patients from a large clinic and obtains \( \bar{x} = 148.5 \) mmHg and \( s = 12.3 \) mmHg. The data show no strong skewness or outliers.

(a) Check the conditions for constructing a one-sample t-interval.

(b) Construct a 95% confidence interval for the true mean systolic blood pressure. Use \( t^* = 2.045 \) (df = 29).

(c) Interpret the interval in context.
problems.correct_answer:
State: We want to estimate the true mean systolic blood pressure of adults with hypertension at this clinic.

Plan: We will use a one-sample t-interval.
Conditions:
(1) Random: The sample is a random sample from the clinic (stated).
(2) 10%: 30 patients is less than 10% of all patients at a large clinic. Check.
(3) Normal/Large Sample: n = 30 >= 30 and no strong skewness or outliers. Check.

Do: x-bar = 148.5, s = 12.3, n = 30, t* = 2.045.
SE = 12.3/sqrt(30) = 2.246.
ME = 2.045 x 2.246 = 4.593.
CI: 148.5 +/- 4.593 = (143.907, 153.093).

Conclude: We are 95% confident that the true mean systolic blood pressure of adults with hypertension at this clinic is between 143.9 and 153.1 mmHg.

hints.text: Check Random, 10%, and Normal/Large Sample conditions. Then apply the formula \( \bar{x} \pm t^* \cdot s/\sqrt{n} \).
SE = 12.3/sqrt(30) = 2.246. ME = 2.045 x 2.246 = 4.593. CI = (143.9, 153.1). Interpret: We are 95% confident the true mean is in this range.

solution_steps.text: (a) Random: Stated as a random sample. 10%: 30 < 10% of all clinic patients (large clinic). Normal/Large Sample: \( n = 30 \geq 30 \) and no strong skewness or outliers. All conditions met.
(c) We are 95% confident that the true mean systolic blood pressure of adults with hypertension at this clinic is between 143.9 and 153.1 mmHg.

problems.question_html:
A physical therapist wants to know if a new stretching routine reduces knee pain. She recruits 15 patients and measures their pain level (0-10 scale) before and after the routine. The differences (before \( - \) after) yield \( \bar{d} = 1.8 \) points and \( s_d = 1.2 \) points. A dotplot of the differences shows approximate symmetry with no outliers.

(a) Explain why this is a matched-pairs design.

(b) Construct a 90% confidence interval for \( \mu_d \). Use \( t^* = 1.761 \) (df = 14).

(c) Interpret the interval. Does the interval suggest the routine is effective?
problems.correct_answer:
State: We want to estimate the true mean difference in pain level (before - after) for patients using this stretching routine.

Plan: This is a matched-pairs design because the same 15 patients are measured twice (before and after). We use a one-sample t-interval on the differences.
Conditions:
(1) Random: Assume these patients are representative (note: not explicitly random — a limitation).
(2) 10%: 15 is less than 10% of all potential patients.
(3) Normal/Large Sample: n = 15, dotplot shows approximate symmetry, no outliers. Check.

Do: d-bar = 1.8, s_d = 1.2, n = 15, t* = 1.761.
SE = 1.2/sqrt(15) = 0.3098.
ME = 1.761 x 0.3098 = 0.546.
CI: 1.8 +/- 0.546 = (1.254, 2.346).

Conclude: We are 90% confident that the true mean reduction in pain level is between 1.25 and 2.35 points. Since the entire interval is positive (above 0), there is convincing evidence that the stretching routine reduces knee pain.

hints.text: Matched pairs: the same subjects are measured twice. Use the differences. Check conditions on the differences, not the original data.
SE = 1.2/sqrt(15) = 0.3098. ME = 1.761 x 0.3098 = 0.546. CI = (1.254, 2.346). Since the interval is entirely above 0, the routine appears effective.

solution_steps.text: (a) This is matched pairs because each patient serves as their own control — pain is measured on the same person before and after the routine.

(c) We are 90% confident that the true mean reduction in pain (before − after) is between 1.25 and 2.35 points. Since the entire interval is above 0, there is convincing evidence the stretching routine reduces pain.

concepts.title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Mean Difference
concepts.content_html:
Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval

Once you have a confidence interval, you can use it to evaluate claims about the population mean \( \mu \). This is a powerful tool: a confidence interval does double duty as both an estimate and an informal hypothesis test.

The Decision Rule

  • If the claimed value of \( \mu \) is inside the confidence interval, the data are consistent with the claim. There is not convincing evidence against it.
  • If the claimed value of \( \mu \) is not inside the confidence interval, there is convincing evidence against the claim at the corresponding significance level.

Connection to Significance Level

A 95% CI corresponds to a two-sided test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \):

  • Value inside 95% CI \( \Leftrightarrow \) p-value \( > 0.05 \) \( \Leftrightarrow \) fail to reject \( H_0 \)
  • Value outside 95% CI \( \Leftrightarrow \) p-value \( < 0.05 \) \( \Leftrightarrow \) reject \( H_0 \)

Matched Pairs and Zero

For a matched-pairs CI for \( \mu_d \):

  • If 0 is in the interval, there is no convincing evidence of a mean difference.
  • If 0 is not in the interval, there is convincing evidence that the treatment has an effect (the mean difference is not zero).

If the entire interval is positive, the evidence suggests an increase. If entirely negative, a decrease.

Worked Example

A manufacturer claims that its energy bars contain an average of 250 calories. A consumer group tests a random sample and constructs a 95% confidence interval: \( (253.2, 261.8) \).

Since 250 is not in the interval \( (253.2, 261.8) \), there is convincing evidence at the 5% significance level that the true mean calorie content is not 250. In fact, since the entire interval is above 250, the evidence suggests the bars contain more than 250 calories on average.

Key Idea: A confidence interval tells you the plausible values for \( \mu \). If a claimed value is not among them, the claim is not supported by the data.
AP Exam Trap: Don't overstate your conclusion. If the claimed value is in the interval, you cannot say "the claim is proven true." You can only say the data are consistent with the claim — other values in the interval are equally plausible.
concepts.content_raw: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for a Population Mean or Mean Difference

problem_sets.title: Practice: Justifying a Claim Based on a CI

problems.question_html: A health organization claims that adults sleep an average of 7 hours per night. A researcher constructs a 95% confidence interval for the mean sleep time: \( (6.4, 7.3) \). What can the researcher conclude about the claim?

choices.text: There is convincing evidence that the true mean is not 7 hours.
The data provide convincing evidence that adults sleep exactly 7 hours.
The data are consistent with the claim that the true mean is 7 hours, since 7 is in the interval.
The confidence interval proves that the claim is correct.

hints.text: Check: is the claimed value (7) inside the confidence interval?
Since 7 is inside (6.4, 7.3), the data are consistent with the claim. We cannot say the claim is proven — only that it is plausible.

solution_steps.text: The claimed value \( \mu = 7 \) is inside the 95% CI (6.4, 7.3).
Therefore, the data are consistent with the claim. There is not convincing evidence against it at the 5% significance level.

problems.question_html: A school district claims the mean math SAT score for its students is 520. A 90% confidence interval based on a random sample gives \( (528, 556) \). Which conclusion is appropriate?

choices.text: The data are consistent with a mean of 520.
There is convincing evidence that the true mean math SAT score is greater than 520.
The true mean is definitely between 528 and 556.
The sample was not random, so no conclusion can be drawn.

hints.text: Is 520 inside the interval (528, 556)?
No — 520 is below the entire interval. Since all plausible values are above 520, there is convincing evidence the true mean exceeds 520.

solution_steps.text: The claimed value 520 is not in the 90% CI (528, 556). The entire interval is above 520.
There is convincing evidence at the 10% significance level that the true mean math SAT score exceeds 520.

problems.question_html: A tutoring company claims its program raises SAT scores by at least 50 points on average. A matched-pairs 95% CI for \( \mu_d \) (after \( - \) before) is \( (32, 47) \). Which conclusion is correct?

choices.text: The data support the claim because the interval shows a positive improvement.
There is convincing evidence that the true mean improvement is less than 50 points, contradicting the claim.
The data are consistent with the claim because 50 is close to the interval.
No conclusion can be drawn because the interval does not contain 0.

hints.text: The claim is \( \mu_d \geq 50 \). Is 50 inside the interval (32, 47)?
50 is above the entire interval (32, 47). All plausible values are below 50, so there is convincing evidence the true improvement is less than 50.

solution_steps.text: The claim is that \( \mu_d \geq 50 \). The 95% CI is (32, 47), and 50 is not in the interval.
Since the entire interval is below 50, there is convincing evidence the true mean improvement is less than 50 points.

problems.question_html: A pharmaceutical company constructs a 95% CI for the mean reduction in cholesterol (before \( - \) after) from a new drug: \( (5.2, 18.6) \) mg/dL. A competing drug is known to reduce cholesterol by 12 mg/dL on average. Based on the interval, is there convincing evidence that the new drug is more effective than the competitor?

choices.text: Yes, because the interval shows the new drug reduces cholesterol.
Yes, because the center of the interval (11.9) is close to 12.
No, because 12 is inside the interval, so the new drug could be equally effective.
No, because the lower bound (5.2) is less than 12.

hints.text: To show the new drug is more effective, you'd need all plausible values above 12. Is 12 in the interval?
12 is inside (5.2, 18.6), so the data are consistent with the new drug being equally effective. No convincing evidence it's better.

solution_steps.text: The value 12 is inside the CI (5.2, 18.6).
Since 12 is a plausible value for the new drug's mean reduction, there is not convincing evidence the new drug is more effective than the competitor.

problems.question_html: A matched-pairs study compares blood pressure before and after a new medication. The 95% CI for \( \mu_d \) (before \( - \) after) is \( (-2.1, 8.3) \). Is there convincing evidence that the medication changes blood pressure? Answer "yes" or "no".
problems.correct_answer: no

hints.text: For matched pairs, check whether 0 is inside or outside the CI for \( \mu_d \).
Since 0 is inside the interval \( (-2.1, 8.3) \), there is no convincing evidence of a mean difference. Answer: no.

solution_steps.text: The value 0 (no difference) is inside the CI \( (-2.1, 8.3) \).
Therefore, there is not convincing evidence that the medication changes blood pressure. The answer is no.

problems.question_html: A 99% confidence interval for the mean weight of bags of flour is \( (4.92, 5.14) \) lb. A consumer claims the bags are underfilled (mean less than 5 lb). Based on this interval, is there convincing evidence of underfilling? Answer "yes" or "no".
problems.correct_answer: no

hints.text: The consumer's claim is that \( \mu < 5 \). Check whether 5 is inside the interval.
Since 5 is inside the interval (4.92, 5.14), the data are consistent with \( \mu = 5 \). There is not convincing evidence of underfilling.

solution_steps.text: The value \( \mu = 5 \) is inside the 99% CI (4.92, 5.14).
Since 5 is a plausible value, there is not convincing evidence that the bags are underfilled. Answer: no.

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for the mean daily screen time of teenagers is \( (4.8, 6.2) \) hours. A researcher claims the true mean is 4.5 hours. Is the claim supported? Explain briefly, including whether the mean could be higher or lower than claimed.
problems.correct_answer: no||No

hints.text: Check if 4.5 is inside the interval (4.8, 6.2).
4.5 is below the interval. The claim is not supported; in fact, the evidence suggests the true mean is higher than 4.5 hours.

solution_steps.text: 4.5 is not inside the 95% CI (4.8, 6.2). The entire interval is above 4.5.
There is convincing evidence the true mean screen time exceeds 4.5 hours, so the claim is not supported.

problems.question_html: A 90% CI for the mean difference in test scores (new method \( - \) old method) is \( (0.5, 4.3) \). A teacher claims the new method is better. Does the interval support this claim? Answer "yes" or "no" and state the key reasoning.
problems.correct_answer: yes||Yes

hints.text: If the new method is better, \( \mu_d > 0 \). Is the entire interval above 0?
The entire interval (0.5, 4.3) is above 0, so there is convincing evidence the new method produces higher scores.

solution_steps.text: The CI for \( \mu_d \) is (0.5, 4.3). Since 0 is below the entire interval, all plausible values for the mean difference are positive.
Yes — there is convincing evidence that the new method produces higher test scores on average.

problems.question_html:
A gym owner claims that members lose an average of at least 10 pounds after 3 months of membership. A random sample of 25 members yields a 95% confidence interval for the mean weight loss: \( (7.2, 13.8) \) pounds.

(a) Is there convincing evidence that the true mean weight loss differs from 10 pounds?

(b) Is there convincing evidence that the true mean weight loss is less than 10 pounds (contradicting the owner's claim)?

(c) Explain your reasoning using the relationship between the CI and the claimed value.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) No. Since 10 is inside the 95% CI (7.2, 13.8), the data are consistent with a true mean weight loss of 10 pounds. There is not convincing evidence that the mean differs from 10.

(b) No. Although the interval includes values below 10, it also includes values above 10. Since 10 is inside the interval, we cannot conclude that the mean is less than 10.

(c) The CI (7.2, 13.8) contains the claimed value of 10, meaning 10 is a plausible value for the population mean. The data do not provide convincing evidence against the owner's claim. However, the interval also includes values below 10, so we cannot confirm the claim is true either — we simply lack evidence to reject it.

hints.text: For each part, ask: is the relevant value (10, or values below 10) inside or outside the interval?
10 is inside (7.2, 13.8), so the data are consistent with 10. The interval includes values both above and below 10, so we can't conclude the mean is specifically less than or greater than 10.

solution_steps.text: (a) 10 is inside the 95% CI (7.2, 13.8), so the data are consistent with a mean of 10. No convincing evidence the mean differs from 10.
(b) Since 10 is in the interval, we cannot conclude that \( \mu < 10 \). The data do not contradict the owner's claim.
(c) The CI contains 10, meaning it is among the plausible values. We lack evidence to reject the claim, but we also cannot confirm it — values as low as 7.2 and as high as 13.8 are all plausible.

problems.question_html:
Two 95% confidence intervals are constructed from independent random samples:

  • Brand A battery life: \( (48.2, 52.8) \) hours
  • Brand B battery life: \( (50.5, 55.3) \) hours

(a) Is there convincing evidence that Brand B has a longer mean battery life than Brand A?

(b) A student says: "Since the intervals overlap, there is definitely no difference between the brands." Is the student's reasoning correct? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) We cannot make a definitive conclusion based on comparing two separate CIs. The intervals overlap (both include values near 50.5-52.8), which means the difference could be zero. However, overlapping CIs do not guarantee no difference — a proper two-sample inference procedure would be needed.

(b) The student's reasoning is incorrect. Overlapping confidence intervals do NOT guarantee that there is no significant difference between the means. Two separate CIs can overlap even when a two-sample test would find a significant difference. The correct approach to compare two means is to construct a single confidence interval for the difference (mu_A - mu_B) or perform a two-sample t-test — not to visually compare two separate intervals.

hints.text: Can you make a valid comparison by looking at two separate CIs? Think about what each interval estimates individually.
Overlapping CIs do not necessarily mean no significant difference. The proper approach is a two-sample t-interval for \( \mu_A - \mu_B \), not comparing two individual CIs.

solution_steps.text: (a) The intervals overlap (both contain values around 50.5–52.8), so we cannot conclude Brand B is definitively better based on separate CIs alone. A two-sample inference procedure is needed.

(b) The student is wrong. Overlapping CIs do not prove the means are equal. A two-sample t-test or a CI for \( \mu_A - \mu_B \) is the correct way to compare two means. Overlapping CIs can occur even when there is a statistically significant difference.

concepts.title: Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean or Mean Difference
concepts.content_html:
Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean or Mean Difference

A significance test (hypothesis test) assesses whether sample data provide convincing evidence against a claim about a population parameter. Before performing any calculations, you must clearly set up the hypotheses.

The Null and Alternative Hypotheses

The null hypothesis \( H_0 \) represents the "no change" or "no difference" claim — the status quo:

\[ H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \]

The alternative hypothesis \( H_a \) is what the researcher suspects or hopes to show:

  • Two-sided: \( H_a: \mu eq \mu_0 \) — the mean differs from \( \mu_0 \)
  • One-sided (left): \( H_a: \mu < \mu_0 \) — the mean is less than \( \mu_0 \)
  • One-sided (right): \( H_a: \mu > \mu_0 \) — the mean is greater than \( \mu_0 \)

Matched-Pairs Hypotheses

In matched-pairs designs, we test whether the mean difference is zero:

\[ H_0: \mu_d = 0 \]\[ H_a: \mu_d eq 0 \quad ext{(or } < 0 ext{ or } > 0 ext{)} \]

where \( \mu_d \) is the true mean of the paired differences.

Choosing One-Sided vs. Two-Sided

  • Use one-sided when the research question specifically asks about one direction ("is it greater than," "does it reduce," "is it less than").
  • Use two-sided when the question asks if there is any difference, without specifying direction.

Important: You must choose the direction of \( H_a \) before looking at the data. Choosing \( H_a \) based on the data is called "data snooping" and invalidates the test.

Defining the Parameter

Always define the parameter in context before writing the hypotheses. For example:

"Let \( \mu \) = the true mean weight (in oz) of cereal boxes produced at this factory."

Worked Example

A teacher believes that a new curriculum has changed students' test scores compared to the historical mean of 72. She collects a random sample.

Parameter: Let \( \mu \) = the true mean test score for all students using the new curriculum.

Hypotheses:

\[ H_0: \mu = 72 \]\[ H_a: \mu eq 72 \]

This is two-sided because the teacher wants to know if scores changed (could be higher or lower).

Key Idea: \( H_0 \) always uses \( = \). The alternative uses \( eq \), \( < \), or \( > \). The value \( \mu_0 \) in \( H_0 \) is the claimed/hypothesized value, not a sample statistic.
AP Exam Trap: Always write hypotheses using population parameters (\( \mu \)), not sample statistics (\( ar{x} \)). Writing \( H_0: ar{x} = 72 \) is wrong and will cost you points. Also, never forget to define the parameter in context.
