problem_sets.title: Practice: Setting Up a Test for a Population Mean

problems.question_html: A manufacturer claims that its light bulbs last an average of 1,200 hours. A consumer group suspects the bulbs last less than advertised. Which hypotheses should the consumer group test?

hints.text: The consumer group suspects the bulbs last less than 1200 hours. Which direction is the alternative?
Since the suspicion is that bulbs last less than claimed, \( H_a: \mu < 1200 \). The null is always \( H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \). Also, hypotheses must use \( \mu \), not \( \bar{x} \).

solution_steps.text: The null hypothesis states the claimed value: \( H_0: \mu = 1200 \).
The consumer group suspects less than 1200, so \( H_a: \mu < 1200 \) (one-sided, left).

problems.question_html: A hospital administrator wants to determine if the mean wait time in the emergency room has changed from the previous year's average of 45 minutes. Which set of hypotheses is appropriate?

hints.text: The administrator wants to know if the wait time has changed — not specifically increased or decreased. One-sided or two-sided?
"Changed" implies either direction, so use \( H_a: \mu \neq 45 \) (two-sided).

solution_steps.text: "Changed" does not specify a direction, so the test is two-sided.

problems.question_html: Students in a study measured their sleep before and after adopting a "no screens" rule. The researcher uses \( d = \text{after} - \text{before} \) and wants to test if the rule increases sleep. What is the correct \( H_a \)?

choices.text: \( H_a: \mu_d \neq 0 \)

hints.text: If sleep increases, after > before. What sign does \( d = \text{after} - \text{before} \) have?
After > before means \( d > 0 \), so \( H_a: \mu_d > 0 \).

solution_steps.text: The rule is expected to increase sleep, so after > before.
Since \( d = \text{after} - \text{before} \), an increase means \( d > 0 \). Thus \( H_a: \mu_d > 0 \).

problems.question_html: A researcher tests whether a new fertilizer changes the mean yield of tomato plants from the known average of 8.5 kg per plant. She defines \( \mu \) and writes \( H_0: \mu = 8.5 \), \( H_a: \mu > 8.5 \). After collecting data, she finds the sample mean is below 8.5. What mistake did the researcher make?

choices.text: She should have used \( \bar{x} \) instead of \( \mu \) in the hypotheses.
She should have written a two-sided alternative since the question asks about "change" without specifying direction.
She should have set \( H_0: \mu > 8.5 \).
No mistake was made; the test is correctly set up.

hints.text: Re-read the research question: does it specify a direction for the change?
The question says "changes the mean yield" — this is non-directional, requiring \( H_a: \mu \neq 8.5 \). The researcher chose one-sided without justification.

solution_steps.text: The research question asks if the fertilizer "changes" yield — no specific direction.
The correct alternative is \( H_a: \mu \neq 8.5 \) (two-sided). Using \( H_a: \mu > 8.5 \) imposes a direction not justified by the question.

problems.question_html: A nutritionist claims a new diet increases the average daily protein intake above 50 g. Write the null hypothesis. Enter your answer in the form "mu = [value]".
problems.correct_answer: mu = 50

hints.text: The null hypothesis always states the boundary value with an equals sign.
The claim is about 50 g. \( H_0: \mu = 50 \).

solution_steps.text: The claimed value is 50 g. The null hypothesis is \( H_0: \mu = 50 \).
The alternative would be \( H_a: \mu > 50 \) since the nutritionist claims an increase.

problems.question_html: A coach measures the mile times of 12 athletes before and after a training program. She wants to test whether the training reduced mile times. Define the parameter and state the hypotheses using \( \mu_d \) where \( d = \text{after} - \text{before} \). Write \( H_a \) using a symbol like \( < \), \( > \), or \( \neq \) and the number 0. Enter only the \( H_a \) (e.g., "mu_d < 0").
problems.correct_answer: mu_d < 0

hints.text: If times were reduced, the after times are shorter. What does that imply about \( d = \text{after} - \text{before} \)?
If after < before, then \( d = \text{after} - \text{before} < 0 \). So \( H_a: \mu_d < 0 \).

solution_steps.text: Let \( \mu_d \) = true mean difference in mile time (after − before) for athletes using this program.
If training reduces times, after < before, so \( d < 0 \). Thus \( H_0: \mu_d = 0 \), \( H_a: \mu_d < 0 \).

problems.question_html: A city official says the mean commute time is 30 minutes. A transportation planner suspects it's longer. She writes: "\( H_0: \bar{x} = 30 \), \( H_a: \bar{x} > 30 \)." Identify the error and write the correct hypotheses. Enter the correct \( H_0 \) in the form "mu = [value]".
problems.correct_answer: mu = 30

hints.text: Hypotheses must be about the population parameter, not the sample statistic.
Replace \( \bar{x} \) with \( \mu \). Correct: \( H_0: \mu = 30 \), \( H_a: \mu > 30 \).

solution_steps.text: The error is using \( \bar{x} \) (sample mean) instead of \( \mu \) (population mean).
Correct hypotheses: \( H_0: \mu = 30 \), \( H_a: \mu > 30 \).

problems.question_html: A company claims its employees work an average of 40 hours per week. The HR department suspects the true average is different. A random sample of 50 employees shows \( \bar{x} = 42.3 \) hours. The HR director then writes \( H_a: \mu > 40 \) because the sample mean is above 40. What is wrong with this approach?
problems.correct_answer: data snooping||chose direction after seeing data||looked at data first

hints.text: When must the direction of the alternative hypothesis be chosen?
The direction of \( H_a \) must be determined before examining the data. Choosing \( H_a: \mu > 40 \) because \( \bar{x} = 42.3 \) is data snooping, which invalidates the test.

solution_steps.text: The HR director chose the direction of \( H_a \) after seeing that \( \bar{x} > 40 \). This is data snooping.
The alternative must be chosen based on the research question before collecting data. Since the question was whether the mean "differs" from 40, the correct alternative is \( H_a: \mu \neq 40 \).

problems.question_html:
A pharmaceutical company develops a new pain medication and wants to test whether it reduces pain scores compared to a placebo. Patients are randomly assigned to medication or placebo, and each patient's pain score is recorded. A matched-pairs design is NOT used.

(a) Explain why this is not a matched-pairs design.

(b) What type of test would be appropriate? (Note: this is a preview — two-sample t-tests are covered in a later unit.)

(c) If the study were redesigned as matched pairs (each patient receives both treatments in random order), write the hypotheses using \( \mu_d \) where \( d = \text{medication} - \text{placebo} \).
problems.correct_answer:
(a) This is not matched pairs because different patients are in each group. There is no natural pairing — one group gets medication and a separate group gets placebo.

(b) A two-sample t-test (or two-sample t-interval) for the difference of two means would be appropriate, since we are comparing two independent groups.

(c) If redesigned as matched pairs:
Let mu_d = the true mean difference in pain scores (medication - placebo) for patients receiving both treatments.
H_0: mu_d = 0 (no difference in mean pain between medication and placebo)
H_a: mu_d < 0 (the medication reduces pain compared to placebo, meaning medication scores are lower)

hints.text: Matched pairs require each subject to provide two measurements, or subjects must be paired. Are the same subjects in both groups here?

Different patients in each group = independent samples = two-sample test. For matched pairs (same patients, both treatments), use \( H_0: \mu_d = 0 \). If medication reduces pain, medication < placebo, so \( d < 0 \).

solution_steps.text: (a) Different patients receive medication vs. placebo — no pairing. This is a two-sample (independent groups) design.
(b) A two-sample t-test for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) (covered in a later unit).
(c) Let \( \mu_d \) = true mean difference (medication − placebo). \( H_0: \mu_d = 0 \), \( H_a: \mu_d < 0 \) (medication reduces pain → lower scores).

problems.question_html:
A school board wants to test whether a new math curriculum changes student performance from the district average of 78 on a standardized test. A random sample of 35 students using the new curriculum will be tested.

(a) Define the parameter of interest in context.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses.

(c) A board member argues for using \( H_a: \mu > 78 \) because "we wouldn't adopt a curriculum that makes scores worse." Evaluate this argument. Should the test be one-sided or two-sided?
problems.correct_answer:
State: (a) Let mu = the true mean standardized test score for all students in the district who would use the new math curriculum.

(b) H_0: mu = 78
    H_a: mu != 78

(c) The board member's argument is problematic. The research question asks whether scores "changed" — this is non-directional. While the board may hope for improvement, using a one-sided test would prevent them from detecting a harmful decrease. A two-sided test is more appropriate because:
- It allows detection of both improvement and decline
- The direction of Ha should be based on the research question, not on hoped-for outcomes
- If the curriculum lowers scores, the board needs to know that too
The test should be two-sided: H_a: mu != 78.

hints.text: Define the parameter in context (what does \( \mu \) represent specifically?). For part (c), consider what happens if scores actually decrease.

Parameter: true mean test score for students using the new curriculum. The question says "changes" (non-directional → two-sided). A one-sided test would miss a potential decrease, which the board also needs to detect.

solution_steps.text: (a) Let \( \mu \) = the true mean standardized test score for all students in the district using the new math curriculum.

(c) The board member's reasoning is flawed. The research question asks about change (non-directional). A one-sided test would fail to detect a harmful decrease in scores. The board needs to know about any change. Use two-sided.

concepts.title: Carrying Out a Test for a Population Mean or Mean Difference
concepts.content_html:
Carrying Out a Test for a Population Mean or Mean Difference

Now we put everything together: set up hypotheses, check conditions, compute the test statistic and p-value, and draw a conclusion. This is the complete 4-step significance test that the AP exam expects.

The One-Sample t-Test

The test statistic for testing \( H_0: \mu = \mu_0 \) is:

\[ t = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}} \]

with \( df = n - 1 \). This measures how many standard errors \( \bar{x} \) is from the hypothesized value \( \mu_0 \).

The p-Value

The p-value is the probability of getting a test statistic as extreme as (or more extreme than) the observed value, assuming \( H_0 \) is true.

  • Left-tailed (\( H_a: \mu < \mu_0 \)): p-value = \( P(t \leq t_{\text{obs}}) \)
  • Right-tailed (\( H_a: \mu > \mu_0 \)): p-value = \( P(t \geq t_{\text{obs}}) \)
  • Two-tailed (\( H_a: \mu \neq \mu_0 \)): p-value = \( 2 \cdot P(t \geq |t_{\text{obs}}|) \)

Conditions (Same as CI)

  1. Random: Data from a random sample or randomized experiment.
  2. 10%: \( n \leq 0.10N \) when sampling without replacement.
  3. Normal/Large Sample: Population is normal, OR \( n \geq 30 \), OR \( 15 \leq n < 30 \) with no strong skew/outliers.

The 4-Step Process

  1. State: Define parameter, state hypotheses, choose \( \alpha \).
  2. Plan: Name the procedure (one-sample t-test), check conditions.
  3. Do: Compute the test statistic and p-value.
  4. Conclude: Compare p-value to \( \alpha \). If p-value \( \leq \alpha \), reject \( H_0 \). If p-value \( > \alpha \), fail to reject \( H_0 \). State conclusion in context.

Worked Example

A cereal company claims boxes contain a mean of 16 oz. A random sample of 25 boxes has \( \bar{x} = 15.85 \) oz and \( s = 0.4 \) oz. Test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) whether the mean is less than 16 oz.

State: Let \( \mu \) = true mean fill weight. \( H_0: \mu = 16 \), \( H_a: \mu < 16 \). \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

Plan: One-sample t-test. Random: stated. 10%: 25 is less than 10% of all boxes. Normal/Large Sample: \( n = 25 \), assume no strong skewness (not stated otherwise).

Do:

\[ t = \frac{15.85 - 16}{0.4 / \sqrt{25}} = \frac{-0.15}{0.08} = -1.875 \]

\( df = 24 \). Using the t-table, the p-value for \( t = -1.875 \) (left-tailed) is between 0.025 and 0.05. Calculator: p-value \( \approx 0.0365 \).

Conclude: Since the p-value (0.0365) \( < \alpha = 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the true mean fill weight of cereal boxes is less than 16 oz.

Key Idea: The conclusion must be stated in context and must reference the p-value and significance level. Use language like "convincing evidence" (reject) or "not convincing evidence" (fail to reject). Never say you "accept \( H_0 \)."
AP Exam Trap: The conclusion must link back to the alternative hypothesis. Don't just say "reject \( H_0 \)" — state what that means in context. Also, always say "fail to reject \( H_0 \)" rather than "accept \( H_0 \)." We never prove the null is true.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Carrying Out a Test for a Population Mean

problems.question_html: A random sample of 20 energy drinks has a mean caffeine content of \( \bar{x} = 168 \) mg and \( s = 14 \) mg. The company claims the mean is 160 mg. What is the value of the t test statistic for testing \( H_0: \mu = 160 \) vs. \( H_a: \mu > 160 \)?

hints.text: Use \( t = (\bar{x} - \mu_0) / (s / \sqrt{n}) \).

problems.question_html: A t-test yields \( t = -2.45 \) with \( df = 18 \) for a two-sided test. Using the t-table, which range contains the p-value?

hints.text: For a two-sided test, the p-value = \( 2 \times P(t > |t_{\text{obs}}|) \). Look up \( |t| = 2.45 \) in the t-table with df = 18.

With df = 18, \( t = 2.101 \) gives upper-tail probability 0.025 and \( t = 2.552 \) gives 0.01. Since 2.101 < 2.45 < 2.552, one-tail area is between 0.01 and 0.025. Two-sided p-value is between 0.02 and 0.05. More precisely, between 0.02 and 0.04.

solution_steps.text: Since \( 2.101 < 2.45 < 2.552 \), the one-tail probability is between 0.01 and 0.025.
Two-sided p-value = \( 2 \times \) (one-tail) = between 0.02 and 0.05. The best answer is 0.02 < p-value < 0.04.

problems.question_html: A random sample of 36 packages from a shipping company has a mean weight of \( \bar{x} = 24.8 \) lb and \( s = 3.6 \) lb. The company claims the mean package weight is 25.5 lb. Test \( H_0: \mu = 25.5 \) vs. \( H_a: \mu \neq 25.5 \) at \( \alpha = 0.10 \). What is the test statistic? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: \( t = (\bar{x} - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt{n}) \). Plug in the values.

solution_steps.text: With df = 35 and a two-sided test, the p-value \( \approx 0.25 \), which is greater than 0.10. Fail to reject \( H_0 \).

problems.question_html: A fitness study tests whether the mean resting heart rate of athletes is below 60 bpm. A random sample of 18 athletes gives \( \bar{x} = 57.2 \) bpm and \( s = 5.4 \) bpm. Which condition is most difficult to verify, and why?

choices.text: Random — because the study may not have used random selection.
10% — because there may be fewer than 180 athletes in the population.
Normal/Large Sample — because \( n = 18 < 30 \), so we need to check for skewness and outliers in the sample.
All conditions are automatically satisfied for any sample.

hints.text: With \( n = 18 \), which condition requires extra verification? What does the Normal/Large Sample condition require for moderate sample sizes?
Since \( 15 \leq n = 18 < 30 \), we need the sample data to show no strong skewness or outliers. This requires examining a graph (dotplot, histogram, or boxplot) of the data.

solution_steps.text: With \( n = 18 \), the sample is moderate (between 15 and 30).
The Normal/Large Sample condition requires checking a graph of the data for strong skewness or outliers. This is the most difficult to verify without seeing the actual data.

problems.question_html: A t-test for \( H_0: \mu = 50 \) vs. \( H_a: \mu < 50 \) gives a p-value of 0.032. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), what is the correct conclusion? Enter "reject" or "fail to reject".
problems.correct_answer: reject

hints.text: Compare the p-value to \( \alpha \). If p-value \( \leq \alpha \), reject \( H_0 \).

solution_steps.text: Reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that \( \mu < 50 \).

problems.question_html: A researcher tests \( H_0: \mu = 100 \) vs. \( H_a: \mu \neq 100 \) and gets a p-value of 0.08. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), she writes: "We accept \( H_0 \) and conclude the true mean is 100." What is wrong with this conclusion? Enter "accept" or "fail to reject" for what she should have said.
problems.correct_answer: fail to reject

hints.text: In hypothesis testing, we never use the word "accept" for \( H_0 \). What is the correct phrasing?
We say "fail to reject \( H_0 \)" because we cannot prove the null is true — we simply lack sufficient evidence against it.

solution_steps.text: We never "accept" \( H_0 \). The correct language is "fail to reject \( H_0 \)."
Correct conclusion: Since the p-value (0.08) > \( \alpha \) (0.05), we fail to reject \( H_0 \). There is not convincing evidence that the true mean differs from 100.

problems.question_html: A one-sample t-test yields \( t = 1.83 \) with \( df = 14 \) for a right-tailed test. Using the t-table, the p-value is between 0.025 and 0.05. At \( \alpha = 0.05 \), what decision do you make? Enter "reject" or "fail to reject".
problems.correct_answer: reject

hints.text: If the p-value is between 0.025 and 0.05, is it less than or equal to \( \alpha = 0.05 \)?
The p-value is at most 0.05 (since it's between 0.025 and 0.05). We reject \( H_0 \) at \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

solution_steps.text: The p-value is between 0.025 and 0.05, which means p-value \( < 0.05 = \alpha \).
Reject \( H_0 \).

problems.question_html: A matched-pairs experiment tests a new study technique. The differences (new \( - \) old) for 10 students yield \( \bar{d} = 4.2 \) points and \( s_d = 6.0 \) points. Calculate the t-statistic for \( H_0: \mu_d = 0 \) vs. \( H_a: \mu_d > 0 \). Round to three decimal places.

hints.text: Use the same t-formula with the differences: \( t = \bar{d} / (s_d / \sqrt{n}) \).

problems.question_html: A health clinic claims the mean cholesterol level of its patients is 200 mg/dL. A doctor suspects it is higher. She randomly selects 30 patient records and finds \( \bar{x} = 212 \) mg/dL and \( s = 28 \) mg/dL. Perform a complete 4-step t-test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
problems.correct_answer:
State: Let mu = the true mean cholesterol level (mg/dL) of patients at this clinic.
H_0: mu = 200
H_a: mu > 200
alpha = 0.05

Plan: We will use a one-sample t-test.
Conditions:
(1) Random: The sample is randomly selected from patient records (stated).
(2) 10%: 30 patients is less than 10% of all patients at the clinic (reasonable for a clinic).
(3) Normal/Large Sample: n = 30 >= 30. The CLT applies.

Do: t = (212 - 200)/(28/sqrt(30)) = 12/5.112 = 2.347.
df = 29. Using the t-table with df = 29, the one-tail p-value is between 0.01 and 0.025. Calculator: p-value = 0.013.

Conclude: Since the p-value (between 0.01 and 0.025) is less than alpha = 0.05, we reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that the true mean cholesterol level of patients at this clinic is greater than 200 mg/dL.

hints.text: Follow the 4 steps: State (parameter, hypotheses, alpha), Plan (name test, check conditions), Do (compute t and p-value), Conclude (decision in context).
t = (212-200)/(28/sqrt(30)) = 12/5.112 = 2.347. df = 29. One-tailed p-value between 0.01 and 0.025. Since p < 0.05, reject H_0.

solution_steps.text: State: Let \( \mu \) = true mean cholesterol (mg/dL) of patients. \( H_0: \mu = 200 \), \( H_a: \mu > 200 \). \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
Plan: One-sample t-test. Random: stated. 10%: 30 < 10% of all clinic patients. Normal/Large Sample: \( n = 30 \geq 30 \).
Conclude: Since the p-value (0.013) < 0.05, we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the true mean cholesterol level exceeds 200 mg/dL.

problems.question_html: An education researcher wants to know if a new reading program changes comprehension scores from the national average of 65. She randomly selects 22 students, teaches them with the new program, and measures their scores: \( \bar{x} = 69.3 \), \( s = 8.5 \). A dotplot of the data shows approximate symmetry with one mild outlier. Perform a full 4-step test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
problems.correct_answer:
State: Let mu = the true mean reading comprehension score for students taught with the new program.
H_0: mu = 65
H_a: mu != 65 (two-sided, since the question asks about "change")
alpha = 0.05

Plan: We will use a one-sample t-test.
Conditions:
(1) Random: The students were randomly selected (stated).
(2) 10%: 22 students is less than 10% of all potential students.
(3) Normal/Large Sample: n = 22. Since 15 <= 22 < 30, we check the data: the dotplot shows approximate symmetry with only one mild outlier. This is acceptable — proceed with caution.

Do: t = (69.3 - 65)/(8.5/sqrt(22)) = 4.3/1.812 = 2.373.
df = 21. For a two-tailed test, p-value = 2 x P(t > 2.373). From the t-table with df = 21: t = 2.080 corresponds to upper-tail 0.025, t = 2.518 corresponds to 0.01. So one-tail is between 0.01 and 0.025. Two-tailed p-value is between 0.02 and 0.05. Calculator: p-value = 0.028.

Conclude: Since the p-value (between 0.02 and 0.05) is less than alpha = 0.05, we reject H_0. There is convincing evidence that the true mean comprehension score for students using the new reading program differs from 65. The sample mean of 69.3 suggests scores may be higher.

hints.text: The question asks about "change" — use a two-sided test. With n = 22, check the Normal/Large Sample condition carefully.
t = (69.3-65)/(8.5/sqrt(22)) = 4.3/1.812 = 2.373. df = 21. Two-tailed p-value between 0.02 and 0.05. Reject H_0 at alpha = 0.05.

solution_steps.text: State: \( \mu \) = true mean comprehension score for students using the new program. \( H_0: \mu = 65 \), \( H_a: \mu \neq 65 \). \( \alpha = 0.05 \).
Plan: One-sample t-test. Random: stated. 10%: 22 < 10% of all students. Normal/Large Sample: \( n = 22 \), approximate symmetry, one mild outlier is acceptable.
Conclude: p-value (0.028) < 0.05, so reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence the new program changes mean comprehension scores from 65. The sample suggests an increase.

concepts.title: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means
concepts.content_html:
Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means

When we want to compare two populations — for example, whether a new drug lowers blood pressure more than a placebo — we take independent random samples from each population and look at the difference in sample means, \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \).

Shape, Center, and Spread

If we repeatedly took pairs of random samples (one from each population) and computed \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \) each time, those differences would form a sampling distribution.

Center:

\[ \mu_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \mu_1 - \mu_2 \]

The mean of the sampling distribution equals the difference of the population means. This makes the statistic \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \) an unbiased estimator of \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \).

Spread:

\[ \sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}} \]

Because the two samples are independent, their variances add. We add the variances (not standard deviations) and then take the square root.

Shape: The sampling distribution of \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \) is approximately Normal when both populations are Normal, or when both sample sizes are large enough (Central Limit Theorem).

Conditions for Using This Model

  1. Independent Samples: The two samples must be taken independently of each other. Knowing the values in one sample gives no information about the other.
  2. 10% Condition (both samples): \( n_1 \le 0.10 N_1 \) and \( n_2 \le 0.10 N_2 \). Each sample must be no more than 10% of its respective population.
  3. Normal/Large Sample (both samples): Each population is Normal, or \( n_1 \ge 30 \) and \( n_2 \ge 30 \). If sample sizes are small, check for strong skewness or outliers in both samples.

Worked Example

A nutritionist compares the daily calorie intake of adults in City A (\( \mu_1 = 2200 \), \( \sigma_1 = 300 \)) and City B (\( \mu_2 = 2050 \), \( \sigma_2 = 280 \)). She takes independent random samples of \( n_1 = 40 \) from City A and \( n_2 = 50 \) from City B.

Mean of the sampling distribution:

\[ \mu_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = 2200 - 2050 = 150 \text{ calories} \]

Standard deviation of the sampling distribution:

\[ \sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{300^2}{40} + \frac{280^2}{50}} = \sqrt{\frac{90000}{40} + \frac{78400}{50}} = \sqrt{2250 + 1568} = \sqrt{3818} \approx 61.79 \text{ calories} \]

Shape: Approximately Normal because \( n_1 = 40 \ge 30 \) and \( n_2 = 50 \ge 30 \).

Key Idea: When combining independent random variables, variances add. For the difference \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \), we still add the variances — we never subtract them. The spread of a difference is always larger than the spread of either individual sampling distribution.
AP Exam Trap: Students often try to subtract the standard deviations or subtract the variances when finding the spread of a difference. Remember: variances always add when the random variables are independent, regardless of whether you are looking at a sum or a difference.
concepts.content_raw: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Sample Means

problem_sets.title: Practice: Sampling Distributions for the Difference Between Two Means

problems.question_html: Researchers take independent random samples from two populations with \( \mu_1 = 85 \), \( \sigma_1 = 12 \), \( n_1 = 36 \), and \( \mu_2 = 78 \), \( \sigma_2 = 10 \), \( n_2 = 49 \). What is the mean of the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \)?

choices.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the shape of the populations.

hints.text: The mean of the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \) is simply \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \).
\( \mu_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = 85 - 78 = 7 \). The shape of the populations does not affect the center.

solution_steps.text: The mean of the sampling distribution of the difference is \( \mu_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \mu_1 - \mu_2 \).

problems.question_html: Two independent random samples are drawn: \( n_1 = 50 \) from a population with \( \sigma_1 = 15 \) and \( n_2 = 40 \) from a population with \( \sigma_2 = 20 \). Which expression gives the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \)?

hints.text: Recall that variances add for independent random variables. Write the formula using variances in the numerators.
\( \sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{15^2}{50} + \frac{20^2}{40}} \). We add the variance terms, never subtract.

solution_steps.text: The standard deviation of \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \) is \( \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}} \).

problems.question_html: Which of the following is the best explanation for why we add the variances (rather than subtract them) when computing the standard deviation of \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \)?

choices.text: Subtracting would sometimes give a negative variance, which is impossible.
The formula only works for sums, and a difference is just a sum where one term is negative, so the squared standard deviation is still positive.
Adding gives a larger value, which makes the interval wider and more conservative.
We only add variances when the populations have equal standard deviations.

hints.text: Think about what happens when you compute \( \text{Var}(X - Y) \) for independent variables. How does the negative sign interact with squaring?
\( \text{Var}(X - Y) = \text{Var}(X + (-Y)) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(-Y) = \text{Var}(X) + (-1)^2\text{Var}(Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) \). The negative sign gets squared away.

solution_steps.text: For independent random variables: \( \text{Var}(aX + bY) = a^2 \text{Var}(X) + b^2 \text{Var}(Y) \).
A difference \( X - Y \) is the same as \( X + (-1)Y \). So \( \text{Var}(X - Y) = (1)^2\text{Var}(X) + (-1)^2\text{Var}(Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) \).
The negative sign is squared, so it becomes positive. Variances always add for independent variables, whether we compute a sum or a difference.

problems.question_html: A factory has two assembly lines. Line 1 produces widgets with a mean weight of \( \mu_1 = 5.2 \) oz and \( \sigma_1 = 0.4 \) oz. Line 2 produces widgets with \( \mu_2 = 5.0 \) oz and \( \sigma_2 = 0.5 \) oz. An inspector takes independent random samples of \( n_1 = 25 \) from Line 1 and \( n_2 = 30 \) from Line 2. Which condition is most likely not satisfied for using the Normal model for \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \)?

choices.text: The 10% condition, because the factory likely produces far more than 250 and 300 widgets
The independence condition, because the two lines are in the same factory
The Normal/Large Sample condition, because \( n_1 = 25 < 30 \) and we don't know if the Line 1 population is Normal
None — all conditions are clearly met

hints.text: Check each condition one by one. Pay special attention to the sample size threshold for the Central Limit Theorem.

The CLT requires \( n \ge 30 \) for each sample (unless the population is known to be Normal). Since \( n_1 = 25 < 30 \) and we have no information about the shape of Line 1's distribution, the Normal/Large Sample condition may not be met for sample 1.

solution_steps.text: 10% condition: A factory produces far more than 250 and 300 widgets, so both samples are less than 10% of their populations. ✓
Independence: The two lines operate independently, so the samples are independent of each other. ✓
Normal/Large Sample: \( n_2 = 30 \ge 30 \) ✓, but \( n_1 = 25 < 30 \) and we don't know whether Line 1's weight distribution is Normal. This condition is questionable.

problems.question_html: Suppose \( \mu_1 = 120 \), \( \sigma_1 = 18 \), \( n_1 = 45 \), and \( \mu_2 = 110 \), \( \sigma_2 = 15 \), \( n_2 = 60 \). Find the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \). Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Use the formula \( \sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{\sigma_2^2}{n_2}} \).

solution_steps.text: Apply the formula: \( \sigma_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{18^2}{45} + \frac{15^2}{60}} \).

problems.question_html: Independent random samples of size \( n_1 = 64 \) and \( n_2 = 81 \) are drawn from populations with \( \mu_1 = 50 \), \( \sigma_1 = 8 \) and \( \mu_2 = 44 \), \( \sigma_2 = 9 \). Find \( P(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 > 8) \). Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: First find the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution, then standardize to find the z-score for 8.

solution_steps.text: Using the z-table: \( P(Z > 1.41) = 1 - 0.9207 = 0.0793 \). Using technology: \( P(Z > 1.4142) \approx 0.0786 \). Acceptable answers: 0.0778 to 0.0793 depending on rounding.

problems.question_html: Two populations have \( \mu_1 = 200 \), \( \sigma_1 = 25 \) and \( \mu_2 = 180 \), \( \sigma_2 = 30 \). Independent random samples of \( n_1 = 100 \) and \( n_2 = 100 \) are taken. Find \( P(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 < 15) \). Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Find the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution, then compute the z-score for 15.

solution_steps.text: \( P(Z < -1.28) \approx 0.1003 \) from z-table. Using technology: \( P(Z < -1.2804) \approx 0.1002 \). Acceptable: 0.0853 to 0.1003 depending on precision.

problems.question_html: A study compares the reaction times (in milliseconds) of professional gamers (\( \mu_1 = 180 \), \( \sigma_1 = 22 \)) and casual gamers (\( \mu_2 = 210 \), \( \sigma_2 = 35 \)). Independent samples of \( n_1 = 50 \) and \( n_2 = 70 \) are taken. What is the probability that \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \) is positive (i.e., the sample mean for professional gamers exceeds that for casual gamers)? Round to four decimal places.

hints.text: Find the mean and SD of the sampling distribution, then find the z-score for 0.

solution_steps.text: P(Z > 5.75) ≈ 0.0000. It is essentially impossible for the professional gamers' sample mean to exceed the casual gamers' sample mean, since professional gamers have much faster (lower) reaction times.

problems.question_html:
A researcher wants to compare the average daily water consumption (in liters) of adults in two cities. She takes independent random samples of \( n_1 = 35 \) adults from City X and \( n_2 = 42 \) adults from City Y. The population parameters are unknown, but she observes \( \bar{x}_1 = 2.8 \), \( s_1 = 0.6 \), \( \bar{x}_2 = 2.5 \), \( s_2 = 0.7 \).

(a) Verify all conditions for using the sampling distribution model for \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \).

(b) Calculate the standard error of \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \).

(c) Explain whether \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 = 0.3 \) provides strong evidence that \( \mu_1 > \mu_2 \), using your answer from (b).
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Random: Both samples are described as independent random samples. ✓ 10%: It is reasonable that both cities have more than 350 and 420 adults, respectively, so each sample is less than 10% of its population. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 35 ≥ 30 and n₂ = 42 ≥ 30, so by the CLT both sampling distributions are approximately Normal. ✓ Independence: The two samples are taken independently from different cities. ✓

(b) SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂) = √(0.36/35 + 0.49/42) = √(0.01029 + 0.01167) = √0.02195 ≈ 0.1482 liters.

(c) The observed difference is 0.3 liters. z = 0.3/0.1482 ≈ 2.02. Since the observed difference is about 2 standard errors above 0, it would be somewhat unusual (about a 2% chance) to observe a difference this large or larger if μ₁ = μ₂. This provides moderately strong evidence that μ₁ > μ₂.

hints.text: For part (a), check each condition explicitly: random sampling, 10% rule for both samples, and Normal/Large Sample for both. For part (b), use sample standard deviations since population values are unknown.
SE = √(0.6²/35 + 0.7²/42). For part (c), compute how many standard errors the observed difference of 0.3 is from 0, and interpret.

solution_steps.text: (a) Random: Both are described as independent random samples. ✓ 10%: Both cities have far more than 350 and 420 adults. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 35 ≥ 30 and n₂ = 42 ≥ 30. ✓

(c) z = (0.3 − 0)/0.1482 ≈ 2.02. The observed difference is about 2 standard errors above 0. P(Z > 2.02) ≈ 0.022. Since there is only about a 2.2% chance of observing a difference this large if the population means were equal, this provides moderately strong evidence that μ₁ > μ₂.

problems.question_html:
A pharmaceutical company tests two formulations of a pain reliever. In a clinical trial, 60 patients receive Formulation A and 55 patients receive Formulation B. The time to pain relief (in minutes) is recorded.

Formulation AFormulation B
Sample size6055
Sample mean18.4 min22.1 min
Sample SD4.2 min5.8 min

(a) Define the parameter of interest and state appropriate hypotheses to test whether Formulation A provides faster relief.

(b) Verify conditions for inference.

(c) Calculate the standard error of \( \bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B \) and the test statistic.

(d) Interpret the test statistic in context.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Let μ_A = the true mean time to pain relief for Formulation A and μ_B = the true mean time to pain relief for Formulation B. H₀: μ_A − μ_B = 0 (no difference in mean relief time). Hₐ: μ_A − μ_B < 0 (Formulation A provides faster relief, meaning lower time).

(b) Random: Patients were assigned to treatments in a clinical trial (assuming random assignment). ✓ 10%: There are more than 600 and 550 potential patients for each formulation. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n_A = 60 ≥ 30 and n_B = 55 ≥ 30. ✓

(c) SE = √(4.2²/60 + 5.8²/55) = √(17.64/60 + 33.64/55) = √(0.294 + 0.6116) = √0.9056 ≈ 0.9517 min. t = (18.4 − 22.1)/0.9517 = −3.7/0.9517 ≈ −3.889.

(d) The test statistic of t ≈ −3.89 means the observed difference in sample means (Formulation A was 3.7 minutes faster) is about 3.89 standard errors below 0. This is very far from what we would expect if there were no difference, providing very strong evidence that Formulation A provides faster pain relief than Formulation B.

hints.text: For part (a), think carefully about the direction: 'faster relief' means lower time, so μ_A < μ_B, which means μ_A − μ_B < 0.
SE = √(s_A²/n_A + s_B²/n_B) = √(4.2²/60 + 5.8²/55). Then t = (x̄_A − x̄_B − 0)/SE. For part (d), explain what the t-value means in terms of standard errors from 0.

solution_steps.text: (a) Let μ_A and μ_B be the true mean times to pain relief for Formulations A and B. H₀: μ_A − μ_B = 0. Hₐ: μ_A − μ_B < 0 (A is faster → lower time).
(b) Random: Clinical trial with (assumed) random assignment. ✓ 10%: Far more than 600 and 550 potential patients exist. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: 60 ≥ 30 and 55 ≥ 30. ✓

(d) The sample mean for Formulation A was 3.7 minutes less than for B. This difference is about 3.89 standard errors below 0, which would be extremely unlikely if the formulations had equal mean relief times. This provides very strong evidence that Formulation A provides faster pain relief.

concepts.title: Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means
concepts.content_html:
Constructing a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

When population standard deviations are unknown (which is almost always the case in practice), we use a two-sample t-interval to estimate the difference \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \).

The Two-Sample t-Interval Formula

\[ (\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) \pm t^* \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}} \]

where:

  • \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \) is the point estimate (the observed difference in sample means)
  • \( t^* \) is the critical value from the t-distribution for the desired confidence level
  • \( \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}} \) is the standard error (SE) of the difference

Degrees of Freedom

The exact degrees of freedom are computed using the Welch-Satterthwaite formula, which is complicated. On the AP exam:

  • Use your calculator's output for df (the exam expects this)
  • Or use the conservative approach: \( df = \min(n_1 - 1, n_2 - 1) \)

Conditions (Must Check All)

  1. Random: Both samples are randomly selected or data come from two randomly assigned treatment groups.
  2. 10% Condition: \( n_1 \le 0.10 N_1 \) and \( n_2 \le 0.10 N_2 \).
  3. Normal/Large Sample: Both populations are Normal, or \( n_1 \ge 30 \) and \( n_2 \ge 30 \). For small samples, check dotplots/boxplots for strong skewness or outliers in both groups.

Worked Example

A teacher wants to estimate the difference in mean test scores between two teaching methods. She randomly assigns 32 students to Method A and 28 students to Method B.

Method AMethod B
\( n \)3228
\( \bar{x} \)78.573.2
\( s \)8.49.1

Step 1: Check conditions.

  • Random: Students were randomly assigned to methods. ✓
  • 10%: Not needed for experiments with random assignment (but if sampling: 32 and 28 are < 10% of all students). ✓
  • Normal/Large Sample: \( n_1 = 32 \ge 30 \) ✓ and \( n_2 = 28 \) — close to 30 and we assume no strong skewness. ✓

Step 2: Compute the interval (95% confidence).

\[ SE = \sqrt{\frac{8.4^2}{32} + \frac{9.1^2}{28}} = \sqrt{\frac{70.56}{32} + \frac{82.81}{28}} = \sqrt{2.205 + 2.9575} = \sqrt{5.1625} \approx 2.272 \]

Using conservative df = min(31, 27) = 27: \( t^* \approx 2.052 \) for 95% confidence.

\[ (78.5 - 73.2) \pm 2.052(2.272) = 5.3 \pm 4.662 = (0.638, 9.962) \]

Step 3: Interpret.

We are 95% confident that the true difference in mean test scores (Method A − Method B) is between 0.64 and 9.96 points. Since the entire interval is positive, we have evidence that Method A produces higher mean scores than Method B.

Key Idea: The interpretation must include: confidence level, the parameter (difference in population means), the interval bounds, and context. On the AP exam, saying "We are 95% confident that the true difference in mean [context] is between [lower] and [upper]" earns full credit.
AP Exam Trap: Do not pool the sample variances. The AP Statistics curriculum uses the unpooled (Welch) two-sample t-procedure. Never use a pooled t-test, even if the problem says the variances are equal.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Two-Sample t-Interval

problems.question_html: A 95% two-sample t-interval for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) is calculated to be \( (2.3, 8.7) \). Which interpretation is correct?

choices.text: There is a 95% probability that \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) is between 2.3 and 8.7.
We are 95% confident that the true difference in population means is between 2.3 and 8.7.
95% of all sample differences fall between 2.3 and 8.7.
We are 95% confident that the sample mean difference is between 2.3 and 8.7.

hints.text: Confidence intervals estimate population parameters, not sample statistics. And we say 'confident,' not 'probability,' because the parameter is fixed.

The correct interpretation uses 'We are [confidence level]% confident that the true [parameter in context] is between [lower] and [upper].' The parameter is the difference in population means, not sample means.

solution_steps.text: A confidence interval estimates a population parameter. The parameter here is \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \), the true difference in population means.
We say 'confident' rather than 'probability' because the parameter is a fixed (unknown) number — it either is or is not in the interval.
Correct: We are 95% confident that the true difference in population means is between 2.3 and 8.7.

problems.question_html: Two independent random samples yield: \( \bar{x}_1 = 45.2 \), \( s_1 = 6.3 \), \( n_1 = 40 \) and \( \bar{x}_2 = 41.8 \), \( s_2 = 7.1 \), \( n_2 = 35 \). Which formula gives the correct standard error for the two-sample t-interval?

hints.text: The SE formula keeps each sample's variance divided by its own sample size, then adds those two fractions under a single square root.
\( SE = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{6.3^2}{40} + \frac{7.1^2}{35}} \). Do not pool the variances or add the SDs.

solution_steps.text: The standard error for a two-sample t-interval is \( SE = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}} \).

problems.question_html: Which of the following would decrease the width of a two-sample t-interval for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \)?

choices.text: Increasing the confidence level from 90% to 99%
Decreasing both sample sizes
Increasing both sample sizes
Using sample standard deviations that are larger

hints.text: The width of the interval is 2 × t* × SE. Think about what makes SE smaller or t* smaller.
Larger sample sizes reduce SE (since n appears in the denominator under the square root) and also increase df, which decreases t*. Both effects make the interval narrower.

solution_steps.text: The width = 2 × t* × SE = 2 × t* × √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).
Increasing sample sizes reduces SE (n₁ and n₂ are in the denominators) and increases df (which reduces t*). Both effects narrow the interval.
Higher confidence levels increase t*, larger SDs increase SE, and smaller samples increase SE — all of which widen the interval.

problems.question_html: A health researcher takes random samples of systolic blood pressure from 50 adults who exercise regularly (\( \bar{x}_1 = 118 \), \( s_1 = 11 \)) and 45 adults who do not exercise regularly (\( \bar{x}_2 = 129 \), \( s_2 = 14 \)). She wants to construct a 99% confidence interval. Using conservative df = 44 and \( t^* = 2.692 \), which of the following is closest to the confidence interval?

hints.text: Calculate SE first: \( \sqrt{\frac{11^2}{50} + \frac{14^2}{45}} \). Then the interval is \( (118 - 129) \pm 2.692 \cdot SE \).

solution_steps.text: Point estimate: 118 − 129 = −11.

problems.question_html: A researcher computes a 90% confidence interval for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) using \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 = 12.5 \), \( SE = 3.8 \), and \( t^* = 1.684 \). What is the upper bound of the confidence interval? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: The upper bound of a confidence interval is the point estimate plus the margin of error: \( (\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) + t^* \cdot SE \).

solution_steps.text: Upper bound = point estimate + margin of error = \( (\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) + t^* \cdot SE \).

problems.question_html: A study measures the typing speed (words per minute) of participants before and after a training program, but uses different groups of people for before and after. The before group: \( n_1 = 22 \), \( \bar{x}_1 = 38 \), \( s_1 = 8 \). The after group: \( n_2 = 25 \), \( \bar{x}_2 = 45 \), \( s_2 = 10 \). What is the standard error for \( \bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2 \)? Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: Since different people are in each group, this is a two-sample (not paired) situation. Use the two-sample SE formula.

solution_steps.text: Since the groups consist of different people, this is a two-sample situation (not paired).

problems.question_html: Two independent random samples give \( \bar{x}_1 = 52.0 \), \( s_1 = 5.0 \), \( n_1 = 25 \) and \( \bar{x}_2 = 48.0 \), \( s_2 = 6.0 \), \( n_2 = 30 \). Using the conservative degrees of freedom, find the 95% confidence interval for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \). Enter the lower bound rounded to two decimal places.

hints.text: Conservative df = min(n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1) = min(24, 29) = 24. Look up t* for 95% confidence with 24 df.

solution_steps.text: Point estimate: \( 52.0 - 48.0 = 4.0 \).
Conservative df = min(24, 29) = 24. For 95% confidence: \( t^* \approx 2.064 \).

problems.question_html: Two independent random samples give: \( \bar{x}_1 = 105.3 \), \( s_1 = 12.4 \), \( n_1 = 38 \) and \( \bar{x}_2 = 98.7 \), \( s_2 = 10.8 \), \( n_2 = 42 \). Using conservative df and \( t^* = 2.026 \) for 95% confidence, find the margin of error. Round to two decimal places.

hints.text: First calculate SE = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂), then multiply by t*.

problems.question_html:
A university wants to compare the mean study hours per week of STEM majors and humanities majors. Independent random samples are taken:

STEMHumanities
\( n \)4538
\( \bar{x} \)22.4 hrs17.8 hrs
\( s \)6.2 hrs5.5 hrs

(a) Check all conditions for constructing a two-sample t-interval.

(b) Construct a 95% confidence interval for \( \mu_{\text{STEM}} - \mu_{\text{Hum}} \). Use conservative df and show your work.

(c) Interpret the interval in context.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Random: Both samples are independent random samples. ✓ 10%: The university has far more than 450 STEM majors and 380 humanities majors. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 45 ≥ 30 and n₂ = 38 ≥ 30, so by the CLT both sampling distributions are approximately Normal. ✓

(b) Point estimate: 22.4 − 17.8 = 4.6 hrs. SE = √(6.2²/45 + 5.5²/38) = √(38.44/45 + 30.25/38) = √(0.8542 + 0.7961) = √1.6503 ≈ 1.2846. Conservative df = min(44, 37) = 37. t* ≈ 2.026 for 95% confidence. ME = 2.026 × 1.2846 ≈ 2.603. CI: 4.6 ± 2.603 = (1.997, 7.203), or approximately (2.00, 7.20).

(c) We are 95% confident that the true difference in mean weekly study hours (STEM minus Humanities) is between 2.00 and 7.20 hours. Since the entire interval is positive, we have evidence that STEM majors study more hours per week on average than humanities majors.

hints.text: For conditions, check random, 10%, and Normal/Large Sample for both groups. For the interval, use conservative df = min(n₁ − 1, n₂ − 1).
SE = √(6.2²/45 + 5.5²/38). Conservative df = 37, giving t* ≈ 2.026 for 95%. Interval: (22.4 − 17.8) ± 2.026 × SE. Interpret in context with confidence level.

solution_steps.text: (a) Random: Both are independent random samples. ✓ 10%: University has far more than 450 and 380 students in these majors. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: 45 ≥ 30 and 38 ≥ 30. ✓

(c) We are 95% confident that the true difference in mean weekly study hours (STEM − Humanities) is between 2.00 and 7.20 hours. Since the entire interval is positive, STEM majors study more on average.

problems.question_html:
A consumer group wants to compare the battery life (in hours) of two smartphone brands. They randomly select 30 phones of Brand A and 35 phones of Brand B and fully charge and drain each phone.

Brand ABrand B
\( n \)3035
\( \bar{x} \)11.2 hrs10.5 hrs
\( s \)1.8 hrs2.1 hrs

(a) Verify conditions for a two-sample t-interval.

(b) Construct and interpret a 90% confidence interval for \( \mu_A - \mu_B \). Use conservative df.

(c) A Brand B executive claims there is no difference in battery life. Does your interval support or refute this claim? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Random: Both samples are randomly selected. ✓ 10%: There are far more than 300 Brand A phones and 350 Brand B phones in existence. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 30 ≥ 30 and n₂ = 35 ≥ 30. ✓

(b) Point estimate: 11.2 − 10.5 = 0.7 hrs. SE = √(1.8²/30 + 2.1²/35) = √(3.24/30 + 4.41/35) = √(0.108 + 0.126) = √0.234 ≈ 0.4837. Conservative df = min(29, 34) = 29. t* ≈ 1.699 for 90% confidence. ME = 1.699 × 0.4837 ≈ 0.822. CI: 0.7 ± 0.822 = (−0.122, 1.522).

Interpretation: We are 90% confident that the true difference in mean battery life (Brand A − Brand B) is between −0.12 and 1.52 hours.

(c) The interval contains 0, so we do not have convincing evidence of a difference in mean battery life at the 90% confidence level. The Brand B executive's claim is plausible based on this data — the true difference could be zero (or even slightly favoring Brand B).

hints.text: For part (c), check whether 0 is inside or outside the confidence interval. If 0 is inside the interval, we cannot rule out 'no difference.'
SE ≈ 0.484. With df = 29 and 90% confidence, t* ≈ 1.699. CI: 0.7 ± 0.822 = (−0.12, 1.52). Since 0 is in this interval, the claim of no difference is plausible.

solution_steps.text: (a) Random: randomly selected samples. ✓ 10%: far more than 300 and 350 phones exist. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: 30 ≥ 30 and 35 ≥ 30. ✓
We are 90% confident that the true difference in mean battery life (A − B) is between −0.12 and 1.52 hours.
(c) Since 0 is contained in the interval, we do not have convincing evidence of a difference. The executive's claim is plausible.

concepts.title: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means
concepts.content_html:
Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

Once you have a confidence interval for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \), you can use it to evaluate claims about how two populations compare. The key question is: Does the interval contain 0?

Three Scenarios

IntervalContains 0?Conclusion
Entirely positive, e.g. (2.1, 5.8)NoConvincing evidence that \( \mu_1 > \mu_2 \)
Entirely negative, e.g. (−7.3, −1.4)NoConvincing evidence that \( \mu_1 < \mu_2 \)
Contains 0, e.g. (−1.2, 4.6)YesNo convincing evidence of a difference

Why Does 0 Matter?

If \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \), the two population means are equal. So:

  • If 0 is a plausible value (inside the interval), we cannot conclude the means are different.
  • If 0 is not a plausible value (outside the interval), we have evidence that the means differ.

Connecting to Significance Tests

A confidence interval and a two-sided significance test are related:

  • If a 95% CI for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) does not contain 0, then a two-sided test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) would reject \( H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 \).
  • If a 95% CI does contain 0, then a two-sided test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) would fail to reject \( H_0 \).

Worked Example

A 95% CI for the difference in mean test scores (tutoring − no tutoring) is (1.5, 8.3).

Since the entire interval is positive and does not contain 0, there is convincing evidence that students who received tutoring scored higher on average than those who did not. We are 95% confident the mean difference is between 1.5 and 8.3 points.

If the interval had been (−0.8, 8.3), we could not conclude there is a difference because 0 is a plausible value for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \).

Key Idea: The location of 0 relative to the confidence interval tells you everything. Interval entirely above 0 → \( \mu_1 > \mu_2 \). Entirely below 0 → \( \mu_1 < \mu_2 \). Straddling 0 → no convincing evidence of a difference.
AP Exam Trap: When an interval contains 0, do NOT say "the means are equal" or "there is no difference." Instead say "there is no convincing evidence of a difference." Failing to reject \( H_0 \) is not the same as accepting \( H_0 \).
concepts.content_raw: Justifying a Claim Based on a Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Means

problem_sets.title: Practice: Justifying Claims with Two-Sample CIs

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) is \( (3.2, 11.5) \). What can we conclude?

choices.text: There is no convincing evidence that the population means differ.
There is convincing evidence that \( \mu_1 > \mu_2 \).
There is convincing evidence that \( \mu_1 < \mu_2 \).
The means are definitely equal because the interval does not include negative values.

hints.text: Check whether 0 is inside or outside the interval (3.2, 11.5). If it's outside, the direction of the interval tells you which mean is larger.
Since 0 < 3.2, the value 0 is not in the interval. The entire interval is positive, meaning \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \), so \( \mu_1 > \mu_2 \).

solution_steps.text: The interval (3.2, 11.5) is entirely positive and does not contain 0.
Since all plausible values for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) are positive, there is convincing evidence that \( \mu_1 > \mu_2 \).

problems.question_html: A researcher calculates a 90% confidence interval for the difference in mean recovery time (Drug A − Drug B) as \( (-2.1, 0.8) \). Which statement is the best conclusion?

choices.text: Drug A leads to significantly faster recovery than Drug B.
Drug B leads to significantly faster recovery than Drug A.
There is no convincing evidence of a difference in mean recovery times between the two drugs.
The two drugs have exactly the same mean recovery time.

hints.text: Does the interval (−2.1, 0.8) contain 0?
Yes, 0 is between −2.1 and 0.8, so 0 is a plausible value for \( \mu_A - \mu_B \). We cannot conclude the means are different. But we also cannot say they are 'exactly the same.'

solution_steps.text: The interval (−2.1, 0.8) contains 0.
Since 0 is a plausible value for \( \mu_A - \mu_B \), there is no convincing evidence of a difference. We do not say the means are equal — only that we lack evidence of a difference.

problems.question_html: A nutritionist compares two diets. A 95% CI for \( \mu_A - \mu_B \) (weight loss in pounds over 12 weeks) is \( (0.1, 5.9) \). A colleague says, "Since the interval barely excludes 0, the result is practically meaningless." Which response best addresses this?

choices.text: The colleague is wrong; since 0 is not in the interval, Diet A is definitively better.
The colleague has a point: statistical significance does not necessarily imply practical significance. A difference as small as 0.1 pounds may not be meaningful.
The colleague is wrong; the interval should be widened to include 0.
The colleague is right; we should redo the study with a 99% confidence level.

hints.text: Think about the distinction between statistical significance and practical significance.

While the interval excludes 0 (statistically significant), the lower bound of 0.1 pounds is very small. A weight loss difference of 0.1 pounds over 12 weeks is likely not practically meaningful. Statistical significance \(
eq\) practical significance.

solution_steps.text: The interval (0.1, 5.9) does exclude 0, so there is statistically significant evidence that Diet A leads to more weight loss.
However, the lower bound of 0.1 pounds is trivially small. The true difference could be as small as 0.1 pounds over 12 weeks, which is not practically meaningful.
This illustrates the important distinction between statistical significance (is there a real difference?) and practical significance (is the difference large enough to matter?).

problems.question_html: A 95% CI for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) is \( (-1.8, 3.4) \) and a 99% CI for the same data is \( (-3.2, 4.8) \). A student claims that since the 99% CI is wider, it provides stronger evidence of a difference. Is this correct?

choices.text: Yes, the wider interval captures more possible values, giving stronger evidence.
No, a wider interval is less informative and both intervals contain 0, so neither provides convincing evidence of a difference.
Yes, the 99% confidence level is more reliable, so its conclusion is stronger.
No, the 95% CI is better because it is narrower and therefore more precise.

hints.text: Check whether each interval contains 0. A wider interval does not mean stronger evidence — it means less precision.
Both intervals contain 0, so neither provides convincing evidence of a difference. A wider interval is less precise, not more informative. The student's reasoning is incorrect.

solution_steps.text: The 95% CI (−1.8, 3.4) contains 0, and the 99% CI (−3.2, 4.8) also contains 0.
Neither interval provides convincing evidence that the means differ. A higher confidence level makes the interval wider (more cautious), not stronger. Width reflects precision, not evidence.

problems.question_html: A 99% confidence interval for \( \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{old}} \) is \( (-15.3, -4.7) \). The entire interval is negative. In the context where higher values are better, which group performed better? Enter "new" or "old".
problems.correct_answer: old

hints.text: If \( \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{old}} \) is negative, which mean is larger?
A negative difference means \( \mu_{\text{new}} < \mu_{\text{old}} \). Since higher values are better, the old group performed better.

solution_steps.text: The entire interval is negative, so \( \mu_{\text{new}} - \mu_{\text{old}} < 0 \), meaning \( \mu_{\text{new}} < \mu_{\text{old}} \).
Since higher values are better and \( \mu_{\text{old}} \) is larger, the old group performed better.

problems.question_html: A 95% CI for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) is \( (0.2, 6.4) \). Would a two-sided hypothesis test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) reject \( H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 \)? Enter "yes" or "no".
problems.correct_answer: yes

hints.text: There is a direct connection between a C% confidence interval and a two-sided test at α = (1 − C/100).
A 95% CI that does not contain 0 means a two-sided test at α = 0.05 would reject H₀. Since (0.2, 6.4) does not contain 0, we would reject.

solution_steps.text: A 95% CI corresponds to a two-sided test at α = 0.05.
Since 0 is not in the interval (0.2, 6.4), we would reject H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ at the 0.05 significance level. Answer: yes.

problems.question_html: A 95% confidence interval for \( \mu_{\text{treatment}} - \mu_{\text{control}} \) is \( (4.2, 12.6) \). The treatment is a new fertilizer and the response is plant height in centimeters. The researcher claims the fertilizer increases average plant height by about 8 cm. Is this claim supported by the interval? Round the center of the interval to one decimal place to check.

hints.text: The center of a confidence interval is the point estimate. Find the midpoint of (4.2, 12.6).
Center = (4.2 + 12.6)/2 = 16.8/2 = 8.4. The claim of 'about 8 cm' is close to the point estimate of 8.4 cm and is within the interval, so it is supported.

solution_steps.text: The center of the interval = (4.2 + 12.6)/2 = 8.4 cm.
The researcher's claim of about 8 cm is close to the point estimate of 8.4 cm and falls within the interval, so it is supported by the data.

problems.question_html: A 90% CI for the difference in mean SAT scores (private school − public school) is \( (12, 48) \). How would the conclusion change if the confidence level were increased to 99% (keeping the same data)? Enter "might contain 0" or "still excludes 0".
problems.correct_answer: might contain 0

hints.text: When you increase the confidence level, the interval gets wider. Think about whether a wider interval might expand enough to include 0.

The 90% CI is (12, 48), with center 30 and half-width 18. At 99% confidence, the margin of error would be much larger. The lower bound could drop below 0, meaning the wider interval might contain 0. We can't be certain without calculating, but it is possible.

solution_steps.text: The 90% CI is (12, 48), centered at 30 with ME = 18.
Increasing to 99% confidence makes the interval wider. The t* value increases substantially (from about 1.68 to about 2.68 for typical df), roughly increasing ME by a factor of 1.6.

New ME ≈ 18 × (2.68/1.68) ≈ 28.7. New interval ≈ (30 − 28.7, 30 + 28.7) = (1.3, 58.7). This still excludes 0, but with different df the result could change. In general, a wider interval 'might contain 0' — we cannot guarantee the conclusion holds.

problems.question_html:
A school district compares math achievement scores between two elementary schools. Independent random samples of 40 students from School A (\( \bar{x}_A = 82.3 \), \( s_A = 9.5 \)) and 35 students from School B (\( \bar{x}_B = 78.1 \), \( s_B = 11.2 \)) are collected.

(a) Construct a 95% confidence interval for \( \mu_A - \mu_B \). Use conservative df.

(b) Based on the interval, is there convincing evidence that the schools differ in mean achievement? Explain.

(c) The district superintendent claims School A outperforms School B by at least 8 points. Does the interval support this claim? Explain.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Point estimate: 82.3 − 78.1 = 4.2. SE = √(9.5²/40 + 11.2²/35) = √(90.25/40 + 125.44/35) = √(2.256 + 3.584) = √5.840 ≈ 2.417. Conservative df = min(39, 34) = 34. t* ≈ 2.032. ME = 2.032 × 2.417 ≈ 4.911. CI: 4.2 ± 4.911 = (−0.711, 9.111), approximately (−0.71, 9.11).

(b) The interval (−0.71, 9.11) contains 0, so there is no convincing evidence at the 95% confidence level that the two schools differ in mean math achievement scores. The true difference could be zero (or even slightly favoring School B).

(c) The superintendent's claim that School A outperforms by at least 8 points means μ_A − μ_B ≥ 8. The interval (−0.71, 9.11) contains values both below and above 8. Since most of the plausible values are below 8, the claim is not well-supported by the data. We cannot be confident the difference is at least 8 points.

hints.text: Compute SE, find t* with conservative df, build the interval. Then check if 0 is in it (part b) and if 8 is plausible (part c).

SE ≈ 2.42, df = 34, t* ≈ 2.032. CI ≈ (−0.71, 9.11). For part (b), 0 is in the interval. For part (c), 8 is barely inside the interval but most values are below 8, so the claim of 'at least 8' is not well-supported.

solution_steps.text: (b) Since 0 is in the interval, there is no convincing evidence of a difference in mean scores.
(c) The claim of at least 8 points is not well-supported. While 8 is barely inside the interval, the vast majority of plausible values are below 8. The point estimate is only 4.2, far less than 8.

problems.question_html:
Two versions of a website are tested to compare user engagement. Version X is shown to 50 randomly selected users and Version Y to 55 randomly selected users. Time spent on the site (in minutes) is recorded.

Version XVersion Y
\( n \)5055
\( \bar{x} \)8.4 min6.9 min
\( s \)3.2 min2.8 min

(a) Calculate a 95% confidence interval for \( \mu_X - \mu_Y \). Use conservative df.

(b) Based on the interval, is there convincing evidence that Version X leads to greater engagement? Justify.

(c) If the company considers a difference of less than 0.5 minutes to be practically insignificant, what can you say about the practical significance of the result?
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Point estimate: 8.4 − 6.9 = 1.5 min. SE = √(3.2²/50 + 2.8²/55) = √(10.24/50 + 7.84/55) = √(0.2048 + 0.1425) = √0.3473 ≈ 0.5893. Conservative df = min(49, 54) = 49. t* ≈ 2.010. ME = 2.010 × 0.5893 ≈ 1.185. CI: 1.5 ± 1.185 = (0.315, 2.685), approximately (0.32, 2.69).

(b) Yes. The entire interval (0.32, 2.69) is above 0, so there is convincing evidence that Version X leads to greater mean time on site than Version Y.

(c) The entire interval is above 0.5 minutes (the lower bound is 0.32, which is below 0.5 — actually 0.32 < 0.5). Since the lower bound is below 0.5, the true difference could be less than 0.5 minutes, which the company considers practically insignificant. While there is statistical significance, practical significance is not guaranteed. The company should consider whether a difference as small as 0.32 minutes is worth the cost of implementing Version X.

hints.text: For part (c), compare the lower bound of the interval to the threshold of 0.5 minutes. If the lower bound is above 0.5, practical significance is confirmed. If below, it's uncertain.
SE ≈ 0.589. With df = 49, t* ≈ 2.010. CI: (0.32, 2.69). The lower bound (0.32) is below 0.5, so while statistically significant, the true difference might be practically insignificant.

solution_steps.text: (b) The entire interval is positive (does not contain 0), so there is convincing evidence Version X leads to more engagement.

(c) The lower bound of 0.32 is below the practical significance threshold of 0.5 minutes. While statistically significant, the true difference could be smaller than what the company considers meaningful. Statistical significance does not guarantee practical significance.

concepts.title: Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means
concepts.content_html:
Setting Up a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means

When we want to test whether two population means are different (or whether one is larger than the other), we use a two-sample t-test. Setting up the test correctly is critical and worth significant credit on the AP exam.

Defining the Parameters

Always start by defining the parameters in context:

  • \( \mu_1 \) = the true mean [response variable] for [population 1 / treatment 1]
  • \( \mu_2 \) = the true mean [response variable] for [population 2 / treatment 2]

Writing the Hypotheses

The null hypothesis always states "no difference":

\[ H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \quad \text{(equivalently, } \mu_1 = \mu_2\text{)} \]

The alternative hypothesis depends on the research question:

  • Two-sided: \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0 \) ("Is there a difference?")
  • One-sided (greater): \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \) ("Is \( \mu_1 \) greater than \( \mu_2 \)?")
  • One-sided (less): \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \) ("Is \( \mu_1 \) less than \( \mu_2 \)?")

Choosing the Significance Level

The significance level \( \alpha \) is chosen before collecting data, typically \( \alpha = 0.05 \) unless stated otherwise.

Checking Conditions

Before proceeding with the test, verify:

  1. Random: Both samples are random, or data come from a randomized experiment.
  2. 10%: \( n_1 \le 0.10 N_1 \) and \( n_2 \le 0.10 N_2 \) (for sampling without replacement).
  3. Normal/Large Sample: Both populations are Normal, or \( n_1 \ge 30 \) and \( n_2 \ge 30 \). For smaller samples, check for strong skewness/outliers.

Worked Example

A fitness trainer wants to test whether a new workout program produces greater mean weight loss than the standard program. She randomly assigns 40 participants to the new program and 35 to the standard program.

Define parameters:

  • \( \mu_1 \) = the true mean weight loss (in pounds) for participants using the new workout program
  • \( \mu_2 \) = the true mean weight loss (in pounds) for participants using the standard workout program

State hypotheses:

\[ H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \]\[ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \]

(One-sided because the trainer specifically wants to test if the new program produces greater weight loss.)

Significance level: \( \alpha = 0.05 \)

Key Idea: On the AP exam, always (1) define both parameters in context, (2) write hypotheses using proper notation, and (3) justify one-sided vs. two-sided based on the research question. These are separate scoring components.
AP Exam Trap: Writing \( H_0: \bar{x}_1 = \bar{x}_2 \) is wrong. Hypotheses are always about population parameters (\( \mu \)), never about sample statistics (\( \bar{x} \)). Also, the null hypothesis must contain an equality (=), never < or >.
