problem_sets.title: Practice: Setting Up Two-Sample t-Tests

problems.question_html: A researcher wants to test whether there is a difference in mean commute times between employees who work in the city center and those who work in the suburbs. Which set of hypotheses is appropriate?

hints.text: Hypotheses use population parameters (μ), not sample statistics (x̄). Also, the research question asks about 'a difference' — not a specific direction.
Since the question is about whether there IS a difference (not which is larger), use a two-sided alternative: \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0 \). Hypotheses must use μ, not x̄.

solution_steps.text: The research question asks about 'a difference' without specifying a direction, so the test should be two-sided.
Hypotheses are about population parameters, so we use μ, not x̄.

problems.question_html: A teacher believes that students who study with background music score lower on tests than students who study in silence. She randomly assigns students to two groups. Which alternative hypothesis should she use?

choices.text: \( H_a: \mu_{\text{music}} - \mu_{\text{silence}} \neq 0 \)
\( H_a: \mu_{\text{music}} - \mu_{\text{silence}} > 0 \)
\( H_a: \mu_{\text{music}} - \mu_{\text{silence}} < 0 \)
\( H_a: \mu_{\text{music}} > \mu_{\text{silence}} \)

hints.text: The teacher believes music students score LOWER. If μ_music < μ_silence, what does that mean for μ_music − μ_silence?
If music students score lower, then \( \mu_{\text{music}} < \mu_{\text{silence}} \), which means \( \mu_{\text{music}} - \mu_{\text{silence}} < 0 \). This is a one-sided (less than) alternative.

solution_steps.text: The teacher suspects music students score lower: \( \mu_{\text{music}} < \mu_{\text{silence}} \).
Writing this as a difference: \( \mu_{\text{music}} - \mu_{\text{silence}} < 0 \).
So \( H_a: \mu_{\text{music}} - \mu_{\text{silence}} < 0 \).

problems.question_html: A student writes the following hypotheses for a two-sample t-test comparing mean heights of adult men and women: \( H_0: \mu_M - \mu_W > 0 \), \( H_a: \mu_M - \mu_W = 0 \). Identify both errors in the hypotheses.

choices.text:
The null should have = and the alternative should have \(
eq\), and the subscripts are wrong.

The null and alternative are swapped: \( H_0 \) should have = and \( H_a \) should have >, <, or \(
eq\).
The student should use x̄ instead of μ, and the null should be two-sided.
The student should have written \( H_0: \mu_M = \mu_W \) and \( H_a: \mu_M > \mu_W \), but the parameters are defined incorrectly.

hints.text:
Two rules: (1) H₀ always contains = and (2) Hₐ contains \(
eq\), <, or >. Check which hypothesis has the equality.

Error 1: The null hypothesis must contain an equality (=), but the student wrote > in H₀. Error 2: The alternative hypothesis cannot contain an equality, but the student wrote = in Hₐ. The null and alternative are essentially swapped.

solution_steps.text: Error 1: \( H_0 \) must always contain an equality (=). The student incorrectly wrote \( H_0: \mu_M - \mu_W > 0 \), which should be in the alternative.

Error 2: \( H_a \) must contain an inequality (\(
eq\), <, or >). The student wrote \( H_a: \mu_M - \mu_W = 0 \), which should be in the null.

Corrected: \( H_0: \mu_M - \mu_W = 0 \), \( H_a: \mu_M - \mu_W > 0 \) (or \(
eq\) 0 for two-sided).

problems.question_html: A researcher randomly selects 15 patients from Hospital A and 18 patients from Hospital B to compare mean recovery times after knee surgery. Hospital A has 200 knee surgery patients per year and Hospital B has 150. The dotplot of recovery times for Hospital A shows a strong right skew. Which condition for a two-sample t-test is not met?

choices.text: Random
Normal/Large Sample
Independence of samples

hints.text: Check each condition. Random? Yes, random selection. 10%? 15/200 = 7.5% and 18/150 = 12%. Normal/Large Sample? Both n < 30, so check shape.

Actually, 18/150 = 12% > 10%, so the 10% condition fails for Hospital B. Also, with n₁ = 15 < 30 and strong right skew in Hospital A's data, the Normal/Large Sample condition is also problematic. The most concerning issue is Normal/Large Sample due to strong skewness with a small sample.

solution_steps.text: Random: Yes, both are randomly selected. ✓
10%: 15/200 = 7.5% ✓, but 18/150 = 12% > 10%. ✗ (However, this condition is about the 10% rule.)
Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 15 < 30 and n₂ = 18 < 30. Since Hospital A shows strong right skew with only 15 observations, the Normal/Large Sample condition is not met.
The Normal/Large Sample condition is the most clearly violated. With strong skewness and small sample sizes, the t-distribution may not be a good approximation.

problems.question_html: A car manufacturer wants to test if their new engine design produces better fuel efficiency than the current design. Define \( \mu_1 \) as the true mean MPG for the new engine and \( \mu_2 \) as the true mean MPG for the current engine. Write the null hypothesis. Enter your answer using the format "mu1 - mu2 = 0" or "mu1 = mu2".
problems.correct_answer: mu1 - mu2 = 0||mu1 = mu2

hints.text: The null hypothesis always states 'no difference' between the parameters.
\( H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \) or equivalently \( H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 \). The null always contains an equality.

solution_steps.text: The null hypothesis states there is no difference: \( H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \), or equivalently \( H_0: \mu_1 = \mu_2 \).

problems.question_html: A study examines whether there is a difference in mean wait times (in minutes) between two hospital emergency departments. Explain why the researcher should choose a two-sided alternative rather than a one-sided alternative. Enter "two-sided" if the researcher has no prior belief about which ER is faster, or "one-sided" if there is a directional claim.
problems.correct_answer: two-sided

hints.text: The research question asks about 'a difference' — does it specify which ER should have shorter wait times?
Since the question asks whether there IS a difference (not which is larger), and the researcher has no prior directional belief, a two-sided test is appropriate.

solution_steps.text: The research question asks whether there is a difference, without specifying a direction.
A two-sided alternative (\( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0 \)) is appropriate when the researcher has no prior expectation about which mean is larger.

problems.question_html: A pharmaceutical company tests whether a new drug lowers cholesterol more than the existing drug. They plan to use \( \alpha = 0.01 \). With \( \mu_1 \) = mean cholesterol reduction for the new drug and \( \mu_2 \) = mean cholesterol reduction for the existing drug, write the alternative hypothesis. Enter "mu1 - mu2 > 0", "mu1 - mu2 < 0", or "mu1 - mu2 != 0".
problems.correct_answer: mu1 - mu2 > 0

hints.text: The company wants to show the new drug lowers cholesterol MORE. If μ₁ is the mean reduction for the new drug and it's larger, what's the sign of μ₁ − μ₂?
If the new drug reduces cholesterol more, then μ₁ > μ₂, so μ₁ − μ₂ > 0. The alternative is \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \).

solution_steps.text: The company wants to show the new drug has a GREATER mean cholesterol reduction: \( \mu_1 > \mu_2 \).
As a difference: \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \).

problems.question_html: An agronomist wants to compare the mean yield (in bushels per acre) of two corn varieties. She plants Variety A on 20 randomly selected plots and Variety B on 25 randomly selected plots. There are 500 plots available. For the 10% condition, what must be true about the number of plots available for each variety?
problems.correct_answer: 200||at least 200 for A and 250 for B

hints.text: The 10% condition requires each sample to be no more than 10% of its population. What population size is needed for a sample of 20?

For Variety A: need \( n_1 \le 0.10 N_1 \), so \( 20 \le 0.10 N_1 \), meaning \( N_1 \ge 200 \). For Variety B: \( 25 \le 0.10 N_2 \), so \( N_2 \ge 250 \). There must be at least 200 plots available for Variety A and 250 for Variety B.

solution_steps.text: For Variety A: \( n_1 = 20 \le 0.10 N_1 \), so \( N_1 \ge 200 \).
For Variety B: \( n_2 = 25 \le 0.10 N_2 \), so \( N_2 \ge 250 \).
There must be at least 200 plots suitable for Variety A and at least 250 plots suitable for Variety B.

problems.question_html:
A sports scientist wants to determine whether a new training regimen improves sprint times compared to the current regimen. She randomly assigns 28 athletes to the new regimen and 32 to the current one. After 8 weeks, she records each athlete's 100-meter sprint time.

(a) Define the parameters of interest in context.

(b) State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses. Justify your choice of one-sided or two-sided.

(c) Check all conditions for performing the test.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Let μ₁ = the true mean 100-meter sprint time (in seconds) for athletes who use the new training regimen. Let μ₂ = the true mean 100-meter sprint time (in seconds) for athletes who use the current training regimen.

(b) H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 (there is no difference in mean sprint times between the two regimens). Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ < 0 (the new regimen results in faster — lower — mean sprint times). One-sided is appropriate because the scientist specifically wants to know if the new regimen IMPROVES (lowers) sprint times, not just whether there is any difference.

(c) Random: Athletes were randomly assigned to the two regimens. ✓ 10%: Not needed for an experiment with random assignment. If sampling, 28 and 32 are less than 10% of all athletes. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 28 < 30 and n₂ = 32 ≥ 30. For the new regimen group, we need to check the data for strong skewness or outliers. If no strong skewness or outliers are present, the condition is approximately met. ⚠️ (Need to check data)

hints.text: For part (a), define μ₁ and μ₂ using the specific context (sprint times). For part (b), 'improves' means lower sprint time. For part (c), note that n₁ = 28 < 30.

Parameters: μ₁ = true mean sprint time for new regimen, μ₂ = true mean sprint time for current. 'Improves' = lower time, so Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ < 0. Conditions: random assignment ✓, 10% not needed for experiment, but n₁ = 28 < 30 needs shape check.

solution_steps.text: (a) μ₁ = true mean 100-m sprint time (sec) for athletes using the new regimen. μ₂ = true mean 100-m sprint time (sec) for athletes using the current regimen.
(b) H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ < 0. One-sided because the scientist wants to test if the new regimen specifically improves (lowers) times.
(c) Random: random assignment to groups ✓. 10%: not needed for experiments ✓. Normal/Large Sample: n₂ = 32 ≥ 30 ✓, n₁ = 28 is close to 30 — check data for skewness/outliers.

problems.question_html:
A school principal wants to compare the mean number of absences between students who participate in extracurricular activities and those who do not. She takes random samples of 50 participants and 45 non-participants.

(a) Define the parameters and state hypotheses. The principal suspects that participants have fewer absences.

(b) Identify the type of test (one-sided or two-sided) and justify.

(c) State the significance level and explain what a Type I error would mean in this context.

(d) Verify all conditions.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) Let μ₁ = the true mean number of absences per year for students who participate in extracurricular activities. Let μ₂ = the true mean number of absences per year for students who do not participate in extracurricular activities. H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0 (no difference in mean absences). Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ < 0 (participants have fewer absences on average).

(b) One-sided (less than). The principal has a specific directional suspicion: participants have FEWER absences, meaning μ₁ < μ₂, or μ₁ − μ₂ < 0.

(c) Use α = 0.05 (standard). A Type I error would mean concluding that students who participate in extracurricular activities have fewer absences on average than non-participants, when in fact there is no difference (or participants do not have fewer absences). This could lead to policies promoting extracurriculars based on a false finding.

(d) Random: Both samples are randomly selected. ✓ 10%: The school has far more than 500 participants and 450 non-participants (assuming a large school). ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 50 ≥ 30 and n₂ = 45 ≥ 30, so CLT applies. ✓

hints.text: The principal 'suspects' fewer absences for participants — this determines the direction of Hₐ. A Type I error = rejecting H₀ when it is true. Describe what that means in the context of absences.
Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ < 0 (participants have fewer absences). Type I error: concluding participants have fewer absences when they actually don't. Both samples ≥ 30, so Normal/Large Sample condition is met.

solution_steps.text: (a) μ₁ = true mean absences for participants, μ₂ = true mean absences for non-participants. H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ < 0.
(b) One-sided. The principal suspects participants have fewer absences (a specific direction).
(c) α = 0.05. Type I error: concluding participants have fewer absences when actually there is no difference. Could lead to misguided policies.
(d) Random ✓. 10%: samples are < 10% of populations (assuming large school) ✓. Normal/Large Sample: 50 ≥ 30 and 45 ≥ 30 ✓.

concepts.title: Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means
concepts.content_html:
Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means

After setting up the hypotheses and checking conditions, we carry out the two-sample t-test using the full 4-step process expected on the AP exam: State, Plan, Do, Conclude.

The Test Statistic

\[ t = \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - 0}{\sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}} \]

This measures how many standard errors the observed difference is from 0 (the hypothesized difference under \( H_0 \)).

Degrees of Freedom

The exact df uses the Welch-Satterthwaite formula (your calculator computes this). The conservative approach uses \( df = \min(n_1 - 1, n_2 - 1) \).

Finding the P-value

  • Two-sided (\( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0 \)): p-value = \( 2 \cdot P(t > |t_{\text{obs}}|) \)
  • One-sided greater (\( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \)): p-value = \( P(t > t_{\text{obs}}) \)
  • One-sided less (\( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \)): p-value = \( P(t < t_{\text{obs}}) \)

The 4-Step Process (Full Worked Example)

A dietitian wants to test whether a low-carb diet results in more weight loss than a low-fat diet. She randomly assigns 35 participants to the low-carb diet and 40 to the low-fat diet for 12 weeks.

Low-CarbLow-Fat
\( n \)3540
\( \bar{x} \)14.2 lbs11.5 lbs
\( s \)5.3 lbs4.8 lbs

STATE:

Let \( \mu_1 \) = true mean weight loss for participants on the low-carb diet. Let \( \mu_2 \) = true mean weight loss for participants on the low-fat diet.

\[ H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \]\[ H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \]

Significance level: \( \alpha = 0.05 \).

PLAN:

We will use a two-sample t-test for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \).

Conditions:

  • Random: Participants were randomly assigned to diets. ✓
  • 10%: Not needed for a randomized experiment. ✓
  • Normal/Large Sample: \( n_1 = 35 \ge 30 \) and \( n_2 = 40 \ge 30 \). ✓

DO:

\[ SE = \sqrt{\frac{5.3^2}{35} + \frac{4.8^2}{40}} = \sqrt{\frac{28.09}{35} + \frac{23.04}{40}} = \sqrt{0.8026 + 0.576} = \sqrt{1.3786} \approx 1.174 \]\[ t = \frac{(14.2 - 11.5) - 0}{1.174} = \frac{2.7}{1.174} \approx 2.300 \]

Using conservative df = min(34, 39) = 34: p-value = \( P(t > 2.300) \approx 0.0139 \).

CONCLUDE:

Since the p-value (0.0139) is less than \( \alpha = 0.05 \), we reject \( H_0 \). There is convincing evidence that the true mean weight loss for the low-carb diet is greater than for the low-fat diet.

Key Idea: The conclusion must (1) compare p-value to α, (2) state reject or fail to reject H₀, and (3) interpret in context. Always say "convincing evidence that..." when rejecting, or "not convincing evidence that..." when failing to reject. Never say "accept H₀."
AP Exam Trap: Do NOT pool the variances. The AP Statistics curriculum explicitly uses the unpooled (Welch) two-sample t-test. Even if a problem states the population variances are equal, use the unpooled version. Also, never use z-procedures when σ₁ and σ₂ are unknown — always use t.
concepts.content_raw: Carrying Out a Test for the Difference Between Two Population Means

problem_sets.title: Practice: Carrying Out Two-Sample t-Tests

problems.question_html: Two independent random samples produce: \( \bar{x}_1 = 56.8 \), \( s_1 = 7.2 \), \( n_1 = 30 \) and \( \bar{x}_2 = 52.3 \), \( s_2 = 8.5 \), \( n_2 = 35 \). What is the two-sample t test statistic for testing \( H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \)? Round to three decimal places.

choices.text: \( t \approx 2.292 \)
\( t \approx 2.311 \)
\( t \approx 1.964 \)
\( t \approx 3.012 \)

hints.text: Use the formula \( t = \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - 0}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1 + s_2^2/n_2}} \).

problems.question_html: A two-sample t-test produces \( t = 1.85 \) with \( df = 40 \) for \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \). Using the t-table, which range contains the p-value?

hints.text: For a one-sided (greater) test, p-value = P(t > 1.85) with 40 df. Use the t-table to find where 1.85 falls.
With df = 40: t* = 1.684 for α = 0.05 (one-sided) and t* = 2.021 for α = 0.025 (one-sided). Since 1.684 < 1.85 < 2.021, the p-value is between 0.025 and 0.05.

solution_steps.text: This is a one-sided test (greater), so p-value = P(t > 1.85) with 40 df.
From the t-table with df = 40: t₀.₀₅ ≈ 1.684, t₀.₀₂₅ ≈ 2.021.

problems.question_html: Why does the AP Statistics curriculum use the unpooled (Welch) two-sample t-test rather than the pooled version?

choices.text: The pooled version is mathematically incorrect.
The unpooled version does not require the assumption that the two population variances are equal, making it more widely applicable.
The pooled version always gives larger p-values.
The unpooled version uses fewer degrees of freedom, making it more conservative.

hints.text: Think about what assumption the pooled t-test requires that the unpooled version does not.

The pooled t-test assumes σ₁ = σ₂ (equal population variances). If this assumption is wrong, the test can give incorrect results. The Welch (unpooled) version works whether or not variances are equal, making it safer and more general.

solution_steps.text: The pooled two-sample t-test requires the assumption that σ₁² = σ₂² (equal population variances). If this assumption is violated, the pooled test can produce inaccurate p-values.

The Welch (unpooled) version does not require this assumption. It works correctly regardless of whether the variances are equal, making it more broadly applicable and the preferred method for AP Statistics.

problems.question_html: Two independent samples give: \( \bar{x}_1 = 102.4 \), \( s_1 = 9.8 \), \( n_1 = 42 \) and \( \bar{x}_2 = 97.6 \), \( s_2 = 11.3 \), \( n_2 = 38 \). A two-sided test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) is performed. Which of the following is closest to the p-value?

hints.text: First compute the t-statistic, then find the two-sided p-value. Remember: for two-sided, multiply the one-sided p by 2.

solution_steps.text: Using conservative df = 37, two-sided p-value ≈ 2 × P(t > 2.02) ≈ 0.051. With Welch df from a calculator (larger df), p ≈ 0.044.

problems.question_html: A two-sample t-test yields a p-value of 0.032 with \( \alpha = 0.05 \). The hypotheses are \( H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \), \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 \neq 0 \). The context: comparing mean test scores of two schools. What is the correct conclusion? Enter "reject" or "fail to reject".
problems.correct_answer: reject

hints.text: Compare the p-value to α. If p-value < α, we reject H₀.
Since 0.032 < 0.05, we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence that the mean test scores of the two schools are different.

solution_steps.text: Since the p-value is less than the significance level, we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence of a difference in mean test scores between the two schools.

problems.question_html: A test for \( H_0: \mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0 \) vs. \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 > 0 \) yields \( t = 1.45 \) with \( df = 28 \) and \( \alpha = 0.05 \). The p-value is approximately 0.079. State the conclusion in context if the study compares mean reaction times of caffeine users (group 1) vs. non-users (group 2) in milliseconds. Enter "reject" or "fail to reject".
problems.correct_answer: fail to reject

hints.text: Compare p-value = 0.079 to α = 0.05.
Since 0.079 > 0.05, we fail to reject H₀. There is not convincing evidence that caffeine users have a higher mean reaction time than non-users.

solution_steps.text: We fail to reject H₀. There is not convincing evidence that the mean reaction time for caffeine users is greater than for non-users.

problems.question_html: A researcher obtains a p-value of 0.048 for a two-sided test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \). She rejects \( H_0 \). Her colleague argues that with \( \alpha = 0.01 \), the result would not be significant. What would the conclusion be at \( \alpha = 0.01 \)? Enter "reject" or "fail to reject".
problems.correct_answer: fail to reject

hints.text: Compare the p-value to the new significance level α = 0.01.
Since 0.048 > 0.01, we fail to reject H₀ at the α = 0.01 level. The result is significant at 0.05 but not at 0.01.

solution_steps.text: p-value = 0.048. At α = 0.01: 0.048 > 0.01, so we fail to reject H₀.
The result is statistically significant at the 0.05 level but not at the 0.01 level. The choice of α affects the conclusion.

problems.question_html: A two-sample t-test gives \( t = -2.58 \) with \( df = 45 \) for \( H_a: \mu_1 - \mu_2 < 0 \). Using the t-table, find the approximate one-sided p-value. Round to three decimal places.

hints.text: For Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ < 0, the p-value = P(t < −2.58) = P(t > 2.58) with 45 df.
With df = 45: t₀.₀₁ ≈ 2.412 and t₀.₀₀₅ ≈ 2.690. Since 2.412 < 2.58 < 2.690, the p-value is between 0.005 and 0.01. More precisely, P(t > 2.58) ≈ 0.007.

solution_steps.text: p-value = P(t < −2.58) with 45 df = P(t > 2.58) by symmetry.
From the t-table: t₀.₀₁ ≈ 2.412 and t₀.₀₀₅ ≈ 2.690. Since 2.412 < 2.58 < 2.690, the p-value is between 0.005 and 0.01.
Using technology: P(t > 2.58 | df = 45) ≈ 0.007.

problems.question_html:
An environmental scientist compares the dissolved oxygen levels (in mg/L) in two lakes. Independent random samples are taken.

Lake AlpineLake Basin
\( n \)3640
\( \bar{x} \)8.4 mg/L7.1 mg/L
\( s \)1.5 mg/L1.8 mg/L

Carry out a complete two-sample t-test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) to determine whether there is a significant difference in mean dissolved oxygen levels. Use the full 4-step process: State, Plan, Do, Conclude.
problems.correct_answer:
STATE: Let μ₁ = the true mean dissolved oxygen level (mg/L) in Lake Alpine. Let μ₂ = the true mean dissolved oxygen level (mg/L) in Lake Basin. H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ \(
eq\) 0. α = 0.05.

PLAN: Two-sample t-test for μ₁ − μ₂. Conditions: Random: Both samples are independent random samples. ✓ 10%: Both lakes have far more than 360 and 400 possible water samples. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 36 ≥ 30 and n₂ = 40 ≥ 30. ✓

DO: SE = √(1.5²/36 + 1.8²/40) = √(2.25/36 + 3.24/40) = √(0.0625 + 0.081) = √0.1435 ≈ 0.3788. t = (8.4 − 7.1)/0.3788 = 1.3/0.3788 ≈ 3.432. Using conservative df = min(35, 39) = 35: p-value = 2 × P(t > 3.432) ≈ 2 × 0.0008 ≈ 0.0016.

CONCLUDE: Since the p-value (≈ 0.0016) is less than α = 0.05, we reject H₀. There is convincing evidence that the true mean dissolved oxygen levels in Lake Alpine and Lake Basin are different. Specifically, the data suggest Lake Alpine has a higher mean dissolved oxygen level.

hints.text: Follow the 4 steps: State (define parameters, hypotheses, α), Plan (name the test, check conditions), Do (calculate SE, t, p-value), Conclude (compare p to α, interpret in context).

solution_steps.text:
STATE: μ₁ = true mean dissolved oxygen (mg/L) in Lake Alpine, μ₂ = true mean in Lake Basin. H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ \(
eq\) 0. α = 0.05.
PLAN: Two-sample t-test. Random ✓, 10% ✓, Normal/Large Sample (36 ≥ 30, 40 ≥ 30) ✓.
CONCLUDE: p = 0.0016 < 0.05 = α. Reject H₀. There is convincing evidence of a difference in mean dissolved oxygen levels between the two lakes.

problems.question_html:
A company tests whether employees who use standing desks have different mean productivity scores than those who use traditional desks. Employees are randomly assigned to desk type for one month.

Standing DeskTraditional Desk
\( n \)2832
\( \bar{x} \)87.383.9
\( s \)7.58.2

(a) Carry out a complete two-sample t-test at \( \alpha = 0.05 \) using the full 4-step process.

(b) Based on your result, would a 95% confidence interval for \( \mu_1 - \mu_2 \) contain 0? Explain without computing the interval.

(c) What type of error (Type I or Type II) could you be making? Explain in context.
problems.correct_answer:
(a) STATE: Let μ₁ = the true mean productivity score for employees using standing desks. Let μ₂ = the true mean productivity score for employees using traditional desks. H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0. Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ \(
eq\) 0. α = 0.05.

PLAN: Two-sample t-test for μ₁ − μ₂. Conditions: Random: Employees were randomly assigned to desk types. ✓ 10%: Not needed for a randomized experiment. ✓ Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 28 and n₂ = 32. n₂ ≥ 30 ✓. n₁ = 28 < 30, but close to 30. Without evidence of strong skewness/outliers, we proceed. ✓ (approximately)

DO: SE = √(7.5²/28 + 8.2²/32) = √(56.25/28 + 67.24/32) = √(2.009 + 2.101) = √4.110 ≈ 2.027. t = (87.3 − 83.9)/2.027 = 3.4/2.027 ≈ 1.677. Conservative df = min(27, 31) = 27. p-value = 2 × P(t > 1.677 | df = 27) ≈ 2 × 0.053 ≈ 0.105.

CONCLUDE: Since the p-value (≈ 0.105) is greater than α = 0.05, we fail to reject H₀. There is not convincing evidence that the mean productivity scores differ between standing desk and traditional desk users.

(b) Yes, a 95% CI for μ₁ − μ₂ would contain 0. Since we failed to reject H₀ at α = 0.05 using a two-sided test, the corresponding 95% CI must contain the hypothesized value of 0.

(c) Since we failed to reject H₀, we could be making a Type II error: failing to detect a real difference in mean productivity scores when one actually exists. In context, this would mean that standing desks do improve (or decrease) mean productivity, but our study did not have enough evidence to detect it.

hints.text: For part (b), remember the connection: if a two-sided test at α fails to reject, the corresponding (1 − α) CI contains the null value. For part (c), identify which type of error is possible based on your decision.
SE ≈ 2.027, t ≈ 1.677, df = 27, p ≈ 0.105 > 0.05 → fail to reject. The 95% CI would contain 0. Since we didn't reject, a Type II error is possible (missing a real difference).

solution_steps.text:
(a) STATE: μ₁ = true mean productivity for standing desks, μ₂ for traditional. H₀: μ₁ − μ₂ = 0, Hₐ: μ₁ − μ₂ \(
eq\) 0, α = 0.05.
PLAN: Two-sample t-test. Random assignment ✓, Normal/Large Sample: n₁ = 28 (close to 30), n₂ = 32 ≥ 30 ✓.
CONCLUDE: 0.105 > 0.05, fail to reject H₀. No convincing evidence of a difference.
(b) Yes, the 95% CI contains 0 because we failed to reject at α = 0.05 (two-sided test ↔ CI correspondence).
(c) Type II error is possible: we may have failed to detect a real difference. Standing desks might truly affect productivity, but the study lacked power to detect it.

topics.name: Unit 5: Regression Analysis
topics.description: Explore relationships between two quantitative variables. Construct and interpret scatterplots, calculate correlation, build least-squares regression models, analyze residuals, and understand the effects of influential points.

concepts.title: Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables
concepts.content_html:
Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables

When we want to explore the relationship between two quantitative variables, we use a scatterplot. Scatterplots display ordered pairs \((x, y)\) as points in a coordinate plane, revealing patterns between two measured quantities.

Explanatory and Response Variables

The explanatory variable (independent variable) is placed on the \(x\)-axis. It is the variable we suspect may help explain or predict changes in the other variable.

The response variable (dependent variable) is placed on the \(y\)-axis. It is the outcome we are interested in measuring or predicting.

For example, if we study how hours of study affect exam scores, then hours studied is the explanatory variable (\(x\)) and exam score is the response variable (\(y\)).

Describing Association in Scatterplots

When describing a scatterplot, you must address four features — remember DOFS:

  • Direction: Is the association positive (both variables increase together) or negative (as one increases, the other decreases)?
  • Outliers / Unusual Features: Are there any points that fall far from the general pattern? Are there distinct clusters or gaps?
  • Form: Is the overall pattern linear (roughly a straight line) or nonlinear (curved)?
  • Strength: How tightly do the points follow the form? Strong means points cluster closely around the pattern; weak means points are widely scattered.

Worked Example

A researcher collects data on the age (years) and price (dollars) of 15 used cars of the same model:

The scatterplot shows a negative, roughly linear, strong association between age and price. As the age of the car increases, the price tends to decrease. There are no obvious outliers or clusters.

Key Idea: Always describe the association in context. Don't just say "negative linear" — say "As car age increases, price tends to decrease in an approximately linear pattern."
AP Exam Tip: On the AP exam, you must mention direction, form, and strength to receive full credit when describing a scatterplot. Forgetting any one of these costs points. Always include context (reference the actual variables by name).
concepts.content_raw: Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables

problem_sets.title: Practice: Graphical Representations Between Two Quantitative Variables

problems.question_html: A biologist measures the height (cm) and wingspan (cm) of 30 birds of the same species and creates a scatterplot. The points rise from left to right and cluster tightly around a straight line. Which of the following best describes the association?

choices.text: Strong, positive, linear association
Weak, positive, linear association
Strong, negative, linear association
Strong, positive, nonlinear association

hints.text: "Rise from left to right" tells you the direction. "Cluster tightly" tells you the strength. "Around a straight line" tells you the form.
Rising left to right = positive direction. Tight clustering = strong. Straight line = linear form. The answer is strong, positive, linear.

solution_steps.text: The points rise from left to right, indicating a positive association (as height increases, wingspan tends to increase).
The points cluster tightly around a straight line, so the association is strong and linear. The best description is: strong, positive, linear association.

diagram.alt_text: Scatterplot with points rising tightly from left to right showing strong positive linear association between height and wingspan
diagram.caption: Scatterplot of bird height vs wingspan showing strong positive linear association

problems.question_html: A teacher records the number of absences and final exam scores for 25 students. She plots absences on the \(x\)-axis and exam score on the \(y\)-axis. In this study, which variable is the explanatory variable and which is the response variable?

choices.text: Explanatory: exam score; Response: number of absences
Explanatory: number of absences; Response: exam score
Both are response variables since neither causes the other
It is impossible to determine without seeing the scatterplot

hints.text: The explanatory variable is the one we think might help predict or explain changes in the other variable. Which one could plausibly affect the other?
We suspect that missing class (absences) might affect exam performance, so absences is the explanatory variable (\(x\)) and exam score is the response variable (\(y\)).

solution_steps.text: We ask: which variable might help explain changes in the other? It is reasonable to think that the number of absences could affect exam scores.
Therefore, number of absences is the explanatory variable (placed on the \(x\)-axis) and exam score is the response variable (placed on the \(y\)-axis).

problems.question_html: A scatterplot of car weight (pounds) versus fuel efficiency (miles per gallon) for 40 vehicles shows a clear downward trend that follows a straight-line pattern with a few points clustered tightly and one point far above the rest. Which of the following best describes this scatterplot?

choices.text: Negative, linear, strong association with no unusual features
Positive, linear, strong association with an outlier
Negative, linear, moderate-to-strong association with an outlier
Negative, nonlinear, weak association with an outlier

hints.text: A "downward trend" tells you the direction. A "straight-line pattern" tells you the form. One point far from the rest is an unusual feature.
Downward = negative. Straight-line = linear. The point far above the rest is an outlier. Most points cluster tightly, so strength is moderate-to-strong.

solution_steps.text: The downward trend indicates a negative association. The straight-line pattern means the form is linear.

Most points cluster tightly, suggesting moderate-to-strong strength, but the point far above the rest is an outlier. The description is: negative, linear, moderate-to-strong association with an outlier.

diagram.alt_text: Scatterplot showing downward trend from left to right with one point far above the rest, representing a car with unusually high fuel efficiency
diagram.caption: Scatterplot of car weight vs fuel efficiency showing negative linear trend with one outlier above

problems.question_html: A researcher measures the distance (miles) from the city center and the median home price (thousands of dollars) for 20 neighborhoods. The scatterplot shows points that follow a curved pattern — prices drop steeply at first, then level off. Which description of the form is most appropriate?

choices.text: Linear
No association
Nonlinear (curved)
Positive and linear

hints.text: If points follow a curved pattern rather than a straight line, the form is not linear.
A pattern that drops steeply then levels off is curved. The form is nonlinear.

solution_steps.text: The scatterplot shows prices dropping steeply at first and then leveling off. This curved pattern does not follow a straight line.
Since the overall shape is curved, the form is nonlinear. A linear model would not be appropriate for this relationship.

problems.question_html:
A scatterplot of daily high temperature (°F) versus number of ice cream cones sold at a shop shows a pattern that rises from left to right with points loosely scattered around a general upward trend. Describe the direction and strength of the association.

The association is __________ and __________.
problems.correct_answer: positive and weak||positive, weak||positive and moderate||positive, moderate

hints.text: "Rises from left to right" tells you the direction. "Loosely scattered" tells you about the strength.
Rising from left to right means positive direction. Loosely scattered means weak (or moderate) strength. The association is positive and weak.

solution_steps.text: The scatterplot rises from left to right, which indicates a positive association — as temperature increases, ice cream sales tend to increase.
The points are loosely scattered, indicating the strength is weak (or moderate at best). The association is positive and weak.

problems.question_html: In a scatterplot, the variable placed on the \(x\)-axis is called the __________ variable.
problems.correct_answer: explanatory||independent||predictor

hints.text: This is the variable we think might help explain or predict changes in the other variable.
The variable on the \(x\)-axis is the explanatory variable (also called the independent or predictor variable).

solution_steps.text: In a scatterplot, the horizontal axis (\(x\)-axis) displays the explanatory variable.
The explanatory variable (also called the independent or predictor variable) is the one we believe may help explain or predict the response variable on the \(y\)-axis.

problems.question_html: A scatterplot of study time (hours) versus test score (%) for 30 students shows a pattern where the points generally rise from left to right but are spread out. One student studied 8 hours but scored only 55%. This student's point would be considered a(n) __________.
problems.correct_answer: outlier||unusual point||unusual observation

hints.text: A point that falls far from the overall pattern in a scatterplot has a special name in statistics.
A point that deviates substantially from the general trend is called an outlier (or an unusual point).

solution_steps.text: The general trend is positive — more study time is associated with higher scores. A student who studied 8 hours but scored only 55% falls well below the expected pattern.
A point that is far from the overall pattern in a scatterplot is called an outlier.

problems.question_html: When describing the association in a scatterplot on the AP exam, the three characteristics you must address are direction, __________, and strength.
problems.correct_answer: form||shape

hints.text: Direction tells you positive/negative. Strength tells you how tightly clustered. The third characteristic describes whether the pattern is linear or curved.
The three key characteristics are direction, form (linear vs. nonlinear), and strength.

solution_steps.text: When describing a scatterplot, you must address direction (positive or negative), form (linear or nonlinear), and strength (strong, moderate, or weak).
The missing characteristic is form — whether the overall pattern follows a straight line or a curve.

problems.question_html:
A nutritionist collects data on daily caloric intake (\(x\)) and body mass index (BMI, \(y\)) for 50 adults. The scatterplot shows a moderate, positive, linear association with two clusters: one group around 1800–2200 calories with BMIs of 20–25, and another group around 2800–3500 calories with BMIs of 28–35.

(a) Identify the explanatory and response variables in context.

(b) Describe the overall association using direction, form, strength, and any unusual features — all in context.

(c) Explain why the clustering might occur and whether it affects the appropriateness of a linear model.
problems.correct_answer: (a) The explanatory variable is daily caloric intake and the response variable is BMI. (b) There is a moderate, positive, linear association between daily caloric intake and BMI. As caloric intake increases, BMI tends to increase. There are two distinct clusters of data. (c) The clusters might represent different subpopulations (e.g., active vs. sedentary individuals). While the overall trend is linear, the clustering suggests there may be a lurking variable influencing the relationship, and a single linear model may not be the best fit.

hints.text: For part (a), think about which variable might help predict the other. For part (b), remember to address direction, form, strength, and unusual features — all in context.
For part (c), clusters often indicate subgroups within the data. Think about what characteristic might divide these adults into two groups and how that affects modeling.

solution_steps.text: (a) The explanatory variable is daily caloric intake (measured in calories) because we suspect it may influence BMI. The response variable is BMI because it is the outcome we are trying to understand.

(b) The scatterplot shows a moderate, positive, linear association between daily caloric intake and BMI. As caloric intake increases, BMI tends to increase. There are two distinct clusters: one group with lower caloric intake and healthy BMI, and another with higher caloric intake and higher BMI.

(c) The clustering likely reflects a lurking variable such as activity level or diet quality that divides the sample into subpopulations. While the overall trend is roughly linear, a single linear model may oversimplify the relationship. Fitting separate models for each cluster or including additional variables could be more appropriate.

diagram.alt_text: Scatterplot showing two clusters of points: one around 1800-2200 calories with BMI 20-25, another around 2800-3500 calories with BMI 28-35
diagram.caption: Scatterplot of daily caloric intake vs BMI showing moderate positive association with two clusters

problems.question_html:
A city planner collects data on the distance from downtown (miles, \(x\)) and average commute time (minutes, \(y\)) for residents at 35 locations. The scatterplot shows a positive, roughly linear association. However, two points — one very close to downtown with an unusually long commute and one very far from downtown with a short commute — stand out.

(a) Describe the overall association in context, addressing direction, form, and strength.

(b) For each of the two unusual points, explain why it might deviate from the pattern. Provide a plausible real-world explanation for each.

(c) If the two unusual points were removed, would you expect the strength of the association to increase, decrease, or stay the same? Justify your answer.
problems.correct_answer: (a) There is a positive, roughly linear, moderate association between distance from downtown and commute time. As distance increases, commute time tends to increase. (b) The point close to downtown with a long commute might represent a resident who commutes against typical traffic patterns or uses public transit with many transfers. The far point with a short commute might represent someone who works from home or lives near a highway with fast access. (c) Removing these outliers would likely increase the strength of the association because the remaining points would more tightly follow the positive linear trend.

hints.text: For part (a), describe the trend for the majority of points. For part (b), think about real-world reasons why someone's commute might not follow the typical distance-time pattern.
For part (c), consider what happens to the scatter of points when outliers that deviate from the trend are removed. Do the remaining points follow the pattern more closely?

solution_steps.text: (a) The overall association between distance from downtown and commute time is positive, roughly linear, and moderate in strength. As distance from downtown increases, average commute time tends to increase.

(b) The point near downtown with a long commute could represent a resident who uses slow public transit, has a job in a different direction, or deals with unusual local congestion. The point far from downtown with a short commute could represent someone who works remotely, has a reverse commute, or lives near a highway interchange.

(c) Removing both outliers would likely increase the strength of the association. These two points deviate from the overall positive linear pattern, adding variability. Without them, the remaining points would cluster more tightly around the linear trend, resulting in a stronger association.

diagram.alt_text: Scatterplot showing positive linear trend with two outlier points: one close to downtown with long commute, one far from downtown with short commute
diagram.caption: Scatterplot of distance from downtown vs commute time with two unusual points

diagrams.alt_text: Scatter plot with points trending upward from left to right. A regression line is drawn through the data with r equals 0.87 displayed
diagrams.caption: Scatter plot of study hours vs exam score showing a strong positive linear relationship with least-squares regression line and r = 0.87

concepts.title: Correlation
concepts.content_html:
Correlation

The correlation coefficient, denoted \( r \), is a numerical measure of the strength and direction of the linear association between two quantitative variables.

Properties of \( r \)

  • Range: \( -1 \le r \le 1 \)
  • \( r = 1 \): perfect positive linear association
  • \( r = -1 \): perfect negative linear association
  • \( r = 0 \): no linear association (but there could still be a nonlinear relationship!)
  • Unitless: \( r \) has no units — it does not depend on the units of \( x \) or \( y \).
  • Symmetric: The correlation between \( x \) and \( y \) equals the correlation between \( y \) and \( x \).
  • Sensitive to outliers: A single extreme point can dramatically increase or decrease \( r \).

Interpreting \( r \)

\(|r|\)Strength
0.8 to 1.0Strong
0.5 to 0.8Moderate
0.0 to 0.5Weak

The Coefficient of Determination: \( r^2 \)

\( r^2 \) tells us the proportion of the variability in the response variable \( y \) that is explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable \( x \).

For example, if \( r = 0.9 \), then \( r^2 = 0.81 \), meaning 81% of the variability in \( y \) is explained by the linear relationship with \( x \).

Correlation vs. Causation

A strong correlation does not mean that changes in \( x \) cause changes in \( y \). Correlation only measures association. Confounding variables, lurking variables, or coincidence could explain the relationship.

Key Idea: \( r \) only measures the strength and direction of linear relationships. A dataset with a strong curved pattern could have \( r \approx 0 \). Always look at the scatterplot before relying on \( r \).
AP Exam Tip: When interpreting \( r^2 \), you must say it in context: "\( r^2 \)% of the variability in [response variable in context] is explained by the linear relationship with [explanatory variable in context]." Using generic language ("y" and "x") will lose credit.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Correlation

problems.question_html: The correlation between the number of hours spent studying and exam score for a class of 30 students is \( r = 0.85 \). Which of the following is a correct interpretation?

choices.text: 85% of the variability in exam scores is explained by study time.
There is a strong, positive, linear association between study time and exam scores.
Studying more hours causes higher exam scores.
For each additional hour of study, exam scores increase by 0.85 points.

hints.text: Remember that \( r \) measures the strength and direction of a linear association — it does not indicate causation, and 0.85 is not the same as \( r^2 \).

\( r = 0.85 \) is close to 1, so the linear association is strong and positive. It does not mean 85% of variability is explained (that would be \( r^2 = 0.7225 \)), and correlation never proves causation.

solution_steps.text: \( r = 0.85 \) is positive and close to 1. This indicates a strong, positive, linear association between study time and exam scores.
Choice A confuses \( r \) with \( r^2 \). Choice C claims causation, which correlation cannot establish. Choice D treats \( r \) as a slope. The correct answer is B.

problems.question_html: A researcher finds \( r = -0.42 \) for the relationship between age of a used car (years) and its resale value (dollars). If the researcher converts the car prices from dollars to euros, what happens to \( r \)?

choices.text: \( r \) changes to a positive value because euros are smaller units.
\( r \) becomes closer to \(-1\) because the values are smaller.
\( r \) stays the same at \(-0.42\).
\( r \) cannot be determined without knowing the exchange rate.

hints.text: Recall that \( r \) is unitless. Think about what happens when you apply a linear transformation (multiplying by a constant) to one of the variables.
Correlation is not affected by changes of units. Converting dollars to euros multiplies each price by a positive constant, which does not change \( r \).

solution_steps.text: The correlation coefficient \( r \) is unitless. It is not affected by linear transformations of the variables such as changing units.
Converting from dollars to euros multiplies each price by a positive constant (the exchange rate). This does not change the relative positions of the data points, so \( r \) remains \(-0.42\).

problems.question_html: A data set of 50 homes shows a correlation of \( r = 0.92 \) between house size (square feet) and sale price (dollars). One luxury mansion of 8,000 sq ft sold for a surprisingly low price due to needed repairs. If this data point is removed, what is the most likely effect on \( r \)?

choices.text: \( r \) would decrease because the sample size is smaller.
\( r \) would increase because the outlier was weakening the linear pattern.
\( r \) would stay the same because one point cannot change the correlation.
\( r \) would become negative because the mansion had a low price.

hints.text: The mansion sold for a surprisingly low price relative to its size. This point deviates from the positive trend. How does removing a point that weakens a pattern affect \( r \)?
An outlier that falls away from the linear trend makes \( r \) weaker (closer to 0). Removing it allows the remaining points to better reflect the strong positive trend, so \( r \) increases.

solution_steps.text: The mansion with 8,000 sq ft and a surprisingly low price falls below the positive linear trend of the rest of the data, weakening the correlation.
Removing this outlier removes the point that was pulling \( r \) away from the strong positive pattern. The remaining points follow the linear trend more tightly, so \( r \) would increase.

problems.question_html: A study finds \( r = 0.95 \) between per-capita ice cream consumption and drowning rates across U.S. cities during summer months. A newspaper reports: "Eating ice cream increases your risk of drowning." Which of the following best explains why this conclusion is flawed?

choices.text: The sample size was too small to draw conclusions.
The correlation is not statistically significant.
Correlation does not imply causation; a lurking variable (hot weather) likely explains both.
The correlation should be negative if ice cream causes drowning.

hints.text: Think about whether a third variable could be driving both ice cream consumption and drowning rates.
Hot weather is a lurking variable: it increases both ice cream consumption and swimming (and thus drowning risk). Correlation does not prove causation.

solution_steps.text: The newspaper is claiming causation based only on correlation. A strong \( r \) does not mean one variable causes the other.

Hot weather is a lurking (confounding) variable that plausibly increases both ice cream consumption and drowning rates. The conclusion that ice cream causes drowning is flawed because correlation does not imply causation.

problems.question_html: If the correlation between two variables is \( r = 0.7 \), then \( r^2 = \) __________. (Express as a decimal.)

hints.text: To find \( r^2 \), simply square the value of \( r \).
\( r^2 = (0.7)^2 = 0.49 \). This means 49% of the variability in the response variable is explained by the linear relationship.

solution_steps.text: The coefficient of determination is found by squaring the correlation coefficient: \( r^2 = (0.7)^2 = 0.49 \).
This means 49% of the variability in the response variable is explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable.

problems.question_html: The correlation coefficient \( r \) can only take values in the range from __________ to __________.

hints.text: Think about the most extreme possible values for \( r \) — one for perfect negative association and one for perfect positive association.
\( r \) ranges from \(-1\) (perfect negative linear association) to \( 1 \) (perfect positive linear association).

solution_steps.text: By definition, the correlation coefficient \( r \) is bounded: \(-1 \le r \le 1\).
\( r = -1 \) means a perfect negative linear relationship, and \( r = 1 \) means a perfect positive linear relationship.

problems.question_html: A correlation of \( r = 0.60 \) is found between hours of exercise per week and resting heart rate. The value of \( r^2 \) is __________%, meaning this percentage of the variability in resting heart rate is explained by the linear relationship with weekly exercise hours. (Round to the nearest whole number.)

hints.text: First square \( r \), then convert to a percentage.
\( r^2 = (0.60)^2 = 0.36 = 36\% \). So 36% of the variability in resting heart rate is explained by the linear relationship with exercise hours.

solution_steps.text: \( r^2 = (0.60)^2 = 0.36 \), which as a percentage is 36%.
Interpretation: 36% of the variability in resting heart rate is explained by the linear relationship with hours of exercise per week.

problems.question_html: The correlation between the \( x \) and \( y \) variables is \( r = 0.75 \). If we swap the variables and compute the correlation between \( y \) and \( x \), the new correlation is __________.

hints.text: One of the key properties of \( r \) is that it is symmetric. What does that mean?
Correlation is symmetric: the correlation between \( x \) and \( y \) is the same as the correlation between \( y \) and \( x \). So the answer is 0.75.

solution_steps.text: Correlation is symmetric: \( r_{xy} = r_{yx} \). Swapping which variable is \( x \) and which is \( y \) does not change \( r \).
Therefore, the correlation between \( y \) and \( x \) is also 0.75.

problems.question_html:
A college admissions office collects data on applicants' SAT scores (\( x \)) and first-year college GPA (\( y \)) for 200 students. They find \( r = 0.68 \).

(a) Interpret the value of \( r \) in context.

(b) Calculate and interpret \( r^2 \) in context.

(c) A parent says, "This proves that getting a high SAT score causes a higher GPA in college." Explain why this conclusion is not supported by the correlation alone.
problems.correct_answer: (a) There is a moderate, positive, linear association between SAT scores and first-year college GPA. Students with higher SAT scores tend to have higher first-year GPAs. (b) r² = 0.68² = 0.4624 ≈ 0.462. About 46.2% of the variability in first-year college GPA is explained by the linear relationship with SAT score. (c) Correlation does not imply causation. There may be lurking variables such as study habits, motivation, socioeconomic background, or quality of high school preparation that influence both SAT scores and college GPA.

hints.text: For part (a), describe \( r \) using strength, direction, and form — all in context. For part (b), square \( r \) and use the standard \( r^2 \) interpretation template.
For part (c), think about other factors that could affect both SAT scores and GPA. Correlation from an observational study cannot prove causation.

solution_steps.text: (a) The correlation \( r = 0.68 \) indicates a moderate, positive, linear association between SAT scores and first-year college GPA. Students with higher SAT scores tend to earn higher GPAs in their first year.
(b) \( r^2 = (0.68)^2 = 0.4624 \). About 46.2% of the variability in first-year college GPA is explained by the linear relationship with SAT score. The remaining 53.8% is due to other factors.

(c) Correlation does not imply causation. This is an observational study, and lurking variables — such as study habits, intellectual curiosity, socioeconomic status, or quality of high school instruction — could influence both SAT scores and college GPA. A strong correlation alone cannot establish a causal relationship.

problems.question_html:
A teacher plots quiz scores versus homework completion percentage for her class and finds \( r = 0.03 \). However, when she looks at the scatterplot, she notices a clear U-shaped pattern.

(a) Explain why \( r \approx 0 \) even though there appears to be a relationship between the variables.

(b) Would it be appropriate to say there is "no association" between homework completion and quiz scores? Justify your answer.

(c) Suggest a more appropriate method for describing the association than reporting \( r \).
problems.correct_answer: (a) The correlation coefficient r only measures the strength of LINEAR association. A U-shaped (nonlinear) pattern can produce r ≈ 0 because the positive and negative trends cancel each other out. (b) No. There is an association — it is just not linear. Saying 'no association' would be incorrect. There is a nonlinear association. (c) The teacher should describe the form of the pattern (U-shaped/quadratic) based on the scatterplot rather than relying on r. She could also consider fitting a quadratic model or reporting separate correlations for different parts of the data.

hints.text: Remember that \( r \) only measures linear association. What happens to \( r \) when the relationship is curved?
A U-shaped pattern has both positive and negative slopes at different parts, which cancel out and make \( r \approx 0 \). But there is clearly still a relationship — just not a linear one.

solution_steps.text: (a) \( r \) only measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship. In a U-shaped pattern, one part of the data has a negative trend and another part has a positive trend. These opposing trends cancel out, producing \( r \approx 0 \) even though a clear relationship exists.

(b) It would be incorrect to say there is "no association." \( r \approx 0 \) means no linear association, but the U-shaped pattern in the scatterplot reveals a nonlinear association between the variables.

(c) Instead of reporting \( r \), the teacher should describe the scatterplot visually: the relationship is U-shaped (quadratic). She could fit a quadratic regression model, or she could describe the association qualitatively, noting the direction of change across different ranges of homework completion.

concepts.title: Linear Regression Models
concepts.content_html:
Linear Regression Models

When a scatterplot shows a roughly linear pattern, we can model the relationship with a least-squares regression line (LSRL):

\[ \hat{y} = a + bx \]

Here, \( \hat{y} \) ("y-hat") is the predicted value of the response variable, \( b \) is the slope, and \( a \) is the y-intercept. Some textbooks write this as \( \hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x \).

The Slope \( b \)

The slope is calculated as:

\[ b = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x} \]

where \( r \) is the correlation coefficient, \( s_y \) is the standard deviation of the \( y \)-values, and \( s_x \) is the standard deviation of the \( x \)-values.

Interpretation: "For each additional [unit] increase in [\( x \) in context], the predicted [\( y \) in context] changes by \( b \) [units of \( y \)]."

The Y-Intercept \( a \)

The y-intercept is calculated using the fact that the LSRL always passes through \( (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) \):

\[ a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} \]

Interpretation: "When [\( x \) in context] is 0, the predicted [\( y \) in context] is \( a \) [units]." Note: this interpretation is only meaningful if \( x = 0 \) is within or near the range of the data.

Prediction vs. Extrapolation

Prediction uses the regression equation to estimate \( \hat{y} \) for an \( x \)-value within the range of the data. This is appropriate.

Extrapolation uses the regression equation to estimate \( \hat{y} \) for an \( x \)-value outside the range of the data. This is risky because the linear pattern may not continue beyond the observed data.

Key Idea: The LSRL always passes through the point \( (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) \) — the mean of the \( x \)-values and the mean of the \( y \)-values. This is a guaranteed fact you can use on the AP exam.
AP Exam Tip: When interpreting the slope, never say "for every increase" — always say "for each additional one-unit increase in [\( x \) in context], the predicted [\( y \) in context] increases/decreases by \( |b| \) [units]." The word "predicted" is essential for full credit.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Linear Regression Models

problems.question_html: A regression equation for predicting a student's exam score (\( y \)) from the number of hours studied (\( x \)) is \( \hat{y} = 52 + 4.5x \). Which of the following correctly interprets the slope?

choices.text: For each additional hour studied, the exam score increases by exactly 4.5 points.
For each additional hour studied, the predicted exam score increases by 4.5 points.
For each additional 4.5 points on the exam, a student studies one more hour.
A student who does not study will score exactly 52 on the exam.

hints.text: The slope tells you the change in the predicted \( y \) for each one-unit increase in \( x \). Pay attention to the word "predicted."
The slope \( b = 4.5 \) means: for each additional hour studied, the predicted exam score increases by 4.5 points. We say "predicted" because the LSRL gives estimates, not exact values.

solution_steps.text: The slope in \( \hat{y} = 52 + 4.5x \) is 4.5. This represents the change in the predicted response for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable.
Correct interpretation: For each additional hour studied, the predicted exam score increases by 4.5 points. Choice A omits "predicted," which is essential.

problems.question_html: A regression model for predicting the price (in thousands of dollars) of a used car based on its age (years) is \( \hat{y} = 28.5 - 2.3x \). The data used to build the model included cars aged 1 to 10 years. A buyer uses this equation to predict the price of a 15-year-old car. What concern should the buyer have?

choices.text: The prediction is too high because older cars are worth more.
The prediction involves extrapolation, which is unreliable because the model may not hold outside the data range.
The prediction is invalid because the slope is negative.
The prediction is fine because the regression equation can be used for any value of \( x \).

hints.text: The model was built using cars aged 1 to 10 years. A 15-year-old car falls outside this range. What is this called?
Using a regression equation to predict outside the range of the data is called extrapolation. The linear trend may not continue, making the prediction unreliable.

solution_steps.text: The data range is 1 to 10 years. A 15-year-old car is outside this range, so using the model is extrapolation.

Extrapolation is dangerous because the linear relationship may not hold beyond the observed data. The model might predict a negative price for very old cars, which is impossible. The concern is that the prediction is unreliable.

problems.question_html: Data on 40 houses shows a regression equation \( \hat{y} = 15.2 + 0.085x \), where \( x \) is house size in square feet and \( y \) is monthly electric bill in dollars. The houses ranged from 800 to 3,500 square feet. Which of the following is the best interpretation of the y-intercept?

choices.text: A house with 0 square feet would have a predicted electric bill of $15.20, but this interpretation is not meaningful.
For each additional square foot, the electric bill increases by $15.20.
The minimum electric bill in the data set is $15.20.
A house of average size has an electric bill of $15.20.

hints.text: The y-intercept is the predicted value of \( y \) when \( x = 0 \). Does \( x = 0 \) make sense in this context?
A house with 0 square feet does not exist, and 0 is far below the data range (800–3500). The y-intercept is technically $15.20, but this interpretation has no practical meaning.

solution_steps.text: The y-intercept \( a = 15.2 \) is the predicted electric bill when house size is 0 square feet.

Since a house with 0 square feet does not exist and is far outside the data range (800 to 3,500 sq ft), this interpretation is not meaningful in context. The y-intercept simply serves to anchor the regression line.

problems.question_html: A regression model predicts travel time \( \hat{y} \) (minutes) based on distance \( x \) (miles) for commuters: \( \hat{y} = 5.2 + 1.4x \). A commuter lives 20 miles from work and their actual commute takes 38 minutes. What is the residual for this commuter?

choices.text: \( 33.2 \) minutes
\( -4.8 \) minutes
\( 4.8 \) minutes
\( 38 \) minutes

hints.text: First find the predicted value by plugging \( x = 20 \) into the equation. Then use residual = observed - predicted.

solution_steps.text: Find the predicted value: \( \hat{y} = 5.2 + 1.4(20) = 5.2 + 28 = 33.2 \) minutes.
Residual = observed - predicted = \( 38 - 33.2 = 4.8 \) minutes. The positive residual means the actual commute was 4.8 minutes longer than predicted.

problems.question_html: Given that \( r = 0.8 \), \( s_y = 10 \), and \( s_x = 4 \), the slope of the LSRL is \( b = \) __________.

hints.text: Use the formula \( b = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x} \).

solution_steps.text: Apply the slope formula: \( b = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x} = 0.8 \cdot \frac{10}{4} \).
\( b = 0.8 \cdot 2.5 = 2 \). The slope of the LSRL is 2.

problems.question_html: The least-squares regression line always passes through the point \( (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) \). If \( \bar{x} = 5 \) and \( \bar{y} = 20 \), and the slope is \( b = 3 \), then the y-intercept \( a = \) __________.

hints.text: Use the formula \( a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} \).

solution_steps.text: Since the LSRL passes through \( (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) \), we use: \( a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} \).
\( a = 20 - 3(5) = 20 - 15 = 5 \). The y-intercept is 5.

problems.question_html: A regression equation predicts that \( \hat{y} = 120 - 8.5x \), where \( x \) is the age of a laptop (years) and \( y \) is its resale value (dollars). The slope \( b = -8.5 \) means that for each additional year of age, the predicted resale value __________ by $__________.
problems.correct_answer: decreases by $8.50||decreases by 8.5||decreases by $8.5

hints.text: A negative slope means the predicted \( y \) decreases as \( x \) increases. By how much does it decrease for each one-unit increase in \( x \)?
The slope of \(-8.5\) means: for each additional year of age, the predicted resale value decreases by $8.50.

solution_steps.text: The slope \( b = -8.5 \) tells us the change in predicted \( y \) for each one-unit increase in \( x \).
Since the slope is negative, the predicted resale value decreases by $8.50 for each additional year of laptop age.

problems.question_html: If \( \bar{x} = 12 \), \( \bar{y} = 50 \), and the slope of the LSRL is \( b = 2.5 \), then the equation of the LSRL is \( \hat{y} = \) __________ \( + \) __________ \( x \).

hints.text: First find the y-intercept using \( a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} \), then write the full equation.

solution_steps.text: Find the y-intercept: \( a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} = 50 - 2.5(12) = 50 - 30 = 20 \).
The equation of the LSRL is \( \hat{y} = 20 + 2.5x \).

problems.question_html:
A fitness researcher collects data on 25 adults, recording their weekly running distance (\( x \), in miles) and resting heart rate (\( y \), in beats per minute). Summary statistics:

  • \( \bar{x} = 15 \) miles, \( s_x = 6 \) miles
  • \( \bar{y} = 68 \) bpm, \( s_y = 8 \) bpm
  • \( r = -0.75 \)

(a) Calculate the slope \( b \) and y-intercept \( a \) of the LSRL.

(b) Write the equation of the LSRL and interpret the slope in context.

(c) A new participant runs 25 miles per week. Use the equation to predict their resting heart rate. Is this prediction reliable? Explain.
problems.correct_answer: (a) b = r(s_y/s_x) = -0.75(8/6) = -1. a = ȳ - bx̄ = 68 - (-1)(15) = 83. (b) ŷ = 83 - x. For each additional mile of weekly running distance, the predicted resting heart rate decreases by 1 bpm. (c) ŷ = 83 - 25 = 58 bpm. This may involve some extrapolation if 25 miles is outside the range of the data (the mean is 15 with SD 6, so 25 is about 1.67 SDs above the mean). The prediction should be used with caution.

hints.text: For part (a), use \( b = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x} \) and \( a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} \). For part (b), plug in the values and interpret the slope in context using the word "predicted."
For part (c), plug \( x = 25 \) into your equation. Then consider: is 25 miles within the range of the data? The mean is 15 and \( s_x = 6 \), so think about what values were likely in the data set.

solution_steps.text: (a) Slope: \( b = r \cdot \frac{s_y}{s_x} = -0.75 \cdot \frac{8}{6} = -0.75 \cdot 1.\overline{3} = -1 \). Y-intercept: \( a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} = 68 - (-1)(15) = 68 + 15 = 83 \).
(b) The LSRL is \( \hat{y} = 83 - x \). Interpretation of slope: For each additional mile of weekly running distance, the predicted resting heart rate decreases by 1 beat per minute.

(c) \( \hat{y} = 83 - 25 = 58 \) bpm. This prediction may be unreliable if 25 miles is outside the range of the original data. With \( \bar{x} = 15 \) and \( s_x = 6 \), the data likely ranges from roughly 3 to 27 miles, so 25 is near the upper edge. While not extreme extrapolation, caution is warranted.

problems.question_html:
The table shows the age (years) and value (thousands of dollars) for 6 used cars of the same model:

Age (\(x\))123578
Value (\(y\))24211914107

The LSRL for this data is \( \hat{y} = 26.0 - 2.35x \).

(a) Interpret the slope and y-intercept of this equation in context. Comment on whether the y-intercept interpretation is meaningful.

(b) Use the equation to predict the value of a 4-year-old car. Is this interpolation or extrapolation?

(c) A dealer uses this equation to predict the value of a 12-year-old car. Calculate the prediction and explain why it may be problematic.
problems.correct_answer: (a) Slope: For each additional year of age, the predicted value of the car decreases by $2,350. Y-intercept: When the car is brand new (age 0), the predicted value is $26,000. This is reasonably meaningful since new cars do have value, though age 0 is just outside the data range (1–8). (b) ŷ = 26.0 - 2.35(4) = 26.0 - 9.4 = 16.6 thousand dollars. This is interpolation because 4 is within the data range of 1 to 8 years. (c) ŷ = 26.0 - 2.35(12) = 26.0 - 28.2 = -2.2 thousand dollars. The model predicts a negative value, which is impossible. This is extrapolation (12 is outside the range 1–8), demonstrating why predicting beyond the data range is unreliable.

hints.text: For part (a), interpret slope as change in predicted \( y \) per unit increase in \( x \). For the y-intercept, does \( x = 0 \) (a brand-new car) make sense? For parts (b) and (c), plug in values and check whether each is within or outside the data range.
For part (c), \( x = 12 \) is well outside the data range of 1 to 8. Plug it in and see what happens — the result demonstrates why extrapolation is dangerous.

solution_steps.text: (a) Slope: For each additional year of age, the predicted value of the car decreases by $2,350 (or $2.35 thousand). Y-intercept: When the car is brand new (age = 0 years), the predicted value is $26,000. This interpretation is somewhat meaningful — a new car does have a value — though \( x = 0 \) is slightly outside the data range of 1 to 8 years.
(b) \( \hat{y} = 26.0 - 2.35(4) = 26.0 - 9.4 = 16.6 \) thousand dollars ($16,600). Since 4 years is within the data range (1 to 8), this is interpolation and the prediction is appropriate.

(c) \( \hat{y} = 26.0 - 2.35(12) = 26.0 - 28.2 = -2.2 \) thousand dollars. The model predicts a negative value, which is impossible. This is extrapolation because 12 years is well outside the data range of 1 to 8 years. The linear pattern does not hold indefinitely — car values level off rather than become negative.

concepts.title: Residuals
concepts.content_html:
Residuals

A residual measures how far an observed value falls from the value predicted by the regression line:

\[ \text{Residual} = y - \hat{y} = \text{observed} - \text{predicted} \]
  • A positive residual means the actual value is above the regression line (the model underpredicted).
  • A negative residual means the actual value is below the regression line (the model overpredicted).
  • A residual of 0 means the point falls exactly on the line.

Residual Plots

A residual plot graphs the residuals on the vertical axis against the explanatory variable (or predicted values) on the horizontal axis. It helps us evaluate whether a linear model is appropriate.

What to Look for in a Residual Plot

  • Good model: Residuals are randomly scattered around the horizontal line at 0, with no clear pattern. Points are spread roughly equally above and below zero.
  • Curved pattern: Indicates a nonlinear relationship. A linear model is not appropriate — consider a transformation or different model.
  • Fanning (megaphone shape): The spread of residuals increases (or decreases) as \( x \) increases. This indicates non-constant variance (heteroscedasticity).

Important Property

For the least-squares regression line, the sum of the residuals is always 0:

\[ \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i) = 0 \]

This is a mathematical consequence of how the LSRL is calculated.

Key Idea: The residual plot is your primary diagnostic tool. Even if \( r \) is high, a pattern in the residual plot means the linear model is not appropriate. Always check the residual plot!
AP Exam Tip: When asked whether a linear model is appropriate, reference the residual plot — not just \( r \) or \( r^2 \). Say: "The residual plot shows [random scatter / a pattern], so a linear model [is / is not] appropriate." The AP graders want you to use the residual plot as evidence.
