problem_sets.title: Practice: Residuals

problems.question_html: The regression equation for predicting test score (\( y \)) from study hours (\( x \)) is \( \hat{y} = 45 + 6x \). A student who studied 5 hours scored 82. What is the residual for this student?

hints.text: First calculate the predicted score using \( x = 5 \), then find residual = observed - predicted.
\( \hat{y} = 45 + 6(5) = 75 \). Residual = \( 82 - 75 = 7 \). The student scored 7 points higher than predicted.

solution_steps.text: Calculate the predicted value: \( \hat{y} = 45 + 6(5) = 45 + 30 = 75 \).
Residual = observed - predicted = \( 82 - 75 = 7 \). The positive residual means the student scored 7 points above the regression line.

problems.question_html: A residual plot for a linear regression model shows a clear U-shaped (curved) pattern. What does this suggest?

choices.text: The linear model is a good fit for the data.
The relationship between the variables is nonlinear, so a linear model is not appropriate.
There are no outliers in the data.
The correlation coefficient is close to 1.

hints.text: A good residual plot should show random scatter. A U-shaped pattern is not random — what does it indicate about the form of the relationship?
A curved pattern in the residual plot means the linear model systematically overpredicts and underpredicts in different ranges. The relationship is nonlinear.

solution_steps.text: A good linear model produces a residual plot with no pattern — residuals randomly scattered around zero.
A U-shaped curve in the residual plot indicates the relationship between the variables is nonlinear. The linear model is not appropriate, and a curved model should be considered.

diagram.alt_text: Residual plot with points forming a U-shape: negative residuals at low and high x values, positive residuals in the middle
diagram.caption: Residual plot showing a clear U-shaped curved pattern indicating a non-linear relationship

problems.question_html: A scatterplot of temperature (°F) vs. number of hot chocolates sold shows a strong negative linear association, and the regression equation is \( \hat{y} = 120 - 1.5x \). The residual plot shows residuals that fan out — the spread of residuals increases as temperature increases. What does this pattern indicate?

choices.text: The linear model is appropriate because \( r \) is strong.
The variance of the response variable is not constant across all values of the explanatory variable.
There is a positive association between the variables.
The residuals sum to a value greater than zero.

hints.text: A fanning pattern in the residual plot has a special name. It relates to the spread (variance) of residuals across different \( x \)-values.
Fanning (megaphone shape) indicates non-constant variance — the predictions are less accurate for some values of \( x \) than others. This violates an assumption of linear regression.

solution_steps.text: A fanning pattern (residuals spreading out) in the residual plot indicates that the variability of the response variable is not constant across all values of the explanatory variable.

This is called heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance). Even though the overall trend may be linear, the predictions are less reliable at higher temperatures. This suggests the linear model, while capturing the trend, has a violation of constant variance.

diagram.alt_text: Scatterplot showing clear downward trend: as temperature increases, hot chocolate sales decrease
diagram.caption: Scatterplot of temperature vs hot chocolate sales showing strong negative linear relationship

problems.question_html: A regression equation gives \( \hat{y} = 200 - 3x \). For a data point where \( x = 30 \) and \( y = 105 \), the residual tells us that the model __________ (overpredicted/underpredicted) by __________ units.

choices.text: Overpredicted by 5 units
Underpredicted by 5 units
Overpredicted by 95 units
Underpredicted by 110 units

hints.text: First calculate \( \hat{y} \) at \( x = 30 \). Then find the residual (observed - predicted) and determine whether the model predicted too high or too low.
\( \hat{y} = 200 - 3(30) = 110 \). Residual = \( 105 - 110 = -5 \). The negative residual means the model overpredicted by 5 units.

solution_steps.text: Residual = \( 105 - 110 = -5 \). The negative residual means the model predicted 110 but the actual value was only 105 — the model overpredicted by 5 units.

problems.question_html: The residual for a data point is \(-5\). This means the observed value is __________ the predicted value by 5 units.
problems.correct_answer: below||less than||under

hints.text: Residual = observed - predicted. If the residual is negative, what does that tell you about the observed value relative to the predicted value?
A negative residual means observed < predicted. The observed value is below (or less than) the predicted value by 5 units.

solution_steps.text: Residual = observed - predicted = \(-5\). This means observed = predicted \(-5\).
The observed value is 5 units below (less than) the predicted value. The regression line overpredicted for this data point.

problems.question_html: For the least-squares regression line, the sum of all residuals always equals __________.
problems.correct_answer: 0||zero

hints.text: This is a mathematical property of how the LSRL is calculated. The positive and negative residuals balance out.
For the LSRL, \( \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i) = 0 \). The sum of all residuals is always 0.

solution_steps.text: A fundamental property of the least-squares regression line is that the residuals sum to zero: \( \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i) = 0 \).
This occurs because the LSRL passes through \( (\bar{x}, \bar{y}) \), ensuring that overpredictions and underpredictions cancel out exactly.

problems.question_html: If five data points have residuals of \( 3, -2, 5, -4 \), and one unknown residual, the unknown residual must equal __________. (Assume the line is the LSRL.)

hints.text: Use the property that the sum of all residuals for the LSRL equals zero.

solution_steps.text: For the LSRL, the sum of all residuals equals 0. Sum the known residuals: \( 3 + (-2) + 5 + (-4) = 2 \).
Let the unknown residual be \( r \). Then \( 2 + r = 0 \), so \( r = -2 \).

problems.question_html: A residual plot that shows random scatter with no discernible pattern indicates that a __________ model is appropriate for the data.
problems.correct_answer: linear

hints.text: If the residuals show no pattern, it means the model is capturing the relationship well. What type of model produces a residual plot?
Random scatter in a residual plot means the linear model is a good fit — there is no systematic error in the predictions.

solution_steps.text: A residual plot with random scatter around zero and no pattern indicates that the model is appropriate.
Since residual plots are used to assess linear regression models, random scatter confirms that a linear model is appropriate for the data.

problems.question_html:
A researcher fits a linear regression model to predict plant height (cm) from the amount of fertilizer used (grams). The LSRL is \( \hat{y} = 10 + 2.4x \). Data for five plants:

Fertilizer (\(x\))246810
Height (\(y\))1619253033

(a) Calculate the predicted height and the residual for each data point.

(b) Verify that the sum of the residuals equals 0 (or approximately 0).

(c) Based on the pattern of residuals, does a linear model appear appropriate? Explain.
problems.correct_answer: (a) x=2: ŷ=14.8, residual=16-14.8=1.2; x=4: ŷ=19.6, residual=19-19.6=-0.6; x=6: ŷ=24.4, residual=25-24.4=0.6; x=8: ŷ=29.2, residual=30-29.2=0.8; x=10: ŷ=34.0, residual=33-34.0=-1.0. (b) Sum = 1.2+(-0.6)+0.6+0.8+(-1.0) = 1.0 ≈ 0 (small rounding). (c) The residuals alternate in sign without a clear curved pattern. They are relatively small compared to the y-values. A linear model appears appropriate.

hints.text: For part (a), plug each \( x \)-value into \( \hat{y} = 10 + 2.4x \) and subtract from the observed height. For part (b), add up all the residuals.
For part (c), look at the signs and magnitudes of the residuals. Do they show a curved pattern (like +, +, -, -, +) or random scatter?

solution_steps.text: (b) Sum of residuals: \( 1.2 + (-0.6) + 0.6 + 0.8 + (-1.0) = 1.0 \). This is close to 0 (the small discrepancy is due to the LSRL coefficients being rounded).

(c) The residuals show no clear curved pattern — they alternate between positive and negative without systematic trends. The magnitudes are small relative to the observed values. A linear model appears appropriate for these data.

diagram.alt_text: Residual plot with five points: residuals at x=2,4,6,8,10 showing values of 1.2, -0.6, 0.6, -0.2, 1.0
diagram.caption: Residual plot for plant height vs fertilizer regression showing slight positive pattern

problems.question_html:
A student fits a linear model to data on advertising spending (\$ thousands, \( x \)) and monthly revenue (\$ thousands, \( y \)) for 12 months at a small business. The residual plot shows the following pattern: residuals are negative for low and high \( x \)-values but positive for middle \( x \)-values.

(a) Sketch a rough description of what this residual pattern looks like and name the shape.

(b) What does this pattern tell you about the appropriateness of the linear model?

(c) Suggest a more appropriate type of model and explain your reasoning.
problems.correct_answer: (a) The residuals form an inverted-U or arch pattern: negative at the ends and positive in the middle. This is a curved pattern. (b) The curved pattern in the residual plot indicates that the linear model is not appropriate. The model systematically underpredicts revenue at moderate spending levels and overpredicts at low and high spending levels. (c) A quadratic (curved) model would be more appropriate since the residual pattern suggests the relationship between advertising spending and revenue is nonlinear — possibly with diminishing returns at higher spending levels.

hints.text: For part (a), think about what shape you get when residuals are negative on both sides and positive in the middle. For part (b), any pattern in a residual plot is a red flag.
For part (c), since the residual plot shows a curve, the relationship between the variables is likely curved. What kind of model captures a curved relationship?

solution_steps.text: (a) The residuals form a curved (arch or inverted-U) pattern: they start negative at low \( x \)-values, rise to positive values in the middle, and return to negative at high \( x \)-values.

(b) A curved pattern in the residual plot indicates that the linear model is not capturing the true relationship. The model systematically underpredicts for moderate advertising spending and overpredicts for low and high spending. A linear model is not appropriate.

(c) A quadratic or polynomial model would better capture the curved relationship. The pattern suggests diminishing returns — revenue increases with advertising up to a point, then the rate of increase slows or reverses. A model like \( \hat{y} = a + bx + cx^2 \) would be more appropriate.

diagram.alt_text: Residual plot with points negative at low x, positive in middle x, and negative at high x, forming an inverted-U shape
diagram.caption: Residual plot showing negative-positive-negative pattern indicating quadratic relationship

diagrams.alt_text: Residual plot with points scattered randomly above and below the dashed line at residual equals zero, showing no systematic pattern
diagrams.caption: Residual plot showing randomly scattered points around the horizontal line at zero, indicating a good linear fit with no pattern

concepts.title: Least-Squares Regression
concepts.content_html:
Least-Squares Regression

The least-squares regression line (LSRL) is the line that minimizes the sum of the squared residuals:

\[ \text{Minimize } \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \]

This criterion ensures that the line is, on average, as close as possible to all the data points.

Interpreting \( r^2 \) in Context

The coefficient of determination \( r^2 \) tells us the proportion of the variability in the response variable that is explained by the linear model:

"\( r^2 \times 100 \)% of the variability in [response variable in context] is explained by the linear relationship with [explanatory variable in context]."

For example, if \( r^2 = 0.81 \) for a model predicting test scores from study hours: "81% of the variability in test scores is explained by the linear relationship with study hours."

Standard Deviation of the Residuals (\( s \))

The standard deviation of the residuals, denoted \( s \), measures the typical distance of the observed \( y \)-values from the LSRL:

\[ s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n - 2}} \]

A smaller \( s \) means predictions are more precise. Interpretation: "The actual [\( y \) in context] values typically differ from the values predicted by the LSRL by about \( s \) [units]."

Influential Points

An influential point is a data point whose removal substantially changes the regression results (slope, intercept, \( r \), or \( r^2 \)).

  • High leverage point: A point with an \( x \)-value far from \( \bar{x} \). It may or may not be influential — it depends on whether it follows the trend.
  • Outlier in regression: A point with a large residual (far from the LSRL). It may or may not be influential depending on its \( x \)-value.
  • A point that is both high leverage and has a large residual is almost always influential.

Effect of Removing Influential Points

  • Removing a point that follows the trend but is far from \( \bar{x} \) (high leverage, on the line): little change to slope, may increase \( r^2 \) slightly.
  • Removing an outlier that does not follow the trend: the slope, \( r \), and \( r^2 \) typically move toward what the remaining data suggest (usually stronger).
  • Removing a point that is both high leverage and an outlier: can dramatically change slope, intercept, \( r \), and \( r^2 \).
Key Idea: Not all outliers are influential, and not all high leverage points are influential. A point is influential only if removing it substantially changes the regression line or correlation. Always check by comparing results with and without the point.
AP Exam Tip: When asked to interpret \( s \), do not confuse it with \( r \) or \( r^2 \). The correct template is: "The actual [\( y \) in context] values typically differ from the predicted values by about \( s \) [units]." Saying "average distance" instead of "typical distance" is also acceptable.

problem_sets.title: Practice: Least-Squares Regression

problems.question_html: The least-squares regression line is defined as the line that minimizes which of the following?

choices.text: The sum of the residuals
The sum of the absolute values of the residuals
The sum of the squared residuals
The largest residual

hints.text: The name "least-squares" gives a clue about what quantity is being minimized.
The LSRL minimizes \( \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \) — the sum of the squared residuals. Note: the sum of the residuals (not squared) is always 0 for any LSRL.

solution_steps.text: "Least-squares" means the line minimizes the sum of the squares of the residuals: \( \sum (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2 \).

Choice A (sum of residuals) is always 0 for the LSRL — it is not the minimized quantity. Choice B (absolute values) is a different criterion (least absolute deviations). The LSRL minimizes squared residuals.

problems.question_html: A linear regression model for predicting a student's college GPA (\( y \)) from their high school GPA (\( x \)) gives \( r^2 = 0.64 \). Which of the following is the correct interpretation?

choices.text: 64% of students have a college GPA predicted by their high school GPA.
The correlation between high school GPA and college GPA is 0.64.
64% of the variability in college GPA is explained by the linear relationship with high school GPA.
A student with a high school GPA of 0.64 will have a college GPA of 0.64.

hints.text: \( r^2 \) represents the proportion of variability in the response variable explained by the linear model. Use the standard interpretation template.
64% of the variability in college GPA is explained by the linear relationship with high school GPA. Note: \( r^2 = 0.64 \) means \( r = \pm 0.8 \), not 0.64.

solution_steps.text: \( r^2 = 0.64 \) means 64% of the variability in the response variable (college GPA) is explained by the linear relationship with the explanatory variable (high school GPA).
Choice B is wrong because \( r = \sqrt{0.64} = 0.8 \), not 0.64. Choices A and D misinterpret what \( r^2 \) represents.

problems.question_html: A data set of 20 students shows the relationship between hours of sleep (\( x \)) and reaction time in milliseconds (\( y \)). The LSRL is \( \hat{y} = 450 - 25x \) with \( r^2 = 0.72 \). One student slept only 2 hours and had a reaction time of 500 ms. The rest of the data ranges from 5 to 9 hours of sleep. Which of the following best describes this student's data point?

choices.text: It has high leverage but is not an outlier, so it is not influential.
It has high leverage and a large residual, so it is likely influential.
It is an outlier with a small residual, so it is not influential.
It is neither high leverage nor an outlier.

hints.text: First check leverage: is 2 hours far from the rest of the data (5–9 hours)? Then check the residual: plug \( x = 2 \) into the equation and compare to the observed \( y = 500 \).

\( x = 2 \) is far from the 5–9 range, so it has high leverage. Predicted: \( \hat{y} = 450 - 25(2) = 400 \). Residual = \( 500 - 400 = 100 \), which is large. Both conditions make it likely influential.

solution_steps.text: Leverage: The student's \( x \)-value (2 hours) is far from the range of the other data (5 to 9 hours), so this point has high leverage.

Residual: \( \hat{y} = 450 - 25(2) = 400 \). Observed = 500. Residual = \( 500 - 400 = 100 \) ms, which is large. Since the point has both high leverage and a large residual, it is likely influential — removing it would substantially change the regression line.

problems.question_html: In a study of 30 cities, a regression model predicts average home price (\( y \), in thousands) from median household income (\( x \), in thousands). The model gives \( r^2 = 0.58 \) and \( s = 45.3 \) thousand dollars. When one very wealthy city (\( x = 150 \), much higher than the other cities) is removed, \( r^2 \) drops to 0.41. What does this tell you about the removed city?

choices.text: The city was an outlier in the \( y \)-direction but not influential.
The city was influential because its removal substantially changed \( r^2 \).
The city had no effect on the regression because it followed the overall trend.
The city was not high leverage because it had a typical \( y \)-value.

hints.text: A point is influential if removing it substantially changes the regression results. Did \( r^2 \) change a lot when this city was removed?

\( r^2 \) dropped from 0.58 to 0.41 — a decrease of 0.17. This is a substantial change, confirming the city was an influential point. Its extreme \( x \)-value (150, much higher than others) made it a high leverage point that was pulling the line toward it.

solution_steps.text: A point is influential if removing it substantially changes key regression statistics. Here, \( r^2 \) dropped from 0.58 to 0.41 when the city was removed — a decrease of 0.17.

This substantial change confirms the city was influential. With \( x = 150 \) being much higher than other cities, it was a high leverage point that was inflating \( r^2 \) by pulling the regression line toward it.

problems.question_html: A regression model predicting fuel efficiency (mpg) from car weight (lbs) has a standard deviation of residuals \( s = 3.2 \) mpg. This means the actual fuel efficiency values typically differ from the predicted values by about __________ mpg.

hints.text: The standard deviation of the residuals \( s \) measures the typical distance of observed values from the regression line.
\( s = 3.2 \) mpg means the actual fuel efficiency values typically differ from the values predicted by the LSRL by about 3.2 mpg.

solution_steps.text: The standard deviation of the residuals (\( s = 3.2 \) mpg) measures the typical size of prediction errors.
Interpretation: The actual fuel efficiency values typically differ from the predicted values by about 3.2 mpg.

problems.question_html: A point with an \( x \)-value far from \( \bar{x} \) is called a __________ point.
problems.correct_answer: high leverage||leverage

hints.text: This type of point has the potential to strongly influence the regression line because of its extreme \( x \)-position.
A point with an \( x \)-value far from the mean of \( x \) is called a high leverage point. It may or may not be influential depending on whether it follows the trend.

solution_steps.text: A point whose \( x \)-value is far from \( \bar{x} \) is called a high leverage point.
High leverage points have the potential to pull the regression line toward them, but they are only considered influential if removing them substantially changes the regression results.

problems.question_html: If \( r^2 = 0.85 \) for a linear model, then __________% of the variability in the response variable is not explained by the linear model.

hints.text: If 85% is explained, how much is left unexplained?
\( 100\% - 85\% = 15\% \). So 15% of the variability is not explained by the linear model.

solution_steps.text: \( r^2 = 0.85 \) means 85% of the variability in the response variable is explained by the linear model.
The remaining \( 100\% - 85\% = 15\% \) of the variability is not explained — it is due to other factors or random variation.

problems.question_html: A regression model has \( s = 12.5 \) pounds. This value is calculated using \( n - 2 \) in the denominator rather than \( n \) because the regression uses __________ estimated parameter(s) (slope and intercept).
problems.correct_answer: 2||two

hints.text: Think about how many parameters the LSRL estimates from the data. Each estimated parameter costs one degree of freedom.
The LSRL estimates two parameters: the slope \( b \) and the y-intercept \( a \). We lose 2 degrees of freedom, so we divide by \( n - 2 \).

solution_steps.text: The formula for \( s \) uses \( n - 2 \) in the denominator: \( s = \sqrt{\frac{\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{n-2}} \).
We subtract 2 because the LSRL estimates 2 parameters from the data: the slope \( b \) and the y-intercept \( a \). Each estimated parameter reduces the degrees of freedom by 1.

problems.question_html:
A researcher studies the relationship between weekly advertising spending (\$ hundreds, \( x \)) and weekly sales revenue (\$ thousands, \( y \)) for a small business over 24 weeks. Computer output:

Predictor    Coef    SE Coef
Constant     2.14    0.85
Advertising  0.368   0.042

S = 1.82    R-Sq = 76.3%

(a) Write the equation of the LSRL and interpret the slope in context.

(b) Interpret \( r^2 \) in context.

(c) Interpret \( s \) in context.

(d) One week the business spent $800 on advertising (\( x = 8 \)) and earned $6,200 in revenue (\( y = 6.2 \)). Calculate the residual and explain what it means in context.
problems.correct_answer: (a) ŷ = 2.14 + 0.368x. For each additional hundred dollars spent on advertising, the predicted weekly sales revenue increases by $368 (0.368 thousand dollars). (b) 76.3% of the variability in weekly sales revenue is explained by the linear relationship with weekly advertising spending. (c) The actual weekly sales revenue values typically differ from the values predicted by the LSRL by about $1,820 (1.82 thousand dollars). (d) ŷ = 2.14 + 0.368(8) = 2.14 + 2.944 = 5.084 thousand. Residual = 6.2 - 5.084 = 1.116 thousand ($1,116). The business earned $1,116 more than predicted that week.

hints.text: For part (a), the coefficients come from the "Coef" column. Pay attention to units — \( x \) is in hundreds of dollars and \( y \) is in thousands. For parts (b) and (c), use the standard interpretation templates with context.
For part (d), plug \( x = 8 \) into the equation to get \( \hat{y} \), then find residual = observed - predicted. A positive residual means the business did better than predicted.

solution_steps.text: (a) The LSRL is \( \hat{y} = 2.14 + 0.368x \). Slope interpretation: For each additional hundred dollars spent on advertising, the predicted weekly sales revenue increases by 0.368 thousand dollars ($368).

(b) \( R^2 = 76.3\% \). Interpretation: 76.3% of the variability in weekly sales revenue (thousands of dollars) is explained by the linear relationship with weekly advertising spending (hundreds of dollars).
(c) \( S = 1.82 \) thousand dollars. Interpretation: The actual weekly sales revenue values typically differ from the values predicted by the LSRL by about $1,820.

(d) Predicted: \( \hat{y} = 2.14 + 0.368(8) = 2.14 + 2.944 = 5.084 \) thousand. Observed: 6.2 thousand. Residual = \( 6.2 - 5.084 = 1.116 \) thousand ($1,116). The actual revenue exceeded the predicted revenue by $1,116 that week.

problems.question_html:
A regression analysis of 15 data points relating distance from school (miles, \( x \)) to commute time (minutes, \( y \)) yields \( \hat{y} = 8.5 + 2.1x \), \( r = 0.89 \), \( r^2 = 0.792 \), and \( s = 4.6 \) minutes. One student lives 25 miles away — much farther than the rest (1–12 miles) — and commutes 45 minutes.

(a) Explain why this student's data point is a high leverage point.

(b) Calculate the residual for this student. Is this student also an outlier in the regression?

(c) When this student's data point is removed, the new regression gives \( r^2 = 0.91 \) and slope \( b = 2.8 \). Explain how the removal affected \( r^2 \) and the slope, and classify the student's point as influential or not.

(d) Which set of regression results — with or without the student — would you recommend using to predict commute times for students living 1–12 miles from school? Justify your answer.
problems.correct_answer: (a) The student lives 25 miles away while the rest live 1–12 miles. The x-value is far from x̄, making it a high leverage point. (b) ŷ = 8.5 + 2.1(25) = 61.0. Residual = 45 - 61.0 = -16.0 minutes. The absolute residual is large compared to s = 4.6, so this is also an outlier. (c) r² increased from 0.792 to 0.91, and slope changed from 2.1 to 2.8. Both changed substantially, confirming the point is influential. The student's point was pulling the slope down (toward the outlying x-value) and reducing r². (d) For predictions within 1–12 miles, the regression without the distant student is more appropriate. That model better represents the relationship for the range of interest, with higher r² and a slope more representative of the remaining data.

hints.text: For part (a), compare the student's \( x \)-value to the range of the rest. For part (b), compute the predicted value and compare the residual to \( s \). For parts (c)–(d), compare the statistics before and after removal.

For part (c), if removing a point changes \( r^2 \) by more than a few percentage points and noticeably changes the slope, the point is influential. For part (d), consider which model best represents the population you are predicting for.

solution_steps.text: (a) The student's \( x \)-value of 25 miles is far from the rest of the data (1–12 miles). Since this \( x \)-value is far from \( \bar{x} \), it is a high leverage point.

(b) Predicted: \( \hat{y} = 8.5 + 2.1(25) = 8.5 + 52.5 = 61.0 \) minutes. Residual = \( 45 - 61.0 = -16.0 \) minutes. Since \( |{-16}| = 16 \) is much larger than \( s = 4.6 \), this point is also an outlier in the regression context.

(c) Removing the student increased \( r^2 \) from 0.792 to 0.91 (a jump of 0.118) and changed the slope from 2.1 to 2.8. Both changes are substantial, confirming the point is influential. The student's point was pulling the regression line downward (reducing the slope) and adding unexplained variability (reducing \( r^2 \)).

(d) For predicting commute times for students living 1–12 miles away, the regression without the distant student (\( r^2 = 0.91 \), \( b = 2.8 \)) is more appropriate. This model better captures the linear relationship within the relevant range and provides more accurate predictions for the population of interest.

course_info.introduction_html:
AP Statistics introduces students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing, and drawing conclusions from data. The course is equivalent to a one-semester introductory college statistics course.

This course covers 9 units aligned with the College Board’s Course and Exam Description (CED): Exploring One-Variable Data, Exploring Two-Variable Data, Collecting Data, Probability & Random Variables, Sampling Distributions, and four units on statistical inference covering proportions, means, chi-square, and regression slopes.

Every concept includes clear explanations with real-world data examples, AP exam tips, and practice problems that mirror the format of the AP exam. Calculator instructions are included where applicable.
